Recognition makes relationships, never a hub; the center stays empty. **Registry-free recognition is where a sovereign social life begins -- peers who know each other, owing no directory, which the series builds on.** The reason recognition matters is that a sovereign peer is not meant to be alone. When strangers can become recognized peers with no registry, a sovereign social life becomes possible — peers who know and are known by others, entirely on their own terms, which the later volumes build into cooperation and federation. So this volume is the social ground floor of the final series: recognition from which delegation, pools, and federation all follow. The strangers are peers; the registry is absent; the social life can build — recognition among sovereigns, owing no directory. Registry-free recognition is where sovereign society begins. **Peers who recognize one another with no registry are Lasting Generational Prosperity in the social dimension -- a society available to anyone.** The deepest meaning of registry-free recognition, at the volume's close: a society of peers who recognize one another with no central authority is lasting generational prosperity in its social form — a way for sovereign people to know, help, and rely on one another without a captor in the middle, available to anyone who holds their own key. Everything the series will build — delegation, pools, federation — rests on this: that a sovereign society requires no registry, only peers recognizing peers. So recognition is not only a technical capacity but a human one: the door to a sovereign society, open to anyone. From stranger to peer — and from recognized peers, a sovereign society.

title: S14 03 Sovereign Peerhood
text: You will see how ordinary sponsorship turns into permanent capture.

title: S14 03 Sovereign Peerhood
text: **Ordinary help turns into leverage -- whatever assists a peer can acquire a lasting claim on it.** The core danger in cooperation is leverage, and this chapter names it. In the ordinary pattern, help comes with a hold: the sponsor that assists acquires a claim, the delegation that is granted becomes an open-ended dependency, and the assistance that was offered turns into a lever the helper can pull. So accepting help commonly means surrendering a piece of sovereignty — a lasting claim the helper retains long after the help is given. Help that creates a lasting claim is capture wearing a generous face; the leverage is the trap. Ordinary sponsorship turns help into a permanent hold. **The weakest party is most exposed to leverage -- the peer that most needs help has most to lose.** Leverage falls hardest on the peer that most needs help. A peer with little — few resources, few alternatives, an urgent need — is exactly the one most exposed to accepting help on capturing terms, because it can least afford to refuse and has the least power to negotiate. So the leverage problem is a weakest-party problem: the peer that most needs cooperation to survive is the one most likely to be captured by it. That is why help must be built to leave the weakest peer free — the one with the greatest need must be able to accept help without surrendering itself. The neediest peer is most at risk from leverage, and so it is for the neediest that help must leave no claim. **The kill-target is the sponsor that turns help into leverage -- delegation must not create it.** This volume names its enemy plainly. The kill-target is the sponsor that turns help into permanent leverage — the helper, delegate, or protector that converts an act of assistance into a lasting claim on the peer's identity, acts, or future. So the whole design refuses it: help must not create leverage, or it becomes the capture it was meant to relieve. That refusal is the volume's organizing principle — everything that follows exists to make help possible without a lasting hold. The sponsor that turns help into leverage is refused; assistance owes nothing after it is given. **Leverage hides in open-endedness -- help with no time bound becomes a standing claim.** Leverage's usual disguise is open-endedness. A delegation with no expiry, a sponsorship with no defined end, a protection with no exit — each is open-ended, and open-endedness is how help quietly becomes a standing claim: what has no end does not end. So the antidote begins with bounds: help that is time-bound, scoped, and revocable cannot silently become permanent. That is why the design insists on limits — an open-ended assistance is a leverage waiting to be exercised. Open-endedness is where leverage hides; bounds are where it is refused. **Scored credit is leverage by another name -- a standing an authority owns can be revoked.** Leverage also hides in scores. When the help a peer gives or receives is recorded as a scored credit an authority owns — a rating, a creditworthiness number, a standing on someone's ledger — that score becomes a lever: the authority that owns it can revoke, downgrade, or gate the peer by it. So scored credit is leverage in a numeric disguise, and this volume refuses it: help and standing here are receipts the peer carries, homed to their receipt-based place, never a score an authority holds over it. Scored credit is a lever; owned receipts are not. The score is refused; standing stays the peer's own. **Refusing leverage is what makes help sovereign -- assistance without a lasting claim, which the chapters build.** The reason to refuse leverage is that help that captures is not real help. When help leaves no lasting claim — time-bound, revocable, boundary-preserving, un-scored — a peer can accept all the cooperation it needs and remain sovereign, which is what governed delegation (Ch 2), sponsorship without claim (Ch 4), and first-class revocation (Ch 6) build. So this chapter frames the whole volume: cooperation that never becomes capture. Leverage is the trap; refusing it is the design; sovereign help is the result — assistance a peer can take and stay free. Refusing leverage is where sovereign cooperation begins. **Help that leaves no claim is help both parties can trust -- neither is captured by giving or receiving it.** The deepest gain of refusing leverage is mutual trust. When help creates no lasting claim, both parties can trust it: the receiver knows it is not being captured, and the giver knows it is not acquiring a dependent it must manage — the assistance is clean on both sides. So refusing leverage does not weaken cooperation; it strengthens it, by making help safe to give and to accept. That mutual safety is the point of the whole design — help that leaves both free is help both can offer without fear. Clean on both sides, help that captures no one is help everyone can trust.

title: S14 03 Sovereign Peerhood
text: You will issue a time-bound, receipted, human-gated delegation the recipient can verify and revoke.

title: S14 03 Sovereign Peerhood
text: **Delegation is a time-bound, human-gated act -- delegate_governed cannot be open-ended.** The foundation of capture-free delegation is bounds and a human gate, and this chapter builds it. `delegate_governed` issues a delegation that is time-bound and human-gated (composing the sealed gate, Full Production ERP, Series 5, Vol 16), signed with the peer's own key — and it refuses to proceed without an expiry or a named approver. So a delegation cannot be open-ended or unattended: it has a defined end and passes a human hand. That combination is what keeps delegation from becoming leverage — bounded in time, deliberate in the making. Delegation is time-bound and human-gated, never open-ended. **The delegation must be time-bound -- no open-ended grant that becomes a standing claim.** Delegation refuses the open-ended grant. `delegate_governed` requires an expiry and refuses a delegation without one — the acceptance test proves it — because an open-ended delegation is exactly how authority quietly becomes a standing claim. So every delegation has a defined end: the authority returns to the peer when the time is up, unless deliberately renewed. That time-bound requirement is the structural antidote to leverage: what ends cannot become permanent. Time-bound by construction, a delegation cannot silently harden into a hold. **The delegation is human-gated -- granting authority passes a human hand.** Delegation passes a human gate. `delegate_governed` is human-gated — composing the sealed gate (Full Production ERP, Series 5, Vol 16) — so granting authority to another requires a named approver, and the acceptance test proves it is refused without one. So a peer never delegates unattended or by default; a human hand attends each grant of authority. That human primacy over delegation keeps the peer in control of what it hands out: authority is delegated deliberately, by a decision the peer makes. The delegation is human-gated; granting authority is a choice, not a default. **Both sides hold a receipt and the recipient can verify -- delegation is transparent and checkable.** Delegation is a shared, verifiable record. The delegation is a governed object both the peer and the recipient hold, and `verify_delegation` lets the recipient (or anyone) confirm it public-only against the peer's own key. So the delegation is transparent: both sides have the receipt, and its authenticity is checkable by anyone from the public key. That transparency is what makes delegation trustworthy — the recipient can prove what it was granted, and the peer can prove what it delegated, with no ambiguity. Both hold the receipt; anyone can verify it — delegation on the record, the peer's own. **A leverage field is refused -- delegation cannot smuggle in a permanent claim.** Delegation is fenced against leverage. `delegate_governed` refuses any leverage or permanent-claim field, so a delegation cannot quietly carry a lasting hold beyond the bounded authority it grants. So a peer cannot accidentally delegate in a way that captures it; the fence keeps delegation time-bound and claim-free. That refusal in code is what keeps delegation sovereign: the authority granted is exactly the bounded, revocable capability, and nothing more. No leverage rides along; delegation stays bounded and clean. **Delegation as a governed act is what makes handing out authority safe -- bounded, gated, verifiable, revocable, which mandate and revocation complete.** The reason to build delegation this way is that authority handed out carelessly becomes leverage over its grantor. When a delegation is time-bound, human-gated, verifiable, and revocable, a peer can hand out authority safely — knowing it will return, it was deliberate, it is provable, and it can be taken back — which mandate-and-quorum (Ch 5) and revocation (Ch 6) complete. So this chapter is the foundation of capture-free cooperation: delegation that a peer can grant without endangering itself. Bounded, gated, verifiable, revocable — delegation that stays the peer's own. Governed delegation is authority handed out without being handed over. **Delegation keeps the peer's authority theirs even while shared -- the grantee acts, the peer still owns.** Delegation shares authority without surrendering it. Because the delegation is bounded, revocable, and under the peer's own mandate, the grantee can act on the delegated capability while the underlying authority remains the peer's — shared for a time, never transferred. So delegation is not a handover of sovereignty but a lending of a specific capability, which the peer can reclaim. That distinction — lend, not transfer — is what makes delegation compatible with sovereignty: the peer stays the owner throughout. Authority is lent, not given; the peer remains sovereign while it shares.

title: S14 03 Sovereign Peerhood
text: You will join a mutual-protection arrangement that has no central insurer.

title: S14 03 Sovereign Peerhood
text: **Mutual protection has no central insurer -- join_mutual_protection is a signed peer commitment.** Protection among peers needs no insurer, and this chapter builds it. `join_mutual_protection` joins a mutual-protection arrangement that has no central insurer — the join is a governed commitment signed with the peer's own key, portable with the peer. So protection is a mutual commitment among peers, not a policy an insurer sells and can cancel: the peers protect one another directly, and each carries its own signed membership. That absence of an insurer is what keeps protection sovereign — there is no central party that underwrites, prices, or drops the peers. Protection is a signed peer commitment, with no insurer in the middle. **No central insurer can drop the peer -- protection is mutual, not underwritten.** Mutual protection cannot be cancelled by an underwriter. Because there is no central insurer, no party can drop, deny, or price out the peer — protection is a mutual commitment the peers make to one another, not coverage an underwriter grants and can revoke. So the peer's protection does not depend on satisfying an insurer's terms or staying in its good graces; it depends only on the mutual commitments the peers hold. That absence of an underwriter is what makes protection dependable for the weakest peer — no one can decide it is uninsurable. Mutual, not underwritten; no insurer can drop the peer. **Protection is portable with the peer -- membership travels, not locked to a provider.** Mutual protection travels. Because the join is an owned, signed commitment, the peer's protection is portable — it moves with the peer, not locked to a provider or a jurisdiction. So a peer carries its protection standing as it carries its recognitions and its keys: owned, portable, and its own. That portability is a direct benefit of the insurer-free design — protection you hold goes where you go, and no provider's closure strips it. The membership is the peer's own; protection is portable, not captive to a provider. **Reputation-as-receipts homes to Series 11 -- this volume joins protection, it does not score it.** The volume is honest about what it builds. It builds the signed join to a mutual-protection arrangement; the reputation and risk mechanics of protection — who is trustworthy, how claims are weighed — home to Sovereign Risk & Mutual Protection (Series 11, Vol 1), where reputation is receipts a party carries. So this volume does not re-implement risk scoring or reputation; it composes the peer's signed membership and homes the protection mechanics to their sealed place. That honest boundary keeps the volume focused: join here, protection mechanics homed to Series 11. The join is built; the risk mechanics are homed, not rebuilt. **An insurer field is refused -- protection cannot acquire a central underwriter.** Mutual protection is fenced against the insurer. `join_mutual_protection` refuses any insurer or underwriter field, so the arrangement cannot quietly acquire a central party that underwrites and could cancel it. So a peer cannot accidentally convert mutual protection into insurance held by a provider; the fence keeps it mutual and insurer-free. That refusal is what preserves the sovereignty of protection — it stays a commitment among peers, never a policy someone sells. No insurer enters; protection stays mutual and the peers' own. **Mutual protection without an insurer is what makes safety sovereign -- mutual, portable, un-cancellable, which sponsorship and mandate build on.** The reason to build protection without an insurer is that safety bought from an underwriter can be revoked by it. When protection is a mutual, portable, insurer-free commitment, a peer's safety is sovereign — no one can drop it, price it out, or lock it to a provider — which is the ground sponsorship without claim (Ch 4) and mandate-and-quorum (Ch 5) build on. So this chapter is what makes safety among peers dependable without surrendering it. Mutual, portable, un-cancellable — protection the peers wholly hold. Mutual protection without an insurer is safety that no provider owns. **Protection strengthens as the web of peers grows -- more mutual commitments, more resilience, no central cost.** Mutual protection compounds with the peer web. Because protection is a set of mutual commitments, it strengthens as more peers join and commit to one another — more links, more resilience — with no central insurer to price or bottleneck it. So a growing federation of peers becomes more protective simply by being more connected, and the strength is distributed, not concentrated in an underwriter. That compounding resilience is a benefit unique to insurer-free mutual protection: safety that grows with the community, owned by all of it. More peers, more protection; resilience is distributed and the peers' own.

title: S14 03 Sovereign Peerhood
text: You will accept or offer help that creates no lasting claim on identity or future acts.

title: S14 03 Sovereign Peerhood
text: **Help creates no lasting claim -- sponsor_without_claim keeps the boundary intact and the exit open.** The heart of capture-free sponsorship is help that leaves no hold, and this chapter builds it. `sponsor_without_claim` accepts or offers help that creates no lasting claim on identity or future acts — the help is receipted and signed with the peer's own key, the peer's birth trust boundary (composing the sealed boundary, Inter-Node Sovereignty, Series 6, Vol 5) stays intact, and the exit path is open by construction. So a peer can take help without surrendering anything permanent: the assistance is real, but it leaves no claim behind it. That claim-free help is what makes sponsorship safe — a peer accepts what it needs and remains free. Help is given; the boundary holds; the exit stays open. **The peer's boundary stays intact through the help -- assistance opens no ownership claim.** Help never breaches the boundary. When a peer accepts sponsorship, its birth trust boundary stays intact — the help composes the sealed boundary (Inter-Node Sovereignty, Series 6, Vol 5) rather than overriding it, so the assistance opens no ownership claim over the peer. So being helped does not mean being admitted-into or owned-by the helper; the peer's default-deny boundary holds throughout, admitting only what the peer allows. That boundary-preservation is the structural guarantee against capture: help cannot cross the line the peer drew at birth. The boundary holds through the help; assistance claims no ownership. **The exit path is open by construction -- the peer can always leave the arrangement.** Sponsorship keeps the door open. `sponsor_without_claim` marks the exit path open by construction — the peer can always leave the helping arrangement, taking nothing owed and leaving nothing claimed. So help is never a one-way door: what the peer entered, it can exit, at will and without penalty. That open exit is what makes sponsorship safe to accept — a peer can take help knowing it can always walk away, rather than being bound to a helper it cannot leave. The exit is open by construction; help is never a trap. **Help is receipted and signed -- both parties hold a clean record of assistance without claim.** Sponsorship leaves a clean record. The help is a governed record signed with the peer's own key, so both parties hold a receipt of the assistance — a documented account that the help was given and that it created no lasting claim. So there is no ambiguity about the terms: the receipt records help-without-claim, and both sides can prove it. That documented clarity is what keeps sponsorship honest — the absence of a lasting claim is on the record, not merely promised. Both hold the receipt; the no-claim terms are proven, not assumed. **A lasting-claim field is refused -- sponsorship cannot smuggle in leverage.** Sponsorship is fenced against leverage. `sponsor_without_claim` refuses any leverage or lasting-claim field, so help cannot quietly carry a permanent hold on the peer. So a peer cannot accidentally accept help on capturing terms; the fence keeps sponsorship claim-free by construction. That refusal in code is what makes sponsorship reliably safe: the help is exactly assistance, with no lever attached. No lasting claim rides along; sponsorship stays clean. **Sponsorship without claim is what makes help safe to accept -- boundary-preserving, exitable, claim-free, which mandate and revocation complete.** The reason to build sponsorship this way is that a peer that cannot safely accept help is not truly sovereign — it is isolated. When help preserves the boundary, keeps the exit open, and leaves no claim, a peer can accept all the assistance it needs and remain free, which mandate-and-quorum (Ch 5) and revocation (Ch 6) complete by keeping control and allowing clean unwinding. So this chapter is what makes cooperation compatible with sovereignty: help a peer can take without being taken. Boundary-preserving, exitable, claim-free — help that leaves the peer whole. Sponsorship without claim is help that captures no one who accepts it. **Claim-free help lets a peer accept from anyone -- it need not trust the helper's intentions, only the terms.** Sponsorship without claim lowers the trust barrier. Because the terms guarantee no lasting claim, a peer can accept help even from a party whose long-term intentions it cannot fully judge — it need not trust the helper's motives, only the claim-free terms enforced in the receipt and the fence. So help becomes widely acceptable: the peer is protected by the structure, not by having to vet every helper's heart. That structural safety is what makes cooperation extend among strangers — a peer can take help broadly, because the terms, not the trust, keep it free. Trust the terms, not the motives; claim-free help is safe to accept from anyone.

title: S14 03 Sovereign Peerhood
text: You will use owner's mandate and family quorum so delegation stays under the peer's constitutional control.

title: S14 03 Sovereign Peerhood
text: **Delegation stays under the peer's constitutional control -- mandate_and_quorum keeps the key with the peer.** Capture-free delegation must stay under the peer's own control, and this chapter builds that control. `mandate_and_quorum` keeps delegation under the peer's constitutional control by composing the owner's mandate (Full Production ERP, Series 5, Vol 28) — carried on every governed act — with the family quorum (composing the sealed succession, Generational Transfer, Series 12, Vol 1) over the peer's own fingerprint. So control never leaves the peer's key: the peer's own mandate scopes every delegation, and a threshold of the peer's own family governs recovery, with no external authority. Delegation stays constitutionally the peer's own — mandate and quorum keep control at home. **The owner's mandate scopes every delegation -- authority is exercised only within the peer's constitution.** The owner's mandate bounds every act. Every governed delegation the peer makes carries the peer's own mandate (composing the owner's mandate, Full Production ERP, Series 5, Vol 28), which scopes what the delegation can do to what the peer's own constitution allows. So a delegation cannot exceed the peer's mandate — it is exercised only within the constitutional bounds the peer set, never beyond them. That mandate-scoping is what keeps delegated authority faithful to the peer's own rules: the grantee acts within the peer's constitution, or not at all. Every delegation carries the peer's mandate; authority stays within the peer's own rules. **The family quorum governs recovery -- a threshold of the peer's own people, no external authority.** Control of delegation is recoverable by the peer's own quorum. `mandate_and_quorum` composes the family quorum (Generational Transfer, Series 12, Vol 1) over the peer's own fingerprint — so if control must be recovered, a threshold of the peer's own family keys governs it, with no external authority involved. So even the recovery of constitutional control stays within the peer's own people: the same family-quorum path that recovers the peer's identity governs its delegations. That keeps delegation sovereign end to end — its control, and the recovery of that control, are both the family's own. The family quorum governs; no external authority touches the peer's control. **Control never leaves the peer's key -- delegation is lent from a control the peer always holds.** Constitutional control is inalienable. Because delegation is scoped by the peer's mandate and governed by the peer's family quorum, control never leaves the peer's own key — a delegation lends a capability from a control the peer always retains. So no delegation, however broad, transfers the peer's constitutional control; it lends within it. That inalienability is the deepest guarantee against capture through delegation: the peer cannot accidentally delegate away the control itself, only exercise it. Control stays with the peer's key; delegation lends from it, never gives it away. **A custodian field is refused -- constitutional control cannot be handed to an outside party.** Mandate-and-quorum is fenced against a custodian. `mandate_and_quorum` refuses any custodian field, so the peer's constitutional control cannot be quietly handed to an outside party that would hold or govern it. So control stays with the peer and its family quorum; no custodian may insert itself between the peer and its own delegations. That refusal is what keeps constitutional control sovereign — it is the peer's own, recoverable by the peer's own people, held by no one else. No custodian governs; control is the peer's and its family's alone. **Mandate and quorum are what keep delegation sovereign end to end -- scoped, recoverable, inalienable, which revocation completes.** The reason to build mandate-and-quorum is that delegation without constitutional control could leak sovereignty. When every delegation is scoped by the peer's mandate, its control recoverable by the peer's family quorum, and that control inalienable from the peer's key, delegation stays sovereign end to end — which the first-class revocation (Ch 6) completes by letting the peer unwind any delegation cleanly. So this chapter is what keeps the peer constitutionally in control of everything it delegates. Scoped, recoverable, inalienable — delegation the peer governs by its own constitution. Mandate and quorum keep delegated authority the peer's own, always. **Constitutional control makes delegation inheritable -- the same family quorum carries it to an heir.** Mandate-and-quorum ties delegation to the inheritable estate. Because the family quorum that governs the peer's delegations is the same sealed succession that carries the peer's identity, a peer's constitutional control of its delegations is inheritable — it passes to an heir with the rest of the estate. So delegation is not only sovereign within a life but continuable beyond it: the heir inherits the mandate and the quorum that govern the peer's cooperative relationships. That inheritability is what makes delegation a durable part of a generational sovereign life. The control passes with the estate; delegation is inheritable, governed by the family's own quorum across the generations.

title: S14 03 Sovereign Peerhood
text: You will revoke a delegation without creating a hostage.

title: S14 03 Sovereign Peerhood
text: **Revocation is a first-class signed act -- revoke_delegation leaves no residual claim.** The final guarantee of capture-free delegation is clean revocation, and this chapter builds it. `revoke_delegation` revokes a delegation as a first-class signed act — signed with the peer's own key — that leaves no residual claim; the delegated capability returns wholly to the peer. So a peer can always take back what it delegated, cleanly and completely: revocation is a real, owned act, and nothing lingers after it. That first-class revocation is what makes delegation safe to grant — a peer is never stuck with a delegation it wants to end. Revocation is a clean, signed act; the authority returns whole. **Revocation returns the capability wholly to the peer -- nothing of the delegation remains.** Revocation is complete. When a peer revokes a delegation, the delegated capability returns wholly to it — nothing of the delegation remains with the grantee, no residual authority, no lingering access. So revocation is not a partial unwinding but a full reclaiming: what was lent comes entirely back. That completeness is what makes revocation a real guarantee — a peer knows that revoking truly ends the delegation, leaving no remnant the grantee could still exercise. The capability returns whole; revocation leaves nothing behind. **Revocation is signed with the peer's own key -- only the peer can revoke its own delegation.** Revocation is the peer's own sovereign act. `revoke_delegation` signs the revocation with the peer's own key and requires one — the acceptance test proves a keyless peer cannot revoke. So a revocation is unmistakably the peer's own decision; no one revokes on its behalf, and no one can prevent it from revoking. That self-signed revocation is what makes it sovereign: the peer's power to take back what it granted is exercised by its own hand, on its own key. Only the peer revokes its own delegation; the power is its own. **Revocation leaves no hostage -- ending a delegation leaves the peer free.** Revocation never traps the revoking peer. Because it leaves no residual claim, revoking a delegation leaves the peer entirely free — no lingering obligation, no penalty, no leverage the grantee retains. So a peer can always unwind a delegation without cost, which means delegation never becomes a trap: what was granted can be cleanly reclaimed. That hostage-free revocation is the final guarantee of the delegation layer — an authority you can always take back is an authority you never truly surrendered. Revocation frees the peer completely; no hostage remains after it. **A residual-claim field is refused -- revocation cannot be turned into a cost.** Revocation is fenced against becoming costly. `revoke_delegation` refuses any leverage or residual-claim field, so a revocation cannot be quietly attached to a penalty or a claim the grantee retains. So the clean reclaiming stays clean: the fence prevents revocation from being converted into a hostage-making act. That refusal-of-residue is what keeps revocation sovereign — taking back is always free and complete. No residual claim attaches; revocation stays clean and costless. **Revocation as a first-class act is what makes delegation safe to grant -- a clean take-back, which help-that-leaves-both-free completes.** The reason to guarantee first-class revocation is that delegation is only safe to grant if it can be cleanly taken back. When a peer can always revoke without penalty, hostage, or residual claim, delegation becomes safe to grant freely — which is what the closing vision of help that leaves both free (Ch 8) completes into a full cooperative capacity. So this chapter is the guarantee that makes the whole delegation layer trustworthy: nothing it grants can trap you. Revoke cleanly; reclaim wholly; owe nothing — the take-back that makes delegation safe. Revocation as a first-class act is the freedom that makes delegation sovereign. **Because revocation is always available, every delegation is freely chosen -- the take-back validates the grant.** Clean revocation validates every delegation. Because a peer can always take back what it granted, every delegation it maintains is one it currently chooses to maintain — not one it is stuck with — which means its delegations are genuine, freely-willed grants. So the power to revoke is what makes delegation meaningful: an authority you can reclaim at will is one you truly consent to lend. That is the quiet strength of the whole layer — delegation matters because revocation is always there. Freely revocable, therefore freely granted; revocation is what makes delegation real.

title: S14 03 Sovereign Peerhood
text: You will know the hard limits: no permanent leverage, no scored authority.

title: S14 03 Sovereign Peerhood
text: **Delegation claims only what it proves -- and this chapter states the limits plainly.** A sovereign layer must be exact about its limits, and this chapter draws the line. Delegation here claims exactly what it builds — governed delegation, mutual protection, sponsorship without claim, mandate-and-quorum control, and first-class revocation — and nothing more; there is no permanent leverage, no scored credit authority, no capability quietly overclaimed. So the reader closes knowing precisely what delegation does and does not do, with every out-of-scope capability honestly homed. That exactness is the whole point of this chapter: honest boundaries around a real, capture-free delegation. Delegation claims its five capabilities and names the rest OUT. **No permanent leverage is created -- the very thing delegation refuses is not smuggled back.** Delegation builds no leverage. There is no permanent leverage created anywhere in this volume — the kill-target is refused, not quietly reintroduced as a "relationship" or a "commitment." So delegation stays capture-free by construction: every delegation is time-bound and revocable, every help leaves no claim, and no lasting hold accumulates. That refusal is the sharpest honesty of the volume — it does not build the very leverage it warns against. No permanent leverage is created; capture stays refused. **No scored credit authority is built -- scored credit and reputation home to Series 11.** Delegation builds no credit score. Any scored credit or reputation — a creditworthiness number, a rating an authority owns — is OUT of this volume and homes to Sovereign Risk & Mutual Protection (Series 11, Vol 1), where reputation is receipts a party carries, never an issued score. So the reader is not led to think delegation includes a credit system; the volume builds receipted help and homes scoring to its receipt-based place. That honest homing keeps delegation free of the scored leverage it warns against. Scored credit is OUT, homed to where standing is receipts, not a number. **No passphrase protection is claimed -- each peer's key is self-held file-custody.** Delegation is honest about key protection, as genesis and recognition were. Each peer's self-held key is file-custody on its own iron under the operator's control, and this volume claims **no passphrase protection, no enclave, no encryption at rest** beyond that file-custody. So the reader is told the exact protection delegation rests on: the peers' own keys, protected as their own files. That precise honesty carries the series discipline forward: delegation overclaims nothing about the keys it depends on. Each key is file-custody on its peer's iron; no passphrase protection is claimed. **External value and settlement are out -- they home to the Port.** Delegation moves no value. Any crossing or settlement of value between peers is OUT of delegation and homes to the sealed Sovereign Port (Inter-Node Sovereignty, Series 6, Vol 7) — delegation lends authority and offers help, it does not move money. So the reader knows delegation is a pure cooperation layer: it shares capability and assistance, not payments. That the value rails are OUT and homed keeps delegation honest about its money-path: there isn't one. External value is OUT; delegation holds and settles none. **Knowing what delegation does not claim is what makes its claims trustworthy -- honest limits, which help-that-leaves-both-free rests on.** The reason to state the limits is that honest limits make honest claims believable. When delegation names exactly what is OUT — permanent leverage, scored credit, passphrase protection, value settlement — and homes each honestly, its five present claims stand on believable ground, which is what the closing vision (Ch 8) rests on. So this chapter is the conscience of the volume: it keeps capture-free delegation honest by refusing to overclaim. The limits are named; the homes are real; the five claims hold — delegation whose honesty about what it is not makes what it is trustworthy. Knowing the OUT list is knowing delegation is honest. **Option B honesty protects the weakest peer -- it is the one that cannot afford a false capability.** The honesty of delegation serves the weakest party most. A peer with little margin, relying on help to survive, is exactly the one that cannot afford a capability claimed but not real — a protection that turns out to have an insurer, a delegation that turns out to be leverage. So Option B honesty, present-or-OUT with a named home, is protection for the weakest peer: it ensures the least-resourced knows precisely what it can rely on. That is why delegation states its limits so plainly — the peer with the least cushion is the one an overclaim would hurt worst. Honest limits protect the weakest peer; that is who Option B is for.

title: S14 03 Sovereign Peerhood
text: You will leave able to give and receive help without creating a new intermediary.

title: S14 03 Sovereign Peerhood
text: **Help leaves both parties free -- delegation and sponsorship create no new intermediary.** The volume closes with a full cooperative capacity, and this chapter marks it. A peer can now give and receive help — delegating authority, joining mutual protection, accepting sponsorship — with every act leaving both parties free: no lasting claim, no central intermediary, no capture on either side. So cooperation is complete and capture-free: peers can help one another as much as they need, and both remain sovereign. Help that leaves both free is help that builds no new hub, no insurer, no leverage — only a relationship both can end. Cooperation is whole, and it captures no one. **Every act was signed with the peer's own key -- the whole cooperative capacity flows from the self-held key.** Cooperation, like genesis and recognition, flows from the key. Every act in this volume — delegation, protection, sponsorship, revocation — was signed with the peer's own self-held key, so a peer's whole capacity to cooperate flows from the identity genesis established. So cooperation is not a separate system a peer joins but an extension of its own sovereign identity: the same key that made the peer now delegates, accepts help, and revokes with it. That continuity keeps cooperation sovereign — there is no help a peer gives or takes that some authority signs for it. The key that made the peer cooperates for it; help is the peer's own act. **Both parties can always exit -- neither is captured by giving or receiving help.** Cooperation keeps both doors open. Because every delegation is revocable, every help leaves the exit open, and every protection is insurer-free, both parties can always exit — the giver and the receiver alike remain free to end the arrangement. So cooperation is symmetric in its safety: neither the helper nor the helped is captured, and either can walk away clean. That mutual exitability is what makes help between sovereigns trustworthy — it is safe to give because it is safe to receive, and both because it is always leavable. Both can exit; help captures neither the giver nor the receiver. **The path to pool bridging is open -- cooperating peers can now form and join pools without capture.** Cooperation opens the way to pools. Peers who can delegate and help one another without capture can now form and join value pools and federations — which the next Sovereign Peerhood volume builds — so cooperation is not an end but the ground for a wider sovereign economy. So the arc continues: peers who can help each other can now pool their efforts, bridge into federations, and share value, all without capture. That the path to pool bridging is open is what connects this volume to the series to come. Cooperation makes pooling possible; bridging is the next step, and the door is open. **No new intermediary is created -- delegation builds cooperation, not a new center.** Cooperation, like genesis and recognition, builds no center. Enabling peers to help one another creates no new hub, no insurer, no delegation authority, no intermediary — it makes bilateral cooperative relationships, and nothing that sits above them. So delegation solves the helping-each-other problem without building the very captor it warns against: the web of cooperating peers has no center, only relationships. That refusal to create an intermediary is what keeps cooperation sovereign rather than a nicer patronage system — there is no "it" the peers depend on, only each other. Cooperation makes relationships, never a hub; the center stays empty. **Capture-free cooperation is where a sovereign economy begins -- peers who help each other, owing no intermediary, which the series builds on.** The reason cooperation matters is that a sovereign peer cannot thrive alone. When peers can give and receive help with no capture, a sovereign cooperative economy becomes possible — peers who delegate, protect, and sponsor one another entirely on their own terms, which the later volumes build into pools and federations. So this volume is the cooperative ground floor of the final series: help from which pools, bridging, and a whole sovereign economy follow. The help is given; the leverage is absent; the economy can build — cooperation among sovereigns, owing no intermediary. Capture-free cooperation is where a sovereign economy begins. **Peers who help each other without capture are Lasting Generational Prosperity in the cooperative dimension -- an economy available to anyone.** The deepest meaning of capture-free cooperation, at the volume's close: an economy of peers who help one another with no leverage on either side is lasting generational prosperity in its cooperative form — a way for sovereign people to delegate, protect, and sponsor one another without a captor in the middle, available to anyone who holds their own key. Everything the series will build — pools, bridging, federation — rests on this: that a sovereign economy requires no intermediary, only peers helping peers freely. So cooperation is not only a technical capacity but a human one: the door to a sovereign economy, open to anyone. Help that leaves both free — and from free cooperation, a sovereign economy.

title: S14 04 Sovereign Peerhood
text: You will see how ordinary value pools recreate platform lock-in.

title: S14 04 Sovereign Peerhood
text: **Ordinary value pools recreate platform lock-in -- a hub, a captive token, a central settlement.** The core danger in pooling value is the pool becoming a platform, and this chapter names it. An ordinary value pool commonly comes with a hub that mediates every bridge, a membership token the operator holds that a peer needs to belong, and a central settlement where value is netted and held in the middle — so joining the pool means depending on an operator that can freeze, gate, or expel the peer. So a pool, meant to be mutual, silently becomes a platform: a center the peers depend on, with the power to lock them in. A pool with a hub is a platform by another name; the lock-in is the trap. Ordinary pools recreate the capture peers came to escape. **The weakest party is most exposed to a pool hub -- the peer that most needs the pool has most to lose.** The pool hub's power falls hardest on the weakest. A peer with little — few alternatives, an urgent need to pool resources — is exactly the one most exposed to a hub's power to freeze its value, revoke its membership, or gate its bridges, because it can least afford to leave. So the pool capture risk is a weakest-party problem: the peer that most needs the pool is the one a hub can most easily control. That is why bridging must be built from the weakest party up — the peer with nothing must be able to pool value and federate without a hub's permission. The neediest peer is most trapped by a pool hub, and so it is for the neediest that bridging must be hub-free. **The kill-target is the bridging hub that holds you -- bridging must not depend on it.** This volume names its enemy plainly. The kill-target is the bridging hub that mediates every bridge, holds a membership token you cannot leave with, and settles value in the middle — the operator your pool membership, your bridges, and your value depend on, which can lock you in. So the whole design refuses it: bridging must not depend on any hub, or it inherits the hub's power to trap the peer. That refusal is the volume's organizing principle — everything that follows exists to make pooling and federating possible with no hub, no captive token, and no central settlement. The bridging hub that holds you is refused; the pool owes it nothing. **A captive membership token is the subtlest lock-in -- what a third party holds, it can withhold.** Lock-in hides in the membership token. When belonging to a pool requires a token the operator issues and holds, that token is a leash: the peer belongs only while the operator lets it, and cannot leave with its membership because the operator, not the peer, holds it. So the captive token is the subtlest capture — it looks like belonging and functions as a hostage. The antidote is that membership must be the peer's own record: a receipt the peer holds and can carry out, not a token a third party keeps. What the peer holds, the peer can leave with; what a hub holds, it can withhold. Membership must be owned, not issued and kept. **Central settlement is where value is trapped -- what nets in the middle can be frozen there.** Lock-in also hides in settlement. When a pool nets and settles value in the middle — a central balance the operator maintains — that value is trapped: it sits where the operator can freeze, delay, or condition it, and the peer cannot simply carry it out. So the antidote is that the pool must hold no value and settle nothing internally: value rides the sealed Port, member by member, and the node nets nothing. What never sits in the middle cannot be frozen there. Value on the Port only, never a central balance — that is how settlement stays uncapturable. The pool holds no value, so there is nothing in the middle to trap. **Refusing the hub, the token, and the central settlement is what makes bridging sovereign -- which the chapters build.** The reason to refuse all three is that a pool with any of them is a platform. When bridging has no hub, no captive token, and no central settlement — membership owned and reversible, value on the Port — a peer can pool value and federate and remain sovereign, which is what peer pools (Ch 2), the bridging ceremony (Ch 3), and value attribution (Ch 5) build. So this chapter frames the whole volume: pooling and federating that owe nothing to any center. The hub is refused; the token is owned; the settlement is on the Port — sovereign bridging is the result. Refusing the center is where sovereign pooling begins. **A pool you can always leave with your value is the only pool worth joining -- the exit validates the membership.** The deepest gain of refusing the center is that the peer can always leave whole. When membership is the peer's own reversible receipt and value never sits in the middle, a peer can always leave a pool carrying its membership record and its value — so every pool it belongs to is one it currently chooses to belong to, not one it is trapped in. That guaranteed exit is what makes pool membership meaningful: a pool you can leave with everything is a pool you truly consent to join. Freely leavable, therefore freely joined; the exit is what makes the pool sovereign.

title: S14 04 Sovereign Peerhood
text: You will join or form a value pool that is itself a set of receipted, governed peer acts.

title: S14 04 Sovereign Peerhood
text: **A peer pool holds no value and appoints no custodian -- form_peer_pool is only who is in.** The foundation of sovereign pooling is a pool that holds nothing, and this chapter builds it. `form_peer_pool` forms or joins a value pool composing the sealed Networked Value Pools (Sovereign Livelihood, Series 10, Vol 2): the pool holds no value, has no balance, and appoints no custodian — it is only *who is in*, a set of members and their receipted acts. So a pool is not a container of value someone holds but a membership of peers whose contributions are their own receipts. That construction is what keeps the pool from becoming a platform: there is no balance to freeze and no custodian to hold it. The pool holds no value; it is only its members and their receipts. **Membership is the peer's own reversible record -- not a token a hub holds.** Belonging is owned, not issued. In a peer pool, membership is the peer's own record — signed with its own key and reversible at will — not a token an operator issues and holds. So a peer belongs by holding its own membership receipt, which it can carry, prove, and revoke, rather than by possessing a token a hub could withhold. That owned, reversible membership is the structural antidote to the captive token: what the peer holds, the peer keeps and can leave with. Membership is a receipt you own and can reverse, never a token a third party keeps. Belonging is the peer's own, always leavable. **The pool is a set of receipted, governed peer acts -- its substance is the members' own records.** The pool's substance is receipts. A peer pool is itself a set of receipted, governed peer acts — memberships, contributions, votes — each a record its author owns, so the pool is not a thing above the peers but the sum of their own acts. So there is no pool-object that holds power over the members; the pool is exactly the receipts they hold, aggregated. That construction is what makes the pool sovereign by design: it has no existence apart from the members' own records. The pool is its members' receipts, nothing more — no entity above them to capture them. **The pool needs at least two members and refuses the empty case -- a real mutual pool, not a shell.** The pool primitive refuses the degenerate case. `form_peer_pool` (through the sealed floor) requires at least two members — a pool of one is a solo livelihood, not a mutual pool — so a claimed pool is a real mutual arrangement, not an empty shell or a single-party construct. So the pool is genuinely mutual: it exists only as an arrangement among multiple peers, each holding their own membership. That requirement keeps the pool honest — it is a real cooperation, or it is refused. A pool is at least two peers pooling; anything less is not a pool. **A bridging-hub or membership-token field is refused -- the pool cannot acquire a captor.** Peer pools are fenced against the platform they replace. `form_peer_pool` refuses any bridging-hub or membership-token field, so the pool cannot quietly acquire a hub that mediates it or a captive token that holds its members. So a peer cannot accidentally form or join a pool that captures it; the fence keeps the pool hub-free and token-free by construction. That refusal in code is what keeps the pool a genuine peer arrangement: no operator may insert itself, and no captive token may be introduced. No hub, no captive token; the pool stays the peers' own. **Peer pools by construction are what make pooling sovereign -- no value held, no custodian, owned membership, which the bridge and attribution build on.** The reason to build the pool this way is that a pool that holds value or issues membership is a platform. When the pool holds no value, appoints no custodian, and makes membership the peer's own reversible record, pooling is sovereign — which is the ground the bridging ceremony (Ch 3) and value attribution (Ch 5) build on. So this chapter is the foundation of sovereign bridging: a pool that is only its members and their receipts. No value held; no custodian; membership owned — a pool that captures no one who joins it. Peer pools by construction are pooling with no platform inside. **Forming or joining is a single sovereign act -- the peer needs no operator's approval to belong.** Belonging is the peer's own act. Because the pool is only its members and their signed receipts, forming or joining one is a single sovereign act the peer takes with its own key — no operator approves the membership, no gatekeeper admits the peer. So a peer joins a pool the way it does everything else sovereign: by its own signed act, needing no permission. That self-admission is part of what makes the pool hub-free — there is no admitting authority, only peers recording their own membership. The peer joins by its own hand; belonging needs no operator's leave.

title: S14 04 Sovereign Peerhood
text: You will execute a receipted bridge into a pool or federation both sides can verify and reverse.

title: S14 04 Sovereign Peerhood
text: **A bridge is a receipted, signed act both sides can verify -- bridge_into_pool needs no hub.** The heart of sovereign bridging is a signed, verifiable bridge, and this chapter builds it. `bridge_into_pool` executes a receipted bridge into a pool or federation — a bridge message composing the sealed inter-node messaging (Inter-Node Sovereignty, Series 6, Vol 1) signed with the peer's own key — that both sides can verify. So a bridge is not a hub-mediated enrollment but a two-sided receipt: the peer signs its bridge, and anyone can verify it against the peer's public key, with no operator in the middle. That signed, verifiable bridge is what keeps entering a pool sovereign — it is the peer's own act, provable to all. A bridge is a signed receipt, verifiable by anyone, mediated by no hub. **The bridge is verifiable public-only -- both sides confirm it with no attesting operator.** The bridge is checkable by anyone. `verify_bridge` confirms a bridge public-only — its signature checks against the bridging peer's own public key — so both sides, and anyone, can confirm the bridge is genuinely the peer's, with no hub attesting it. So the bridge's authenticity depends on nothing but the peer's key: there is no operator whose confirmation is required, and none that could deny it. That public-only verifiability is what keeps the bridge hub-free — it is self-evident, not operator-certified. The bridge verifies against the peer's own key; no operator attests it. **The bridge is first-class reversible -- a peer can always unbridge.** A bridge is not a one-way door. `bridge_into_pool` marks the bridge reversible — a peer can always unbridge, undoing its entry with a signed act, so entering a pool or federation never traps it. So the bridge is symmetric with the exit: what the peer bridged into, it can bridge out of, on its own signed decision. That reversibility is what makes bridging safe — a peer can enter a pool knowing it can always leave, rather than being enrolled irrevocably. The bridge can always be reversed; entering is never a trap. **Each peer must hold its own key -- a bridge requires a sovereign actor.** Bridging presupposes sovereignty. `bridge_into_pool` requires the peer to hold its own key and refuses to proceed without one — the acceptance test proves a keyless peer cannot bridge. So a bridge is an act between sovereign actors, each signing with its own identity; it cannot be performed on behalf of a peer that does not hold its own key. That requirement keeps bridging genuine: it is a real sovereign act, not an enrollment a hub performs for a hollow member. The peer holds its own key; the bridge is its own sovereign act. **A bridging-hub field is refused -- the bridge cannot acquire a mediator.** The bridge is fenced against the hub. `bridge_into_pool` refuses any bridging-hub field, so the bridge cannot quietly acquire an operator that mediates it. So a peer cannot accidentally bridge through a hub; the mechanism stays peer-signed and hub-free. That refusal in code is what keeps the bridge genuinely direct: no mediator may insert itself between the peer and the pool. No hub mediates the bridge; the crossing is the peer's own. **The bridging ceremony is what makes entering a pool sovereign -- signed, verifiable, reversible, hub-free, which federation and attribution build on.** The reason to build the bridge as a ceremony is that entering a pool through a hub is entering it captured. When a bridge is signed, verifiable, reversible, and hub-free, a peer can enter any pool or federation sovereignly — which is the ground federation without directory (Ch 4) and value attribution (Ch 5) build on. So this chapter is the act of entering, done right: the peer's own signed crossing, provable and reversible. Signed, verifiable, reversible, hub-free — a bridge the peer wholly owns. The bridging ceremony is entering a pool with no one in the middle. **Many bridges compose a federation without a hub -- each crossing is its own receipt.** A federation of pools needs no center. Because each bridge is a self-contained signed receipt, a peer can bridge into many pools and federations, and they into it, without any hub coordinating — the federation is just many independent bridges, each held by its parties. So a whole web of pooled peers can form with no central operator at all: the structure is the sum of bilateral bridges, not a hub of enrollments. That composability without a hub is what lets sovereign bridging reach beyond one pool to a whole federation. Many bridges, no hub; the federation is hub-free at every crossing.

title: S14 04 Sovereign Peerhood
text: You will participate in federation discovery and introduction without any central directory.

title: S14 04 Sovereign Peerhood
text: **Federation needs no central directory -- federate_without_directory reconciles independent roots.** Sovereign federation happens without a directory, and this chapter builds it. `federate_without_directory` participates in federation discovery and introduction by composing the sealed directory-free recognition (Volume 2): federating peers reconcile their independent roots, opt-in and local, with no central index. So peers find and introduce each other into a federation directly, as equals, with no directory that lists them or mediates their federating. That directory-free federation is what keeps the wider network sovereign — there is no central index a peer must appear in to belong. Federation is peers reconciling their own roots, needing no directory. **Discovery is opt-in and local -- no peer is listed in a federation directory.** Federating is the peer's own choice. Because it composes directory-free discovery, participating in a federation is opt-in and local — no peer appears in any central federation directory, and none is discoverable without choosing to present itself. So there is no directory that enrolls peers into a federation whether they like it or not; a peer federates only by opting to. That opt-in locality is what keeps federation sovereign: the peer controls its own participation, rather than being listed in an index it cannot leave. Federation happens by the peer's choice, never by inclusion in a directory. **The federation composes the sealed recognition layer -- it invents no new discovery mechanism.** Federation is built on a sealed floor. `federate_without_directory` composes the sealed directory-free discovery of Recognition (Volume 2) — it adds no new discovery mechanism, but reuses the proven, registry-free introduction the earlier volume sealed. So federating rides the same tested, directory-free machinery that recognition established, which is what makes it trustworthy: the discovery is already proven. That composition-not-reinvention is the volume's discipline — federation is recognition applied to pools, not a new index invented for a wider network. The federation reuses sealed recognition; it invents no directory. **A registry or directory field is refused -- federation cannot smuggle in a central index.** Federation is fenced against the directory. `federate_without_directory` refuses any registry or directory field, so federating cannot quietly acquire the central index it exists to avoid. So a peer cannot accidentally reintroduce a directory into its federation; the mechanism stays root-to-root, opt-in, and local. That refusal in code is what keeps federation genuinely directory-free: no index may insert itself. The directory is refused; federation stays a meeting of roots, not a listing. **Federation without a directory is what makes the wider network sovereign -- opt-in, local, index-free, which value attribution and governance build on.** The reason to federate without a directory is that a network organized by a central index is controlled by it. When peers federate by reconciling their own roots — opt-in, local, index-free — the wider network is sovereign at every link, which is the ground value attribution (Ch 5) and pool governance (Ch 6) build on for the pooled economy. So this chapter extends sovereign discovery from two peers to a whole federation: peers finding and introducing each other with no directory. Opt-in, local, index-free — a federation the peers wholly own. Federation without a directory is a sovereign network with no center. **A directory-free federation cannot be gated at the door -- no index decides who may join.** The deepest gain of directory-free federation is open entry. Because there is no central directory that lists members and mediates joining, no index can gate the door — a peer federates by reconciling roots with willing peers, not by being admitted to a registry. So the federation cannot exclude a peer by omission from a list, throttle its participation, or expel it from an index, because there is no index to do so. That absence of a gatekeeping directory is what keeps federation open to the weakest peer: it needs no one's listing to belong. No directory at the door; the federation is open to any peer with willing counterparts.

title: S14 04 Sovereign Peerhood
text: You will see earned value recorded as an owned receipt that travels with the peer.

title: S14 04 Sovereign Peerhood
text: **Earned value is an owned receipt that travels -- attribute_pool_value makes it the member's own.** Value in a sovereign pool is owned, not held, and this chapter builds it. `attribute_pool_value` records earned value as the member's own receipt — composing the sealed pool contribution over the income primitive (Sovereign Livelihood, Series 10, Vols 2 and 1) — so the pool holds nothing and the member owns the record. So a peer's earned value is a receipt it carries, not a balance a pool keeps: value attribution is an owned, portable record, not a number in someone's ledger. That ownership is what keeps pooled value sovereign — it travels with the peer, and no pool holds it. Earned value is the member's own receipt, portable and held by no pool. **Value settles only via the Port -- the node nets nothing and settles nothing.** Settlement rides the Port. When pooled value is settled, `settle_pool_on_port` composes the sealed pool settlement — per-member Port directives, member by member — and the node nets nothing, holds no balance, and performs no in-node settlement. So value never sits in the middle: it crosses only across the sealed Sovereign Port (Inter-Node Sovereignty, Series 6, Vol 7), and the pool has no balance to freeze. That Port-only settlement is the structural guarantee against trapped value — what never nets in the middle cannot be held there. Value rides the Port, per member; the node settles nothing, so nothing is captured. **The pool holds no value -- there is no balance for anyone to freeze.** The pool is value-free by construction. Because attribution is the member's own receipt and settlement rides the Port, the pool holds no value at any point — there is no pool balance, no netted total, no central account. So there is nothing for an operator to freeze, condition, or expropriate: the pool cannot hold value hostage because it holds no value at all. That absence of a balance is what makes the pool sovereign about value — the capture risk is removed by construction, not policed. No balance in the pool; no value to trap. **A held-value or pool-balance field is refused -- settlement cannot move into the middle.** Value attribution is fenced against central settlement. Both `attribute_pool_value` and `settle_pool_on_port` refuse any held-value, pool-balance, or netting field — the acceptance test proves an in-node pool-value settlement is refused — so value cannot quietly be netted or held in the middle. So a peer cannot accidentally route pooled value through a central settlement; the fence keeps value on the Port and out of the pool. That refusal in code is what enforces value sovereignty: settlement stays on the Port, member by member. No held value, no netting; settlement rides the Port only. **Value attribution on the record is what keeps pooled value sovereign -- owned, portable, Port-settled, which governance completes.** The reason to build value attribution this way is that pooled value held in the middle is captured value. When earned value is the member's own portable receipt, the pool holds no balance, and settlement rides the Port, pooled value is sovereign — which the human-gated pool governance (Ch 6) completes by keeping the pool's decisions the members' own. So this chapter is what makes pooling value safe: value the peer owns and carries, settled with no center. Owned, portable, Port-settled — pooled value the peer wholly holds. Value attribution on the record is pooling value with nothing in the middle. **Owned value receipts compose the peer's whole livelihood -- pooled earnings join the rest of what the peer holds.** Pooled value integrates with the peer's sovereign economy. Because attribution is an owned receipt like any other income, a peer's pooled earnings join the rest of its owned value — its livelihood, its recognitions, its standing — as portable receipts it holds. So pooling value does not create a separate captive account; it adds to the coherent body of value the peer already owns and carries. That integration is what makes pool value a genuine part of a sovereign livelihood rather than a walled-off balance. Pooled value is the peer's own, joining everything else it holds.

title: S14 04 Sovereign Peerhood
text: You will participate in pool decisions through human-gated, receipted votes.

title: S14 04 Sovereign Peerhood
text: **Pool decisions pass a human gate -- pool_vote is human-gated and receipted.** Governing a sovereign pool keeps human primacy, and this chapter builds it. `pool_vote` participates in a pool decision through a human-gated, receipted vote — composing the sealed pool governance (`enforce_decision` over a governance skin, Sovereign Risk & Mutual Protection, Series 11, Vol 4) and the sealed human gate (Full Production ERP, Series 5, Vol 16), signed with the peer's own key. So consequential pool decisions pass a human hand and are recorded as owned receipts: governance is deliberate and documented, not automated or opaque. That human-gated, receipted vote is what keeps pool governance sovereign — the members decide, by their own rules, with a human on the consequential. Pool decisions are human-gated votes the members own. **A gated pool decision is refused without a human -- no automated pool authority decides.** The pool gate is real and enforced. `pool_vote` is refused without a named human's approval — the acceptance test proves a gated pool decision attempted with no approver raises rather than silently passing. So a consequential pool decision cannot happen unattended or by an automated pool authority; a human the members trust puts their hand on it. That human primacy over pool decisions is the same principle that governs every material act in the sovereign stack, applied to the pool: the decisions that shape it pass a human. A pool decision is never automatic; it passes a human, or it does not pass. **The vote is the members' own, not a pool operator's -- governance stays with the peers.** Pool governance is the members'. The governance skin `pool_vote` composes is the members' own rules, and the vote is signed with the peer's own key — so pool decisions are governed by the members, not by a pool operator that owns the rules. So there is no operator whose governance the members must accept; the pool is governed by its own peers, by rules they hold. That member-ownership of governance is what keeps the pool sovereign in its decisions: the rules are the peers', not a platform's. The members govern the pool; no operator owns its rules. **The vote is a receipt the peer holds -- pool governance is on the record and owned.** Pool governance documents itself. Because each vote is a receipted governed act signed with the peer's key, the peer holds a record of its participation — what was decided, and that it passed a human hand — an owned, verifiable account of the pool's governance. So the pool's decisions are on the record and owned by their participants, rather than kept in an operator's opaque log. That owned record of governance is part of what makes the pool trustworthy: its decisions can be proven by the members who made them. The vote is a receipt the peer holds; pool governance is owned and provable. **A hub or second-authority field is refused -- no operator governs the pool.** Pool governance is fenced against the operator. `pool_vote` refuses any bridging-hub or second-authority field, so pool governance cannot quietly acquire an operator that decides for the members. So a peer cannot accidentally cede the pool's governance to a hub; the fence keeps decisions with the members and their own rules. That refusal in code is what keeps pool governance sovereign: no authority may govern the pool but its own peers. No operator governs; the pool's decisions are the members' own. **Pool governance under human primacy is what makes the pool self-governing and sovereign -- human-gated, owned, operator-free, which the peer-to-pooled-peer close completes.** The reason to build pool governance this way is that a pool governed by an operator is a platform, and a pool governed automatically has no human primacy. When pool decisions are human-gated, receipted, and governed by the members' own rules, the pool is self-governing and sovereign — which the closing arc from peer to pooled peer (Ch 8) completes into a full sovereign pooled life. So this chapter is what keeps a pool the members' own to govern: deliberate, documented, operator-free. Human-gated, owned, operator-free — a pool the peers govern themselves. Pool governance under human primacy is a pool that governs itself sovereignly. **Human-gated governance governs a growing pool without automating its judgment -- the members' judgment holds as the pool grows.** Human primacy holds as the pool grows. The gate does not automate the members' judgment; it ensures the members' judgment is actually applied — deliberately, to the decisions the skin gates — even as the pool grows larger and its decisions more frequent. So human primacy is what keeps a growing pool from outrunning its own members' judgment: the gate is the pause that ensures the members' considered decision governs the consequential moment. Growing a pool without automating its judgment is exactly what the gate provides. The judgment stays the members', and it holds as the pool grows.

title: S14 04 Sovereign Peerhood
text: You will know the hard limits: no permanent membership token, no central settlement.

title: S14 04 Sovereign Peerhood
text: **Bridging claims only what it proves -- and this chapter states the limits plainly.** A sovereign layer must be exact about its limits, and this chapter draws the line. Bridging here claims exactly what it builds — peer pools, a bridging ceremony, federation without directory, value attribution, and human-gated pool governance — and nothing more; there is no permanent membership token, no central settlement, no capability quietly overclaimed. So the reader closes knowing precisely what bridging does and does not do, with every out-of-scope capability honestly homed. That exactness is the whole point of this chapter: honest boundaries around a real, hub-free bridging. Bridging claims its five capabilities and names the rest OUT. **No permanent membership token is created -- the very thing bridging refuses is not smuggled back.** Bridging builds no captive token. There is no permanent membership token created anywhere in this volume — the kill-target is refused, not quietly reintroduced as a "credential." So bridging stays token-free by construction: membership is the peer's own reversible receipt, and no operator-held token accumulates. That refusal is the sharpest honesty of the volume — it does not build the very captive token it warns against. No membership token is created; the captive token stays refused. **No central settlement is performed -- value rides the Port, and this volume settles nothing in the middle.** Bridging settles nothing centrally. There is no central settlement anywhere in this volume — value rides the sealed Port, member by member, and the node holds no balance, nets nothing, and settles nothing internally. So the reader knows the pool has no settlement in the middle: value crosses only via the Port, and the pool holds no value. That refusal of central settlement is the volume's hardest money-fence — the node moves and holds no value, and where value crosses is the sealed Port, named. No central settlement; value rides the Port only. **No passphrase protection is claimed -- each peer's key is self-held file-custody.** Bridging is honest about key protection, as the whole series has been. Each peer's self-held key is file-custody on its own iron under the operator's control, and this volume claims **no passphrase protection, no enclave, no encryption at rest** beyond that file-custody. So the reader is told the exact protection bridging rests on: the peers' own keys, protected as their own files. That precise honesty carries the series discipline forward: bridging overclaims nothing about the keys it depends on. Each key is file-custody on its peer's iron; no passphrase protection is claimed. **Scored reputation is out -- it homes to Series 11.** Bridging builds no rating. Any scored reputation — a pool-standing number, a rating an authority owns — is OUT of this volume and homes to Sovereign Risk & Mutual Protection (Series 11, Vol 1), where reputation is receipts a party carries. So the reader is not led to think bridging includes a pool-reputation score; the volume builds owned receipts and homes scoring to its receipt-based place. That honest homing keeps bridging free of a scored authority. Scored reputation is OUT, homed to where standing is receipts, not a number. **Knowing what bridging does not claim is what makes its claims trustworthy -- honest limits, which peer-to-pooled-peer rests on.** The reason to state the limits is that honest limits make honest claims believable. When bridging names exactly what is OUT — a membership token, central settlement, passphrase protection, scored reputation — and homes each honestly, its five present claims stand on believable ground, which is what the close from peer to pooled peer (Ch 8) rests on. So this chapter is the conscience of the volume: it keeps hub-free bridging honest by refusing to overclaim. The limits are named; the homes are real; the five claims hold — bridging whose honesty about what it is not makes what it is trustworthy. Knowing the OUT list is knowing bridging is honest. **Option B honesty protects the weakest peer -- it is the one that cannot afford a false capability.** The honesty of bridging serves the weakest party most. A peer with little margin, relying on a pool to survive, is exactly the one that cannot afford a capability claimed but not real — a settlement that turns out to be central, a membership that turns out to be a captive token. So Option B honesty, present-or-OUT with a named home, is protection for the weakest peer: it ensures the least-resourced knows precisely what it can rely on. That is why bridging states its limits so plainly — the peer with the least cushion is the one an overclaim would hurt worst. Honest limits protect the weakest peer; that is who Option B is for.

title: S14 04 Sovereign Peerhood
text: You will leave able to enter and leave pools without ever becoming a platform dependent.

title: S14 04 Sovereign Peerhood
text: **A peer becomes a pooled peer with no platform -- bridging is complete and hub-free.** The volume closes with a full pooled capacity, and this chapter marks it. What began as a solitary peer can now pool value and join federations with no platform at all: it forms or joins pools that hold no value, bridges with a signed and reversible act, federates with no directory, attributes value it owns and settles on the Port, and votes in pool decisions by human-gated acts. So bridging is complete and hub-free: a peer can become a pooled, federated actor without ever becoming a platform dependent. From peer to pooled peer, with no one in the middle. Bridging is whole, and the peer is never captured. **Every act was signed with the peer's own key -- the whole pooled capacity flows from the self-held key.** Pooling, like everything sovereign, flows from the key. Every act in this volume — forming, bridging, federating, attributing, voting — was signed with the peer's own self-held key, so a peer's whole capacity to pool and federate flows from the identity genesis established. So pooling is not a separate system a peer joins but an extension of its own sovereign identity: the same key that made the peer now pools value and federates with it. That continuity keeps the pooled life sovereign — there is no pooled act a peer takes that some operator signs for it. The key that made the peer pools for it; pooling is the peer's own act. **The peer can always leave with its membership and value -- the exit is guaranteed by construction.** The pooled peer is always free to go. Because membership is the peer's own reversible receipt and value rides the Port with no pool balance, a peer can always leave a pool carrying its membership record and its value — the exit is guaranteed by construction, not granted by an operator. So pooling never traps the peer: what it entered, it can leave, whole. That guaranteed exit is the deepest test of whether the pool was ever capture — and here it never is, because leaving costs nothing and takes everything the peer owns. The peer leaves with all it holds; the exit is always open. **The path to the clean-exit covenant is open -- the pooled peer can leave any arrangement cleanly, which the capstone completes.** Pooling opens the way to the series' close. The pooled, federated peer is ready for the clean-exit covenant — the capstone that synthesizes the whole series into the peer's guaranteed ability to leave any arrangement cleanly, which the next and final Sovereign Peerhood volume builds. So the arc completes: a peer that can pool and federate without capture is a peer whose clean exit from everything is the covenant that closes the series. That the path to the clean-exit covenant is open is what connects this volume to the end of the whole ladder. Pooling completes the sovereign life; the clean exit is the final word, and the door is open. **No hub, token, or central settlement is created -- bridging builds pooling, not a platform.** Bridging, like every peerhood layer, builds no center. Enabling peers to pool and federate creates no hub, no membership token, no central settlement, no intermediary — it makes pooled relationships among peers, and nothing that sits above them. So bridging solves the pooling-and-federating problem without building the very captor it warns against: the pooled economy has no center, only peers and their receipts.
