A reviewer months later does not find an order that is simply "completed" with no story; they find the transition that completed it, and the transition that put it in process, and the release before that, and can trace the build's progress back through the governed acts that produced it. **The work order the floor executes is the same governed obligation the planning chapter framed, now moving through its life.** A work order in this series is an obligation -- committed work, opened, approved, and closed with evidence -- and the production order's lifecycle is that obligation's life on the shop floor: released is the human commitment to build, in process is the work underway, completed is the obligation discharged with the evidence the next chapters require. This module holds the manufacturing lifecycle and refuses the transitions that would break it; the governance that approves a release and records the closing evidence composes the sealed obligation ledger and access surface. The floor does the work; the record refuses to let the work's status outrun the work itself. **What runs here is the fail-closed lifecycle; the real-time capture of what the equipment is doing composes the port.** A modern shop floor also wants live execution data -- machine states, cycle counts, operator confirmations streamed from the equipment -- and none of that is claimed here as running, because it is the concern of the sovereign port (S6-V07), where the sovereign core meets the machines. This chapter presents the governed lifecycle the execution data would advance, and names the telemetry seam at its edge. The distinction is the series' discipline: the lifecycle is governed on the core; the wire to the PLC is earned at the port. **For Ridgeline, a fail-closed lifecycle means a production order's status is always something the build reached, never something the floor set.** When Ridgeline releases a bracket order and its shop-floor lead works it, the order moves planned to released to in process to completed only by passing through each state, and an order cannot be reported finished that was never released or never worked. When Ridgeline's auditor asks how a completed order came to be finished, the answer is its transition history -- released, in process, completed -- each a governed event, not a status someone typed at quarter-end. The next chapter adds the gate that stands between in process and completed: the quality check a build must pass before it can be called finished.

title: S5 19 Manufacturing Erp
chapter_title: Quality — the Gate a Build Must Pass to Be Called Finished
text: You will gate completion on quality, fail-closed -- so a production order that has not passed its quality check does not complete, and a finished good that reaches inventory is one that was inspected and passed by construction.

title: S5 19 Manufacturing Erp
chapter_title: Quality — the Gate a Build Must Pass to Be Called Finished
text: **Quality control is the manufacturing discipline most often overridden under pressure, and a governed operation makes passing the quality gate a precondition of finishing rather than a step that can be waved through.** When a shipment is due and a line is behind, the quality check is the control that quietly gives: an inspection deferred, a result marked pass to keep the order moving, a unit shipped on the promise that quality will catch it next time. Every override makes the schedule and breaks the guarantee, and the defect that reaches a customer is almost always one a quality gate was supposed to stop and someone was allowed to bypass. A manufacturing record that lets completion happen without a passed inspection is a record whose "finished goods" include units no one can prove were ever inspected. **This chapter gates completion on a passed quality check, fail-closed, so an uninspected or failed build cannot be called finished.** `complete` refuses to move a production order to completed unless two conditions hold: the materials are fully issued (the concern of the next chapter) and the quality gate has passed. A build that has not passed its quality check is not completed with a warning attached; it is refused, and the order stays in process until quality passes or the build is honestly scrapped. Completion is not a status an operator sets when the units are off the line; it is a governed act the process permits only when the quality evidence supports it. The finished good that results is, by construction, one that passed its gate -- because the process declined to finish it otherwise. **A failed or missing inspection refuses completion, and that refusal is the whole of the control.** The value of a quality gate is entirely in what it stops: a build that failed inspection, or that was never inspected at all, must not become finished goods. Here neither can. A failed quality result refuses completion; a completion attempted without a passed quality event refuses just the same. There is no path from in process to completed that does not run through a passed quality check, so a finished good cannot claim an inspection it did not receive. This is the same fail-closed posture the series takes everywhere -- the default is refusal, and quality is not an exception the schedule can purchase. **The quality event a build must pass is a receipted piece of evidence, not a checkbox that can be un-checked.** In this series, evidence is a governed, hash-accumulated record -- the sealed evidence and accumulator primitives Manufacturing & Quality (Vol 10) presented -- and a passed inspection is exactly such a record on those sealed primitives: the receipted proof that the build met its quality requirement. The completion gate requires that pass result -- it composes the sealed evidence and refuses to finish a build whose quality did not pass. A non-conformance is not a failed inspection quietly deleted; it is a governed state the order can carry -- reworked and re-inspected, or scrapped -- with the failing evidence preserved. A reviewer does not find a finished good with an inspection that was edited to pass; they find the quality event, receipted, that the completion gate required, and can re-derive that the gate held. **Process control -- keeping the build within its specification as it runs -- composes the same governed evidence, not a separate quality system.** The measurements a process control regime takes -- the dimensions, the tolerances, the in-process checks -- are receipted evidence over the governed order, and whether the process stayed in control is a re-runnable question over that evidence rather than an attestation beside it. This volume presents the completion gate that quality passes through; the statistical machinery of process control composes the sealed evidence primitives and the sealed Analytics & Decision Intelligence (Vol 19) surface over them. There is one quality record -- the governed evidence on the order -- and process control is a view of it, never a rival system that can disagree. **What runs here is the fail-closed quality gate; the instruments and lab systems that produce a measurement compose the port.** The gauges, the coordinate-measuring machines, the lab information systems that generate an inspection result live at the equipment, and integrating them is the concern of the sovereign port (S6-V07). This chapter presents the gate that a passed result opens and a failed or missing result holds shut, and names the instrument seam at its edge. The measurement is earned at the port; the gate that acts on it is governed on the core. **For Ridgeline, gating completion on quality means a finished bracket is one that was inspected and passed, provably.** When Ridgeline finishes a production order, the order completes only if its quality gate has passed; a run that failed inspection stays in process until it is reworked and re-inspected or honestly scrapped, and no uninspected unit reaches finished goods. When Ridgeline's auditor -- Ilse Vogt, returning from Volume 2 -- asks whether every finished good this quarter passed its quality gate, the answer is the receipted quality event the completion of each order required, re-runnable, not a quality log whose pass marks no one can vouch for. The next chapter adds the second gate completion depends on: the materials, conserved exactly to the bill of materials, and the value-conserving cost the finished good carries into the ledger.

title: S5 19 Manufacturing Erp
chapter_title: Materials — Value-Conserving Issue and the Cost the Build Carries
text: You will issue materials to a production order value-conserving -- an over-issue beyond the bill of materials refused, and completion held until the issued materials conserve exactly to the requirement -- and see the produced-good cost post to the ledger as a balanced entry.

title: S5 19 Manufacturing Erp
chapter_title: Materials — Value-Conserving Issue and the Cost the Build Carries
text: **Materials are where a manufacturing operation leaks value most quietly, and a governed issue closes the leak by conserving every unit consumed against the bill of materials the build committed to.** Raw material flows to the floor, is consumed in the build, and becomes -- most of it -- the finished good; the difference between what was issued and what the bill of materials required is shrink, and in most plants it is discovered only at a physical count, as a variance no one can attribute to a cause. Material issued without a governing requirement is material that can walk: over-issued to an order and diverted, under-recorded and lost, or simply unreconciled until the count forces a write-off. A manufacturing record that lets materials be issued freely is a record whose raw-material inventory and whose finished goods never quite tie to the builds between them. **This chapter issues materials to a production order value-conserving, against the requirement the order was opened with.** `issue_materials` records materials issued to an in-process order, and every issue is held to the bill of materials: a component not on the order's bill is refused, and a cumulative issue that would exceed the requirement is refused -- an over-issue beyond what the build was planned to consume does not happen. The order accumulates what has been issued, and the conservation the whole build turns on is simple and checkable: `is_fully_issued` is true only when the issued quantity equals the required quantity for every component, exactly. Materials stop being a flow the floor draws from freely and become a value conserved, unit for unit, against the requirement the order committed to. **Completion is held until the issued materials conserve exactly to the requirement, which is the first of the two gates a finished good must pass.** The completion gate of the previous chapter has two conditions, and this is the other: an order cannot be completed while it is short a material. A build whose issued materials do not conserve to its bill of materials -- missing a component, short a quantity -- is refused completion, named by exactly what it is short, and stays in process until the materials conserve or the build is honestly scrapped. There is no finished good that was quietly built from less than its bill of materials, because the process refuses to finish one. A finished good, when it exists, has consumed exactly the materials its bill of materials required -- no phantom build, no silent shrink. **The produced good's cost is exactly the cost of the materials that became it -- a value-conserving posting, not a plug.** When an order is built, the materials it consumed carry a cost, and that cost becomes the finished good's: `cost_posting` sums the issued-material quantities at their unit costs and emits a balanced entry -- the total debited to finished goods, credited out of work in process -- so debits equal credits by construction. Nothing is created or lost in the transformation; value moves from raw materials, through work in process, into the finished good, and the posting conserves it at every step. A finished good whose cost you cannot decompose into the materials it consumed is not a governed build; here the cost is exactly the materials, and it decomposes to them. **That cost posts to the sealed general ledger in the one posting shape the whole system shares.** The balanced entry the build emits is the same `{debits, credits}` shape every ledger-bound act in this series emits, and it composes the sealed posting floor through the general ledger's adapter -- the produced-good cost becomes a governed posting the trial balance nets to zero, exactly as a supplier payable or a payroll run does. Manufacturing does not keep its own private cost ledger that a controller must later reconcile to the general ledger; it emits the canonical posting shape, and the one ledger records it. The floor and the finance function share a single record of what the build cost, because the build posts to it directly. **What runs here is the value-conserving issue and the balanced cost; the physical movement of stock composes the sealed supply surface.** The on-hand inventory the materials are drawn from, and the movements that record a stock issue, are the concern of the sealed supply-chain surface (Supply Chain Execution, Vol 9) -- this chapter composes that surface for the material reality and governs the conservation against the bill of materials. The warehouse execution is the supply volume's; the conservation and the cost are manufacturing's. Each is governed in its own place, and they compose without a second copy of the truth. **For Ridgeline, value-conserving issue means its materials always tie to its builds, and its finished goods carry a cost it can prove.** When Ridgeline issues steel and flux to a bracket order, an over-issue is refused, and the order cannot be finished until the issued steel and flux conserve exactly to what the bill of materials required -- so Ridgeline's raw-material inventory bleeds nowhere the record cannot name, and its finished brackets carry a cost that is exactly the steel and flux that became them, posted balanced to the general ledger. When Ridgeline's auditor reconciles finished goods to the materials consumed, the builds tie out to the unit and the cost decomposes to the materials. The next chapter lifts from the single build to the whole of manufacturing compliance and reporting -- composed, as projections, over the governed production records this volume has built.

title: S5 19 Manufacturing Erp
text: You will see manufacturing compliance and production reporting as projections composed over the governed production records this volume built -- every compliance check and every production figure decomposing to the orders, issues, quality events, and postings beneath it -- rather than as separate systems maintained beside the floor.

title: S5 19 Manufacturing Erp
text: **Once manufacturing is governed at the level of the individual build -- the order opened against its bill of materials, the fail-closed lifecycle, the value-conserving issue, the quality gate -- compliance and reporting stop being separate systems and become projections over what the governed production records already contain.** A legacy plant runs a production-reporting layer and a quality-compliance function as things apart from the builds: data is extracted from the execution system, cleaned, and loaded into reports and audit binders that are only as true as the extract that fed them. This chapter takes the other path, the one the whole series takes: the governed production orders, material issues, quality events, and cost postings are the single source, and reporting and compliance are views computed from them -- never a second copy of production truth that can drift from the floor. **Production reporting composes the sealed analytics surface over the governed builds, so every production figure decomposes to the orders beneath it.** How many units were built, at what yield, at what material cost, over a period? In a governed operation these are not numbers a reporting system asserts; they are projections over the completed production orders and their conserved materials and costs, and they decompose -- ask which builds make up a period's output and the answer is the specific orders, with their issues and quality events and postings, not an aggregate no one can open. The analytics that produce these views are the sealed Analytics & Decision Intelligence (Vol 19) surface, composed here rather than duplicated, so a production metric inherits the discipline the series applies to every figure: it is trustworthy exactly to the degree it decomposes to the governed transactions under it, and here it decomposes all the way to the metal. **Manufacturing compliance composes the sealed compliance surface, so a regulatory or traceability requirement is run over the governed record rather than attested beside it.** Was every finished good built from its full bill of materials and passed by its quality gate? Can a lot be traced to the materials that became it and the inspections it passed? Are the process controls a regulated product requires evidenced on every build? These are compliance questions, and in a governed operation they are answered by running the checks over the governed orders, issues, quality events, and postings -- the sealed Compliance & Audit (Vol 16) surface, composed over the very records this volume produces. Genealogy and traceability stop being a binder assembled for an audit and become a re-runnable query over the governed builds: a finished good's materials, its inspections, and its cost are already linked in the record, because the record refused to finish the good without them. **The most demanding manufacturing requirement -- forward and backward traceability -- is satisfied by the governed record itself, not a traceability system bolted beside it.** Because a production order links its finished good to the exact materials it conserved and the quality events it passed, tracing a defect backward to the material lot that caused it, or forward from a suspect material to every finished good that consumed it, is a query over the governed orders rather than a reconstruction from scattered logs. The traceability a recall depends on is a property the governed build already has, composed through the sealed compliance surface -- not a promise a separate system makes and an audit tests. **Composition rather than duplication is the point, and it is what keeps manufacturing from growing a second, divergent truth.** The failure mode this chapter refuses is the one every large manufacturer eventually suffers: an execution system, a quality database, and a production-reporting warehouse each holding its own copy of what was built, each subtly out of step with the others and with the floor, so that three answers to the same production question disagree. By composing reporting and compliance over the single governed record instead of copying it, the volume ensures there is one production truth and many views of it -- and a view that disagrees with the builds is a bug in the view, not a rival account of what the plant made. **What is present in this chapter is the composition; the analytics and compliance engines it composes are sealed elsewhere and named here.** This chapter introduces no new module -- deliberately. Its work is to show that manufacturing's higher-order questions are answered by projecting the sealed analytics and compliance surfaces over the governed production records the earlier chapters built, and to draw the boundary at the sovereign port for the plant-floor connectivity that is genuinely outside the core. The governed order, the conserved materials, and the passed quality gate are the substance; reporting and compliance are the views; and the port is the edge. Nothing here overstates what runs: the composed surfaces are sealed, and the connectivity is named as the sovereign port's (S6-V07), not implied as this volume's. **For Ridgeline, composed compliance and reporting mean it can answer the hard questions about its production from the builds themselves.** When Ridgeline's operations lead asks how many brackets shipped this quarter at what material cost and yield, or whether every finished good passed its quality gate, or which finished goods consumed a suspect steel lot, the answers are projections over the governed production records -- decomposable to the specific orders, issues, quality events, and postings -- not reports from a system that might have missed something in its last extract. And when Ridgeline is ready to wire its gauges and machine controllers into the record, it knows exactly where that work lives: the sovereign port, governed in its own volume, not bolted onto the manufacturing core as an unproven promise. The final chapter draws the volume together -- the governed build as something a successor inherits and can prove.

title: S5 19 Manufacturing Erp
text: You will see the governed production order -- opened against its bill of materials, moved through a fail-closed lifecycle, conserved in its materials, gated on its quality, and posted at its cost -- as one inheritable manufacturing record a successor can re-run to prove every finished good was built, from the right materials, and inspected.

title: S5 19 Manufacturing Erp
text: **The governed production order -- its bill of materials, its fail-closed lifecycle, its value-conserving materials, its quality gate, and its balanced cost -- is not five features; it is one inheritable record of how a business makes what it makes.** An order opened against a sealed bill of materials; a lifecycle that reaches no state by skipping the one before it; materials that conserve exactly to the requirement; a completion gated on a passed quality event; a cost that posts balanced to the general ledger -- together these make a build a chain of governed acts a successor can follow from the commitment to the finished good. The volume's work is not a manufacturing execution system bolted onto the core; it is production rebuilt so that its integrity lives in the record rather than in the experienced people who run the floor today. **Every finished good this volume produces is re-derivable, and that is what makes the production provable.** A successor who trusts none of the prior floor team can take the production orders, the bills of materials, the material issues, and the quality events, and re-run the build -- confirming that each finished good conserved its materials to its bill, passed its quality gate, and carried a cost that decomposes to the materials that became it. There is no finished good that rests on an entry someone made under deadline, no completion that bypassed its materials or its inspection. The output that in most plants is the least reconcilable becomes the most provable, because every finished good is a build that the process refused to finish until it was whole. **Manufacturing integrity becomes a generational asset rather than floor knowledge, which is the point of building it this way.** In most manufacturers the knowledge of how a product is really built -- which materials matter, which steps are skipped when the line is behind, which inspections are truly load-bearing -- lives in the heads of a few experienced people, and walks out the door when they retire. This volume moves that integrity into the record: the bill of materials, the lifecycle, the conservation, the quality gate, and the cost are all governed facts, so the discipline survives the departure of the people who established it. A business that changes hands, or outlives its founders, inherits not a folklore of how the floor was run but a governed record it can re-run -- and that continuity is exactly what lasting, generational prosperity asks of the operation through which a business turns materials into product. **The vertical is the sealed core composed, not a parallel manufacturing system -- and that is the discipline that makes it honest.** The temptation in a vertical is to build a second world: a manufacturing suite that reimplements the ledger, the obligations, the evidence, the inventory, and then drifts from the core it was supposed to extend. This volume refuses that. A work order is the sealed obligation; a production state is the sealed object lifecycle; a quality event is the sealed evidence; a material is the sealed supply record; a cost is a posting on the sealed ledger. The one thing genuinely manufacturing -- the governed production order that conserves materials to a bill and gates completion on quality -- is the only new act the volume presents, and it composes everything beneath it rather than copying it. There is one core, and manufacturing is a station on it, not a rival to it. **What the volume presents runs today, and what it composes it names -- and that honesty is part of the inheritance.** The governed production order, its fail-closed lifecycle, its value-conserving material issue, its quality gate, and its balanced cost all run on the public starter and are proven by tests a successor can re-run. The bill of materials composes the sealed supply-chain surface (Supply Chain Execution, Vol 9); the manufacturing and quality primitives compose Manufacturing & Quality (Vol 10); the cost posts on the sealed posting floor; production reporting and compliance compose the sealed Analytics & Decision Intelligence (Vol 19) and Compliance & Audit (Vol 16) surfaces; and the plant-floor connectivity -- PLC, SCADA, instruments, machine telemetry -- is homed in the sovereign port (S6-V07). Nothing is claimed to run that does not, and nothing that runs is left without a home for what it leans on. A successor inherits not a set of promises but a set of proofs, with the boundaries drawn honestly. **For Ridgeline, the inheritable production record is what lets the business outlast the people who built its shop floor.** The day comes when Ridgeline's long-serving shop-floor lead retires, or the company passes to a new owner, and the question is whether manufacturing's integrity leaves with them. Because every order opened against its bill of materials, every lifecycle passed through its states, every issue conserved to its requirement, every completion cleared its quality gate, and every cost posted balanced to the ledger, the answer is that it does not. The new team inherits a manufacturing operation they can re-run and prove -- the builds tie to their materials, the quality gates held, the costs decompose -- and Ridgeline keeps making what it makes, from the right materials, inspected, at a cost it can prove, with the drift between the record and the metal closed by construction. That is what this volume adds to the sovereign ERP -- the first of the vertical band, each a real operation governed on the one core and provable by anyone who inherits it.

title: S5 20 Distribution Wholesale
chapter_title: Distribution — Where the Promise and the Stock Must Agree
text: You will see why distribution is the operation where a business most often promises what it cannot deliver, and what it takes to make a shipment something the record can prove came from real stock, billed for exactly what shipped, within the customer's credit.

title: S5 20 Distribution Wholesale
chapter_title: Distribution — Where the Promise and the Stock Must Agree
text: **Distribution is the operation where a business most often promises what it cannot yet deliver, and where the gap between the promise and the stock is discovered at the moment it is most expensive -- when the truck is at the dock.** A distributor lives on the accuracy of a single number: how much of a thing is actually on the shelf, available to promise to the next customer. Everywhere upstream the record can be a little loose and be corrected later; at the moment of fulfillment the record either matches the metal on the shelf or it does not, and a mismatch means a customer promised product that was never there, a shipment billed for more than left the dock, or an order taken from a customer already past the credit a business should extend. The distributor that lets its record drift from its stock ships against inventory it does not have and bills against shipments it did not make -- and every screen shows the order sailing through. **The record and the stock drift apart in three specific ways, and a governed distribution operation is built to close each.** The first is phantom stock: an order allocated and promised against on-hand that is not really there, so the business commits to a customer it cannot supply and discovers the shortfall at the dock. The second is over-billing: an invoice for more than actually shipped, so revenue is recorded that no shipment supports and a customer is charged for goods they never received. The third is over-extended credit: an order taken from a customer already at or past their limit, so the business ships product it will struggle to collect on. Each is a place where the promise the record makes outruns what the stock, the shipment, or the customer's credit can support -- and each is a failure of the same discipline: the refusal to promise what cannot be delivered. **The legacy answer is the distribution and warehouse-management system, and in most operations it records the promise rather than enforcing the stock.** A distribution system captures the orders taken, the allocations made, the shipments entered, and the invoices raised -- and it is a diligent system of record. But it is not a system of refusal: it will allocate an order against on-hand that is not there, invoice for a quantity the dock never shipped, and take an order from a customer over their limit, because each of those is an entry a user is permitted to make. When an auditor later asks whether every shipment this quarter came from real stock, was billed for exactly what shipped, and stayed within the customer's credit, the honest answer is that the system holds what was entered -- and whether the entries matched the stock is a question no one can settle by re-running them. **This volume makes a sales order a governed act that allocates from real stock, bills only what shipped, and refuses an order over the customer's credit.** The chapters that follow present one thing that runs today: a governed sales-order fulfillment. A sales order allocates against governed on-hand, and an allocation that would drive stock negative -- that would promise what is not there -- is refused fail-closed. It moves through a lifecycle -- open, allocated, shipped, invoiced -- where no state is reached by skipping the one before it, so an order cannot be shipped before it is allocated or invoiced before it shipped. Its invoice is value-conserving: it bills the quantities that shipped, and no more. And it is gated by a fail-closed credit check that refuses an order which would put the customer over their governed limit. The shipment that results is one the record can prove came from real stock, at the quantity that shipped, within the customer's credit -- because the process refused to make the promise otherwise. **The difference is between a distribution record you enter and a distribution record you can re-run.** A legacy system tells an auditor that inventory is tracked, shipments are recorded, and credit is checked. A governed distribution hands the auditor the orders, the inventory movements, and the invoices, and lets them re-run the allocation and watch it refuse the order that would overdraw stock, re-run the invoice and confirm it bills only what shipped, re-run the credit check and watch it refuse the over-limit order. The claim that a shipment was proper becomes a computation that either allocates, conserves, and clears -- or declines. **The value that flows through distribution is conserved from stock to shipment to invoice to ledger, or it is a leak.** Every governed record in this series conserves value; distribution extends that discipline across the whole order-to-cash flow of a wholesaler. The allocation conserves to on-hand -- never more than is there; the invoice conserves to the shipment -- never more than shipped; and the sale posts to the general ledger as a balanced entry -- accounts receivable against sales revenue, debits equal to credits. A shipment whose invoice you cannot tie back to the stock that left the dock is not a governed sale; it is a promise the record made that the stock did not keep. **What this volume presents runs today, and what it leans on it composes rather than rebuilds.** The on-hand it allocates against is the sealed supply-chain surface (Supply Chain Execution, Vol 9); the value-conserving invoice and the fail-closed credit gate are the ones Revenue & Order-to-Cash (Vol 17) already presented; the sale posts on the sealed posting floor. The logistics a modern distributor also wants -- the carrier and transportation systems, the warehouse-management scanners, the EDI to trading partners -- is the concern of the sovereign port (S6-V07), named as a boundary, not smuggled in. Demand planning and distribution analytics compose the sealed Analytics & Decision Intelligence (Vol 19); compliance and traceability compose the sealed Compliance & Audit (Vol 16). **For Ridgeline Fabricated Metals, the composite manufacturer this series follows, distribution is how its product reaches its customers and where its promises are most exposed.** Ridgeline ships fabricated brackets and components to customers from its warehouse, on sales orders through its channels, and every one of those orders is a place where it can promise stock it does not have, bill for more than it ships, or extend credit past what it should. When its fulfillment lead allocates an order and its billing clerk invoices a shipment, the question the rest of this volume answers is whether that allocation and that invoice are governed acts a successor could re-run -- from real stock, for what shipped, within credit -- or promises that left no proof. The next chapter begins where a governed shipment begins: with the allocation, fail-closed against the stock that is really there.

title: S5 20 Distribution Wholesale
chapter_title: The Allocation — Fail-Closed Against the Stock That Is Really There
text: You will allocate a sales order against governed on-hand, fail-closed -- an allocation that would drive stock negative is refused, so a business can never promise a customer inventory that is not there.

title: S5 20 Distribution Wholesale
chapter_title: The Allocation — Fail-Closed Against the Stock That Is Really There
text: **The single number a distributor lives on is how much of a thing is really on the shelf, available to promise, and the allocation is the moment that number is put to the test.** When an order is taken, the business commits to supplying it, and that commitment is only as good as the stock behind it. In a legacy operation, allocation is often a soft reservation against an on-hand figure that may be stale, overstated, or already promised to someone else -- so two orders get allocated the same units, or an order is allocated against stock a cycle count will later reveal was never there. The allocation looks successful on the screen; the failure surfaces at the dock, when the picker cannot find what the system promised. A distribution record that lets an order allocate against stock that is not there is a record that manufactures promises the warehouse cannot keep. **This chapter allocates a sales order against governed on-hand, fail-closed, so an order can never promise what is not there.** `allocate` takes a sales order and the governed inventory movements, and checks each line against the on-hand at the order's warehouse location -- composing the sealed no-phantom-stock guard of the supply-chain surface (Supply Chain Execution, Vol 9). A line whose quantity would drive on-hand negative -- that would allocate stock that is not there -- is refused, and the order is not partly promised and partly not; it is refused as a whole, and the caller may backorder what cannot be covered. The default is refusal: an allocation the stock cannot support does not happen. Available-to-promise stops being a soft figure a salesperson hopes is current and becomes a hard check against the stock that is really there. **The allocation conserves to on-hand, and never exceeds it -- which is the invariant that keeps the promise honest.** Because every line is checked against governed on-hand before it is allocated, an order can never allocate a quantity the governed movements do not support -- the check refuses exactly that. And when each allocation is committed as a governed inventory movement before the next order allocates, that discipline extends across every order the warehouse fulfills: two orders cannot both draw down the last unit, because the second allocation sees the first's commitment in the on-hand it checks against. Allocation is value-conserving in the way the whole series is value-conserving: nothing is promised out that is not really in. A reviewer does not audit a reservation table and hope it reconciles to the stock; they re-run the allocation against the same governed movements and watch it refuse the same over-promises. **A refused allocation is an honest backorder, not a silent shortfall discovered at the dock.** When an order cannot be fully allocated, the refusal is immediate and named -- this line, this quantity, would overdraw this stock -- so the business learns at order entry that it cannot yet supply, rather than at the dock when the truck is waiting. That is the difference between a governed operation and a hopeful one: the governed operation surfaces the shortfall where it can still be managed -- expedite the replenishment, split the shipment, tell the customer the truth -- while the hopeful operation discovers it where it can only be apologized for. Fail-closed allocation turns the stock-out from a dock-side crisis into an order-entry decision. **The on-hand the allocation checks against is the sealed inventory record, not a copy this volume maintains.** The movements that establish on-hand -- the receipts, the issues, the transfers -- are the concern of the sealed supply-chain surface (Supply Chain Execution, Vol 9), and this chapter composes that surface rather than keeping a second inventory of its own. There is one inventory truth, governed in the supply volume, and the allocation is a check against it -- so the availability a distributor promises against is the same on-hand the warehouse actually holds, never a distribution-side copy that has drifted from it. The warehouse governs the stock; the sales order checks against it; and the two never disagree, because there is only one of them. **What runs here is the fail-closed allocation; the physical warehouse operations -- the picking, the bin locations, the scan guns -- compose the port.** The execution of a pick, the directed put-away, the handheld scanner that confirms a location, all live at the equipment, and integrating them is the concern of the sovereign port (S6-V07). This chapter presents the governed check that stands between an order and the stock -- the refusal to promise what is not there -- and names the warehouse-execution seam at its edge. The pick is executed at the port; the promise is governed on the core. **For Ridgeline, fail-closed allocation means it never promises a customer stock it does not have.** When Ridgeline allocates a sales order for fabricated brackets against its warehouse, an order for more than the on-hand shows is refused, named by exactly the line and quantity that would overdraw, and Ridgeline's fulfillment lead learns at order entry -- not at the dock -- that the stock is short and the order must be backordered or split. When Ridgeline's auditor asks whether every allocation this quarter was covered by real stock, the answer is the re-runnable check against the governed on-hand, not a reservation ledger no one can reconcile. The next chapter moves the allocated order down the line -- through the fail-closed lifecycle from allocation to shipment to invoice.

title: S5 20 Distribution Wholesale
chapter_title: Fulfillment — the Sales Order as a Fail-Closed Lifecycle
text: You will move a sales order through a fail-closed lifecycle -- open, allocated, shipped, invoiced -- where no state is reached by skipping the one before it, so an order cannot ship before it is allocated or bill before it shipped.

title: S5 20 Distribution Wholesale
chapter_title: Fulfillment — the Sales Order as a Fail-Closed Lifecycle
text: **Fulfillment is the stretch where an order's status is most tempting to advance ahead of its physical progress, and a governed distribution operation makes each status something the order reached rather than something a clerk set.** Between the moment an order is taken and the moment its invoice goes out, the order passes through allocation, picking, packing, shipment, and billing -- and at every step there is pressure to mark the next status early: to bill before the truck leaves so revenue lands this period, to mark shipped before the carrier confirms so the dashboard looks current. Each early mark makes the screen better and the reconciliation worse, and the classic distribution failure -- an invoice for a shipment that never left, revenue recognized on goods still on the shelf -- is exactly a status advanced ahead of the physical fact it was supposed to record. **This chapter makes the sales order a fail-closed state machine, so its status always reflects its real progress.** A sales order moves through a lifecycle -- `open`, `allocated`, `shipped`, `invoiced` -- and `transition` permits only the moves the lifecycle allows, with the honest exit of cancelled where an order legitimately stops. An attempt to jump a state -- to ship an order that was never allocated, to invoice one that never shipped -- is refused with an error naming the move and the moves that were actually allowed. The default is refusal: a status the lifecycle does not permit does not happen. The order's status stops being a field a clerk advances and becomes a state the order reached by passing through allocation before shipment and shipment before billing. **No ship before allocation, and no invoice before shipment -- and those two refusals are the heart of the control.** The value of the lifecycle is in its edges: because shipped can only be reached from allocated, and invoiced only from shipped, an invoiced order carries in its own history the guarantee that it was allocated from real stock and shipped before it was billed. There is no path to an invoice that bypasses the shipment, so a distributor cannot bill for goods that never left the dock, and no path to a shipment that bypasses the allocation, so a distributor cannot ship what was never confirmed available. The two failures that most corrupt a distribution ledger -- billing an unshipped order and shipping an unallocated one -- are closed not by vigilance but by the shape of the lifecycle. **Every transition is a governed event over the same order, not a silent rewrite of its status.** Moving an order to a new state does not overwrite it in place; it produces a new order at the new state and a transition event describing the move -- which order, from what state, to what state. The prior state is not erased; the transition is a new fact appended to the order's history, the way every governed change in this series is an append rather than an edit. A reviewer months later does not find an order that is simply "invoiced" with no story; they find the invoice that followed a shipment that followed an allocation, and can trace the order's fulfillment back through the governed steps that produced it -- the same discipline the manufacturing volume applies to a production order, applied here to a shipment. **Multi-channel fulfillment is many orders on the one lifecycle, not a separate flow per channel.** A wholesaler sells through several channels -- direct accounts, distributors, marketplaces -- and the temptation is a bespoke fulfillment path for each, which is how channels drift out of step with one another and with the stock. Here every order, whatever channel it came from, moves through the same fail-closed lifecycle and allocates against the same governed on-hand, so the channel is an attribute of the order rather than a separate system. There is one fulfillment truth across all channels, and a channel that reports differently is a view that disagrees with the orders, not a rival account of what shipped. **What runs here is the fail-closed lifecycle; the carrier and transportation execution composes the port.** The booking of a carrier, the printing of a label, the tracking of a truck, the delivery confirmation scanned at the customer's door -- all live at the logistics equipment, and integrating them is the concern of the sovereign port (S6-V07). This chapter presents the governed lifecycle the shipment advances through, and names the carrier seam at its edge. The truck is dispatched at the port; the order's progress is governed on the core. **For Ridgeline, a fail-closed lifecycle means an order's status always matches where the shipment really is.** When Ridgeline fulfills a bracket order, the order moves open to allocated to shipped to invoiced only by passing through each state, and it cannot be invoiced before it shipped or shipped before it was allocated from real stock. When Ridgeline's auditor asks how an invoiced order came to be billed, the answer is its transition history -- allocated, shipped, invoiced -- each a governed event, not a status advanced to make a period's revenue. The next chapter completes the order-to-cash arc: the value-conserving invoice for exactly what shipped, gated by credit, and posted balanced to the ledger.

title: S5 20 Distribution Wholesale
chapter_title: The Sale — Billed for What Shipped, Within Credit, Posted Balanced
text: You will invoice a shipment value-conserving -- billing only the quantities that shipped -- gate the order against the customer's credit fail-closed, and post the sale to the general ledger as a balanced entry, so revenue is never recorded that no shipment or no creditworthy customer supports.

title: S5 20 Distribution Wholesale
chapter_title: The Sale — Billed for What Shipped, Within Credit, Posted Balanced
text: **Billing is the step where revenue is most easily invented ahead of the shipment, and a governed distribution operation ties the invoice to what actually shipped and the order to what the customer can actually pay.** An invoice is a claim on a customer and a line of revenue on the books, and both are only honest if a real shipment of a real quantity backs them and the customer has the credit to settle. In a legacy operation the invoice is often raised from the order rather than the shipment -- so a partial ship gets billed in full, or an order gets invoiced before it leaves -- and the credit check is a soft warning a salesperson can dismiss. The result is revenue recorded that no shipment supports, receivables raised against customers already past their limit, and a quarter's numbers that overstate what the business actually earned and can actually collect. **This chapter invoices a shipment value-conserving, so the bill can never exceed what shipped.** `invoice_shipment` builds the invoice from the SHIPPED quantities -- the quantities the order allocated and shipped -- and composes the sealed value-conserving invoice (Revenue & Order-to-Cash, Vol 17): the line amounts are quantity times unit price, the lines sum to the subtotal, the tax is a named line, and the total is subtotal plus tax. Because the invoice is built from the allocated quantities the order shipped, a distributor cannot bill for more than was allocated and shipped, and an unshipped order cannot be invoiced at all. The invoice stops being a claim raised from the order and becomes a computation over the shipment -- and revenue is recorded only for goods that actually moved. **The order is gated by a fail-closed credit check, so the business does not ship to a customer it should not.** `credit_check` composes the sealed credit gate (Revenue & Order-to-Cash, Vol 17): it takes the order's amount and the customer's governed credit limit and outstanding balance, and refuses the order if it would put the customer over their limit. A refused order is not flagged and passed; it is refused, and taking the order anyway is a governed override, not a value the check quietly returns. The credit gate is the same fail-closed posture the series takes everywhere: the default is refusal, and an over-limit order does not ship on the hope that the customer will pay. A distributor extends credit deliberately, as a governed decision, not by default because a warning was easy to click past. **The sale posts to the general ledger as a balanced entry, so the distribution and the finance functions share one record of what was sold.** `sale_posting` produces the accounting fact of the sale in the one posting shape the whole system shares: accounts receivable is debited the invoice total, sales revenue is credited the subtotal, and the named tax is credited to tax payable -- so debits equal credits by construction, and the total ties to the invoice. That balanced entry composes the sealed posting floor through the general ledger's adapter, and the trial balance nets to zero exactly as it does for a supplier payable or a production cost. Distribution does not keep its own sales ledger that a controller must later reconcile to the general ledger; it emits the canonical posting, and the one ledger records it -- so the revenue the finance function reports is the revenue the shipments actually produced. **Channel and pricing governance is the discipline of which price applies to which order, and it lives on the governed order rather than in a separate pricing engine.** A wholesaler prices differently by channel, customer, and volume, and the price that applies to an order is carried on the order's lines and flows into the value-conserving invoice -- so the price a customer is billed is the price the order recorded, and a change to a pricing policy is a governed act rather than a quiet edit to a rate table. This chapter presents the invoice that prices the shipment and the credit gate that governs the order; the full pricing-policy machinery -- the tiered rates, the channel agreements -- composes the governed order and the sealed access surface for the changes that set them, rather than a pricing black box the invoice trusts. **What runs here is the value-conserving invoice, the fail-closed credit gate, and the balanced sale posting; the tax rate and the external billing rails compose their sealed homes.** The sales-tax amount on the invoice is a named line the invoice conserves (total is subtotal plus the named tax); the statutory rate policy that determines that amount is governed as policy on the sealed Sovereign Tax surface (Vol 3) and supplied to the invoice rather than computed in it, and the electronic invoicing and payment rails that deliver the bill and collect the cash are the concern of the sovereign port (S6-V07). This chapter presents the sale as a governed, value-conserving, balanced act; the tax computation and the payment rail are named homes around it. **For Ridgeline, the governed sale means its revenue always ties to its shipments and its receivables to its creditworthy customers.** When Ridgeline invoices a shipped bracket order, the invoice bills exactly the quantities that shipped at the prices the order recorded, the order is refused if it would put the customer over their credit limit, and the sale posts balanced to the general ledger as receivable against revenue. When Ridgeline's controller reports sales, or Ilse Vogt -- the auditor from Volume 2 -- ties revenue to the shipments that produced it, the invoices re-derive from the shipments and the postings balance to the cent. The next chapter lifts from the single order to the coordination of demand and supply, and the compliance and traceability of the whole distribution operation -- composed over the governed records this volume has built.

title: S5 20 Distribution Wholesale
chapter_title: Demand and Supply, Coordinated over the Governed Record
text: You will see available-to-promise and demand-supply coordination as projections over the governed inventory and orders this volume builds -- every availability figure and every demand plan decomposing to the movements and orders beneath it -- rather than as a separate planning system maintained beside the warehouse.

title: S5 20 Distribution Wholesale
chapter_title: Demand and Supply, Coordinated over the Governed Record
text: **Once distribution is governed at the level of the individual order -- allocated against real stock, shipped through a fail-closed lifecycle, billed for what shipped -- the coordination of demand and supply stops being a separate planning system and becomes a projection over what the governed records already hold.** A legacy operation runs a demand-planning tool and an available-to-promise engine as things apart from the warehouse: inventory positions are extracted, forecasts are layered on, and the resulting plans are only as true as the extract that fed them. This chapter takes the other path, the one the whole series takes: the governed inventory movements and the governed orders are the single source, and available-to-promise and demand coordination are views computed from them -- never a second copy of the availability picture that can drift from the stock. **Available-to-promise is a projection over the governed on-hand and the open orders, so every availability figure decomposes to the movements and allocations beneath it.** How much of an item can the business still promise, at a location, over a horizon? In a governed operation that is not a number a planning engine asserts; it is a projection over the governed inventory movements and the allocations already committed against them, and it decomposes -- ask what makes up an availability figure and the answer is the specific receipts, issues, and allocations, not an aggregate no one can open. Because the same governed on-hand the allocation checks against is the on-hand the availability projects from, the number a salesperson promises against and the number the warehouse actually holds are the same number, always. **Demand planning composes the sealed analytics surface over the governed orders, so a forecast is built on real demand history rather than a disconnected data mart.** The demand a distributor plans for is a pattern in its governed orders -- what shipped, to whom, when -- and forecasting that demand composes the sealed planning and analytics surface (Analytics & Decision Intelligence, Vol 19) over those governed records. The forecast inherits the discipline the series applies to every derived figure: it is a projection over the governed order history, decomposable to the shipments that produced it, rather than a number a planning system emits from an extract that may have missed a channel. Demand planning stops being a parallel forecast the warehouse ignores and becomes a view over the same orders the warehouse fulfilled. **Exceptions are surfaced from the record, not raised in a parallel plan that the warehouse then has to reconcile.** A stock-out that will breach a service level, a demand spike that outruns supply, an allocation that could not be covered -- these are exceptions, and in a governed operation they are surfaced by projecting over the governed on-hand, orders, and allocations, not flagged in a planning system that holds its own copy of the positions. Because the exception is derived from the same record the warehouse acts on, the coordination it prompts -- expedite a replenishment, reallocate stock, tell a customer the truth -- acts on the real positions rather than a planner's stale view. There is one availability picture, and the exceptions are what it shows when it is projected forward. **Composition rather than duplication is the point, and it is what keeps distribution from promising against a picture that has drifted from the stock.** The failure mode this chapter refuses is the one every large distributor eventually suffers: a warehouse system, an available-to-promise engine, and a demand-planning tool each holding its own copy of the inventory position, subtly out of step, so that three answers to "can we promise this?" disagree. By composing availability and demand over the single governed record instead of copying it, the volume ensures there is one availability truth and many views of it -- and a view that disagrees with the movements is a bug in the view, not a rival account of what is on the shelf. **What is present in this chapter is the composition; the analytics and planning engines it composes are sealed elsewhere and named here.** This chapter introduces no new module -- deliberately. Its work is to show that distribution's coordination questions are answered by projecting the sealed inventory over the governed movements and the sealed analytics over the governed orders, and to keep the availability picture single. The governed allocation, the fail-closed lifecycle, and the value-conserving sale are the substance; available-to-promise and demand coordination are the views. Nothing here overstates what runs: the composed surfaces are sealed, and the availability is a projection over the one governed record, not a second planning system this volume ships. **For Ridgeline, coordinated demand and supply mean it can answer "can we promise this, and when?" from the stock and the orders themselves.** When Ridgeline's fulfillment lead asks how much of a bracket it can still promise this week, or its planner forecasts next quarter's demand, the answers are projections over the governed on-hand, allocations, and order history -- decomposable to the specific movements and shipments -- not reports from a planning tool that might have missed a channel in its last extract. The availability Ridgeline promises against is the stock it actually holds, and the demand it plans for is the demand its orders actually recorded. The next chapter turns to the compliance and traceability of the whole distribution operation -- composed, like this, over the governed records the volume has built.

title: S5 20 Distribution Wholesale
text: You will see distribution compliance and end-to-end traceability as projections composed over the governed order, allocation, shipment, and posting records this volume built -- every compliance check and every trace decomposing to the transactions beneath it -- rather than as a separate system maintained beside the flow.

title: S5 20 Distribution Wholesale
text: **Once distribution is governed at the level of the individual order -- the allocation from real stock, the fail-closed shipment, the value-conserving invoice, the balanced posting -- compliance and traceability stop being separate systems and become projections over what the governed records already link.** A legacy distributor runs a compliance function and a traceability database as things apart from the flow: shipment data is extracted, cleaned, and assembled into audit binders and trace reports that are only as true as the extract that fed them. This chapter takes the other path, the one the whole series takes: the governed orders, allocations, shipments, and postings are the single source, and compliance and traceability are views computed from them -- never a second copy of the distribution record that can drift from the flow. **End-to-end traceability is a query over the governed order-to-shipment record, not a trace database assembled beside it.** Which shipments went to a customer; which stock a shipment drew from; which orders consumed a particular lot -- these are traces, and in a governed distribution they are answered by following the links the governed records already hold: an order allocated specific stock, shipped specific quantities, and posted a specific sale, so tracing forward from a suspect lot to every shipment that carried it, or backward from a shipment to the stock it drew from, is a query over the governed orders rather than a reconstruction from scattered logs. The traceability a recall depends on is a property the governed record already has, composed through the sealed compliance surface (Compliance & Audit, Vol 16) -- not a promise a separate system makes and an audit tests. **Distribution compliance composes the sealed compliance surface, so a regulatory requirement is run over the governed record rather than attested beside it.** Was every shipment allocated from real stock and billed for what shipped? Were credit limits and pricing policies honored? Are the licensing and jurisdictional rules a regulated distributor must observe evidenced on every order? These are compliance questions, and in a governed operation they are answered by running the checks over the governed orders, allocations, shipments, and postings -- the sealed Compliance & Audit (Vol 16) surface, composed over the very records this volume produces. Compliance stops being a periodic attestation that controls were followed and becomes a re-runnable check that they were, evidenced by the transactions themselves. **A recall -- the hardest distribution requirement -- is satisfied by the governed record itself, not a traceability system bolted beside it.** Because each order links its shipment to the specific stock it allocated and the specific invoice it produced, identifying every customer who received product from a suspect lot, and every order that lot touched, is a query over the governed records rather than a frantic reconstruction. The genealogy a recall depends on is already in the record, composed through the sealed compliance surface -- so the distributor can answer, within the hour, exactly where a lot went, rather than assembling the answer over days from systems that each hold a piece of it. **Composition rather than duplication is the point, and it is what keeps distribution from growing a second, divergent record of what shipped.** The failure mode this chapter refuses is the one every large distributor eventually suffers: a shipping system, a compliance repository, and a traceability database each holding its own copy of what moved, subtly out of step, so that three answers to "where did this go?" disagree. By composing compliance and traceability over the single governed record instead of copying it, the volume ensures there is one distribution truth and many views of it -- and a view that disagrees with the shipments is a bug in the view, not a rival account of what shipped. **What is present in this chapter is the composition; the compliance and analytics engines it composes are sealed elsewhere and named here.** This chapter introduces no new module -- deliberately. Its work is to show that distribution's higher-order questions are answered by projecting the sealed compliance and analytics surfaces over the governed records the earlier chapters built, and to draw the boundary at the sovereign port for the trading-partner connectivity that is genuinely outside the core. The governed order, the allocated stock, and the value-conserving sale are the substance; compliance and traceability are the views; and the port is the edge. Nothing here overstates what runs: the composed surfaces are sealed, and the connectivity -- EDI to trading partners, the carrier and warehouse systems -- is named as the sovereign port's (S6-V07), not implied as this volume's. **For Ridgeline, composed compliance and traceability mean it can answer the hard questions about its distribution from the shipments themselves.** When Ridgeline is asked which customers received brackets from a particular production lot, or whether every shipment this quarter was allocated from real stock and billed for what shipped, the answers are projections over the governed orders, allocations, shipments, and postings -- decomposable to the specific transactions -- not reports from a system that might have missed something in its last extract. And when Ridgeline is ready to wire its trading partners' EDI or its carriers' tracking into the record, it knows exactly where that work lives: the sovereign port, governed in its own volume, not bolted onto the distribution core as an unproven promise. The final chapter draws the volume together -- the governed distribution record as something a successor inherits and can prove.

title: S5 20 Distribution Wholesale
text: You will see the governed sales order -- allocated from real stock, moved through a fail-closed lifecycle, billed for what shipped, gated on credit, and posted balanced -- as one inheritable distribution record a successor can re-run to prove every shipment came from real stock, was billed for what shipped, and stayed within the customer's credit.

title: S5 20 Distribution Wholesale
text: **The governed sales order -- its fail-closed allocation, its fail-closed lifecycle, its value-conserving invoice, its credit gate, and its balanced posting -- is not five features; it is one inheritable record of how a business turns stock into revenue.** An order allocated only from stock that is really there; a lifecycle that reaches no state by skipping the one before it; an invoice that bills only what shipped; a credit gate that refuses what the customer cannot pay; a sale that posts balanced to the general ledger -- together these make a shipment a chain of governed acts a successor can follow from the order to the receivable. The volume's work is not a distribution-management system bolted onto the core; it is order-to-cash-for-a-distributor rebuilt so that its integrity lives in the record rather than in the people who know the warehouse today. **Every shipment this volume produces is re-derivable, and that is what makes the distribution provable.** A successor who trusts none of the prior warehouse team can take the orders, the inventory movements, and the invoices, and re-run the fulfillment -- confirming that each shipment allocated only from real stock, billed only for what shipped, stayed within the customer's credit, and posted a balanced sale. There is no shipment that rests on a promise the stock could not keep, no invoice that bills more than left the dock. The flow that in most distributors is the least reconcilable -- stock to shipment to invoice to cash -- becomes the most provable, because every shipment is an order the process refused to fulfill until the stock, the shipment, and the credit all supported it. **Distribution integrity becomes a generational asset rather than warehouse knowledge, which is the point of building it this way.** In most distributors the knowledge of what is really on the shelf, which customers to trust with credit, which channels to prioritize when stock is short, lives in the heads of a few experienced people, and walks out the door when they retire. This volume moves that integrity into the record: the allocation, the lifecycle, the invoice, the credit gate, and the posting are all governed facts, so the discipline survives the departure of the people who established it. A business that changes hands, or outlives its founders, inherits not a folklore of how the warehouse was run but a governed record it can re-run -- and that continuity is exactly what lasting, generational prosperity asks of the operation through which a business turns its stock into cash. **The vertical is the sealed core composed, not a parallel distribution system -- and that is the discipline that makes it honest.** The temptation in a vertical is to build a second world: a distribution suite that reimplements the inventory, the invoicing, the credit, the ledger, and then drifts from the core it was supposed to extend. This volume refuses that. The on-hand is the sealed inventory; the invoice is the sealed value-conserving billing; the credit gate is the sealed credit check; the posting is a sealed general-ledger entry. The one thing genuinely distribution -- the governed sales order that allocates from real stock and ties the shipment to the invoice to the ledger -- is the only new act the volume presents, and it composes everything beneath it rather than copying it. There is one core, and distribution is a station on it, not a rival to it. **What the volume presents runs today, and what it composes it names -- and that honesty is part of the inheritance.** The governed sales order, its fail-closed allocation and lifecycle, its value-conserving invoice, its credit gate, and its balanced sale posting all run on the public starter and are proven by tests a successor can re-run. The on-hand composes the sealed supply-chain surface (Supply Chain Execution, Vol 9); the invoice and credit compose Revenue & Order-to-Cash (Vol 17); the sale posts on the sealed posting floor; demand and reporting compose the sealed Analytics & Decision Intelligence (Vol 19); compliance and traceability compose the sealed Compliance & Audit (Vol 16); the tax rate policy is governed on the sealed Sovereign Tax surface (Vol 3); and the logistics connectivity -- carrier, warehouse-management, EDI -- is homed in the sovereign port (S6-V07). Nothing is claimed to run that does not, and nothing that runs is left without a home for what it leans on. A successor inherits not a set of promises but a set of proofs, with the boundaries drawn honestly. **For Ridgeline, the inheritable distribution record is what lets the business outlast the people who ran its warehouse.** The day comes when Ridgeline's long-serving fulfillment lead retires, or the company passes to a new owner, and the question is whether distribution's integrity leaves with them. Because every order allocated from real stock, every lifecycle passed through its states, every invoice billed only what shipped, every order cleared its credit gate, and every sale posted balanced to the ledger, the answer is that it does not. The new team inherits a distribution operation they can re-run and prove -- the shipments tie to the stock, the invoices to the shipments, the receivables to creditworthy customers -- and Ridgeline keeps getting its product to its customers, from real stock, billed for what shipped, within credit, with the drift between the promise and the stock closed by construction. That is what this volume adds to the sovereign ERP, and the second station the vertical band composes on the one core: a real operation governed and provable by anyone who inherits it.

title: S5 21 Professional Services
chapter_title: Professional Services — Where the Hours and the Bill Must Agree
text: You will see why professional services is the operation where a business most often bills what it cannot substantiate, and what it takes to make an invoice something the record can prove came from recorded time, at the agreed rate, within the engagement's budget.

title: S5 21 Professional Services
chapter_title: Professional Services — Where the Hours and the Bill Must Agree
text: **Professional services is the one business whose entire inventory is time, and where the record of that time and the bill sent for it are most easily allowed to drift apart.** A firm that sells its people's hours lives or dies on a single chain: time is worked, time is recorded, time is billed, and the bill is collected. Everywhere a product business has a physical good to reconcile against, a services business has only the record -- and if the record of the hours drifts from what was worked, or the bill drifts from the record, there is no shelf to count that will reveal it. A services firm that lets its billing drift from its recorded time bills for work it cannot substantiate, bleeds past the budget a client agreed to, and charges the wrong rate for the wrong person -- and every timesheet looks full. **The record and the bill drift apart in three specific ways, and a governed services operation is built to close each.** The first is the unsubstantiated bill: an invoice for hours no recorded time entry supports, so a client is charged for work the firm cannot show was done. The second is budget bleed: an engagement that quietly runs past the budget a client agreed to, so the firm either eats the overrun or bills a client who never approved it. The third is the wrong rate: time billed at a rate that does not match the resource who worked it, so a junior's hours are charged as a senior's, or a rate no engagement agreed to is applied. Each is a place where the bill outruns what the recorded time, the budget, or the rate card can support -- and each is a failure of the same discipline: the refusal to bill what cannot be substantiated. **The legacy answer is the professional-services-automation tool, and in most firms it records the bill rather than substantiating the time.** A PSA system captures the timesheets entered, the invoices raised, and the budgets tracked -- and it is a diligent system of record. But it is not a system of refusal: it will bill hours no time entry supports, let an engagement run past its budget, and apply a rate the rate card does not carry, because each is an entry a user is permitted to make. When an auditor -- or a client -- later asks whether every billed hour was recorded, at the agreed rate, within the engagement's budget, the honest answer is that the system holds what was entered, and whether the bill matched the recorded time is a question no one can settle by re-running it. **This volume makes an engagement a governed act that bills only recorded time, at the rate-card rate, within the budget.** The chapters that follow present one thing that runs today: a governed professional-services engagement. Time is recorded against the engagement value-conserving -- a resource not on the rate card, or a non-positive hour, is refused -- so the billable amount is exactly the recorded hours at their agreed rates. The bill is fail-closed on the engagement's governed budget: an engagement whose billable amount would exceed its budget cannot bill without a governed override. And the invoice is value-conserving, built from the recorded time, so the bill can never exceed what was recorded. The invoice that results is one the record can prove came from recorded hours, at the agreed rate, within the budget -- because the process refused to raise it otherwise. **The difference is between a services record you enter and a services record you can re-run.** A legacy PSA tells a partner that time is tracked, budgets are watched, and invoices are raised. A governed services operation hands the auditor the engagements, the recorded time, and the rate cards, and lets them re-run the bill and watch it refuse the invoice that exceeds the recorded time or the budget. The claim that a bill was proper becomes a computation that either conserves the time and clears the budget -- or declines. **The value that flows through services is conserved from recorded time to bill to ledger, or it is a leak.** Every governed record in this series conserves value; services extends that discipline across the whole time-to-cash flow of a firm. The billable amount conserves to the recorded hours at their rates; the invoice conserves to the billable amount; the bill is held within the governed budget; and the sale posts to the general ledger as a balanced entry -- accounts receivable against services revenue, debits equal to credits. A bill you cannot tie back to the recorded time that produced it is not a governed engagement; it is a claim the record made that the timesheets did not keep. **What this volume presents runs today, and what it leans on it composes rather than rebuilds.** The engagement runs against a project, and the project and task structure it bills against is the sealed Project surface (Vol 11), composed here, not rebuilt -- this volume presents the engagement, and the project stays the project volume's. The resources whose rates it carries are the governed people of the sealed human-capital surface (Human Capital & Payroll, Vol 15). The invoice it produces composes the sealed value-conserving invoice (Revenue & Order-to-Cash, Vol 17); the bill posts on the sealed posting floor. The document collaboration and external timesheet tools a modern firm also uses are the concern of the sovereign port (S6-V07), named as a boundary, not smuggled in. Utilization and margin analytics compose the sealed Analytics & Decision Intelligence (Vol 19); services compliance composes the sealed Compliance & Audit (Vol 16). **For Ridgeline Fabricated Metals, the composite manufacturer this series follows, professional services is the engineering it sells alongside its product.** Ridgeline bills clients for custom design and engineering engagements -- senior and junior engineers' hours against a client project, on an agreed rate card and budget -- and every engagement is a place where it can bill unrecorded time, bleed past the budget, or charge the wrong rate. When its engagement lead records time and its billing partner raises an invoice, the question the rest of this volume answers is whether that time and that invoice are governed acts a successor could re-run -- recorded, at the agreed rate, within budget -- or a bill that left no proof. The next chapter begins where a governed engagement begins: with the engagement itself, opened against a governed budget and a rate card.

title: S5 21 Professional Services
chapter_title: The Engagement, Opened Against a Governed Budget and Rate Card
text: You will open an engagement as a governed record with a rate card and a governed budget, moved through a fail-closed lifecycle -- so what an engagement may bill and what it may not are fixed as governed facts before a single hour is worked.

title: S5 21 Professional Services
chapter_title: The Engagement, Opened Against a Governed Budget and Rate Card
text: **An engagement is the frame a professional-services firm puts around a client's work, and in a governed operation it is the record that fixes what the work may bill before the work begins.** When a client engages a firm, the two agree on the terms -- who will work, at what rate, against what budget -- and those terms are the only statement of what the engagement may bill made before the pressure of the work distorts them. In a legacy operation the terms are often soft: a rate anyone can override, a budget the work quietly exceeds, an engagement that drifts from what the client agreed to. A governed services operation treats the terms as exactly what they are: the governed frame the rest of the engagement answers to, fixed at the start, and not a target the work is free to depart from. **This chapter opens an engagement as a governed record with a rate card and a governed budget.** `open_engagement` takes a client, a rate card -- a billing rate per resource -- and a budget, and produces a governed engagement that starts with no time recorded. The rate card fixes what each resource's hours may be billed at; the budget fixes the ceiling the engagement's billing may not exceed without a governed override. Neither is a soft default a partner can quietly change; they are the governed terms the engagement carries, and every later act -- recording time, billing -- is measured against them.
