title: Vol 04 Resonance Coordination
chapter_title: The Resonance Coordination Opportunity — Aligning Without a Central Controller
text: **A federation of sovereign nodes can only act coherently if its members can keep their shared state aligned -- agreeing on what is true across the federation -- so coordination is a capability a federation needs, and the place where a central controller most easily creeps in.** A federation acts together only when its nodes agree on the shared facts: the current plan, the shared ledger position, the state they hold in common. Keeping that alignment is coordination. But coordination raises a question that decides whether the federation stays sovereign: is alignment reached by a central authority declaring the truth and the nodes accepting it, or by the nodes reconciling their own independently-held state as equals? **The tension is between alignment and sovereignty -- the nodes must reach agreement on shared state, but no node may be dictated to by a central controller that declares the truth for all -- and resolving that tension is the design problem.** Alignment without sovereignty is the orchestrator model: a central controller holds the authoritative state and pushes it to the nodes, which accept it. Sovereignty without alignment is drift: nodes that never reconcile diverge until they cannot act together. The sovereign answer resolves the tension by making each node compute its own view of the shared state and reconciling those views as equals -- so the federation reaches agreement, but no controller declares the truth and no node's state is authoritative over another's. **Legacy coordination runs through a central controller or consensus authority that dictates the truth -- an orchestrator holds the master state, or a consensus protocol elects a leader whose view becomes canonical, and the nodes align to it.** The familiar architecture of distributed coordination is a central authority: an orchestrator that owns the state and pushes updates, or a consensus mechanism that elects a leader whose version wins. Either way, one authority's view becomes the truth, and the nodes align to it rather than to each other. Coordination becomes obedience to a center, and a federation coordinated this way is a federation whose shared truth is owned by whatever holds the center -- exactly the central control sovereignty is meant to escape. **This is the weakness of the central orchestrator, and naming it precisely folds the old comparison into the opening -- the controller achieves alignment, but by declaring the truth from a center, so the coordination is only as sovereign as whatever holds the controller.** Traditional coordination systems are built for consistency, and consistency is easily achieved by a central authority declaring the canonical state. Their weakness is not that they fail to align; they align well. Their weakness is that alignment is obedience to a center that owns the truth, so no node's own state is authoritative and coordination depends on the controller. The sovereign advantage is structural: each node computes its own signal, and reconciliation is mutual agreement between equals -- so no controller owns the truth and no node is dictated to. **The sovereign opportunity is not a better orchestrator -- it is each node computing its own coordination signal and two nodes reconciling those signals as equals, so a federation reaches alignment with no central truth and no controller dictating it.** The design commitment of this volume is coordination with no central authority: each node computes the integrity root over its own governed state as its signal, and two nodes coordinate by comparing those signals -- resonant when they agree, a surfaced divergence when they differ. What is genuinely new is this each-node-computes-its-own, reconcile-as-equals discipline. What is deliberately absent is the orchestrator, the master state, and the elected leader whose view the legacy model makes canonical. **The stakes are the whole of Lasting Generational Prosperity, because a federation that can align without a central controller can stay coherent and independent across generations, while one that coordinates through a controller inherits a single point of authority its heirs cannot escape.** Coordination is how a federation stays coherent over time, and coherence owned by a controller is coherence rented. A federation that aligns by reconciling its nodes' own state as equals stays independent: it can grow, outlive any controller, and hand its way of staying aligned to successors. A federation that aligns through a central authority has handed the continuity of its coherence to whatever holds the center. The sovereign discipline is what keeps a federation's alignment its own, which is the precondition for its coherence being generational rather than dependent. **For the Ridgeline federation -- a family office and a partner co-op keeping shared state aligned -- the difference is whether each node computes its own signal and the two reconcile as equals, or whether a controller holds the master state and both align to it.** When the Ridgeline nodes need to confirm they hold the same shared state, the legacy path puts a controller in the middle holding the canonical version. The independent, self-computed integrity root is the Federation Node Governance floor's (S5 Vol 28); this chapter's contribution is to frame it as a coordination signal each node computes for itself. There is the sealed Sovereign Object Model (S5 Vol 5) and Federation Node Governance floor (S5 Vol 28) -- their governed state, their mandate roots, their symmetric reconciliation -- and over them a thin binding: compute each node's own root as its signal, reconcile two signals as equals and never overwrite. The capability inherits every guarantee the sealed floors proved and adds no unproven machinery of its own. **The coordination is, in the end, alignment the federation owns -- its own because each node computes its own signal, sovereign because no node's state is authoritative over another's, and provable because a signal is a faithful root of governed state -- which is exactly what a federation needs to stay coherent without a controller.** A federation that stays coherent needs its alignment to be its own, not dictated from a center. Because each node computes its own signal and reconciliation is between equals, the federation holds its coherence as something it owns and no controller declares. It depends on no orchestrator and no elected leader; it holds coordination that is sovereign in its every reconciliation, and can hand that way of staying aligned to whoever runs the federation next. **A federation that can stay aligned without a central controller holds a capacity that compounds across the generations rather than decaying into a dependency, which is the coherent discipline beneath its shared prosperity.** The capacity to stay coherent is a form of capital, and it compounds when alignment is owned. A federation coordinated by a controller decays into a dependency each generation inherits; a federation coordinated by mutual reconciliation accumulates an ownerless way of staying aligned each generation can extend. The capacity to stay coherent without a controller is what keeps a federation's coherence a compounding asset rather than a rented convenience -- and that capacity is what this volume gives a federation that means to stay aligned for the long run. **This is the coordination foundation of Lasting Generational Prosperity -- alignment the federation owns and hands on -- so the federation endures because the ability to stay coherent, without a controller it cannot escape, endures.** The objective the whole series serves is Lasting Generational Prosperity, and a federation is how sovereign nodes stay coherent together. Prosperity that lasts across a federation depends on the federation's ability to stay aligned, and that ability endures only if alignment is owned rather than dictated from a center. Resonance coordination is exactly that owned alignment: self-computed signals, mutual reconciliation, no central truth, composed from sealed floors. A federation that coordinates this way inherits not just alignment but the proven capacity to stay coherent without a controller, which is what makes its prosperity generational rather than dependent. **For the Ridgeline federation, resonance coordination is now the alignment the family office and the co-op own -- each node's own signal, reconciled as equals, no controller declaring the truth -- the coherence foundation on which their Lasting Generational Prosperity rests.** The Ridgeline nodes began the way most federations do -- reaching for a controller that would hold the canonical state between them. They end holding their alignment as their own: each node computing its own signal over its governed state, the two reconciling as equals, a divergence surfaced for governance rather than overwritten. Generations from now, a Ridgeline node can compute its own signal, reconcile it with a peer as an equal, and hand the whole way of staying coherent to its successors intact. The coordination cockpit the federation uses is the sovereign surface at six-sov.com/seeit; the resonance coordination itself -- self-computed, reconciled, ownerless -- is what this volume built, and it is the coherence layer beneath everything the Ridgeline federation means to hand on.

title: Vol 05 Inter Node Trust Boundaries Handoff
chapter_title: The Trust Boundaries & Handoff Opportunity — Inheriting a Node's Identity Without a Custodian
text: You will see why a federation of sovereign nodes must be able to hand a node's identity and trust anchors to a successor without a custodian, an escrow, or a central recovery authority -- and why the sovereign answer is a receipted, human-gated ceremony over a verifying package.

title: Vol 05 Inter Node Trust Boundaries Handoff
chapter_title: The Trust Boundaries & Handoff Opportunity — Inheriting a Node's Identity Without a Custodian
text: **A node's identity and trust anchors -- its keys, its right to be recognized by its peers -- must be able to outlive the person who first held them, because a federation meant to last across generations cannot lose a node when its steward changes.** A sovereign node is recognized by its peers through its identity and its keys. But people change: a steward retires, a family passes its node to the next generation, an organization changes ownership. If the node's identity cannot survive that change, the federation loses the node -- and a federation that loses nodes with every generational turn cannot endure. So the node's identity must be inheritable: able to pass to a successor intact. The question is how, and the answer decides whether the node stays sovereign. **The tension is between durability and sovereignty -- a node's identity must be recoverable and inheritable across a change of steward, but no custodian, escrow, or central authority may hold its keys -- and resolving that tension is the design problem.** Durability without sovereignty is the custodian model: a third party holds a copy of the keys so they can be recovered, which means the third party could use them. Sovereignty without durability is fragility: a node whose keys are held by no one loses its identity the moment its steward is gone. The sovereign answer resolves the tension by making the node's trust anchor a governed object the node owns, and its handoff a receipted, human-gated ceremony -- so the identity is inheritable, but no custodian ever holds the keys. **Legacy identity recovery runs through a custodian, an escrow, or a central authority that holds the keys -- a recovery service keeps a copy, an escrow releases it on a trigger, or a central directory can reset the identity -- and whoever holds the keys can become the identity.** The familiar answer to "what if the keys are lost" is to have someone else hold them: a key-escrow service, a custodial recovery provider, a central identity authority with reset power. Each solves durability by creating a second holder of the keys -- and a second holder is a second authority who could impersonate the node, be compelled to release the keys, or lose them. Recoverability bought this way is sovereignty sold: the node's identity is only as safe as the custodian, and the custodian is a single point of capture the node cannot escape. **This is the weakness of the key-escrow custodian, and naming it precisely folds the old comparison into the opening -- the custodian makes the identity recoverable, but by holding the keys, so the node's identity is only as sovereign as whoever holds them.** Traditional recovery is built for the worst case -- lost keys -- and solves it by a second holder. Its weakness is not that it fails to recover; it recovers reliably. Its weakness is that recovery runs through a holder of the keys, so the node's identity is never truly its own and the holder is a point of capture. The sovereign advantage is structural: the trust anchor is the node's own governed object, and its handoff is a human-gated ceremony over a verifying package -- so the identity is inheritable, but no one but the node and its named successor ever holds it. **The sovereign opportunity is not a better escrow -- it is a receipted, human-gated ceremony that hands a node's trust anchors to a successor over a verifying package, so a node's identity is inheritable with no custodian, no escrow, and no central recovery authority.** The design commitment of this volume is trust handoff with no key-holder in the middle: the node's trust anchor is a governed object the node owns, and its handoff to a successor is a ceremony that proceeds only when the successor package verifies and a named human approves. What is genuinely new is this inheritable-by-ceremony discipline. What is deliberately absent is the escrow, the custodian, and the central recovery authority that the legacy model makes the unavoidable second holder of the keys. **The stakes are the whole of Lasting Generational Prosperity, because a federation that can hand a node's identity to a successor without a custodian can keep its nodes across generations without ever surrendering their keys, while one that relies on escrow inherits a key-holder it cannot escape.** A node's identity is a generational asset -- the continuity of a family's or an organization's place in the federation. Whether that continuity is owned depends on whether recovery runs through a custodian. A federation whose nodes hand off their trust anchors by receipted ceremony keeps its nodes and its keys: identity passes to successors intact, and no custodian ever holds the keys. A federation that relies on escrow has handed the continuity of its identities to a key-holder each generation inherits. The sovereign discipline is what keeps a node's identity its own across the handoff, which is the precondition for its continuity being generational. **For the Ridgeline federation -- a family office handing its node's trust anchors to the next generation -- the difference is whether the handoff is a receipted, human-gated ceremony the family performs, or a recovery a custodian executes from a copy of the keys it held all along.** When the Ridgeline family office passes its node to the next generation, the legacy path relies on a custodian holding the keys to transfer them. This volume gives them another path: the node's trust anchor is a governed object the family owns, and the handoff to the successor is a ceremony that completes only when the successor package verifies and a named steward approves -- with no custodian ever holding the keys. The chapters that follow build that capability -- the trust anchor as a governed object (Ch 2), the handoff ceremony (Ch 3), the object model it composes (Ch 4), the generational handoff it composes (Ch 5), the recovery constitution and rotation it homes elsewhere (Ch 6), and the owned, inheritable trust it becomes (Ch 7) -- and none of it puts a custodian in the middle.

title: Vol 05 Inter Node Trust Boundaries Handoff
chapter_title: The Trust Anchor as a Governed Object — declare_trust_anchor
text: You will see how a node declares its trust anchor -- its key, its right to be recognized -- as a governed, provenance-carrying object it owns, so the anchor is an inheritable artifact on the record rather than a secret a custodian holds.

title: Vol 05 Inter Node Trust Boundaries Handoff
chapter_title: The Trust Anchor as a Governed Object — declare_trust_anchor
text: **A node's trust anchor -- the key or identity commitment by which its peers recognize it -- must be a governed object the node itself owns and can hand on, not a secret sitting in a custodian's vault, and `declare_trust_anchor` is the act that makes it one.** The first move in inheritable trust is to change what the anchor *is*. In the custodian model the anchor is a secret someone else holds. Here the anchor is a governed object the node registers under its own mandate: authored by the node, carrying its provenance, sealed with its integrity hash. `declare_trust_anchor(reg, node_id, anchor, *, mandate, author, source_ref, at)` performs exactly that registration. The anchor becomes a thing on the record that the node owns -- and a thing on the record can be inherited by ceremony, where a secret in a vault can only be released by its holder. **`declare_trust_anchor` composes the sealed object registry -- it calls `reg.append` with kind `ratify` to register the anchor as a provenance-carrying governed object under the node's own mandate -- so the anchor is created by the same governed-object machinery every sovereign artifact uses.** The function does not build a new store. It composes the sealed Sovereign Object Model: `reg.append(f"trust_anchor:{node_id}", anchor, author=author, source_ref=source_ref, at=at, mandate=mandate, kind="ratify")`. The kind is `ratify` because declaring a trust anchor is a constitutive act -- the node is putting its identity commitment on the record. The registry returns the governed object with its `version_hash`, and that hash is the anchor's integrity: any later handoff can verify the anchor against it. The anchor is governed the moment it is declared, by the machinery Vol 5 of Series 5 sealed. **An empty node id or an empty anchor is refused -- `declare_trust_anchor` raises `TrustError` before it registers anything -- because a trust anchor must name the node it belongs to and must carry an actual identity commitment; an anchor for no one, or an anchor that commits to nothing, is not a trust anchor.** The guard is deliberate and comes first. `if not node_id: raise TrustError(...)` and `if not anchor: raise TrustError(...)`. A trust anchor is a binding between a node and a key: strip either side and there is nothing to inherit. Refusing the empty case keeps the registry honest -- every `trust_anchor:` object names a real node and carries a real commitment, so when a successor inherits one there is something definite to inherit. The refusal is not a validation nicety; it is what makes the anchor an asset rather than a placeholder. **The registered anchor carries its author, its source reference, and its integrity hash -- it is inheritable precisely because it is on the record with its provenance, not because a custodian could hand over a copy.** What the node gets back from `declare_trust_anchor` is a full governed object: `object_id` (`trust_anchor:nodeA`), the `payload` (the key or commitment), and `version_hash`. The provenance travels with it -- who authored it, from what source, when. This is why the anchor is inheritable without a custodian: a successor does not need someone to hand them a secret; they need the governed object and a ceremony that verifies it. The record *is* the inheritance. A custodian's copy is inheritable only through the custodian; a governed object is inheritable through the registry every node already runs. **What `declare_trust_anchor` is not: it is not a key generator, not a secret store, and not a custodian's copy of the node's keys -- the anchor's payload is whatever the node authors (a public key reference, an identity commitment), and the node's private key material never enters this module.** The boundary matters. This function does not generate keys -- the node's own key runtime does that, and that runtime is OUT of this volume (Ch 6). It does not store secrets -- the anchor is a governed reference, and the registry holds governed objects, not vaults of private keys. It does not keep a custodian's copy -- there is no second holder anywhere in the module. The anchor is a public-facing, provenance-carrying commitment the node puts on the record. Everything a custodian would hold stays with the node. **In the acceptance test, node A declares its trust anchor and gets back a governed object with a real `version_hash` and `object_id` `trust_anchor:nodeA` -- and declaring an anchor for no node, or an empty anchor, raises `TrustError` -- so the guarantee is executable, not asserted.** `test_declare_trust_anchor_registers_a_governed_object` declares `{"key": "ecdsa-pub-A"}` under node A's mandate and asserts the returned object has a `version_hash`, the `object_id` `trust_anchor:nodeA`, and the payload key intact. `test_declare_trust_anchor_refuses_empty` confirms both empty guards raise `TrustError`. The receipt is the test: the anchor is a real governed object with provenance, and the empty cases are refused, both demonstrated by running code rather than described in prose. **For the Ridgeline family office, `declare_trust_anchor` is the moment their node's identity stops being a secret their steward holds and becomes a governed object the family owns -- the precondition for handing it to the next generation without a custodian.** Ridgeline's node is recognized by its peers through its trust anchor. Before this, that anchor lived as a secret the current steward held -- inheritable only if the steward, or a custodian, handed it over. `declare_trust_anchor` puts the anchor on the record as a governed object under the family's mandate, carrying its provenance and integrity. Now the anchor is a family asset, not a steward's secret. The handoff ceremony that inherits it -- built in Ch 3 -- has a governed object to verify and pass on, and no custodian to route it through.

title: Vol 05 Inter Node Trust Boundaries Handoff
chapter_title: Handoff as a Receipted, Human-Gated Ceremony — hand_off_trust
text: You will see how a node hands its trust anchors to a successor as a fail-closed ceremony -- the successor package must verify over its own bytes and a named human must approve -- so identity is inherited with no custodian, no escrow, and no central recovery authority.

title: Vol 05 Inter Node Trust Boundaries Handoff
chapter_title: Handoff as a Receipted, Human-Gated Ceremony — hand_off_trust
text: **Handing a node's trust anchors to a successor must be a ceremony the node performs over its own governed objects, gated by a named human -- not a recovery a custodian executes from a copy of the keys -- and `hand_off_trust` is that ceremony.** Once the anchor is a governed object (Ch 2), inheriting it does not require a custodian; it requires a ceremony that assembles what the node owns and completes only under a human's assent. `hand_off_trust(reg, *, at, approver, approval_ref)` is that ceremony. It gathers the node's governed objects into a successor package and governs the handoff fail-closed. Nowhere does it call a custodian, release an escrow, or invoke a central recovery authority. The successor inherits by ceremony, and the node conducts the ceremony itself. **`hand_off_trust` composes the sealed generational-continuity floor -- it assembles the successor package over the node's governed objects with `assemble_successor_package` and governs the handoff with `govern_handoff` -- so the handoff is the same generational-continuity discipline Vol 29 of Series 5 sealed, applied to trust anchors.** The function builds nothing new for the mechanics of inheritance. It calls `assemble_successor_package(reg, at=at)` to gather the node's governed objects into a package carrying its own integrity, then `govern_handoff(package, approver=approver, approval_ref=approval_ref)` to gate the transfer. Trust handoff is generational handoff: the same sealed floor that hands a node's ledgers and constitutions to a successor hands its trust anchors. This volume does not reinvent succession; it points succession at the trust anchor. **The ceremony is deny-by-default: an empty approver or an empty approval reference is refused before anything is handed off -- `hand_off_trust` raises `TrustError` if `approver` is blank or `approval_ref` is empty -- so no handoff proceeds without a named human naming the ceremony.** The guards come first, before assembly completes into a transfer. `if not str(approver).strip(): raise TrustError(...)` and `if not str(approval_ref).strip(): raise TrustError(...)`. A handoff of a node's identity is the highest-materiality act in its life -- it changes who is recognized as the node. So it fails closed: no named human, no handoff; no reference naming the ceremony (a succession deed, a board minute), no handoff. The default is refusal, and only a named human's deliberate, referenced assent moves it off that default. **The handoff completes only when two conditions hold together -- the successor package verifies over its own bytes AND a named human approves -- so the successor inherits an intact identity by a deliberate human act, not by a trigger firing or a custodian releasing.** `govern_handoff` is fail-closed on both axes. First, the package must verify: its integrity is checked against its own bytes, so a tampered or partial package is refused -- the successor inherits exactly what the node owned, or nothing. Second, a named human must approve: the transfer is a person's decision, not an automatic event. Both must hold. This is the whole difference from escrow: an escrow releases on a trigger, mechanically; this ceremony completes on a verified package plus a human's assent. Identity passes by human decision over verified bytes. **There is no second recovery authority, no standing escrow, and no central trust service anywhere in `hand_off_trust` -- the successor package is assembled from the node's own governed objects and the approval is a named human's -- so the kill-target holds: nothing but the node and its named successor ever holds the identity.** The kill-target for this volume is explicit: no recovery authority, no escrow, no central trust service. The function honors it structurally. The package comes from `reg` -- the node's own registry. The approval comes from a named human at the ceremony. No third party holds a copy, releases a secret, or resets an identity. The only parties to the handoff are the node (whose objects are assembled) and the human who approves the succession. A grep of this module for a custodian, an escrow, or a central authority returns nothing, because the design admits none. **In the acceptance test, a node declares its anchor and then hands off trust with a named steward and a succession deed -- the handoff completes with `handed_off` true, the named approver recorded, and a package root -- while an unnamed approver or empty reference raises `TrustError`.** `test_hand_off_trust_receipts_a_named_ceremony` declares node A's anchor, then calls `hand_off_trust(reg, at=..., approver="steward", approval_ref="succession deed #5")` and asserts `handed_off` is true, the approver is recorded, and a `package_root` is returned -- the receipt of a completed ceremony. `test_hand_off_trust_refuses_unnamed_approver_or_ref` confirms a whitespace approver and an empty reference both raise `TrustError`. The ceremony's two conditions are executable: verified package plus named human, or no handoff. **For the Ridgeline family office, `hand_off_trust` is the succession itself -- the retiring steward and the successor perform a receipted ceremony over the family node's governed anchor, and the node's identity passes intact with no custodian ever in the room.** When Ridgeline passes its node to the next generation, the handoff is a deliberate family act: the successor package is assembled from the family node's own governed objects, a named steward approves against a succession deed, and the package verifies over its own bytes. The node's identity passes to the successor generation intact. No custodian held the keys to hand over; no escrow released on a date; no central authority reset the identity. The family performed the ceremony, and the ceremony -- verified and human-gated -- is the whole of the inheritance.

title: Vol 05 Inter Node Trust Boundaries Handoff
chapter_title: The Anchor as a Governed Object — Composing the Sovereign Object Model (S5 Vol 5)
text: You will see that the trust anchor's governance is not new machinery -- it is the sealed Sovereign Object Model (S5 Vol 5), and the anchor is just another provenance-carrying governed object, which is why it is inheritable.

title: Vol 05 Inter Node Trust Boundaries Handoff
chapter_title: The Anchor as a Governed Object — Composing the Sovereign Object Model (S5 Vol 5)
text: **The governance that makes a trust anchor an owned, provenance-carrying object is not machinery this volume invented -- it is the sealed Sovereign Object Model of Vol 5 of Series 5, and the trust anchor is simply another governed object registered in it.** It would be easy to read Ch 2 as introducing a trust-specific store. It does not. `declare_trust_anchor` registers the anchor through the same `ObjectRegistry` that governs every sovereign object -- ledgers, constitutions, contributions, capacity offers. The anchor is not special-cased; it is a governed object like any other, distinguished only by its `object_id` prefix `trust_anchor:`. The trust boundary rides on a sealed floor, which is why it inherits that floor's guarantees without restating them. **When `declare_trust_anchor` calls `reg.append(..., kind="ratify")`, it is invoking the object model's constitutive registration -- the same append that puts any governed object on the record with its author, source, mandate, and time -- so the anchor carries the identical provenance every sovereign object carries.** The object model defines one way to bring a governed object into being: `append`, with its provenance fields and its `kind`. The trust anchor uses it unchanged. The `kind="ratify"` says this is a constitutive act -- the node ratifying its identity commitment -- and the object model records it exactly as it records a ratified constitution or a ratified ledger head. There is no trust-specific registration path. The anchor's provenance is the object model's provenance, which means anyone who can verify a governed object can verify a trust anchor. **The `version_hash` the registry returns is the object model's integrity guarantee -- a hash over the anchor's own bytes -- and it is precisely what the handoff ceremony later verifies, so Ch 3's fail-closed verification is the object model's integrity, reused.** When Ch 3 said the successor package must verify over its own bytes, it was leaning on this: every governed object carries a `version_hash` computed by the sealed object model, and verification means recomputing that hash and comparing. The trust anchor inherits this for free. Its integrity is not a trust-specific checksum; it is the object model's content hash. So the whole verify-before-handoff guarantee is not new code in this volume -- it is the object model's integrity, pointed at the trust anchor and the successor package. **Reusing the sealed object model is the reason the anchor is inheritable at all -- a governed object can be assembled into a successor package and verified by a successor, whereas a trust-specific secret store would have needed its own inheritance path and its own integrity, and would have been a second thing to trust.** Had this volume built a bespoke trust store, inheritance would have required bespoke machinery to package, transfer, and verify its contents -- and that machinery would itself have been an unsealed authority. By making the anchor a governed object, inheritance is already solved: `assemble_successor_package` (Ch 5) gathers governed objects, and verification is the object model's hash. The anchor rides the same succession road every governed object rides. Composition is not just tidiness here; it is what removes the need for a custodian, because the sealed floor already knows how to hand a governed object to a successor. **The boundary of this chapter is strict: it composes the sealed object model, it does not re-implement it -- there is no new registry, no new provenance format, and no new integrity scheme in this volume, only the trust anchor registered in the sealed one.** What this volume adds is two functions and an invariant. What it does not add is a single line of object-model machinery. The registry, the append, the provenance fields, the version hash -- all sealed in Vol 5 of Series 5, all reused. This is the discipline that keeps the trust boundary honest: it cannot smuggle in an unsealed store under the name of trust, because it composes the audited floor. If the object model is sound, the anchor's governance is sound, with nothing new to re-audit. **For the Ridgeline family office, this is the assurance that their node's trust anchor is governed exactly as their ledgers and constitutions are -- one object model, one provenance discipline, one integrity guarantee -- so the anchor is auditable and inheritable by the same rules they already trust.** Ridgeline already relies on the sealed object model for their financial ledgers and their constitution. The trust anchor now sits in that same model. When they audit their node, the anchor audits the same way everything else does; when they hand the node to the next generation, the anchor packages and verifies the same way everything else does. There is no separate trust subsystem for the family to understand or trust. The anchor's inheritability is the object model's inheritability, which they have already proven to themselves.

chapter_title: The Generational Handoff — Composing Generational Continuity (S5 Vol 29)
text: You will see that trust handoff is generational handoff -- the successor package and the fail-closed human gate are the sealed Generational Continuity floor (S5 Vol 29), pointed at the node's trust anchors.

title: Vol 05 Inter Node Trust Boundaries Handoff
chapter_title: The Generational Handoff — Composing Generational Continuity (S5 Vol 29)
text: **Handing a node's trust anchors to a successor is not a new kind of transfer -- it is generational handoff, the same succession Vol 29 of Series 5 sealed, applied to the trust anchor -- so `hand_off_trust` composes the continuity floor rather than inventing a trust-specific one.** A federation already knows how to hand a node from one generation to the next: that is generational continuity. Trust handoff is that same act, focused on the node's identity. `hand_off_trust` therefore reaches for the sealed continuity floor's two moves -- assemble the successor package, govern the handoff -- and points them at the node's governed objects, including its trust anchor. The volume adds the trust-anchor focus and the invariant; the succession mechanism itself is already sealed. **`assemble_successor_package(reg, at=at)` is the continuity floor's packaging step -- it gathers the node's governed objects into a single package carrying its own integrity, so the successor receives a verifiable whole rather than a loose handful of secrets.** The first move of the ceremony is to assemble. The sealed continuity floor's `assemble_successor_package` walks the node's registry and gathers its governed objects into a package with its own root hash. Applied here, the package includes the trust anchor declared in Ch 2 alongside the node's other governed state. The successor does not receive scattered secrets to reassemble; they receive one package with one integrity root. That root is what the next step verifies, and it is what Ch 3's `package_root` receipt records. The packaging is the continuity floor's, reused unchanged. **`govern_handoff(package, approver=..., approval_ref=...)` is the continuity floor's fail-closed gate -- it verifies the package over its own bytes and requires a named human -- so the two conditions of Ch 3's ceremony are the sealed continuity gate, not new guards written for trust.** The second move is to govern. The sealed continuity floor's `govern_handoff` verifies the assembled package's integrity and refuses unless a named human approves against a reference. Ch 3 described these as the ceremony's two conditions; here we name their home: they are `govern_handoff`, sealed in Vol 29 of Series 5. Trust handoff did not write a new verification or a new human gate. It composed the succession gate the continuity floor already sealed, so the same discipline that governs handing a node's ledgers to a successor governs handing its trust anchors. **Reusing the continuity floor is exactly why this volume needs no escrow and no recovery engine -- succession is already solved for governed objects, so the trust anchor inherits by the same path, and the kill-target holds without any new custodial machinery.** The kill-target forbids a recovery authority, an escrow, and a central trust service. Composing the continuity floor is how the volume honors it without building anything that could become one. The floor hands governed objects to successors by assemble-then-govern, with no third party holding anything -- the package comes from the node's own registry and the gate is a named human. Point that at the trust anchor and you have inheritable identity with no custodian, because the succession machinery never needed one. The absence of an escrow is not a restraint bolted on; it is a property of the floor being composed. **The boundary of this chapter is strict: it composes the sealed continuity floor, it invents no succession engine -- there is no new packaging format, no new handoff gate, and no recovery mechanism in this volume, only the trust anchor routed through the sealed `assemble_successor_package` + `govern_handoff`.** This volume writes two functions and an invariant. The succession mechanics -- how objects are packaged, how a package is verified, how a human gate is enforced -- are all Vol 29 of Series 5, composed. If the continuity floor is sound, trust handoff is sound, with no new succession code to re-audit. This is the discipline that keeps the volume from smuggling in an unsealed recovery engine: it cannot, because it delegates every mechanical step to the audited floor and adds only the focus on the trust anchor. **For the Ridgeline family office, this means the succession of their node's identity works exactly like the succession of the node itself -- one continuity discipline they have already lived through -- so passing the trust anchor to the next generation is not a separate, riskier procedure but the same governed handoff.** Ridgeline has a generational-continuity plan for their node: how it passes to the next generation, packaged and human-gated. The trust anchor now rides that same plan. When they perform the succession, the anchor is assembled into the successor package with the rest of the node's governed state and passes under the same named-human gate. There is no separate trust-handoff procedure to design, staff, or trust -- and no custodian to insert. The family's existing continuity discipline carries the identity, which is why the handoff is safe by construction rather than by a new safeguard.

chapter_title: Recovery Constitution, Delivery & Rotation — Naming the Homes This Volume Does Not Build
text: You will see exactly where the recovery constitution, the delivery of a handoff package, and automated key rotation live -- each at a real sealed or named home -- so nothing this volume leaves out floats without an address.

title: Vol 05 Inter Node Trust Boundaries Handoff
chapter_title: Recovery Constitution, Delivery & Rotation — Naming the Homes This Volume Does Not Build
text: **The rules a federation follows when a node's steward is lost -- who may propose a successor, what quorum admits them -- are a recovery constitution, and its home is a governed object of the sealed Constitutions floor (Vol 30 of Series 5), not a new engine in this volume.** A reader might ask where the *policy* of recovery lives: the standing rules for succession when no orderly handoff happened. Those rules are a constitution -- a governed document of articles -- and the sealed Constitutions floor already governs constitutions. A federation writes its recovery rules as articles in a governed constitution object; this volume's `hand_off_trust` executes a handoff under a named human, and the recovery constitution is what names who that human may be and under what quorum. The policy is a governed object at Vol 30 of Series 5; this volume does not build a recovery-policy engine. **Delivering an assembled handoff package to the successor node -- getting the bytes from here to there -- is Receipted Inter-Node Messaging (S6 Vol 1), not a transfer mechanism this volume invents.** `hand_off_trust` assembles a successor package and gates its handoff, but it does not carry the package across the wire. Carriage is delivery, and delivery between nodes has a sealed home: Receipted Inter-Node Messaging (S6 Vol 1), where a message is authored, carried to a peer, and received with its provenance intact. When a handoff package must travel to a successor node on a different machine, it travels as a receipted inter-node message. This volume produces the package and gates the ceremony; the co-wave-independent Messaging volume delivers it. No delivery code lives here. **Automated key rotation orchestration -- rotating a node's keys on a schedule, revoking and re-issuing without a human in the loop each time -- is OUT of this volume: it is designed-toward, homed on the sovereign node's own key runtime -- a Series 6 node capability -- because it needs live key material this proof-first floor does not touch.** The honest boundary. This volume declares a trust anchor and hands it off by ceremony, all over governed objects and pure hashes. It does not rotate keys automatically -- automated rotation needs the node's live private key material and a runtime that touches it, and this floor touches no private keys. So rotation orchestration is homed on the sovereign node's own key runtime, a Series 6 node capability. What is PRESENT is declaring an anchor and handing it off under a human gate; what is OUT here is automating the rotation of that anchor's keys. Naming rotation as OUT, with its home, is the volume refusing to pretend it rotates keys today. **Transport, the surfaces, and the connectors each have their own homes too -- transport is the Port (S6 Vol 7), the human surfaces are six-sov.com and seeit, and connectors are the sovereign port (Series 6) -- so no capability this volume gestures at is left without an address.** Beyond recovery policy, delivery, and rotation, the volume touches the edges of several other capabilities, and each has a home. The transport underneath inter-node delivery is the Port (S6 Vol 7). The places a human watches a handoff or a recovery are the surfaces six-sov.com and seeit. The adapters to a node's existing key infrastructure are connectors at the sovereign port of Series 6. None of these is built here; each is named at its real home. The volume's job is the two PRESENT functions and the invariant, and everything adjacent is pointed at an address rather than implied to be present. **Naming every home precisely is what makes the kill-target credible rather than merely declared -- a volume that said "no escrow" while quietly leaving recovery policy, delivery, and rotation homeless would have smuggled the custodian back in under a vague gesture.** The kill-target -- no recovery authority, no escrow, no central trust service -- is only as honest as the volume's willingness to say where the omitted work lives. If recovery policy floated, a reader could imagine this volume secretly deciding succession; it does not -- policy is a governed constitution (Vol 30 of Series 5). If delivery floated, a reader could imagine a custodial transfer service; there is none -- delivery is receipted messaging (S6 Vol 1). If rotation floated, a reader could imagine an automatic key authority; there is none -- rotation is homed on the node's own key runtime, a Series 6 node capability. Every home named is a place the custodian is *not*. The credibility of the boundary is the precision of the addresses. **For the Ridgeline family office, this chapter is the map of what their node's own systems and other volumes provide around the handoff -- the recovery rules they write as a constitution, the messaging that delivers the package, the key runtime that rotates their keys -- so they know the handoff ceremony is one governed act in a federation where every neighboring capability has a known, sealed or named home.** Ridgeline does not get a monolithic trust product from this volume; they get a precise ceremony and a map. Their recovery rules are articles they ratify in a governed constitution (Vol 30 of Series 5). The delivery of a succession package to a successor node is receipted messaging (S6 Vol 1). The automated rotation of their node's keys is their node's own key runtime, a Series 6 node capability. The transport is the Port (S6 Vol 7); the place they watch is seeit. The family can see the whole neighborhood of the handoff and confirm that nowhere in it is a custodian holding their keys -- because every home is named, and none of them is an escrow.

title: Vol 05 Inter Node Trust Boundaries Handoff
chapter_title: Trust the Federation Owns — Synthesis and the LGP Stakes
text: You will see the whole volume resolve to one invariant -- a node's trust anchor is its own governed object, handed off only by a receipted, human-gated ceremony over a verifying package -- and why that invariant is what lets a federation keep its nodes across generations without ever surrendering their keys.

title: Vol 05 Inter Node Trust Boundaries Handoff
chapter_title: Trust the Federation Owns — Synthesis and the LGP Stakes
text: **The whole of this volume resolves to a single invariant: a node's trust anchor is its own governed object, handed off to a successor only by a receipted, human-gated ceremony over a verifying package -- never by a custodian's recovery or an escrow's release.** Everything built here serves that one sentence. The anchor is a governed object (Ch 2), so it is owned and inheritable. The handoff is a ceremony (Ch 3), fail-closed on a verified package and a named human. The governance is the sealed object model (Ch 4); the succession is the sealed continuity floor (Ch 5); the recovery policy, delivery, and rotation are named at their homes (Ch 6). The invariant is the volume's whole claim, and every chapter is a face of it: trust the node owns, inherited by ceremony. **The two PRESENT functions are small and their power is borrowed honestly: `declare_trust_anchor` composes the sealed object model to make the anchor a governed object, and `hand_off_trust` composes the sealed continuity floor to inherit it under a named human's gate.** `declare_trust_anchor` is a registration -- `reg.append(kind="ratify")` -- and nothing more; its strength is that it makes the anchor a first-class governed object of the sealed Sovereign Object Model (S5 Vol 5). `hand_off_trust` is an assembly plus a gate -- `assemble_successor_package` then `govern_handoff` -- and nothing more; its strength is that it makes trust handoff a case of the sealed Generational Continuity floor (S5 Vol 29). Two functions, two sealed floors composed, one invariant enforced. The volume is honest about how little it invents and precise about what that little guarantees. **The kill-target held at every step: there is no second recovery authority, no standing escrow, and no central trust service anywhere in this volume -- the anchor comes from the node's own registry and the handoff is a named human's ceremony, so nothing but the node and its named successor ever holds the identity.** KM set the kill-target at the wave's arming: no recovery authority, no escrow, no central trust service. The volume honors it structurally, not by promise. There is no custodian to grep for, no escrow trigger to fire, no central directory to reset an identity. The successor package is assembled from the node's own governed objects; the approval is a named human's, against a reference. The recovery policy is a governed constitution the federation owns (Ch 6), not a service that holds keys. The custodian has no place to hide in this design because every capability adjacent to the handoff is named at a home that is not an escrow. **This is why owned, inheritable trust is a generational asset and not merely a security feature: a federation whose nodes hand off their trust anchors by receipted ceremony keeps its nodes and its keys across every generational turn, while one that relies on escrow inherits, each generation, a key-holder it cannot escape.** The stakes named in Ch 1 come home here. A node's identity is the continuity of a family's or an organization's place in the federation. Whether that continuity is owned turns entirely on this invariant. Hand off by ceremony over a governed object, and the identity passes to successors intact with no custodian in the chain -- generation after generation, the keys stay with the node. Rely on escrow, and every generation inherits the same second holder, the same point of capture, the same sovereignty sold for recoverability. The invariant is what makes a node's identity a generational asset the federation actually owns. **What comes next is transport -- delivering these handoff packages across nodes rests on the Port (S6 Vol 7), the must-solo volume this wave arms toward -- and the recovery policy that gates a handoff is written as a governed constitution, the discipline the sealed Constitutions floor (S5 Vol 30) already provides.** This volume produces a verified, human-gated handoff package; carrying it to a successor node rests on transport, and transport's home is the Port (S6 Vol 7), which the wave arms toward next. The rules that decide who may approve a succession are a governed constitution, written with the sealed Constitutions discipline (S5 Vol 30). The trust boundary is complete as a proof-first floor: the anchor is governed, the handoff is a ceremony, and the neighboring capabilities have their homes. What remains is to carry the packages and to write the policies -- both at addresses this volume named and neither a custodian. **For the Ridgeline family office, the volume ends where it began -- their node's identity passing to the next generation -- but now as a receipted ceremony the family performs over an object they own, with no custodian ever in the room, which is what it means for a family's place in the federation to be truly inheritable.** Ridgeline set out to hand their node to the next generation without surrendering its keys. This volume gave them the way: their trust anchor is a governed object they own (Ch 2), and its handoff is a succession ceremony they perform under a named steward's assent over a verifying package (Ch 3), riding the sealed object model and continuity floor (Ch 4, Ch 5), with recovery policy, delivery, and rotation each at a known home (Ch 6). The family's place in the federation passes to the next generation intact, and no custodian ever held the keys. That is trust the federation owns -- and it is the whole of what this volume was for.

title: Vol 06 Sovereign Federation Onboarding
chapter_title: The Node Onboarding Opportunity — Joining a Federation Without a Central Admission Authority
text: You will see why a federation of sovereign nodes must let a new node join by adopting the shared constitution and passing a named human's assent -- not by a central service enrolling it -- and why that is what keeps growth from re-centralizing the federation.

title: Vol 06 Sovereign Federation Onboarding
chapter_title: The Node Onboarding Opportunity — Joining a Federation Without a Central Admission Authority
text: **A federation meant to last across generations must be able to grow -- to admit new nodes as families and organizations join -- because a federation that cannot admit a node is a closed set that shrinks with every departure and never renews.** Growth is not optional for a durable federation. Families form new nodes; organizations spin up new members; the federation that cannot take them in ages into a closed club and dwindles. So onboarding -- the act by which a new node becomes part of the federation -- is a first-class capability. The question is how a node joins, and the answer decides whether the federation stays a federation of sovereigns or quietly becomes a directory a central service controls. **The tension is between growth and sovereignty -- a federation must admit new nodes, but if admission runs through a central authority that enrolls them, that authority becomes the gatekeeper of membership, and a federation with a membership gatekeeper is no longer a federation of sovereigns -- and resolving that tension is the design problem.** Growth without sovereignty is the central directory: one service decides who is in and who is out, and its list *is* the federation. Sovereignty without growth is the closed set: no one may join, so no one central controls membership, but the federation cannot renew. The sovereign answer resolves the tension by making joining an act the node performs -- adopting the federation's constitution as its own governed object -- admitted by a named human's assent, so the federation grows without a gatekeeper who owns the membership list. **Legacy onboarding runs through a central admission authority that enrolls the node -- a directory service adds it, an identity provider issues its membership, an administrator flips it on -- and whoever controls the enrollment controls who belongs.** The familiar answer to "how does a node join" is to have a central service enroll it: a membership directory, an identity provider, an admin console. Each solves growth by making one authority the keeper of the list -- and the keeper of the list is the keeper of membership, who can admit, deny, or remove at will. Growth bought this way is sovereignty sold: the federation's composition is whatever the central authority's list says, and the nodes are entries in someone else's registry rather than sovereigns who chose to join. **This is the weakness of the central admission authority, and naming it precisely folds the old comparison into the opening -- the directory makes joining easy, but by owning the membership list, so the federation belongs to whoever owns the directory.** Traditional onboarding is built for convenience -- one place to add a node -- and solves it by a central list. Its weakness is not that it fails to admit; it admits reliably. Its weakness is that admission runs through an owner of the list, so the federation is only as sovereign as that owner, and the list is a single point of control the nodes cannot escape. The sovereign advantage is structural: the joining node adopts the constitution as its own governed object, and admission is a named human's assent -- so the federation grows by consent, with no central owner of who belongs. **The sovereign opportunity is not a better directory -- it is onboarding by the node's own governed adoption of the constitution plus a named human's assent, so a federation grows with no central admission authority, no automatic enrolment, and no membership registry a central service owns.** The design commitment of this volume is joining-by-consent with no gatekeeper: the node proposes to join by ratifying the federation's articles as its own governed constitution-adoption, and it is admitted only when a named human deliberately assents. What is genuinely new is this adopt-and-assent discipline. What is deliberately absent is the central directory, the automatic enrolment, and the membership registry that the legacy model makes the unavoidable owner of who belongs. **The stakes are the whole of Lasting Generational Prosperity, because a federation that grows by consent stays a federation of sovereigns as it scales, while one that grows through a central directory re-centralizes itself with every node it admits.** Growth is where a decentralized system is most tempted to centralize -- a single onboarding service is so convenient that federations adopt one and, without noticing, hand it their membership. Whether the federation stays sovereign as it grows depends on whether joining runs through a gatekeeper. A federation whose nodes join by adopting the constitution under a human's assent keeps its sovereignty as it grows: each new node is a sovereign who chose in, on the record, with no central owner of the list. A federation that grows through a directory has rebuilt the center it left. The sovereign discipline is what lets a federation grow without re-centralizing, which is the precondition for growth that serves Lasting Generational Prosperity rather than a gatekeeper. **For the Ridgeline federation -- admitting a new family-office node -- the difference is whether the new node joins by adopting the federation's constitution under a named steward's assent, or is enrolled by a central directory that from then on owns the membership list.** When Ridgeline admits a new family-office node, the legacy path enrolls it in a central directory that owns membership from that moment on. This volume gives them another path: the joining node adopts the federation's articles as its own governed constitution-adoption, and a named steward assents to its admission -- with no central directory owning who belongs. The chapters that follow build that capability -- the adoption as a governed object (Ch 2), the human admission gate (Ch 3), the constitution it composes (Ch 4), the compliance gate it composes (Ch 5), the identity and revocation it homes elsewhere (Ch 6), and the federation that grows by consent (Ch 7) -- and none of it puts a central gatekeeper over membership.

title: Vol 06 Sovereign Federation Onboarding
chapter_title: The Adoption as a Governed Object — propose_onboarding
text: You will see how a joining node opens its adoption of the federation's constitution as a governed, provenance-carrying object it authors, so its commitment to the shared rules is on the record rather than a verbal agreement a central service records for it.

title: Vol 06 Sovereign Federation Onboarding
chapter_title: The Adoption as a Governed Object — propose_onboarding
text: **A node joins the federation by an act it performs itself -- adopting the shared constitution as a governed object it authors -- not by a central service enrolling it, and `propose_onboarding` is that act.** The first move in joining-by-consent is to make the joining the node's own governed act. In the directory model, joining is something done *to* the node: a service adds it. Here, joining begins with something the node *does*: it ratifies the federation's articles as its own governed constitution-adoption, under its own mandate, carrying its own provenance. `propose_onboarding(reg, node_id, articles, *, mandate, author, source_ref, at)` performs exactly that. The node's proposal to join is a governed object it authored -- which is what makes its later admission a consent it gave rather than an enrollment it received. **`propose_onboarding` composes the sealed constitution templates -- it calls `open_constitution` (itself over the sealed object registry) to open the node's adoption of the federation's articles as a governed object under the node's own mandate -- so the adoption is created by the same governed-constitution machinery every sovereign constitution uses.** The function builds no new store. It composes the sealed Constitutions floor: `open_constitution(reg, f"onboarding:{node_id}", dict(articles), mandate=mandate, author=author, source_ref=source_ref, at=at)`. The articles the node adopts become a governed constitution object, `object_id` `constitution:onboarding:<node_id>`, carrying the node's authorship and a `version_hash`. Adopting the federation's rules is the same act as ratifying any constitution -- Vol 30 of Series 5 sealed that -- pointed at a joining node. The adoption is governed the moment it is proposed, by machinery already audited. **An empty node id or empty articles is refused -- `propose_onboarding` raises `OnboardingError` before it opens anything -- because a proposal to join must name the node that is joining and must adopt actual articles; a proposal from no one, or a proposal that adopts nothing, is not a proposal to join.** The guards come first. `if not node_id: raise OnboardingError(...)` and `if not articles: raise OnboardingError(...)`. A proposal to join is a binding between a node and the federation's rules: strip either side and there is nothing to admit. Refusing the empty case keeps the record honest -- every `constitution:onboarding:` object names a real joining node and carries the real articles it adopted, so when a human later assents, there is a definite commitment to assent to. The refusal is what makes the proposal a commitment rather than a placeholder. **The opened adoption carries its author, its source reference, and its integrity hash -- the node's commitment to the federation's rules is on the record with its provenance, not a verbal agreement a central service noted on the node's behalf.** What the node gets back from `propose_onboarding` is a full governed object: the `object_id` `constitution:onboarding:<node_id>`, the adopted articles, and a `version_hash`. The provenance travels with it -- who authored the adoption, from what source, when. This is what makes admission a consent rather than an enrollment: the human who later assents is assenting to a governed object the node itself authored and signed with its provenance, not adding a name to a list. The record *is* the commitment. A central directory's entry is a note someone made about the node; this adoption is the node's own governed act. **What `propose_onboarding` is not: it is not a central directory add, not an enrollment, and not a membership list -- it opens one governed object, the joining node's own constitution-adoption, and touches no central registry of who belongs.** The boundary matters. This function does not add the node to a directory -- there is no directory here. It does not enroll the node -- enrollment is a central service's act, and this is the node's own act. It does not maintain a membership list -- the federation's membership is the set of admitted governed adoptions, not a list a service owns. `propose_onboarding` produces exactly one thing: the joining node's governed adoption of the constitution. Everything a central directory would own stays absent by design. **In the acceptance test, node B proposes to join and gets back a governed constitution-adoption with a real `version_hash` and `object_id` `constitution:onboarding:nodeB` -- and proposing with no node id, or with empty articles, raises `OnboardingError` -- so the guarantee is executable, not asserted.** `test_propose_onboarding_opens_a_governed_constitution_adoption` proposes node B's adoption of two articles and asserts the returned object has a `version_hash` and the `object_id` `constitution:onboarding:nodeB`. `test_propose_onboarding_refuses_empty` confirms both empty guards raise `OnboardingError`. The receipt is the test: the adoption is a real governed object with provenance, and the empty cases are refused, both demonstrated by running code. **For the Ridgeline family office, `propose_onboarding` is the moment a new family-office node's decision to join stops being a verbal agreement and becomes a governed object it authored -- the precondition for a named steward admitting it by consent rather than a directory enrolling it.** When a new Ridgeline node decides to join the federation, the legacy path would enroll it in a directory. `propose_onboarding` instead puts the node's adoption of the federation's constitution on the record as a governed object the node itself authored, carrying its provenance and integrity. Now joining is a commitment the node made, not an entry a service created. The admission that follows -- built in Ch 3 -- has a governed adoption to assent to, and no directory to add the node to.

title: Vol 06 Sovereign Federation Onboarding
chapter_title: Admission as a Deny-by-Default Human Gate — admit_node
text: You will see how a node is admitted only when its adoption is a real governed object, node onboarding is a human-gated class, and a named human assents -- fail-closed, in that order -- so the federation grows by consent with no central admission authority and no automatic enrolment.

title: Vol 06 Sovereign Federation Onboarding
chapter_title: Admission as a Deny-by-Default Human Gate — admit_node
text: **Admitting a node to the federation must be a named human's deliberate assent over the node's own governed adoption -- not a central service adding it automatically -- and `admit_node` is that gate.** Once the node's adoption is a governed object (Ch 2), admitting it does not require a directory; it requires a human's assent, gated fail-closed. `admit_node(proposal, *, approver, approval_ref, gate=None)` is that gate. It admits a node only when three conditions hold in order, and its default -- when any condition fails -- is refusal. Nowhere does it add the node to a central list, enroll it automatically, or let admission happen without a person deciding. The federation grows by consent, and the consent is a named human's, recorded against the node's own adoption. **`admit_node` is deny-by-default and fail-closed, checking three conditions in order -- a real governed adoption, a human-gated class, and a named human's approval -- so admission is impossible unless every condition is met and trivially refused if any is not.** The function's structure is deny-first. It does not admit and then check; it refuses unless each condition is satisfied. The order matters: first it verifies there is a real governed adoption to admit, then it confirms onboarding is a gated class, then it requires a named human. Each condition is a separate `raise OnboardingError` on failure. The default across all of them is no admission. This is the whole difference from an auto-enrolling directory: a directory admits unless told not to; `admit_node` refuses unless every gate is passed. **The first condition is that the proposal must be a real governed constitution adoption -- carrying a `version_hash` -- so an admission of nothing, or of an ungoverned proposal, is refused before anything else is checked.** `if not (proposal and proposal.get("version_hash")): raise OnboardingError(...)`. Admission must have something governed to admit. A missing proposal, an empty dict, or a proposal that never became a governed object (no `version_hash`) is refused at the door. This is what ties admission to consent: the human can only admit a node whose adoption is a real, integrity-carrying governed object the node authored. There is no admitting a node that never proposed -- no path by which a central service conjures a membership without the node's own governed act. **Then node onboarding must be a human-gated action class -- `admit_node` composes the sealed `HumanApprovalGate` and refuses unless onboarding requires approval -- AND a named human must approve, with an approver and a non-empty approval reference; a blank approver or empty reference is refused.** The second and third conditions are the human gate. `admit_node` builds a `HumanApprovalGate` and asks `requires_approval("node_onboarding", ...)`; if onboarding is somehow not a gated class, it refuses -- admitting a node is high-materiality and must be gated. Then it requires the human: `if not str(approver).strip(): raise OnboardingError(...)` and `if not str(approval_ref).strip(): raise OnboardingError(...)`. A node is admitted only by a named person, against a reference naming the admission (an admission minute, a board resolution). No named human, no admission; no reference, no admission. Consent is a person's recorded decision, not a flag. **There is no central admission authority and no automatic enrolment anywhere in `admit_node` -- the proposal is the node's own governed adoption and the approval is a named human's -- so the kill-target holds: nothing admits a node but a person assenting to the node's own act.** The kill-target for this volume is explicit: no central admission authority, no automatic enrolment, no membership registry a central service owns. The function honors it structurally. The thing admitted is the node's own governed adoption from `proposal`. The thing that admits is a named human's approval. There is no directory service, no auto-admit path, no membership list being appended. The only parties to an admission are the joining node (whose adoption is verified) and the human who assents. A grep of this module for a central enrolment service returns nothing, because the design admits none. **In the acceptance test, node B proposes and is admitted by a named federation steward against an admission minute -- returning `admitted` true and the adopted constitution's root -- while an admission of a nonexistent proposal, or with a blank approver or empty reference, raises `OnboardingError`.** `test_admit_node_with_named_human` proposes node B, then admits it with `approver="federation-steward"`, `approval_ref="admission minute #12"`, and asserts `admitted` is true, the `constitution_root` equals the adoption's `version_hash`, and the approver is recorded. `test_admit_node_refuses_nonexistent_proposal` confirms admitting `{}` raises. `test_admit_node_refuses_unnamed_approver_or_ref` confirms a whitespace approver and an empty reference both raise. The gate's three conditions are executable: real adoption, gated class, named human -- or no admission. **For the Ridgeline family office, `admit_node` is the admission itself -- a named steward assents to the new node's governed adoption against a recorded minute, and the node joins by consent, with no central directory ever owning the membership.** When Ridgeline admits a new family-office node, the admission is a deliberate act: the new node's governed adoption is verified, onboarding is confirmed a gated class, and a named steward assents against an admission minute. The node joins the federation, and the admission carries the adopted constitution's root as its receipt. No central directory enrolled the node; no automatic process admitted it; no membership list a service owns records it. The steward assented to the node's own act, and that assent -- verified and recorded -- is the whole of the admission.

title: Vol 06 Sovereign Federation Onboarding
chapter_title: The Adoption as a Governed Constitution — Composing Constitutions (S5 Vol 30) over the Object Model (S5 Vol 5)
text: You will see that a joining node's adoption is not new machinery -- it is the sealed Constitutions floor (S5 Vol 30), itself over the sealed Object Model (S5 Vol 5), and the adoption is just a governed constitution, which is why it is auditable and admittable.

title: Vol 06 Sovereign Federation Onboarding
chapter_title: The Adoption as a Governed Constitution — Composing Constitutions (S5 Vol 30) over the Object Model (S5 Vol 5)
text: **The governance that makes a joining node's adoption an owned, provenance-carrying object is not machinery this volume invented -- it is the sealed Constitutions floor of Vol 30 of Series 5, itself built over the sealed Object Model of Vol 5 of Series 5, and the adoption is simply a governed constitution.** It would be easy to read Ch 2 as introducing an onboarding-specific store. It does not. `propose_onboarding` opens the adoption through `open_constitution`, the same machinery that governs every sovereign constitution. The adoption is not special-cased; it is a governed constitution like any other, distinguished only by its `object_id` prefix `constitution:onboarding:`. The onboarding capability rides two sealed floors, which is why it inherits their guarantees without restating them. **When `propose_onboarding` calls `open_constitution`, it is invoking the Constitutions floor's governed-adoption machinery -- the same act that ratifies any set of articles into a governed constitution object -- so the joining node's adoption carries the identical structure every sovereign constitution carries.** The Constitutions floor defines one way to turn articles into a governed constitution: `open_constitution`, with its articles, its mandate, and its provenance. The adoption uses it unchanged. The joining node's articles become a governed constitution object, authored under the node's mandate, exactly as a family's own constitution would. There is no onboarding-specific adoption path. The adoption's structure is the Constitutions floor's structure, which means anyone who can audit a sovereign constitution can audit a node's adoption. **Constitutions themselves ride the sealed Object Model -- `open_constitution` registers the constitution as a governed object with a `version_hash` -- so the adoption's integrity is the Object Model's integrity, and that hash is exactly what Ch 3's `admit_node` verifies when it requires a real governed adoption.** The Constitutions floor does not invent its own storage; it composes the Object Model, registering each constitution as a governed object with a content hash. The adoption inherits this two floors deep: its `version_hash` is the Object Model's integrity, computed over the adoption's bytes. This is why Ch 3's first gate -- the proposal must carry a `version_hash` -- is not an onboarding-specific check; it is the Object Model's integrity, surfaced through the Constitutions floor. Admission verifies the adoption by the same hash every governed object carries. **Reusing the sealed floors is the reason the adoption is auditable and admittable at all -- a governed constitution can be inspected, verified, and assented to, whereas an onboarding-specific membership record would have needed its own audit path and its own integrity, and would have been a second thing to trust.** Had this volume built a bespoke membership store, admission would have required bespoke machinery to inspect and verify it -- and that machinery would itself have been an unsealed authority over who belongs. By making the adoption a governed constitution, admission is already solved: `admit_node` verifies the Object Model's `version_hash` and a human reads the governed articles. The adoption rides the same audit road every constitution rides. Composition is what removes the need for a central membership authority, because the sealed floors already know how to govern and verify a set of adopted articles. **The boundary of this chapter is strict: it composes the sealed Constitutions floor and the sealed Object Model, it re-implements neither -- there is no new constitution format, no new registry, and no new integrity scheme in this volume, only the joining node's adoption opened in the sealed ones.** What this volume adds is two functions and an invariant. What it does not add is a single line of constitution or object-model machinery. The `open_constitution` call, the governed-object registration, the provenance fields, the version hash -- all sealed in Vol 30 and Vol 5 of Series 5, all reused. This is the discipline that keeps onboarding honest: it cannot smuggle in an unsealed membership store under the name of onboarding, because it composes the audited floors. If those floors are sound, the adoption's governance is sound, with nothing new to re-audit. **For the Ridgeline family office, this is the assurance that a joining node's adoption is governed exactly as their own constitution is -- one constitution discipline, one object model, one integrity guarantee -- so the adoption is auditable and admittable by the same rules they already trust.** Ridgeline already relies on the sealed Constitutions floor for their own governing articles and on the sealed Object Model for their ledgers. A joining node's adoption now sits in those same floors. When they review an admission, the adoption reads the same way their own constitution does; when `admit_node` verifies it, it verifies the same hash everything else carries. There is no separate onboarding subsystem for the family to understand or trust. The adoption's admittability is the Constitutions floor's auditability, which they have already proven to themselves.

title: Vol 06 Sovereign Federation Onboarding
chapter_title: The Human Admission Gate — Composing Compliance & Audit (S5 Vol 16)
text: You will see that the admission gate is not a new approval mechanism -- it is the sealed HumanApprovalGate of Compliance & Audit (S5 Vol 16), pointed at node onboarding, so admitting a node is governed by the same deny-by-default human primacy that gates every high-materiality act.

title: Vol 06 Sovereign Federation Onboarding
chapter_title: The Human Admission Gate — Composing Compliance & Audit (S5 Vol 16)
text: **The gate that requires a named human to admit a node is not a new approval mechanism this volume built -- it is the sealed `HumanApprovalGate` of Compliance & Audit (Vol 16 of Series 5), pointed at node onboarding -- so admission is governed by the same human primacy that gates every high-materiality act in the system.** It would be easy to read Ch 3 as introducing an onboarding-specific approval check. It does not. `admit_node` composes `HumanApprovalGate` -- the same gate that requires a human before any high-materiality action. Admitting a node is not special-cased with a bespoke approval; it is a high-materiality action class gated by the sealed compliance floor. The human primacy of admission is the human primacy of the whole system, applied to onboarding. **`admit_node` calls the compliance floor's `requires_approval` -- the deny-by-default gate that returns whether an action class needs human approval -- so the requirement that a human assent to an admission is the compliance floor's requirement, not a guard written for onboarding.** The compliance floor defines one way to ask whether an action needs a human: `requires_approval(action_class, role_spec, mode)`, which returns true when the class is high-materiality and forbidden to automate. `admit_node` asks exactly that for `node_onboarding`, and refuses if the answer is not that approval is required. There is no onboarding-specific approval logic. The gate is the compliance floor's, reused, so the same deny-by-default discipline that gates a large disbursement or a governance change gates the admission of a node. **Node onboarding is declared a high-materiality action class -- admitting a node changes who belongs to the federation, which is as consequential as any governed act -- so `requires_approval` returns that approval is required, and `admit_node` refuses to proceed on its own.** Why is onboarding gated? Because admitting a node is high-materiality: it changes the composition of the federation, and a changed composition changes who may act, who may see, who may vote. An act with consequences that large must not happen without a human.
