chapter_title: Trust Earned Per Request, Not Vouched — Synthesis and the LGP Stakes
text: You will see the volume resolve to one invariant -- a node grants access only by verifying the requester's own evidence and its own declared rule for exactly this resource, every request -- and why trust earned per request rather than vouched is the foundation the rest of Zero-Trust Sovereignty is built on.

title: Vol 01 Zero Trust Node Architecture
chapter_title: Trust Earned Per Request, Not Vouched — Synthesis and the LGP Stakes
text: **The whole of this volume resolves to a single invariant: a node grants access only by verifying the requester's own presented evidence and its own declared rule for exactly this resource, re-checked every request -- never a central attestation, a standing grant, or a hub's vouching.** Everything built here serves that one sentence. The evidence is the node's own governed object (Ch 2), so what is verified is the node's own record. The decision is deny-by-default per request (Ch 3), so there is no standing trust. The identity is the sealed anchor (Ch 4); the authorization is the sealed declared-rule and human gates (Ch 5); onboarding, transport, monitoring, and shields are named at their homes (Ch 6). The invariant is the volume's whole claim, and every chapter is a face of it: never trust, always verify. **The two PRESENT functions are small and their power is borrowed honestly: `present_evidence` composes the sealed object model to make evidence the node's own governed object, and `verify_access` composes the sealed federation-governance check to decide deny-by-default from that evidence and a declared rule -- every request.** `present_evidence` is a registration -- `reg.append(kind="ratify")` -- making evidence a first-class governed object of the sealed Sovereign Object Model (S5 Vol 5). `verify_access` is a two-condition deny-by-default gate -- real evidence, then a node-declared rule (`authorize_crossing`, S5 Vol 28) -- with no standing trust. Two functions, sealed floors composed, one invariant enforced. The volume is honest about how little it invents and precise about what that little guarantees: verification, never vouching. **The kill-target held at every step: there is no second trust authority, no central attestation service, and no hub that vouches anywhere in this volume -- the evidence is the requester's own governed object, the authorization is the node's own declared rule, and both are re-verified each request.** KM set the kill-target at the arm: no second trust authority, no central attestation, no vouching hub. The volume honors each structurally, not by promise. There is no trust store to grep for, no attestation verdict trusted, no standing-grant cache, no hub vouching. The evidence comes from the requester's own governed object; the authorization is a rule the node declared; the decision re-runs from scratch each request. The trust authority has no place to hide in this design because every access is a fresh verification of governed evidence against a declared rule. **This is why trust earned per request is defensible across generations and not merely a security feature: a federation that verifies every access from governed evidence has no trust for an adversary to steal and no authority to compromise, generation after generation, while one that trusts an authority inherits that authority's every breach.** The stakes named in Ch 1 come home here. A federation's security is a generational asset -- it must hold across changes of steward, membership, and threat. Whether it holds turns on this invariant. Verify every access from the requester's own evidence and the node's own rule, and the security has no standing trust to steal and no authority to breach -- it is a property of the federation's own governed records, re-proven each request, inheritable intact. Trust an authority, and every generation inherits the same single point of failure. The zero-trust invariant is what makes a federation's security its own across the generations, which is what Lasting Generational Prosperity requires of a defense. **What comes next is the rest of Zero-Trust Sovereignty, built on this foundation -- the protective shields (S7 Vol 2), the sovereign data storage model (S7 Vol 3), and the verified data flows across nodes (S7 Vol 4) all rest on verify-every-request -- so this opener is the ground the series stands on.** This volume establishes the architecture: access decided per request from governed evidence, deny-by-default, no standing trust. The active protective shields build on it (S7 Vol 2); data-at-rest governance builds on it (S7 Vol 3); verified data flows between nodes build on it (S7 Vol 4). Each later volume of the series assumes this foundation -- that nothing is trusted by default and everything is verified. The opener is complete as a proof-first floor, and the series it opens has its ground: trust earned per request, never vouched. **For the Ridgeline federation, the volume ends where zero-trust always aimed -- a node that grants a peer nothing by default and verifies everything, so its security is its own, re-proven each request, with no central authority it must trust and an adversary cannot compromise.** Ridgeline set out to decide its accesses safely without handing its security to a trusted authority. This volume gave it the way: a node presents its own governed evidence (Ch 2), and access is granted only by verifying that evidence and the node's own declared rule for exactly this request (Ch 3), riding the sealed anchor and governance gates (Ch 4, Ch 5), with onboarding, transport, monitoring, and shields each at a known home (Ch 6). The node's security is its own verification, re-proven every request, with no trust authority to breach. That is trust earned per request, not vouched -- and it is the foundation the whole of Zero-Trust Sovereignty is built on.

title: Vol 02 Shields Protective Layers
chapter_title: The Shields Opportunity — Defense in Depth Without a Trust Authority
text: You will see why a sovereign node must protect a resource with layered, independently-verifiable shields it declares itself -- not a single perimeter and not a central security service that vouches -- and why defense in depth is what makes a resource safe when any one layer is breached.

title: Vol 02 Shields Protective Layers
chapter_title: The Shields Opportunity — Defense in Depth Without a Trust Authority
text: **A resource protected by a single line of defense is a resource one breach away from exposure -- and a sovereign node that guards its resources with one perimeter, or trusts one central security service to guard them, has staked everything on that one thing holding.** Zero-Trust Node Architecture (the volume before this) made every access a verification. But a verified access still reaches a resource, and a resource protected by only one control fails completely the moment that control is bypassed. The discipline that survives a breach is defense in depth: layers of independent protection, so that defeating one still leaves the rest. This volume builds that -- protective shields, layered, each verified on its own terms. **The tension is between protection and sovereignty -- a resource needs layered defense, but if those layers are provided and vouched for by a central security service, the node has handed its protection to whatever it trusts -- and resolving that tension is the design problem of shields.** Layered protection is easy to buy: a security appliance, a managed service, a platform that wraps every resource in its controls and attests they are safe. Its convenience is real and its weakness is the same one zero-trust named -- a central authority that vouches is a central point of capture. Sovereignty demands the layers be the node's own: declared by the resource owner, verified from the resource's own bytes, with no service in the middle attesting. The sovereign answer is protective shields the owner declares and anyone can verify without trusting a vouching authority. **Legacy security stacks a single perimeter or a central security service that vouches for everything inside it -- a firewall, a WAF, a managed security platform that attests a resource is protected -- and whoever breaches the perimeter or compromises the service inherits everything it guarded.** The familiar answer to "protect this resource" is a perimeter or a platform: one wall, or one service that wraps and vouches. Each concentrates protection in a single trusted thing, and a single trusted thing is a single catastrophic failure -- breach the perimeter and you are inside; compromise the service and its every attestation is worthless. Protection bought by a vouching authority is sovereignty mortgaged: the node's resources are only as safe as the one service it trusted, which is exactly what an adversary attacks. **This is the weakness of the security appliance, and naming it precisely folds the old comparison into the opening -- it makes protection easy, but by concentrating it in one vouching thing, so the node's security is only as sound as whatever it trusted.** Traditional layered security is built for convenience -- one platform to protect everything -- and solves it by a central provider. Its weakness is not that it fails to protect; it protects reliably until the provider is breached. Its weakness is that the protection rests on a trusted thing that does not verify from the resource's own bytes, so its compromise is total. The sovereign advantage is structural: each shield is the owner's own declared, governed layer, verified independently from the resource itself -- so defeating one layer leaves the others, and there is no vouching authority to compromise. **The sovereign opportunity is not a stronger appliance -- it is protective shields the resource owner declares, layered, each verified from the resource's own bytes, with no second trust authority, no central attestation service, and no hub that vouches.** The design commitment of this volume is defense in depth with nothing central: a resource carries layered shields its owner declared, and a request clears the resource only when every shield passes, each verified on its own terms from the resource's own record. What is genuinely new is this owner-declared, independently-verifiable layering. What is deliberately absent is the security appliance, the managed service, and the vouching authority the legacy model makes the single point of failure -- and the cryptographic layers are the sealed foundation substrate composed, not new crypto invented here. **The stakes are the whole of Lasting Generational Prosperity, because a federation whose resources are protected by layered shields it owns survives the breach of any single layer, generation after generation, while one that relies on a central security service inherits that service's every compromise.** Protection is a generational asset -- it must hold across changing threats and changing custodians. Whether it holds turns on whether the layers are the node's own or a service's. A federation whose shields it declares and verifies from its own resources loses at most one layer to any breach, and has no vouching authority for an adversary to topple -- its protection is a property of its own records, inheritable intact. A federation that trusts a security service has made its protection that service's to lose. The shields discipline is what keeps a federation's protection defensible across the generations. **For the Ridgeline federation -- protecting a shared record a peer must access -- the difference is whether the record carries layered shields the family declared and the peer verifies from the record itself, or whether a security service wraps it and vouches it is safe.** When a Ridgeline node exposes a shared record to a peer, the legacy path wraps it in a service that attests it is protected. This volume gives it another path: the record carries an integrity shield and a confidentiality shield the family declared, and the peer clears the record only when every shield passes, each verified from the record's own bytes -- with no service vouching. The chapters that follow build that capability -- declaring a shield (Ch 2), clearing every layer deny-by-default (Ch 3), the integrity shield over the sealed foundation (Ch 4), the confidentiality and ready-today capacity (Ch 5), what shields home elsewhere (Ch 6), and protection the node owns layer on layer (Ch 7) -- and none of it trusts a vouching authority.

title: Vol 02 Shields Protective Layers
text: You will see how a resource owner declares a protective shield as a governed object it owns -- and how the integrity shield composes the sealed foundation's Merkle tree to carry a tamper-evident root over the resource -- so a shield is the owner's own layer, not a central attestation.

title: Vol 02 Shields Protective Layers
text: **A protective shield over a resource must be a governed object the resource owner declares -- carrying the protection on the record under the owner's own mandate -- not an attestation a central service issued, and `declare_shield` is the act that makes it one.** The first move in owned protection is to change what a shield *is*. In the appliance model a shield is a control a service applies and vouches for. Here a shield is a governed object the owner registers: authored under its mandate, naming the resource it protects and the kind of protection, carrying its integrity. `declare_shield(reg, resource_id, kind, chunks, *, mandate, author, source_ref, at)` performs exactly that. The shield becomes a thing on the record the owner owns -- verifiable by anyone from the resource itself, with no service in the middle attesting. **`declare_shield` composes the sealed object registry -- it calls `reg.append` with kind `ratify` to register the shield as a provenance-carrying governed object under the owner's own mandate -- so the shield is created by the same governed-object machinery every sovereign artifact uses.** The function builds no new store. It composes the sealed Sovereign Object Model: `reg.append(f"shield:{resource_id}:{kind}", payload, ..., kind="ratify")`. The `ratify` marks it a constitutive act -- the owner putting a protective layer on the record. The registry returns the governed shield with its `version_hash`. The shield is governed the moment it is declared, by the machinery Vol 5 of Series 5 sealed -- which is why a verifier can check it as it checks any governed object. **For the integrity shield, `declare_shield` composes the sealed foundation's Merkle tree -- it computes the Merkle root over the resource's canonical chunks via the sealed `MerkleTree` and stores that root in the shield -- so the shield carries a tamper-evident fingerprint of the resource, built from the sealed P5 substrate rather than crypto invented here.** When `kind` is `integrity`, the function does one cryptographic thing: `payload["root"] = MerkleTree(chunks).get_root()`. The `MerkleTree` is the sealed P5 shield primitive -- now vendored in-tree and reached through the `_lazy_bp` runtime boundary. The shield stores the Merkle root over the resource's chunks, and that root is what a later request is checked against (Ch 3). This volume writes no Merkle code; it composes the sealed one. The integrity shield's strength is the sealed foundation's, reused. **An empty resource id, an empty kind, or (for the integrity shield) empty chunks is refused -- `declare_shield` raises `ShieldError` before it registers anything -- because a shield must name the resource it protects and the protection it applies, and an integrity shield must have something to root over.** The guards come first. A shield with no resource protects nothing; a shield with no kind applies nothing; an integrity shield with no chunks has no fingerprint. Each empty case raises `ShieldError`. Refusing them keeps the record honest -- every `shield:` object names a real resource and a real protection, so when a request is cleared there is a definite layer to clear. The refusal is what makes a shield an accountable protective layer rather than an empty label. **What `declare_shield` is not: it is not new cryptography, not a security service, and not a central attestation -- it registers one governed shield the owner declared, and the crypto it uses is the sealed P5 substrate composed, not invented here.** The boundary matters. This function does not write a Merkle tree -- it composes the sealed one through the `_lazy_bp` boundary, which fails loud if the substrate is absent. It does not run a security service -- there is no service; the shield is the owner's own object. It does not attest centrally -- there is no authority vouching; a verifier checks the shield from the resource's own bytes. `declare_shield` produces exactly one thing: the owner's own governed protective layer. Everything a security service would own stays absent by design. **In the acceptance test, an integrity shield is declared over a resource and comes back a governed object with a real `version_hash`, `object_id` `shield:doc:1:integrity`, and a Merkle root over the chunks -- and declaring a shield with no resource, kind, or chunks raises `ShieldError` -- so the guarantee is executable.** `test_declare_shield_integrity_registers_a_governed_object_with_root` declares an integrity shield over three chunks and asserts the returned object carries a `version_hash`, the right `object_id`, and a non-empty `root` (the sealed P5 Merkle root). `test_declare_shield_refuses_empty` confirms all three empty guards raise. The receipt is the test: the shield is a real governed object carrying a sealed-Merkle root, and the empty cases are refused, both demonstrated by running code. **For the Ridgeline federation, `declare_shield` is the moment a protective layer over a shared record stops being a service's attestation and becomes a governed object the family declared -- carrying a sealed-Merkle fingerprint of the record -- the precondition for a peer to clear the record from its own bytes rather than trust a service.** When Ridgeline protects a shared record, the legacy path has a service wrap it and vouch. `declare_shield` instead puts an integrity shield on the record as a governed object under the family's mandate, carrying the record's Merkle root from the sealed foundation. Now the protection is the family's own governed layer, not a service's word. The clearing that follows -- built in Ch 3 -- has a governed shield with a real root to check, and no service to trust.

title: Vol 02 Shields Protective Layers
chapter_title: Clearing Every Layer, Deny by Default — pass_shield_stack
text: You will see how a request clears a resource only when every declared shield passes, in order -- an integrity shield recomputing the sealed Merkle root and refusing a tampered payload, an unknown shield refusing the stack, an empty stack refusing outright -- so defense in depth is deny-by-default.

title: Vol 02 Shields Protective Layers
chapter_title: Clearing Every Layer, Deny by Default — pass_shield_stack
text: **Clearing a request against a resource must mean passing every protective layer the owner declared, in order -- not satisfying one and assuming the rest, and not passing by default -- and `pass_shield_stack` is that check.** Once a resource carries governed shields (Ch 2), reaching it does not require trusting a service; it requires clearing each declared shield on its own terms. `pass_shield_stack(shields, payload_chunks)` is that verification. It clears the request only when every shield passes, and its default -- when any fails or when there is nothing to clear -- is refusal. Defense in depth is exactly this: one passed layer is not enough; every layer must hold. **`pass_shield_stack` is deny-by-default and fail-closed, checking every shield in order -- a request clears the resource only if all layers pass, and any failure refuses the whole stack.** The function iterates the declared shields and requires each to pass; the first failure raises `ShieldError` and the request is refused. There is no partial clear, no "most layers passed." The default across the stack is no access. This is what makes it defense in depth rather than a single control: an adversary who defeats one layer still faces the rest, and the request clears only when none of them refused. Deny-first, layer by layer. **An integrity shield passes only when the presented payload's Merkle root -- recomputed via the sealed foundation's `MerkleTree` -- equals the shield's declared root, so a tampered or altered payload is refused before the request clears.** For an `integrity` shield, `pass_shield_stack` recomputes `MerkleTree(payload_chunks).get_root()` and compares it to the root the shield declared (Ch 2). If they match, the layer passes; if they differ -- one altered byte, one missing chunk -- the roots diverge and the layer refuses. The Merkle recomputation is the sealed P5 primitive, composed; the volume writes no crypto. So the integrity layer is a tamper check from the resource's own bytes: the presented payload is exactly what was shielded, or the request is refused. **A shield of an unknown kind refuses the stack -- an unrecognized protection is not silently passed -- and an empty stack refuses outright, because an unshielded resource is not implicitly open.** Two deny-by-default guards make the default safe. If a shield names a kind the checker does not recognize, `pass_shield_stack` refuses rather than waving it through -- an unrecognized protection is treated as unmet, never as satisfied. And if there are no shields at all, the function refuses: a resource with no declared protection is not implicitly open; the absence of a shield is not a grant. Both guards close the door that a lenient checker would leave ajar -- there is no path by which a request clears without every declared, recognized layer actually passing. **There is no second trust authority and no central attestation anywhere in `pass_shield_stack` -- each layer is verified from the resource's own bytes against a governed shield the owner declared -- so the kill-target holds: nothing but the resource's own shields, each independently checked, clears a request.** The kill-target for this volume is explicit: no second trust authority, no central attestation service, no hub that vouches. The function honors it structurally. It consults no service, trusts no attestation verdict, and asks no hub. It recomputes the integrity root from the presented bytes and compares it to the owner's declared shield. A grep of this module for a security service, an attestation cache, or a vouching authority returns nothing, because the design admits none. The layers verify; nothing vouches. **In the acceptance test, a matching payload clears the integrity shield, a tampered payload is refused, an empty stack is refused, an unknown kind is refused, and two shields both must pass -- each raising `ShieldError` on failure.** `test_pass_shield_stack_clears_matching_payload` clears one integrity shield with the exact bytes. `test_pass_shield_stack_refuses_tampered_payload` proves an altered chunk refuses (Merkle mismatch). `test_pass_shield_stack_deny_by_default_empty` proves an empty stack refuses. `test_pass_shield_stack_refuses_unknown_kind` proves an unrecognized shield refuses. `test_pass_shield_stack_defense_in_depth_all_must_pass` proves two shields both pass together and that failing either refuses the whole stack. Defense-in-depth and deny-by-default are executable, not asserted in prose. **For the Ridgeline federation, `pass_shield_stack` is the moment a peer's request for a shared record is cleared -- only if the record's integrity shield verifies the peer's payload against the sealed Merkle root and every other declared layer passes too -- so a tampered record, a missing layer, or an unrecognized protection grants the peer nothing.** When a Ridgeline peer requests a shared record, the record's shields decide. The integrity shield recomputes the Merkle root over the presented bytes and refuses any tamper; every other declared layer must pass; an unshielded record is not open. There is no security service vouching, no single control to bypass. The peer clears the record only by satisfying every layer the family declared, each checked from the record's own bytes -- protection the family owns, layer on layer.

title: Vol 02 Shields Protective Layers
chapter_title: The Integrity Shield — Composing the Sealed P5 Merkle over the Object Model (S5 Vol 5)
text: You will see that the integrity shield's cryptography is not new -- it is the sealed P5 Merkle tree, now vendored in-tree and reached through the runtime boundary, over the sealed Sovereign Object Model (S5 Vol 5) -- so a tamper-evident shield composes an audited foundation, not code invented here.

title: Vol 02 Shields Protective Layers
chapter_title: The Integrity Shield — Composing the Sealed P5 Merkle over the Object Model (S5 Vol 5)
text: **The tamper-evidence at the heart of the integrity shield -- the Merkle root that proves a resource is exactly what was shielded -- is not cryptography this volume wrote; it is the sealed P5 Merkle tree of the constitutional foundation, composed.** It would be easy to read Ch 2 as introducing a hashing scheme. It does not. `declare_shield` computes the integrity root by calling the sealed `MerkleTree`, and `pass_shield_stack` verifies by recomputing it. The Merkle tree itself -- its structure, its hashing, its root -- is the sealed P5 shield primitive, audited and byte-verified (the foundation's `bl-verify` walks it). The integrity shield rides that sealed floor, which is why its tamper-evidence needs no fresh cryptographic audit. **The sealed P5 substrate is now vendored in-tree, and the shield composes it through the `_lazy_bp` runtime boundary -- which resolves the sealed `MerkleTree` when the substrate is present and fails loud when it is absent -- so the composition is honest in both the production node and a pure clone.** The foundation crypto was brought into the node tree so the node is self-contained; the shield reaches it the way the whole kernel does, through the `_lazy_bp` adapter. That adapter is the runtime boundary: it returns the sealed `MerkleTree` on a node that carries the substrate, and raises a clear, actionable error on one that does not. So the integrity shield never silently degrades -- it uses the sealed Merkle where it is present and refuses honestly where it is not. **The shield that carries the Merkle root is itself a governed object of the sealed Sovereign Object Model (Vol 5 of Series 5) -- so the root rides the same governed-object integrity every sovereign artifact rides, and a verifier checks the shield the way it checks anything else.** Ch 2 registered the shield through the object registry, so the shield -- root and all -- is a governed object with its own `version_hash`. The Merkle root protects the resource; the object model protects the shield. A verifier confirms the shield is authentic (its own governed integrity) and then checks the resource against the Merkle root it carries. Two sealed floors, layered: the object model governs the shield, the P5 Merkle governs the resource. Neither is new. **Reusing the sealed foundation is the reason the integrity shield is trustworthy without new audit -- a Merkle tree written here would have been unaudited cryptography, the exact thing a sovereign system must not roll itself, whereas the sealed P5 Merkle is byte-verified and battle-tested.** The cardinal sin in a sovereign crypto system is home-rolled primitives. Had this volume written its own Merkle tree, every claim of tamper-evidence would rest on unaudited code. By composing the sealed P5 Merkle -- the same primitive the foundation's `bl-verify` confirms clean -- the integrity shield inherits proven cryptography. Composition here is not convenience; it is the discipline that keeps a security volume from grounding its guarantees on crypto no one audited. **The boundary of this chapter is strict: it composes the sealed P5 Merkle and the sealed Object Model, it re-implements neither -- there is no new hash, no new tree, and no new integrity scheme in this volume, only the sealed Merkle composed to shield a resource.** This volume writes two functions and an invariant. The Merkle tree -- its hashing and root -- is the sealed P5 substrate, composed. The shield's own integrity -- its governed-object hash -- is Vol 5 of Series 5, composed. If those floors are sound, the integrity shield is sound, with no new cryptography to re-audit. This is the discipline that keeps the shields volume honest: it cannot smuggle in home-rolled crypto, because it composes the audited foundation for every cryptographic layer. **For the Ridgeline federation, this is the assurance that the tamper-evidence protecting a shared record is the same sealed Merkle the family already verified via the foundation's `bl-verify` -- one audited primitive, composed, not a security-specific hash the family must take on faith.** Ridgeline already ran the foundation's `bl-verify` and watched the sealed P5 Merkle prove clean. The integrity shield now composes that same Merkle to protect the family's records. There is no separate shield-specific cryptography for the family to trust, and no home-rolled hash to audit. The protection over every record is the sealed foundation's Merkle -- which the family has already proven to itself -- reused through the node's own runtime boundary.

title: Vol 02 Shields Protective Layers
chapter_title: Confidentiality and the Ready-Today Capacity — Composing Sealed P5 with Honest Maturity
text: You will see exactly which cryptographic shields the sealed foundation can back today and to what degree -- confidentiality via Paillier (ready), a zero-knowledge shield with its range HELD, a sandbox shield parser-only -- each composed from the sealed P5 substrate, none over-read.

title: Vol 02 Shields Protective Layers
chapter_title: Confidentiality and the Ready-Today Capacity — Composing Sealed P5 with Honest Maturity
text: **The shields thesis genuinely owns a range of cryptographic protections -- confidentiality, zero-knowledge, sandboxing -- because the sealed P5 foundation provides their substrate; the discipline is to compose each at its honest maturity, claiming exactly what the substrate backs today and no more.** Beyond the integrity shield (Ch 4), the sealed P5 layer carries a homomorphic-encryption primitive, a zero-knowledge primitive, and a WASM runtime. These are real, sealed, and now in-tree. So the shields volume can offer confidentiality, zero-knowledge, and sandbox shields as compositions of them. But sealed and present is not the same as fully mature -- and this chapter states, layer by layer, precisely how far each composition honestly reaches. **The confidentiality shield composes the sealed P5 Paillier homomorphic-encryption layer -- ready today -- so a resource can be protected such that a value is verified or combined without being revealed, using the sealed primitive, not encryption written here.** The sealed P5 provides Paillier: an additively-homomorphic scheme that lets a party add encrypted values without decrypting them. The confidentiality shield composes it, so a shielded value can be checked or combined while staying encrypted -- confidentiality as a protective layer. This is a ready-today composition: the Paillier primitive is sealed and functional (the foundation exercises it). The confidentiality shield is exactly the sealed Paillier, composed to protect a resource's values -- no home-rolled encryption, and no claim beyond what additively-homomorphic Paillier does. **The zero-knowledge shield composes the sealed P5 zero-knowledge primitive, with its range capability HELD -- so the volume discloses plainly that the ZK shield proves what the sealed ZK layer proves today, and the range-proof capacity is held, not presented as complete.** The sealed P5 carries a zero-knowledge primitive, and a ZK shield composes it to let a party prove a statement about a resource without revealing it. But the maturity is bounded and stated: the range-proof capability is **HELD** -- it is not offered as a finished, general range proof. The ZK shield is therefore composed at exactly the sealed layer's current reach, and the held range is disclosed rather than over-read. This is the difference between an honest security book and a brochure: the ZK shield is present as a composition, and its limit is named in the same breath. **The sandbox shield composes the sealed P5 WASM runtime, which is parser-only -- so the volume discloses that the sandbox shield parses and validates a module today, and does not claim full sandboxed execution the runtime does not yet provide.** The sealed P5 includes a WASM runtime, and a sandbox shield composes it to confine untrusted logic touching a resource. Its maturity is stated: the WASM runtime is **parser-only** -- it parses and validates modules, and full sandboxed execution is not claimed. The sandbox shield is therefore composed at parser-only reach, and that boundary is disclosed. The shield is real as far as the sealed runtime goes, and no further -- the volume does not present a parser as an executor. **There is no false-present anywhere in this chapter -- each cryptographic shield is exactly what the sealed P5 substrate backs today (integrity and confidentiality ready; ZK range HELD; WASM parser-only), composed and disclosed, never a capability the foundation does not yet have.** This is the maturity-honesty discipline made explicit. The volume composes the sealed foundation for four shield kinds, and for each it states the reach: integrity (Ch 4) and confidentiality are ready-today compositions; the zero-knowledge shield's range is held; the sandbox shield is parser-only. A reader is told precisely which protection runs to what degree. No shield is presented as more than its sealed substrate provides. The thesis owns these capacities -- as compositions, at their honest maturity, and not one degree beyond. **The line held here is the same line the whole series holds: compose the audited foundation, disclose the maturity, and never let a security promise outrun the cryptography behind it.** A security volume is where over-claiming does the most harm -- a reader who trusts a shield the substrate cannot back is exposed exactly where they thought they were safe. So this chapter refuses the brochure. It names the sealed primitive behind each shield, states how far it reaches, and marks the held and parser-only limits in the text a reader will act on. The shields are real compositions of a sealed foundation; their maturity is stated; and the reader can tell, layer by layer, precisely what protects them and how far. **For the Ridgeline federation, this is the honest menu of what a shield can do today -- an integrity layer and a confidentiality layer they can rely on now, a zero-knowledge layer whose range is held, a sandbox layer that parses -- so the family protects a shared record with exactly the protections the sealed foundation backs, and knows the edges.** When Ridgeline shields a shared record, it can compose the ready-today integrity and confidentiality layers with confidence, add a zero-knowledge layer knowing its range is held, and a sandbox layer knowing it parses. The family gets real, sealed-backed protections and an honest statement of each one's reach -- so it never mistakes a held capability for a finished one, and protects its records with the substrate's true strength, disclosed edge and all.

title: Vol 02 Shields Protective Layers
chapter_title: What Shields Do Not Own — Access, Identity, the Human Gate, Storage, Monitoring
text: You will see exactly where the per-request access decision, a node's identity, the human gate for a material action, data-at-rest governance, and monitoring live -- each at a real sealed home -- so nothing this volume leaves out floats without an address.

title: Vol 02 Shields Protective Layers
chapter_title: What Shields Do Not Own — Access, Identity, the Human Gate, Storage, Monitoring
text: **Whether a requester may reach a resource at all -- the per-request access decision -- is Zero-Trust Node Architecture (Vol 1 of Series 7), not a decision shields make; shields protect a resource in layers, they do not decide who is verified to reach it.** A reader might ask where the *access* decision lives, before the shields even apply. That is zero-trust verification, sealed the volume before this: a node grants an access only by verifying the requester's own evidence and its own declared rule. Shields come after: they add layered protection to the resource an access reaches. This volume decides no accesses; the sealed S7 Vol 1 does. Shields and the access decision compose -- verify the access, then clear the layers -- but the decision is homed, not rebuilt here. **A node's identity -- the anchor a resource owner is known by -- is Trust Boundaries & Handoff (Vol 5 of Series 6), not an identity shields mint; a shield names its owner by an identity the federation already governs.** A shield is declared by a resource owner under its mandate, and that owner's identity is its sealed trust anchor. Shields do not create identities; they reference the sealed ones. The anchor by which a shield's owner is recognized is Trust Boundaries & Handoff (S6 Vol 5), composed. This volume mints no identity; a shield's ownership traces to a sealed anchor, named at its home. **The human gate for a material action on a resource -- a person's deliberate approval where materiality warrants -- is Compliance & Audit (Vol 16 of Series 5), not an approval shields build; a shield is a machine layer, and the human step is the sealed compliance gate, composed.** Some actions on a shielded resource are material enough to need a person, not only passing layers. That escalation is the sealed `HumanApprovalGate` of Compliance & Audit (S5 Vol 16), the same gate the rest of the system uses. Shields verify machine layers; where a human is required, the sealed compliance gate provides it. This volume builds no approval mechanism; the human gate is homed at Vol 16 of Series 5. **Governing a resource's data at rest -- how it is stored, scoped private or shared, and kept integral on disk -- composes the sealed Sovereign Object Model (Vol 5 of Series 5) and the sealed P5 Merkle, and watching the pattern of accesses over time is Analytics & Decision Intelligence (Vol 19 of Series 5); shields protect a resource in the moment, they do not store it or monitor it.** Two neighboring capabilities have their homes. Data at rest -- storage as governed objects with integrity on disk -- composes the Sovereign Object Model (S5 Vol 5) and the sealed P5 Merkle. Continuous monitoring of access patterns is Analytics & Decision Intelligence (S5 Vol 19), never Vol 17. Shields are moment-of-access protection; storage and monitoring are their own volumes, named at their homes and not rebuilt here. **Naming every home precisely is what makes the kill-target credible rather than merely declared -- a volume that said "no trust authority" while quietly leaving access, identity, the human gate, storage, and monitoring homeless would have smuggled a central authority back in under a vague gesture.** The kill-target -- no second trust authority, no central attestation, no hub that vouches -- is only as honest as the volume's willingness to say where the omitted work lives. If the access decision floated, a reader could imagine shields vouching for who may enter; they do not -- access is Zero-Trust Node Architecture (S7 Vol 1). If identity floated, a reader could imagine shields minting it; they do not -- identity is Trust Boundaries (S6 Vol 5). If storage or monitoring floated, a reader could imagine a shields platform owning them; they do not -- each is its own home. Every home named is a place the trust authority is *not*. **For the Ridgeline federation, this chapter is the map of what the rest of the architecture provides around a shielded resource -- who is verified to reach it, whose identity declared it, when a human must approve, where it is stored and monitored -- so they know layering protection is one governed act in a federation where every neighboring capability has a known, sealed home.** Ridgeline does not get a monolithic security product from this volume; it gets precise protective layers and a map. The access decision is zero-trust (S7 Vol 1). The owner's identity is a sealed anchor (S6 Vol 5). A material action's human gate is compliance (S5 Vol 16). The record's data at rest composes the Object Model (S5 Vol 5) + sealed P5 Merkle; the monitoring is Analytics (S5 Vol 19). The family can see the whole neighborhood of a shielded resource and confirm that nowhere in it is a central authority vouching -- because every home is named, and none of them is a security service.

title: Vol 02 Shields Protective Layers
chapter_title: Protection the Node Owns, Layer on Layer — Synthesis and the LGP Stakes
text: You will see the volume resolve to one invariant -- a request clears a resource only when every protective shield the owner declared passes, each verified from the resource's own bytes -- and why layered protection the node owns is defensible across generations.

title: Vol 02 Shields Protective Layers
chapter_title: Protection the Node Owns, Layer on Layer — Synthesis and the LGP Stakes
text: **The whole of this volume resolves to a single invariant: a request clears a resource only when every protective shield its owner declared passes, each verified from the resource's own bytes -- never a central authority's vouching, and never by default.** Everything built here serves that one sentence. A shield is a governed object the owner declared (Ch 2). Clearing is deny-by-default and defense-in-depth (Ch 3). The integrity shield's cryptography is the sealed P5 Merkle over the object model (Ch 4). The confidentiality, zero-knowledge, and sandbox shields are sealed-P5 compositions at honest maturity (Ch 5). Access, identity, the human gate, storage, and monitoring are named at their homes (Ch 6). The invariant is the volume's whole claim, and every chapter is a face of it: protection the owner declares, every layer verified. **The two PRESENT functions are small and their power is borrowed honestly: `declare_shield` composes the object model and the sealed P5 Merkle to make a protective layer the owner's own governed object, and `pass_shield_stack` clears a request deny-by-default only when every declared layer passes.** `declare_shield` registers a shield and, for integrity, computes the sealed-Merkle root -- a first-class governed object of the Sovereign Object Model (S5 Vol 5) carrying a sealed P5 fingerprint. `pass_shield_stack` is a defense-in-depth gate -- every layer must pass, tampered/unknown/empty refused. Two functions, sealed floors composed, one invariant enforced. The volume is honest about how little it invents and precise about what that little guarantees: layered protection, verified, never vouched. **The kill-target held at every step: there is no second trust authority, no central attestation service, and no hub that vouches anywhere in this volume -- each shield is the owner's own governed object, and each layer is verified from the resource's own bytes.** KM set the kill-target at the arm: no second trust authority, no central attestation, no vouching hub. The volume honors each structurally. There is no security service to grep for, no attestation verdict trusted, no vouching hub consulted. A shield is the owner's declared object; a layer passes by recomputing the sealed Merkle from the presented bytes and matching the declared root. The security service has no place to hide in this design because every layer is an independent verification of the resource against a governed shield. **The maturity is stated, not sold: the integrity and confidentiality shields are ready-today compositions of the sealed foundation, the zero-knowledge shield's range is held, and the sandbox shield is parser-only -- so a reader knows precisely what protects them and how far, with no false-present.** A security volume that over-claimed would expose a reader exactly where they felt safe. This one refuses. Ch 5 names the sealed primitive behind each shield and marks the held and parser-only limits in the text a reader acts on. The shields are real compositions of an audited foundation; their reach is disclosed layer by layer. Honest maturity is not a caveat bolted on -- it is part of the invariant: a shield is exactly what the sealed substrate backs, and no more. **This is why layered protection the node owns is defensible across generations and not merely a feature: a federation whose resources carry shields it declared survives the breach of any single layer and has no vouching authority to compromise, generation after generation, while one that relies on a security service inherits that service's every failure.** The stakes named in Ch 1 come home here. Protection is a generational asset -- it must hold across changing threats and custodians. A federation whose shields it declares and verifies from its own resources loses at most one layer to any breach and has no authority to topple; its protection is a property of its own records, inheritable intact. A federation that trusts a security service has made its protection that service's to lose. The shields invariant is what keeps a federation's protection its own across the generations -- defense in depth that no breach of one thing can undo. **For the Ridgeline federation, the volume ends where defense in depth always aimed -- a shared record protected by layered shields the family declared, each cleared from the record's own bytes, so no single breach and no compromised service exposes it, and the family knows exactly which layers protect it and how far.** Ridgeline set out to protect its resources without handing that protection to a security service. This volume gave it the way: a record carries governed shields the family declared (Ch 2), and a request clears it only by passing every layer from the record's own bytes (Ch 3), the cryptographic layers composing the sealed foundation at honest maturity (Ch 4, Ch 5), with access, identity, the human gate, storage, and monitoring each at a known home (Ch 6). The family's protection is layered, owned, and verifiable -- defense in depth that survives the breach of any one layer, which is the whole of what this volume was for.

title: Vol 03 Sovereign Data Storage
chapter_title: The Sovereign Storage Opportunity — Data at Rest Without a Central Store
text: You will see why a sovereign node must hold its data at rest as governed objects it owns -- private or shared by declared scope, integrity provable from the bytes -- rather than in a central store that owns the data and vouches for it, and why that is what keeps data sovereign at rest.

title: Vol 03 Sovereign Data Storage
chapter_title: The Sovereign Storage Opportunity — Data at Rest Without a Central Store
text: **A node is only as sovereign as the store its data rests in -- and a node that keeps its records in a central storage service has handed the durability, the scoping, and the integrity of its data to whatever owns that store.** Zero-trust verified every access and shields protected the resource in the moment; but data spends most of its life at rest, and where it rests decides whether it is sovereign. If it rests in a service's store, the service owns it: it decides who may read it, whether it is intact, and whether it exists tomorrow. The last piece of a sovereign node is the storage model itself -- data at rest the node owns. This volume builds that. **The tension is between durability and sovereignty -- data must be stored durably and scoped for sharing, but if the store owns the data and vouches for it, the node's records are the store's to hold, scope, and attest -- and resolving that tension is the design problem of the storage model.** Durability without sovereignty is the storage service: the data lives in a system a provider owns, and its confidentiality, its access scope, and its integrity are the provider's guarantees. Sovereignty without durability is the isolated node that shares nothing. The sovereign answer resolves the tension by making each datum the owner's own governed object -- scoped private or shared by the owner's declaration, its integrity provable from its own bytes -- so the data is durable and shareable while remaining the node's own. **Legacy storage puts data in a central store that owns it, scopes it, and vouches for its integrity -- a database, an object store, a managed data service that holds every record, decides who may read it, and attests it is unaltered -- and whoever owns the store owns the data.** The familiar answer to "where does the data live" is a central store: a managed database or object store that holds the records and provides access control and integrity. Each concentrates the data in a system a provider owns -- and the owner of the store is the owner of the data: it can read it, alter it, scope it, or lose it, and its integrity is only the store's word. Storage bought this way is sovereignty sold: the node's records are the provider's to govern, which is exactly the dependency a sovereign node cannot carry. **This is the weakness of the storage service, and naming it precisely folds the old comparison into the opening -- it makes durability easy, but by owning the data and vouching for it, so the node's records are only as sovereign as whoever holds the store.** Traditional storage is built for convenience -- one service to hold and scope everything -- and solves it by a central owner. Its weakness is not that it fails to store; it stores reliably. Its weakness is that the data is the store's, its scope the store's decision, its integrity the store's attestation -- so the node never truly owns its records at rest. The sovereign advantage is structural: each datum is the owner's own governed object, scoped by the owner's declared rule, its integrity a Merkle root anyone can recompute from the bytes -- with no store owning it and no service vouching. **The sovereign opportunity is not a better storage service -- it is data at rest as governed objects the owner holds, scoped private or shared by declaration, integrity provable from the bytes, with no central store, no second trust authority, and no hub that vouches.** The design commitment of this volume is data-at-rest the node owns: each datum is a governed object under its owner's mandate, its visibility a declared scope, and its integrity a sealed-Merkle root anyone can verify. What is genuinely new is this governed, scoped, integrity-provable data model. What is deliberately absent is the storage service, the central owner, and the vouching authority the legacy model makes the unavoidable holder of the data -- and the integrity is the sealed foundation Merkle composed, not a scheme invented here. **The stakes are the whole of Lasting Generational Prosperity, because a federation whose data rests as governed objects it owns keeps its records sovereign at rest across generations, while one that relies on a storage service inherits that service's every failure and every claim to the data.** Data at rest is a generational asset -- the records a family or organization keeps for decades. Whether those records are owned turns on where they rest. A federation whose data rests as governed objects it holds -- scoped by its own declaration, integrity it can prove -- keeps its records its own across every custodian and every year: no store owns them, no service scopes them, no authority attests them. A federation that rests its data in a service has made its records that service's to hold and lose. The storage discipline is what keeps a federation's data sovereign at rest, which is the precondition for its records being a generational asset rather than a rented dependency. **For the Ridgeline federation -- storing a private record and sharing another with a peer -- the difference is whether each datum is the family's own governed object, scoped by its declaration and integrity-provable, or a row in a service's store the service owns and vouches for.** When Ridgeline stores a private ledger and shares a report with a partner, the legacy path puts both in a service that owns and scopes them. This volume gives it another path: each datum is the family's own governed object carrying a Merkle integrity root, private or shared by the family's declared scope, retrievable only by a verified, scoped, integrity-checked access -- with no store owning the data. The chapters that follow build that capability -- storing a datum as a governed object (Ch 2), retrieving deny-by-default scoped and integrity-verified (Ch 3), the datum over the sealed floors (Ch 4), private vs shared scope (Ch 5), what storage homes elsewhere (Ch 6), and storage the node owns (Ch 7) -- and none of it puts a central store in the middle.

title: Vol 03 Sovereign Data Storage
chapter_title: Storing a Datum as a Governed Object — store_datum
text: You will see how a node stores a datum as a governed object it owns -- carrying a declared visibility and a sealed-Merkle integrity root over its bytes -- so data at rest is the owner's own provable record, not a row in a service's store.

title: Vol 03 Sovereign Data Storage
chapter_title: Storing a Datum as a Governed Object — store_datum
text: **A datum at rest must be a governed object the owner holds -- carrying its own provenance, visibility, and integrity under the owner's mandate -- not a row in a store a service owns, and `store_datum` is the act that makes it one.** The first move in sovereign storage is to change what a stored datum *is*. In the service model a datum is a row the store owns and scopes. Here a datum is a governed object the owner registers: authored under its mandate, carrying a declared visibility and a Merkle integrity root over its bytes. `store_datum(reg, owner, chunks, *, visibility, mandate, author, source_ref, at)` performs exactly that. The datum becomes a thing on the record the owner owns -- scoped by the owner's declaration and provable from its own bytes, with no store owning it. **`store_datum` composes the sealed object registry -- it calls `reg.append` with kind `ratify` to register the datum as a provenance-carrying governed object under the owner's own mandate -- so the datum is created by the same governed-object machinery every sovereign artifact uses.** The function builds no new store. It composes the sealed Sovereign Object Model: `reg.append(f"datum:{owner}:...", payload, ..., kind="ratify")`. The `ratify` marks it a constitutive act -- the owner putting a record on the ledger. The registry returns the governed datum with its `version_hash`. The datum is governed the moment it is stored, by the machinery Vol 5 of Series 5 sealed -- which is why it is auditable and inheritable like any governed object, with no database in the middle. **The datum carries a declared visibility -- 'private' or 'shared' -- so its access scope is the owner's decision on the record, not a store's access-control setting; a visibility other than private or shared is refused.** Part of the payload is `visibility`, and it must be exactly `private` or `shared`. This is the owner declaring, on the datum itself, how it may be accessed: private (own-mandate only) or shared (crossable by a declared rule, Ch 5). The scope is not a store's ACL that a service enforces and could change; it is a governed property of the datum, authored by the owner. A visibility outside the two allowed values is refused, so every stored datum carries a real, meaningful scope. The datum's access policy travels with the datum, owned by the owner. **The datum carries a sealed-Merkle integrity root over its canonical chunks -- computed via the sealed foundation's `MerkleTree` -- so its integrity at rest is provable from its own bytes, not vouched for by a store.** When it stores a datum, `store_datum` computes `MerkleTree(chunks).get_root()` -- the sealed P5 Merkle primitive, reached through the `_lazy_bp` boundary -- and stores that root in the datum. The root is a tamper-evident fingerprint: anyone can recompute it from the datum's bytes and confirm the datum is exactly what was stored (Ch 3). The volume writes no hashing; it composes the sealed Merkle. So a datum's integrity is not the store's attestation -- it is a root anyone can verify from the bytes, built on the audited foundation. **What `store_datum` is not: it is not a central store, not a database, and not a service that vouches -- it registers one governed datum the owner holds, and the record is the sealed object registry, the scope the owner's declaration, and the integrity the sealed Merkle, none of them a service's.** The boundary matters. This function does not run a store -- there is no store; the datum is a governed object in the sealed registry. It does not implement a database -- the record is the object model, composed. It does not vouch -- there is no authority attesting; the integrity is a root anyone recomputes. `store_datum` produces exactly one thing: the owner's own governed datum. Everything a storage service would own -- the data, the scope, the integrity claim -- stays with the owner by design. **In the acceptance test, a datum is stored under its owner and comes back a governed object with a real `version_hash`, an `object_id` beginning `datum:nodeA:`, its declared visibility, and a sealed-Merkle root -- and storing with no owner, no chunks, or an invalid visibility raises `StorageError` -- so the guarantee is executable.** `test_store_datum_registers_a_governed_object_with_root` stores a private datum and asserts the returned object carries a `version_hash`, the right `object_id` prefix, `visibility` 'private', and a non-empty `root`. `test_store_datum_refuses_empty_or_bad_visibility` confirms empty owner, empty chunks, and a visibility of 'public' each raise. The receipt is the test: the datum is a real governed object with a sealed-Merkle root and a valid scope, and the invalid cases are refused, both demonstrated by running code. **For the Ridgeline family office, `store_datum` is the moment a private ledger or a shared report stops being a row in a service's store and becomes a governed object the family holds -- scoped by the family's declaration and carrying a provable integrity root -- the precondition for retrieving it by a verified, scoped access rather than a store's permission.** When Ridgeline stores a record, the legacy path puts it in a service that owns and scopes it. `store_datum` instead registers it as a governed object under the family's mandate, carrying its declared visibility and a sealed-Merkle root over its bytes. Now the record is the family's own governed datum -- its scope the family's decision, its integrity provable from its bytes. The retrieval that follows -- built in Ch 3 -- has a governed datum with a real root and a real scope to verify, and no store to permit it.

title: Vol 03 Sovereign Data Storage
chapter_title: Retrieving Deny by Default — Scoped and Integrity-Verified — retrieve_datum
text: You will see how a datum is read deny-by-default -- the node must have declared a scope rule for exactly this datum and requester, and the presented bytes must verify against the stored Merkle root -- so private data with no rule is refused and altered data at rest is refused.

title: Vol 03 Sovereign Data Storage
chapter_title: Retrieving Deny by Default — Scoped and Integrity-Verified — retrieve_datum
text: **Reading a datum at rest must be a verified, scoped, integrity-checked act -- the node confirming it declared a rule for exactly this access and that the bytes are intact -- not a store granting permission from an access list, and `retrieve_datum` is that read.** Once a datum is a governed object (Ch 2), reading it does not require a store's permission; it requires the node's own scope rule and an integrity check from the datum's bytes. `retrieve_datum(reg, datum, rules, presented_chunks, *, principal_mandate, want)` is that verification. It returns the datum only when the access is scoped and the integrity holds, and its default -- when either fails -- is refusal. Data is read by the node's own verification, not a store's grant. **`retrieve_datum` is deny-by-default and fail-closed, checking its conditions in order, per request -- a real governed datum, then a node-declared scope, then an integrity match -- so a read is impossible unless all hold.** The function is deny-first. First it verifies there is a real governed datum to read (a `version_hash` and object id). Then it confirms the access is authorized by a node-declared scope rule for exactly this datum and requester. Then it verifies the presented bytes against the datum's stored Merkle root. Each failure raises `StorageError`. The default across all of them is no read. This is the whole difference from a store: a store returns data if the ACL allows; `retrieve_datum` returns nothing until scope and integrity are both re-verified, this request. **The access must be authorized by a node-declared scope rule naming exactly this datum and requester -- composing the sealed `authorize_crossing`, so own-mandate access is whole, a cross-mandate access needs a declared `SharingRule`, and private data with no rule is refused -- there is no standing trust across data.** `authorize_crossing(reg, rules, principal_mandate=..., obj_id=datum["object_id"], want=...)` -- the owner's own access is whole; another mandate's access needs a `SharingRule` the node declared naming exactly this datum. Private data with no declared rule is refused. And the scope is per-datum: a rule granting one datum does not grant another, and an unknown datum denies. There is no standing trust that bleeds across the node's data -- each read is authorized only by a rule declared for exactly that datum. The scope is the sealed federation-governance check, composed. **The presented bytes must verify against the datum's stored Merkle root -- recomputed via the sealed foundation's `MerkleTree` -- so altered or partial data at rest is refused before it is returned.** After the scope check, `retrieve_datum` recomputes `MerkleTree(presented_chunks).get_root()` and compares it to the root the datum stored (Ch 2). If they match, the bytes are exactly what was stored and the datum is returned; if they differ -- one altered byte, one dropped chunk -- the roots diverge and the read is refused. The integrity check is the sealed P5 Merkle, composed. So a datum is not just scoped but proven intact from its own bytes: a read returns exactly the stored data, or nothing. Data at rest that was tampered with cannot be read as if it were sound. **There is no central store and no standing trust anywhere in `retrieve_datum` -- the datum is the owner's own governed object, the scope is the node's own declared rule, and the integrity is the sealed Merkle over the bytes -- so the kill-target holds: data is read only by a per-request verification, never a store's permission.** The kill-target for this volume is explicit: no central store that owns/vouches for the data, no second trust authority, no standing trust across data. The function honors each structurally. The datum comes from the sealed registry -- not a store. The scope is a rule the node declared -- not a store's ACL. The integrity is recomputed from the bytes -- not a store's attestation. A grep of this module for a store, a standing-grant cache, or a vouching authority returns nothing. Data is read by verification; nothing is stored or vouched centrally. **In the acceptance test, an owner reads its own datum with integrity verified, a peer reads a shared datum only with a declared scope rule, a peer with no rule is refused, tampered bytes are refused, and a nonexistent datum is refused -- each raising `StorageError` on failure.** `test_retrieve_datum_own_mandate_whole_integrity_verified` reads the owner's own datum. `test_retrieve_datum_cross_mandate_needs_declared_scope` proves a peer with no rule is refused and with a declared `SharingRule` is granted. `test_retrieve_datum_denies_tampered_at_rest` proves altered bytes are refused (Merkle mismatch). `test_retrieve_datum_denies_nonexistent` proves reading nothing raises. Deny-by-default, scope, and integrity are executable, not asserted in prose. **For the Ridgeline family office, `retrieve_datum` is the moment a record is read -- the family reads its own private ledger with its integrity proven, a partner reads a shared report only if the family declared a scope for it and the bytes verify -- so a stolen access, a broadened ACL, or an altered record grants a reader nothing.** When Ridgeline or a partner reads a record, the legacy path lets the store's ACL decide and trusts the store's copy. This volume gives it a verified read: the family's own datum is checked against the family's declared scope and its integrity recomputed from the bytes. Private data with no rule is refused; a partner reads a shared datum only by a declared scope; altered data is refused. There is no store to permit the read and no standing trust to steal -- the family's data is read only by a per-request, scoped, integrity-checked verification it owns.

title: Vol 03 Sovereign Data Storage
chapter_title: The Datum as a Governed Object with Integrity — Composing the Object Model (S5 Vol 5) and the Sealed P5 Merkle
text: **The two things that make a datum sovereign at rest -- that it is a governed record and that its integrity is provable -- are not machinery this volume invented; the record is the sealed Sovereign Object Model (Vol 5 of Series 5) and the integrity is the sealed P5 Merkle of the constitutional foundation.** It would be easy to read Ch 2 as introducing a storage engine and a hashing scheme. It does neither. `store_datum` registers the datum through the same `ObjectRegistry` that governs every sovereign object, and computes its integrity root with the sealed `MerkleTree`. Data at rest rides two audited floors -- the object model for the record, the P5 Merkle for the integrity -- which is why it needs no database and no crypto of its own. **The datum's record is the sealed object model -- `store_datum` composes `reg.append`, the same constitutive registration every governed object uses -- so a datum carries the identical provenance and integrity every sovereign artifact carries.** The object model defines one way to bring a governed object into being: `append`, with its provenance fields and its `version_hash`. A datum uses it unchanged. There is no storage-specific record path; the datum is a governed object like a ledger entry or a constitution, distinguished only by its `datum:` prefix and its stored root. So a datum's record is auditable and inheritable exactly as any governed object is -- which means storage inherits the object model's guarantees without restating them. **The datum's integrity is the sealed P5 Merkle -- `store_datum` computes the root and `retrieve_datum` recomputes it via the sealed `MerkleTree`, reached through the runtime boundary -- so the tamper-evidence is the audited foundation's, not a hash invented here.** The sealed P5 provides the Merkle tree; storage composes it. The root a datum carries and the root a read recomputes are both the sealed primitive -- the same Merkle the foundation's `bl-verify` confirms clean. Storage writes no hashing. So a datum's provable integrity is not a storage-specific checksum; it is the sealed foundation Merkle, composed. Anyone who can verify a Merkle root can verify a datum's integrity, on cryptography no one had to re-audit for this volume. **Both floors are audited -- the object model byte-consistent and the P5 Merkle `bl-verify`-clean -- so reusing them is exactly why a sovereign storage model needs no store and no crypto of its own, which would each have been an unaudited authority.** Had this volume built a storage engine, it would have been a system owning the data. Had it written a hash, it would have been unaudited crypto. Both are the exact things the kill-target and the no-home-rolled-crypto discipline forbid. By composing the sealed object model and the sealed P5 Merkle, storage owns no data and rolls no crypto: the record is the audited registry, the integrity the audited Merkle. Composition here is not tidiness; it is what keeps the storage model from becoming the central store it was built to replace. **The boundary of this chapter is strict: it composes the sealed object model and the sealed P5 Merkle, it re-implements neither -- there is no new store, no new record format, and no new hash in this volume, only a datum registered in the sealed registry with a sealed-Merkle root.** This volume writes two functions and an invariant. The record -- how a governed object is stored and versioned -- is Vol 5 of Series 5, composed. The integrity -- how a Merkle root is computed -- is the sealed P5 substrate, composed. If those floors are sound, a datum's governance and integrity are sound, with no new storage or crypto code to re-audit. This is the discipline that keeps the storage model honest: it cannot smuggle in a central store or a home-rolled hash, because it composes the audited floors for both. **For the Ridgeline family office, this is the assurance that a stored record is governed exactly as their ledgers are and its integrity is the same sealed Merkle they verified via the foundation's `bl-verify` -- one object model, one audited hash, composed -- so a stored datum is as trustworthy as any figure in their books.** Ridgeline already relies on the sealed object model for their ledgers and has watched the sealed P5 Merkle prove clean. A stored datum now rides both: its record is the object model, its integrity the sealed Merkle. There is no separate storage subsystem for the family to trust and no home-rolled hash to audit. A record at rest is as governed and as provable as everything else the family keeps -- which is why its storage is sovereign, not a service's.
