title: Vol 03 Sovereign Data Storage
chapter_title: Private vs Shared Scope — Composing authorize_crossing (S5 Vol 28) and the Sealed Scope Discipline
text: **What makes a datum private or shared -- who, other than the owner, may read it -- is not machinery this volume invented; it is the sealed Federation Node Governance `authorize_crossing` (Vol 28 of Series 5) and its declared-rule scope discipline.** It would be easy to read Ch 3's scope check as a storage access-control system. It is not. `retrieve_datum` composes `authorize_crossing` -- the sealed cross-mandate check that grants an access only by a rule the node declared naming exactly the object, the peer, and a sufficient scope. A datum's private-or-shared reality is exactly that: own-mandate access is whole (private), and a cross-mandate read needs a declared rule (shared). Storage scopes data by the same sealed rule that governs any federation crossing. **Own-mandate access is whole -- a datum is the owner's, and the owner reads it without a rule, which is precisely what 'private' means -- so private data needs no access grant for its owner and is refused to everyone else by default.** The sealed scope check returns whole access when the requester's mandate is the datum's home mandate. That is private data: the owner reads its own datum with no rule, and no other mandate may read it unless a rule is declared. The `private` visibility a datum carries (Ch 2) is realized by this: own-mandate whole, everyone else denied by default. Privacy is not a store enforcing an ACL; it is the sealed own-mandate rule, composed -- the owner's data is the owner's, full stop, until the owner declares otherwise. **Shared data crosses only by a declared `SharingRule` naming exactly this datum and peer -- so 'shared' is not open; it is the owner declaring a specific, scoped grant, and a rule for one datum never shares another.** The sealed scope check grants a cross-mandate read only when a `SharingRule` names exactly the datum, the peer, and a scope at least as strong. That is shared data: the owner declares a rule sharing a specific datum with a specific peer at a specific scope, and that rule shares exactly that datum -- not the owner's other data, and not a wider scope than declared. `shared` visibility is a scoped, declared grant, not a public flag. The exactness is the sealed discipline's: sharing is always a specific rule, never a broad opening. **Reusing the sealed scope discipline is exactly why no standing trust bleeds across a node's data -- a rule declared for one datum grants that datum only, and an unknown datum denies -- so the storage model's scoping is the federation's own consented, per-datum access, with nothing central deciding.** The kill-target forbids standing trust across data. Composing the sealed `authorize_crossing` is how storage honors it. A declared rule authorizes exactly one datum for one peer; it does not carry to the peer's next request for a different datum, and a datum not on the record denies rather than defaulting open. There is no store-wide permission and no standing grant that spans the node's data. Each read is scoped by a rule declared for exactly that datum, by the node itself. The scoping is the sealed floor's, per-datum, consented. **The boundary of this chapter is strict: it composes the sealed `authorize_crossing` and the sealed scope-rule discipline, it invents no access control -- there is no new ACL, no new permission model, and no new sharing engine in this volume, only a datum scoped by the sealed declared-rule check.** This volume writes two functions and an invariant. The scoping mechanics -- how a declared rule grants a cross-mandate access, how own-mandate is whole -- are Vol 28 of Series 5, composed. If that floor is sound, the storage model's private/shared scoping is sound, with no new access-control code to re-audit. This is the discipline that keeps storage from smuggling in an ACL system: it delegates scoping to the audited federation floor and adds only the datum's declared visibility. **For the Ridgeline family office, this means a datum is scoped exactly like their federation crossings -- own data whole, shared data by a declared rule -- one scope discipline they already live by, so keeping a record private or sharing it with a partner is the same governed act, not a separate storage permission.** Ridgeline already scopes its federation crossings by declared rules. A stored datum now scopes the same way: the family reads its own private records whole, and shares a specific record with a partner by declaring a rule for exactly that record. There is no separate storage ACL for the family to manage, and no standing permission that spans its data. A record's privacy and its sharing are the sealed federation scope discipline, composed -- which is why the family can keep and share its data with the same rule it already trusts, and no central store deciding who reads what.

title: Vol 03 Sovereign Data Storage
chapter_title: What the Storage Model Does Not Own — Access, Identity, Encryption-at-Rest, Delivery, Monitoring
text: You will see exactly where the per-request access decision, a node's identity, encryption-at-rest, delivery between nodes, and monitoring live -- each at a real sealed or named home -- so nothing this volume leaves out floats without an address.

title: Vol 03 Sovereign Data Storage
chapter_title: What the Storage Model Does Not Own — Access, Identity, Encryption-at-Rest, Delivery, Monitoring
text: **Whether a requester is verified to reach a datum at all -- the per-request access decision -- is Zero-Trust Node Architecture (Vol 1 of Series 7), not a decision the storage model makes; storage governs the datum and its scope, it does not decide who is verified to request it.** A reader might ask where the *access* decision lives, before the scope check even applies. That is zero-trust verification, sealed earlier in this series: a node grants an access only by verifying the requester's own evidence and its own declared rule. The storage model's scope check (Ch 5) refines that to per-datum private/shared scope, but the underlying decision that a requester is verified at all is homed at Zero-Trust Node Architecture (S7 Vol 1), composed, not rebuilt here. **A node's identity -- the owner a datum is stored under -- is Trust Boundaries & Handoff (Vol 5 of Series 6), and the human gate for a material read or write is Compliance & Audit (Vol 16 of Series 5); storage names its owner and escalates a material action, it mints neither.** A datum is stored under an owner's mandate, and that owner's identity is its sealed trust anchor (S6 Vol 5). Where a read or write is material enough to need a person, the sealed `HumanApprovalGate` of Compliance & Audit (S5 Vol 16) provides the human step. Storage references the sealed identity and composes the sealed human gate; it creates no identity and builds no approval mechanism. Both are homed at their sealed floors. **Encrypting a datum's value at rest -- so the bytes are unreadable even to a holder of the disk -- composes the sealed P5 Paillier layer where a value must be computed on while encrypted (ready), and otherwise the on-disk encryption a node's own key runtime provides (OUT, designed-toward); the storage model proves integrity, it does not by itself encrypt the bytes.** The storage model makes a datum's integrity provable (the Merkle root), but confidentiality-at-rest -- encrypting the bytes -- is a distinct capability. Where a value must be operated on while encrypted, the sealed P5 Paillier layer composes (ready today). Where the bytes are simply encrypted at rest, that is the node's own key runtime -- OUT, designed-toward, because it touches live key material this proof-first floor does not. The storage model proves integrity from the bytes; encrypting them is homed at the sealed Paillier or the node's key runtime, named honestly. **Delivering a datum to another node is Receipted Inter-Node Messaging (Vol 1 of Series 6), the transport underneath is The Sovereign Port (Vol 7 of Series 6), and watching access patterns over time is Analytics & Decision Intelligence (Vol 19 of Series 5); storage governs the datum at rest, it does not carry or monitor it.** Once a shared datum is authorized to cross to a peer, carrying it is delivery -- Receipted Inter-Node Messaging (S6 Vol 1) -- over the transport the Port (S6 Vol 7) provides. Watching the pattern of reads and writes is Analytics & Decision Intelligence (S5 Vol 19), never Vol 17. Storage governs data at rest; delivery, transport, and monitoring are their own sealed floors, composed or named, and not rebuilt here. **Naming every home precisely is what makes the kill-target credible rather than merely declared -- a volume that said "no central store" while quietly leaving access, identity, encryption, delivery, and monitoring homeless would have smuggled a central store back in under a vague gesture.** The kill-target -- no central store that owns/vouches, no second trust authority, no standing trust across data -- is only as honest as the volume's willingness to say where the omitted work lives. If the access decision floated, a reader could imagine storage vouching for who may read; it does not -- access is Zero-Trust Node Architecture (S7 Vol 1). If encryption floated, a reader could imagine a storage service encrypting and holding the keys; it does not -- encryption is sealed Paillier or the node's key runtime. If delivery floated, a reader could imagine a store that also ships the data; it does not -- delivery is receipted messaging (S6 Vol 1). Every home named is a place the central store is *not*. **For the Ridgeline family office, this chapter is the map of what the rest of the architecture provides around a stored datum -- who is verified to read it, whose identity stored it, when a human must approve, how its value is encrypted, how it is delivered and monitored -- so they know storing a record is one governed act in a federation where every neighboring capability has a known, sealed or named home.** Ridgeline does not get a monolithic storage product from this volume; it gets a precise governed record and a map. The access decision is zero-trust (S7 Vol 1). The owner's identity is a sealed anchor (S6 Vol 5); a material action's human gate is compliance (S5 Vol 16). Encryption-at-rest is sealed Paillier or the family's own key runtime. Delivery is receipted messaging (S6 Vol 1); transport is the Port (S6 Vol 7); monitoring is Analytics (S5 Vol 19). The family can see the whole neighborhood of a stored datum and confirm that nowhere in it is a central store owning the data -- because every home is named, and none of them is a storage service.

title: Vol 03 Sovereign Data Storage

title: Vol 03 Sovereign Data Storage
chapter_title: Storage the Node Owns, Provable and Scoped — Synthesis and the LGP Stakes
text: **The whole of this volume resolves to a single invariant: a node's data at rest is the owner's own governed object with a provable integrity root, read only by a verified, scoped, integrity-checked access -- never a central store's to hold, scope, or vouch for.** Everything built here serves that one sentence. A datum is a governed object the owner holds (Ch 2). Retrieval is deny-by-default, scoped, and integrity-verified (Ch 3). The record is the sealed object model and the integrity the sealed P5 Merkle (Ch 4). The scope is the sealed declared-rule discipline (Ch 5). Access, identity, encryption, delivery, and monitoring are named at their homes (Ch 6). The invariant is the volume's whole claim, and every chapter is a face of it: data the owner owns, provable and scoped. **The two PRESENT functions are small and their power is borrowed honestly: `store_datum` composes the object model and the sealed P5 Merkle to make a datum the owner's own governed object with a provable root, and `retrieve_datum` reads it deny-by-default only when the access is scoped and the integrity holds.** `store_datum` registers a datum with a declared visibility and a sealed-Merkle root -- a first-class governed object of the Sovereign Object Model (S5 Vol 5) carrying a sealed P5 fingerprint. `retrieve_datum` is a deny-by-default read -- real datum, node-declared scope (`authorize_crossing`, S5 Vol 28), and an integrity match. Two functions, sealed floors composed, one invariant enforced. The volume is honest about how little it invents and precise about what that little guarantees: data owned, scoped, and provable, never stored or vouched centrally. **The kill-target held at every step: there is no central store, no second trust authority, and no standing trust across data anywhere in this volume -- each datum is the owner's own governed object, its scope the node's own declared rule, and its integrity the sealed Merkle over its bytes.** KM set the kill-target at the arm: no central store that owns/vouches, no second trust authority, no standing trust across data. The volume honors each structurally. There is no store to grep for, no attestation trusted, no standing grant spanning the node's data. The datum comes from the sealed registry; the scope is a rule the node declared per datum; the integrity is recomputed from the bytes. The central store has no place to hide in this design because every read is a per-request, scoped, integrity-checked verification of a governed object the owner holds. **This is why storage the node owns is a generational asset and not merely a feature: a federation whose data rests as governed, provable, scoped objects it holds keeps its records sovereign at rest across generations, while one that rests its data in a service inherits that service's every failure and claim to the data.** The stakes named in Ch 1 come home here. Data at rest is a generational record -- what a family or organization keeps for decades. Whether it is owned turns on where and how it rests. A federation whose data rests as governed objects it holds -- scoped by its own declaration, integrity it can prove from the bytes -- keeps its records its own across every custodian: no store owns them, no service scopes them, no authority vouches for them, and their integrity is provable years later. A federation that rests its data in a service has made its records that service's to hold and lose. The storage invariant is what keeps a federation's data sovereign at rest across the generations. **What comes next is the rest of Zero-Trust Sovereignty on this owned-data foundation -- private-versus-shared governance at scale, verified data flows across nodes, and resilience and recovery all rest on data the node owns and can prove -- so this volume is the ground the series's storage capabilities stand on.** This volume establishes that data at rest is the owner's own governed, provable, scoped object. The governance of private versus shared storage at scale builds on it; verified data flows between nodes build on it (delivering data whose integrity is provable); resilience and recovery build on it (restoring data the node can prove is intact). Each later capability assumes this foundation -- that a datum is owned, scoped, and provable at rest. The storage model is complete as a proof-first floor, and the series it serves has its owned-data ground. **For the Ridgeline family office, the volume ends where sovereign storage always aimed -- a private ledger and a shared report the family holds as governed objects, scoped by its declaration and provable from their bytes, so no service owns the records, no ACL is broadened behind the family's back, and an altered record cannot be read as sound.** Ridgeline set out to keep its data at rest without handing it to a storage service. This volume gave it the way: each record is a governed object the family holds (Ch 2), read only by a verified, scoped, integrity-checked access (Ch 3), the record and integrity riding the sealed floors (Ch 4, Ch 5), with access, identity, encryption, delivery, and monitoring each at a known home (Ch 6). The family's data at rest is owned, provable, and scoped -- sovereign storage that survives every custodian and proves itself years on, which is the whole of what this volume was for.

title: Vol 04 Verified Data Flows
chapter_title: Data Flow Trust Problems -- Why a Pipe Is Not a Guarantee
text: You will see the risks in uncontrolled data movement across nodes -- lost provenance, unverifiable integrity, compliance gaps -- and why a sovereign flow must be a governed, verified event, not a trusted pipe.

title: Vol 04 Verified Data Flows
chapter_title: Data Flow Trust Problems -- Why a Pipe Is Not a Guarantee
text: **Most systems move data between nodes through a trusted pipe -- an integration, an API call, a message bus -- and the moment the data leaves one node and arrives at another, its provenance and its integrity become assumptions rather than facts.** The sending system believes it sent the right bytes; the receiving system believes it received them intact; and between the two there is a pipe that neither fully governs. When the flow works, no one looks. When it does not -- a truncated payload, a replayed message, a silently altered field -- the failure is discovered downstream, often long after the corrupted data has been acted on. The pipe was trusted, and trust is exactly what a zero-trust node cannot extend to a flow it did not verify. **The first problem is provenance -- a flow that arrives without a verifiable statement of who sent it, under what mandate, and over what content, is a fact with no owner.** In a federation of sovereign nodes, a datum that crosses a boundary must be traceable to the node that sent it and the mandate under which it was sent, or it cannot be governed. Legacy pipes carry payloads, not provenance; the "from" field is a header a sender writes and a receiver believes. There is no governed record that binds the flow to its sender's authority. When a regulator, a partner, or a successor asks "where did this come from, and who authorized it," the honest answer is a log entry, not a proof. **The second problem is integrity -- a flow whose bytes cannot be verified against a commitment made by the sender is a payload that may have changed in transit, and nothing catches it.** Networks drop chunks; intermediaries rewrite fields; a malicious relay can alter a value and pass it on. A pipe that does not carry an integrity commitment over its content leaves the receiver to trust that what arrived is what was sent. For a financial ledger, a supply commitment, or a compliance record, that trust is misplaced: one altered byte, undetected, propagates into every decision the receiver makes on the flow. **The third problem is compliance -- when data movement is a pipe, governance is retrospective, reconstructed from logs after the fact, rather than enforced at the moment the flow is accepted.** Regulated data has rules about where it may go and who may receive it. A pipe enforces none of them; it moves whatever it is given. Compliance teams then reconstruct, from access logs and network captures, whether a flow should have happened -- weeks later, with incomplete evidence. The rule was never in force at the moment that mattered. A sovereign flow must carry its policy at acceptance, not reconstruct it at audit. **The sovereign opportunity is to stop treating a flow as a pipe and start treating it as a governed object -- a receipted, integrity-proven event that the receiver verifies against a declared policy before it accepts a single byte.** This volume builds exactly that. A flow becomes the sender's own governed object, carrying a cryptographic commitment over its content, and the receiver accepts it only when the flow is real, the acceptance is authorized by a rule the node declared, and the delivered bytes verify against the sender's commitment. Provenance is a governed record, integrity is a proof, and policy is enforced at the moment of acceptance -- deny-by-default, no standing trust across flows. **The generational stake is that data flows are how a federation's knowledge moves across time as well as space -- and knowledge that cannot prove its own provenance and integrity decays into rumor the moment the people who remember it are gone.** Lasting Generational Prosperity depends on records that a successor node can trust without trusting the intermediaries that carried them. A verified flow is that trust made structural: a successor can take a flow, check its provenance against the governed record, and verify its integrity from the bytes, without asking anyone to vouch for the pipe. The rest of this volume builds the flow as a governed object (Ch 2), its deny-by-default acceptance (Ch 3), the monitoring and reconciliation that compose over it (Ch 4-5), and the zero-knowledge privacy option that lets a flow prove a property without exposing the data (Ch 6) -- compared against legacy integration (Ch 7) and synthesized as a generational backbone (Ch 8).

title: Vol 04 Verified Data Flows
chapter_title: Receipted and Verifiable Flow Design -- declare_flow
text: You will make a data flow a governed object under the sender's own mandate, carrying a sealed-P5 Merkle integrity root over its content, so the flow's provenance and integrity are provable from its own bytes -- not a trusted pipe.

title: Vol 04 Verified Data Flows
chapter_title: Receipted and Verifiable Flow Design -- declare_flow
text: **A data flow that can be governed must first be a governed object -- attributed to a sender, addressed to a target, and committed to its content -- and `declare_flow` is the act that makes it one.** In legacy integration, a flow is a transient event in a pipe; there is no object to point at afterward. This volume begins by making the flow durable and attributable. `declare_flow(reg, source, target, chunks, *, mandate, author, source_ref, at)` records the flow as a governed object on the sealed object registry, under the sender's own mandate, carrying the source, the target, and a cryptographic commitment over the content. The flow stops being a pipe event and becomes a fact the federation can verify. **`declare_flow` writes the flow as the sender's OWN governed object, composing the sealed object registry's append under the sender's mandate -- so a flow exists only because the sender, acting under its own authority, declared it.** The function calls `reg.append(f"flow:{source}->{target}:...", payload, mandate=mandate, kind="ratify")` -- the same sealed registry the whole object model is built on. The flow is ratified under the sender's mandate; no central flow authority mints it, and no other node can declare a flow on the sender's behalf. This is the first line against a second trust authority: the flow's provenance is the sender's own mandate on the sealed record, not a broker's assertion. **The flow carries a Merkle integrity root over its canonical chunks -- computed via the sealed P5 `MerkleTree` -- so its integrity is provable from its own bytes, not from trust in the pipe that carried it.** The payload records `{"source": source, "target": target, "root": _merkle_root(chunks)}`, where `_merkle_root` composes the sealed P5 `MerkleTree` (vendored in-tree, via the `_lazy_bp` boundary) over the flow's content. The root is a commitment: any receiver holding the delivered bytes can recompute the root and compare. If they match, the bytes are exactly what the sender committed to; if a single chunk was altered or dropped, the roots diverge. The flow's integrity travels with the flow, as a proof, not as a hope. **An empty source, an empty target, or empty content is refused -- there is no anonymous flow, no flow to nowhere, and no empty flow -- so every governed flow names its two ends and commits to real content.** `declare_flow` raises `FlowError` if `source` is empty (a flow needs a sender), if `target` is empty (a flow needs a destination), or if `chunks` is empty (a flow needs content to commit to). These are not conveniences; they are the minimum for a flow to be governable. A flow with no sender cannot be attributed; a flow with no target cannot be scoped; a flow with no content cannot be verified. The refusals keep the governed record free of un-anchorable flows. **The volume rolls no cryptography of its own -- the integrity commitment is the sealed P5 Merkle, composed through the runtime boundary, so a flow's integrity inherits an audited foundation rather than a new, unproven scheme.** `verified_flow.py` imports `MerkleTree` from `_lazy_bp` and computes roots; it implements no hash, no tree, no signature. The integrity guarantee is exactly the sealed P5 Merkle's guarantee, and the module fails loud if that substrate is absent. This is the maturity-honesty discipline: the flow is receipted and integrity-proven because the sealed foundation provides the proof, and the volume claims nothing the foundation does not back. **In the acceptance test, a sender declares a flow and the governed object carries its source, target, and a real Merkle root, and each of the three empty-input cases is refused -- so the declaration is executable, not asserted.** `test_declare_flow_registers_governed_object_with_root` declares `nodeA -> nodeB` over real chunks and asserts the object id, the version hash, and a non-empty root. `test_declare_flow_refuses_empty` proves an empty source, an empty target, and empty content each raise `FlowError`. The flow-as-governed-object is proven in code, in the suite pushed to the starter -- not a claim in prose. **For the Ridgeline federation, `declare_flow` is the moment a member node sends a batch of records to a partner and, instead of pushing them down a pipe, mints a governed flow that names both ends and commits to every byte -- so the partner, and any auditor after, can prove exactly what was sent and that it arrived intact.** When Ridgeline sends a settlement file, a supply commitment, or a compliance extract, the legacy path trusts the transport. This volume gives it a governed flow: the file is the sender's own ratified object, carrying a Merkle root over its content. The partner verifies the bytes against the root; a regulator, years later, verifies the same. The pipe is no longer trusted, because the flow proves itself. The next chapter builds the deny-by-default acceptance that decides whether the partner may accept it at all.

title: Vol 04 Verified Data Flows
chapter_title: Governed Flow Policies -- verify_flow, Deny by Default
text: You will accept a flow deny-by-default -- the receiver must have declared a scope rule for exactly this flow, and the delivered bytes must verify against the flow's Merkle root -- so an unpolicied flow is refused and a flow altered in transit is refused.

title: Vol 04 Verified Data Flows
chapter_title: Governed Flow Policies -- verify_flow, Deny by Default
text: **Accepting a data flow must be a decision the receiver makes -- verifying that it declared a policy for exactly this flow and that the bytes are intact -- not a pipe delivering a payload the receiver never governed, and `verify_flow` is that decision.** Once a flow is a governed object (Ch 2), a receiver does not accept it because it arrived; it accepts it because it verifies. `verify_flow(reg, flow, rules, presented_chunks, *, principal_mandate, want)` is the verification. It returns an acceptance only when the flow is real, the acceptance is authorized by a rule the node declared, and the delivered bytes verify against the flow's committed root. Its default, when any of those fails, is refusal. A flow is accepted by the receiver's own governance, not by the pipe. **`verify_flow` is deny-by-default and fail-closed, checking its conditions in order -- a real governed flow, then a node-declared policy, then an integrity match -- so acceptance is impossible unless all three hold.** The function is deny-first. It confirms there is a real governed flow to accept (a `version_hash` and object id). It confirms the acceptance is authorized by a node-declared scope rule for exactly this flow and requester. It verifies the delivered bytes against the flow's stored Merkle root. Each failure raises `FlowError`; the default across all of them is no acceptance. This is the difference from a pipe: a pipe delivers if the connection is open; `verify_flow` accepts nothing until policy and integrity are both verified for this flow. **The acceptance must be authorized by a node-declared scope rule naming exactly this flow and requester -- composing the sealed `authorize_crossing` -- so own-mandate acceptance is whole, a cross-node acceptance needs a declared rule, and there is no standing trust across flows.** `authorize_crossing(reg, rules, principal_mandate=..., obj_id=flow["object_id"], want=...)` decides. The receiver's own-mandate acceptance is whole; a cross-node acceptance needs a `SharingRule` the receiver declared naming exactly this flow. A flow the node never declared a policy for is refused. And the policy is per-flow: a rule for one flow does not authorize another. There is no standing trust that lets a stream of flows through on the strength of one -- each is authorized only by a rule declared for it. The policy is the sealed federation-governance check, composed. **The delivered bytes must verify against the flow's stored Merkle root -- recomputed via the sealed foundation's `MerkleTree` -- so a flow whose content was altered or truncated in transit is refused before it is accepted.** After the policy check, `verify_flow` recomputes `MerkleTree(presented_chunks).get_root()` and compares it to the root the flow committed (Ch 2). If they match, the bytes are exactly what the sender committed to and the flow is accepted; if they differ -- one altered byte, one dropped chunk -- the roots diverge and the acceptance is refused. Integrity is verified in transit from the flow's own commitment, not trusted to the pipe. A flow that changed on the wire cannot be accepted as if it were sound. **There is no hub that vouches anywhere in `verify_flow` -- the flow is the sender's governed object, the policy is the receiver's own declared rule, and the integrity is the sealed Merkle over the bytes -- so the kill-target holds: a flow is accepted by the receiver's verification, never by an intermediary's assurance.** The kill-target for this volume is explicit: no second trust authority, no central attestation, no hub that vouches. `verify_flow` honors each structurally. The flow comes from the sealed registry -- not a broker. The policy is a rule the receiver declared -- not a hub's attestation. The integrity is recomputed from the bytes -- not a relay's assurance. A grep of the module for a vouching authority or a standing-trust cache returns nothing. A flow is accepted by verification, and nothing central vouches for it. **In the acceptance test, a node accepts its own flow with integrity verified, a peer accepts a cross-node flow only with a declared scope rule, a peer with no rule is refused, tampered bytes are refused, and a non-flow is refused -- each raising `FlowError` on failure.** `test_verify_flow_own_mandate_integrity_verified` accepts an own-mandate flow. `test_verify_flow_cross_node_needs_declared_policy` proves a peer with no rule is refused and with a declared `SharingRule` is accepted. `test_verify_flow_denies_tampered_in_transit` proves altered bytes are refused (Merkle mismatch). `test_verify_flow_refuses_no_real_flow` proves accepting nothing raises. Deny-by-default, policy, and integrity are executable, not asserted. **For the Ridgeline federation, `verify_flow` is the moment a partner node receives an inbound file and, instead of ingesting whatever the pipe delivered, checks that it declared a policy for exactly this flow and that every byte verifies -- so a spoofed sender, an unpolicied stream, or a corrupted payload is refused at the boundary.** When a partner receives a settlement or a supply file, the legacy path ingests what arrives and reconciles problems later. This volume gives it a governed acceptance: the partner accepts only a flow it declared a policy for, and only if the bytes verify against the sender's commitment. An unpolicied flow is refused; a tampered flow is refused. There is no hub to vouch and no standing trust to exploit -- the partner accepts a flow only by its own policy and verification. Chapters 4 and 5 compose the monitoring and reconciliation that watch these flows over time.

title: Vol 04 Verified Data Flows
chapter_title: Real-Time Flow Monitoring -- Composed, Not Connected
text: You will monitor cross-node flows with governed visibility by composing the sealed Analytics & Decision Intelligence floor over the flow receipts -- this volume connects nothing and stores nothing; it emits governed flows that a sealed floor observes.

title: Vol 04 Verified Data Flows
chapter_title: Real-Time Flow Monitoring -- Composed, Not Connected
text: **Monitoring cross-node data movement, in a sovereign system, means observing the governed receipts a flow already produces -- not tapping a pipe or standing up a new surveillance layer -- and this chapter is explicit that the monitoring is composed from a sealed floor, not built here.** Because a flow is a governed object with a receipt (Ch 2) and a verified acceptance outcome (Ch 3), it is already observable: every flow leaves a record of its provenance, the policy that authorized it, and whether its integrity held. Real-time monitoring is the act of reading those records as they land. This volume does not build a monitor; it makes flows observable and homes the observation at the sealed Analytics floor. **The observable surface is the flow receipts themselves -- each carries its source and target, the policy decision that accepted or refused it, and the integrity outcome -- so monitoring reads governed facts, not intercepted traffic.** A monitor that taps the wire sees bytes it must interpret and trust. A monitor that reads flow receipts sees governed facts: this flow was declared by this sender under this mandate, accepted (or refused) under this policy, and verified (or failed) against its Merkle root. The receipts are the truth the flow already committed to. Monitoring them requires no new interception and no new trust -- it reads the same governed record the federation is built on. **Real-time visibility over these receipts composes the sealed Analytics and Decision Intelligence floor (S5 Vol 19) -- the observation, aggregation, and dashboarding of governed events -- so this volume adds no monitoring engine of its own.** Analytics and Decision Intelligence is the sealed floor for consuming governed events and turning them into operational awareness. Flow receipts are governed events; Analytics consumes them. The flow monitoring surface -- volumes moving, acceptance rates, integrity-failure counts -- is Analytics reading flow receipts, homed at S5 Vol 19. This volume connects nothing to a dashboard; it emits governed flows, and the sealed Analytics floor observes them. Naming the home honestly keeps the claim exact: monitoring is composed, not built here. **Anomaly detection and alerting are governed decisions on the flow receipts -- a spike in integrity failures, a flow from an unexpected sender, a policy refusal rate that jumps -- and they home at the same sealed Analytics floor, not a new alerting system.** An anomaly is a pattern in the receipts, and a decision about a pattern is exactly what Decision Intelligence provides. When integrity failures spike, when a sender that never sent before starts sending, when refusals climb, the signal is in the receipts and the decision is Analytics'. This volume does not decide what is anomalous; it produces the governed receipts that make anomalies detectable, and the sealed floor detects them. The alert, when it fires, is a governed decision with its own audit trail -- not a side-channel notification from a pipe tap. **The Atrium monitoring lens is a surface, not a capability -- where an operator watches flows across the federation is the sovereign surface, and this volume homes it there rather than building a console.** A human watching flow health needs a lens, and that lens is the sovereign surface at six-sov.com/seeit, composing the Analytics floor's flow view. This volume builds no console and no visualization; it makes flows observable and names the surface. The distinction matters for maturity honesty: the monitoring the reader gets is real because Analytics is sealed and the surface exists, and this volume claims exactly that composition and no monitoring engine of its own. **Because monitoring is composed and not built, the kill-target holds trivially here -- there is no second trust authority in an observation, no central attestation in a dashboard, and no hub that vouches in an alert -- the monitor reads governed receipts the flows already own.** The risk in a monitoring chapter is inventing a central observer that becomes the thing everyone trusts. This volume refuses it. The monitor is the sealed Analytics floor reading governed flow receipts; it vouches for nothing, attests nothing, and holds no standing trust. The flows own their own provenance and integrity; Analytics merely observes. There is no monitoring hub to compromise because there is no monitoring hub -- only a sealed floor composing governed events. **For the Ridgeline federation, flow monitoring is the operations view where a steward watches settlement and supply flows move across member nodes in real time -- and every number on that view traces to a governed flow receipt, so the view cannot show a flow that did not really happen or hide one that did.** When Ridgeline's steward watches the federation's flows, the legacy path shows a dashboard fed by pipe taps the steward must trust. This volume gives a view fed by governed receipts: every flow shown is a real governed object with a verifiable provenance and integrity outcome, composed into the Analytics floor's lens at the sovereign surface. The steward sees the truth the flows committed to, not a monitor's interpretation. Chapter 5 composes the reconciliation that resolves conflicts when two nodes' views of a flow disagree.

title: Vol 04 Verified Data Flows
chapter_title: Conflict and Reconciliation in Flows -- Composed Against Declared Roots
text: You will detect and resolve conflicts in distributed flows by composing the sealed Federation Node Governance root reconciliation -- conflicts resolve against declared roots and a human witness where material, not a central arbiter.

title: Vol 04 Verified Data Flows
chapter_title: Conflict and Reconciliation in Flows -- Composed Against Declared Roots
text: **In a federation, two nodes can end up with divergent records of the same flow -- one accepted it, one refused it; one holds one version, one holds another -- and a sovereign system must make that divergence detectable and resolved against declared roots, not paper it over with a central arbiter's ruling.** Distributed flows create distributed state, and distributed state diverges. A flow accepted by one node and refused by another, a flow whose bytes one node verified and another did not, a replay that one node caught and another missed -- these are conflicts. This chapter is explicit that the volume detects conflicts through the governed receipts and homes their resolution at the sealed federation floors, building no arbiter of its own. **A flow conflict is a divergence between two nodes' governed records, and because both records are governed objects with roots, the divergence is detectable by comparing roots -- not by trusting one node's word over another's.** When two nodes disagree about a flow, each holds a governed record with a verifiable root. The conflict is the mismatch between those roots. It is not a matter of opinion or of whose log is more trusted; it is a cryptographic divergence, visible to anyone holding both roots. This is why the flow-as-governed-object matters for conflict: it turns a "he-said-she-said" between nodes into a comparison of commitments, where the divergence is a fact, not a dispute. **Reconciliation composes the sealed Federation Node Governance root reconciliation (`reconcile_roots`, S5 Vol 28) -- the sealed mechanism that compares two nodes' roots and identifies the divergence -- so this volume adds no reconciliation engine and no arbiter.** The sealed federation floor already provides `reconcile_roots`, which takes two nodes' roots and reports whether they agree and where they diverge. Flow reconciliation is exactly this mechanism applied to flow records: compare the roots, find the divergence, and resolve it against the governed history. This volume composes that sealed mechanism; it does not build a second one. There is no central arbiter that rules on conflicts, because the reconciliation is against declared, verifiable roots -- the divergence resolves to what the governed records prove, not to what an authority decides. **A material conflict -- one whose resolution changes a financial, compliance, or supply outcome -- is witnessed by a human gate, composing the sealed Compliance and Audit floor (S5 Vol 16), so a consequential reconciliation is never silent or automatic.** Some conflicts are mechanical and resolve to the governed record without human involvement. Others are material: a settlement amount, a compliance record, a supply commitment. For those, the resolution passes through the sealed human-approval gate -- a named human ratifies the reconciled outcome, deny-by-default, with a receipt. This volume does not build that gate; it composes the sealed Compliance and Audit floor for the witness. A material flow conflict is resolved with a human in the loop and an audit trail, exactly as the sealed floor enforces. **No central arbiter decides a flow conflict -- reconciliation is against declared, verifiable roots and, where material, a human witness -- so the kill-target holds: no second trust authority resolves conflicts by fiat.** The temptation in a reconciliation chapter is to build a central conflict-resolution service that everyone must trust to rule fairly. This volume refuses it. Conflicts resolve against the governed records both nodes hold, using the sealed `reconcile_roots`; material conflicts add a sealed human gate. No service adjudicates; no authority's ruling overrides the records. The resolution is what the verifiable roots and the witnessed decision prove -- there is no arbiter to capture, because there is no arbiter. **Because detection uses the receipts and resolution composes sealed floors, this volume's contribution to conflict handling is precise and bounded -- it makes flows conflicts detectable via their governed roots and names the sealed reconciliation and human-witness homes, and it builds neither.** The honest statement of this chapter is a composition: flow records carry roots (Ch 2), which make divergences detectable; `reconcile_roots` (S5 Vol 28) resolves them against the records; the human gate (S5 Vol 16) witnesses material ones. This volume's own code declares and verifies flows; the reconciliation and the witness are sealed floors it composes. Naming those homes -- specific sealed volumes, not a vague "the system handles it" -- keeps the claim exact and refuses a soft-home into an unbuilt arbiter. **For the Ridgeline federation, flow reconciliation is what happens when two member nodes disagree about a settlement flow -- their governed roots are compared, the divergence is found, and a material difference is ratified by a named human with a receipt -- so a conflict resolves to what the records prove, not to whichever node argues hardest.** When two Ridgeline nodes disagree about a flow, the legacy path escalates to whoever administers the integration, who rules from logs. This volume gives a governed reconciliation: the nodes' roots are compared by the sealed `reconcile_roots`, the divergence is a fact, and a material resolution passes the sealed human gate. The conflict resolves against verifiable records and a witnessed decision -- no arbiter, no fiat. Chapter 6 builds the zero-knowledge privacy option that lets a flow prove a property without revealing the data behind it.

title: Vol 04 Verified Data Flows
chapter_title: The Zero-Knowledge Privacy Option -- attest_flow_clears, Proving Without Revealing
text: You will let a flow prove a property -- that a private quantity clears a stated minimum -- without revealing the quantity, composing the sealed P5 zero-knowledge shield (Pedersen commitment + range proof), so a flow satisfies a compliance rule while keeping its payload private.

title: Vol 04 Verified Data Flows
chapter_title: The Zero-Knowledge Privacy Option -- attest_flow_clears, Proving Without Revealing
text: **Some flows must prove a property to be accepted -- that a payment clears a threshold, that a pool meets its minimum, that a match is valid -- and yet the underlying quantity is private, so the flow must prove the property WITHOUT revealing the number, and `attest_flow_clears` is that proof.** A verified flow (Ch 2-3) proves provenance and integrity, but sometimes compliance needs more: the receiver must know a flow satisfies a rule -- clears a minimum -- without the sender exposing the actual figure. A member proving its pooled commitment clears the threshold must not have to reveal its budget. This chapter builds the zero-knowledge privacy option: a flow proves it clears a stated minimum, and the verifier learns only that it clears, never by how much or from what. **`attest_flow_clears` commits the flow's private quantity with a Pedersen commitment and proves the committed value clears the minimum with a range proof over the difference -- so the property is proven and the quantity stays hidden.** The function commits the quantity as `C = quantity*G + r*H` (a Pedersen commitment, which hides the quantity), forms the difference commitment `C - minimum*G` (which commits to `quantity - minimum`), and produces a range proof that this difference lies in `[0, 2^bits)` -- i.e. that `quantity >= minimum`. The output is the commitment and the proof. The quantity never appears; only the commitment (which reveals nothing) and a proof that the hidden value clears the bar. An honest prover cannot prove a false clearance: `attest_flow_clears` refuses to build a proof when `quantity < minimum`. **The proof composes the sealed P5 zero-knowledge shield -- Pedersen commitment, Schnorr, and the range proof -- PRESENT via the authorized ZK overlay, so this volume rolls no cryptography of its own; it composes an audited, executable foundation at its honest maturity.** The zero-knowledge primitives are the sealed P5 ZK layer, made executable under the authorized overlay: the Pedersen commitment and the bit-decomposition range proof (each committed bit proven zero-or-one by a Schnorr OR-proof, the bits bound to the commitment). `verified_flow.py` writes no cryptography; it calls the sealed ZK. The maturity is stated plainly: Pedersen, Schnorr, and Range are PRESENT and tested via the authorized overlay -- the volume composes them and claims exactly that, no more. **`verify_flow_clears` verifies the clearance proof from the public commitment alone -- reconstructing the difference commitment and checking the range proof -- so the verifier confirms the flow clears the minimum while learning nothing about the quantity.** The verifier holds the commitment and the proof, reconstructs `C - minimum*G`, and verifies the range proof against it. If it verifies, the flow provably clears the minimum; if the proof is malformed, tampered, or bound to a different minimum, verification fails, deny-by-default. The verifier never sees the quantity -- only that the hidden value clears the bar it named. This is the privacy option's whole point: a compliance property is checked without the data behind it ever crossing the boundary. **This chapter lands the zero-knowledge privacy option that the Distribution Matrix Governance volume homed here (Distribution Matrix Governance, S5 Vol 6) and discharges the clears-the-minimum clause that Situational Supply and Distributed Manufacturing homed at the S7 series -- prove a pool clears its minimum, or a match is valid, without exposing any member's budget or position.** Distribution Matrix Governance (S5 Vol 6, Ch 6) named its zero-knowledge privacy options as homing at S7 Vol 4; this chapter delivers them. Situational Supply (S5 Vol 40) and Distributed Manufacturing (S5 Vol 41) each named a ZK-shielded form -- proving a pool clears the minimum without exposing budgets, proving a demand-capacity match without exposing either side -- as homing at the S7 series; `attest_flow_clears` is that clears-without-exposure proof, volume-pinned here as Pedersen + Schnorr + Range PRESENT. The Atrium federation lens that Distribution Matrix Governance (S5 Vol 6) also named is a surface, homed at six-sov.com/seeit (OUT). **In the acceptance test, a flow that clears the minimum proves it and verifies true, a flow below the minimum cannot produce a proof, a proof checked against the wrong minimum fails, and a tampered proof fails -- so proving-without-revealing is executable and sound, not asserted.** `test_attest_flow_clears_zero_knowledge` proves a quantity of 120 clears a minimum of 100 and verifies, with the quantity hidden. `test_attest_flow_clears_refuses_below_minimum` proves a quantity below the minimum cannot build a clearance proof. `test_verify_flow_clears_rejects_wrong_minimum` and `test_verify_flow_clears_rejects_tampered_proof` prove soundness -- a proof for one minimum does not verify against another, and a tampered proof is refused. The privacy option is proven in code, composing the sealed ZK overlay. **For the Ridgeline federation, the zero-knowledge privacy option is how a member proves its committed share clears the pool's minimum -- so the valley knows the pool will form -- without any member exposing its budget to the others, ending the choice between proving viability and protecting privacy.** When Ridgeline pools demand to found a supply response, the legacy path forces each member to reveal its commitment for the pool to prove it clears -- exposing budgets to coercion or price discrimination. This volume gives the members `attest_flow_clears`: each proves its share clears without revealing it, and the valley verifies the pool clears without seeing any figure. Viability and privacy hold together. Chapters 7 and 8 compare verified flows to legacy integration and synthesize the volume as a generational trust backbone.

title: Vol 04 Verified Data Flows
text: You will compare sovereign verified flows against traditional integration -- pipes, ETL, and message buses -- seeing where the sovereign model's per-flow provenance, integrity, and privacy hold guarantees that trusted pipes cannot.

title: Vol 04 Verified Data Flows
text: **Legacy integration -- the API pipe, the ETL job, the message bus -- moves data by trusting the channel: the sender trusts the pipe to deliver, the receiver trusts the pipe to have delivered honestly, and the governance is reconstructed afterward from logs.** These technologies are mature and fast, and for decades they have been how enterprises move data between systems. But their trust model is the channel. A pipe delivers whatever it is given; an ETL job transforms whatever it reads; a bus routes whatever is published. Provenance is a header, integrity is assumed, and policy is a review after the fact. For systems inside one trust boundary, that is often acceptable. Across sovereign nodes that do not trust each other, it is exactly the wrong model. **A verified flow inverts the trust model -- it proves provenance from the sender's mandate, verifies integrity from the flow's own commitment, and enforces policy at the moment of acceptance -- so the receiver trusts its own verification, not the channel.** Where a pipe assumes, a verified flow proves. The flow is the sender's governed object (provenance), carries a Merkle root (integrity), and is accepted only by a rule the receiver declared (policy). None of this trusts the transport: the same guarantees hold whether the flow crossed a trusted network or a hostile one, because the proof travels with the flow. This is the zero-trust posture applied to data movement -- never trust the pipe, always verify the flow. **The sovereign model composes sealed floors rather than introducing a new integration engine to trust -- the registry, the federation scope check, the P5 Merkle, and the P5 ZK -- so adopting verified flows adds guarantees without adding a new central dependency.** A common objection to a new integration model is that it becomes one more engine everyone must trust. Verified flows avoid this: the module composes the sealed object registry, the sealed `authorize_crossing`, the sealed P5 Merkle, and the sealed P5 ZK. It introduces no broker, no bus, no central service. The guarantees come from audited, sealed foundations, and the flow logic is a thin governed layer over them. There is nothing new to trust -- only sealed floors composed at their honest maturity. **The honest scope is that verified flows govern movement -- they do not replace the transport that carries bytes or the transformation that reshapes them -- so the sovereign model composes, rather than competes with, the mechanics of integration.** A verified flow does not move bytes; delivery and transport are Receipted Inter-Node Messaging (S6 Vol 1) and the Port (S6 Vol 7). It does not transform data; a flow's content is committed as-is. What it governs is the movement's provenance, integrity, and policy. This is the boundary the volume holds against overclaim: verified flows are the governance layer over movement, not a new pipe or a new ETL engine. The reader gets exactly a governance guarantee, and the transport and transformation stay where they honestly live. **Migration guidance is to wrap existing pipes as governed flows and verify at acceptance -- so a node adopts verified flows incrementally, gaining provenance and integrity without ripping out its transport.** A node need not replace its message bus or its API integrations to adopt verified flows. It wraps what a pipe carries as a governed flow: declare the flow (Ch 2) as the payload leaves, verify the flow (Ch 3) as it arrives. The transport is unchanged; the governance is added at the two ends. Over time, the receipts accumulate into a governed history the node can monitor (Ch 4), reconcile (Ch 5), and prove properties over (Ch 6). The migration is additive -- verified flows govern the movement the existing pipes already perform. **The realism is that per-flow verification has a cost -- a commitment to compute, a policy to declare, a proof to check -- and the sovereign model pays it deliberately where the guarantee is worth it, not everywhere by default.** Verifying every flow is not free: the Merkle root is computed, the policy is evaluated, and a ZK proof, where used, is generated and checked. For high-volume, low-stakes internal traffic, a trusted pipe may remain the right choice. For cross-node flows where provenance, integrity, and privacy matter -- settlement, compliance, supply commitments -- the verification cost buys a guarantee no pipe can. The sovereign model is honest about the tradeoff: it governs the flows that warrant governing, and it names the cost rather than hiding it. **For the Ridgeline federation, the choice between a trusted pipe and a verified flow is the choice between reconstructing what happened after a dispute and proving what happened at the moment it did -- and for the flows that carry money, compliance, and supply, the valley chooses proof.** Ridgeline keeps its ordinary integrations for ordinary traffic. But for the flows that matter -- a settlement between members, a compliance extract to a regulator, a supply commitment to a partner -- it wraps them as verified flows: provenance from the sender's mandate, integrity from the Merkle root, policy at acceptance, and privacy from the ZK proof where a figure must stay hidden. When a dispute comes, the valley does not reconstruct from logs; it verifies from proofs. Chapter 8 synthesizes verified flows as the trust backbone a federation carries across generations.

title: Vol 04 Verified Data Flows
chapter_title: Verified Flows as a Generational Trust Backbone
text: You will see verified flows synthesized as the trust backbone of a sovereign federation -- every movement of data a governed, verifiable event -- so a federation's knowledge moves across nodes and across generations without trusting the pipes that carried it.

title: Vol 04 Verified Data Flows
chapter_title: Verified Flows as a Generational Trust Backbone
text: **This volume built one thing -- data movement between nodes as a governed, verifiable event -- and everything in it composes from that single idea: a flow is the sender's own governed object, carrying its own integrity, accepted only by the receiver's own policy, and able to prove a property without exposing the data.** The chapters are one capability seen from its faces: declare a flow as a governed object with integrity (Ch 2), accept it deny-by-default by policy and verification (Ch 3), monitor it by composing Analytics (Ch 4), reconcile conflicts against declared roots (Ch 5), and prove a compliance property in zero knowledge (Ch 6). The synthesis is that a federation no longer trusts pipes -- it verifies flows. **The volume rolls no cryptography and builds no transport -- `declare_flow`, `verify_flow`, and `attest_flow_clears` compose the sealed object registry, the sealed federation scope check, the sealed P5 Merkle, and the sealed P5 ZK -- so verified flows inherit audited foundations rather than adding unproven machinery.** The honest account of the volume's construction is a list of compositions. The governed record is the sealed registry. The policy is the sealed `authorize_crossing`. The integrity is the sealed P5 Merkle. The privacy is the sealed P5 ZK, Pedersen and Range PRESENT via the authorized overlay. The flow module adds the thin governance layer that turns these into a verified flow -- and nothing else. There is no connector engine, no message bus, no cryptography of its own. The capability is real because the floors beneath it are sealed and proven. **Verified flows integrate with the rest of the federation -- messaging and the Port carry the bytes, storage holds the data at rest, zero-trust node architecture decides the access, and analytics observes the movement -- so a flow is one governed act within a sovereign system, not an island.** A verified flow is where several sealed capabilities meet: Receipted Inter-Node Messaging (S6 Vol 1) and the Port (S6 Vol 7) deliver the bytes; the Sovereign Data Storage Model (S7 Vol 3) holds the data at rest; Zero-Trust Node Architecture (S7 Vol 1) decides who may access; Analytics (S5 Vol 19) monitors. Verified flows govern the movement between these, composing each at its sealed home. The federation is coherent because each capability is a governed floor and the flows verify the movement across them. **The generational handoff is that a successor node can verify a flow from its proofs alone -- provenance from the governed record, integrity from the Merkle root, a property from the ZK proof -- without trusting any intermediary that carried it or any person who remembers it.** This is the deepest reason verified flows matter for Lasting Generational Prosperity. When a federation passes to a new generation of stewards and nodes, the flows in its history are either trustworthy or they are rumor. A verified flow is trustworthy by construction: a successor takes the flow, checks its provenance against the governed record, verifies its integrity from the bytes, and confirms its properties from the proofs -- with no living witness required. The knowledge survives the people, because the flows carry their own proof. **The final synthesis is that knowledge which carries its own proof endures across generations, and knowledge that depends on trusted pipes decays the moment the trust is gone -- so a sovereign federation makes its data movement verifiable precisely so its knowledge can outlast the systems and the people that produced it.** A federation's prosperity is cumulative: each generation builds on the records the last one left. If those records moved through trusted pipes, their provenance and integrity are only as good as the memory of the people who trusted the pipes -- and memory fades. Verified flows make the record self-proving. A settlement, a commitment, a compliance fact, moved as a verified flow, can be checked by anyone, anytime, from the proof. That is how a federation's knowledge compounds across generations instead of decaying: every movement of data is a governed, verifiable event, and the proof outlives the pipe. **For the Ridgeline federation, verified flows are the backbone that lets the valley's knowledge -- who settled what, who committed to which supply, who proved they cleared the minimum -- pass intact to the stewards who come after, so the next generation inherits provable facts rather than trusted logs.** When Ridgeline hands its federation to the next generation, it hands over a history of flows. Because each flow is verified -- provenance, integrity, policy, and privacy proven -- the successors inherit facts they can check, not logs they must trust. The valley's cumulative knowledge, its record of who did what across decades, is a chain of governed, verifiable events. The pipes that carried them are long forgotten; the proofs remain. That is the trust backbone this volume built: data movement made verifiable, so the federation's knowledge endures.

title: Vol 05 Private Shared Storage Governance
chapter_title: The Private vs Shared Dilemma -- Who Owns the Boundary
text: You will see the tension between privacy, collaboration, and compliance in storage -- and why a sovereign node must make the private/shared boundary a governed classification it owns, not a central store's policy.

title: Vol 05 Private Shared Storage Governance
chapter_title: The Private vs Shared Dilemma -- Who Owns the Boundary
text: **Every federation lives on a contradiction it cannot escape: some of its data must stay strictly private, and some must be shared to collaborate -- and where the line between them is drawn, and who may move it, decides who really owns the data.** A family office keeps its ledger private and shares a summary with a partner. A supply network keeps its costs private and shares its capacity. The value is in both the privacy and the sharing, and the danger is in the boundary between them. Draw the line in a central store, and the store owns the line. This volume is about drawing that line as a governance the node holds, not a permission a store grants. **In a central store, the boundary between private and shared is the store's access-control list -- a policy the store enforces, the store can broaden, and the store is trusted to honor -- so the data's owner does not actually control who sees it.** A store scopes data by an ACL: this user may read, that group may not. The ACL is the store's, administered by whoever runs the store. The owner asks the store to keep something private and trusts it to comply. But an ACL is a convention the store enforces; a misconfiguration, a broadened permission, or a compromised admin exposes what was meant to be private. The owner never held the boundary -- the store did. **Compliance for data ownership is retrospective when a store scopes the data -- an audit reconstructs, after the fact, whether a datum should have been shared, rather than the classification being in force at every read.** Regulated data has rules about what may be shared with whom. When a store's ACL scopes it, compliance teams reconstruct from access logs whether each share was permitted -- weeks later, incompletely. The classification was never a governed fact enforced at the moment of access; it was an ACL entry someone set. A sovereign system must make the private/shared classification a governed property of the datum itself, checked at every access, not audited afterward. **The sovereign opportunity is to make the private/shared boundary a governed classification the owner declares and holds -- private, shared, or hybrid -- so that who may see a datum is a property of the datum, checked at every access, not a store's ACL.** This volume builds exactly that. Each datum is the owner's own governed object carrying a declared visibility: private, shared, or hybrid. A private datum is never shareable across mandates. A shared or hybrid datum is accessible only by a scope rule the owner declared for exactly it. The classification travels with the datum, enforced deny-by-default at every read, and no store administers it. The owner holds the boundary, because the boundary is a governed classification, not a permission. **This is the built topology behind the idea of a distribution matrix -- which data is private and which is shared or federated is not a diagram or a convention but a governed classification on the sealed object model, declared per datum and enforced at access.** A "distribution matrix" or "resonant shard" pattern is often drawn as an architecture diagram: these shards here are private, those are shared. This volume makes that diagram a built fact. The partition is `classify_datum` recording each datum's visibility as a governed object; the sharing is `govern_shared_access` granting a scoped read only by a declared rule. The matrix is not a picture of how data is distributed -- it is the governed classification that distributes it, per datum, provable and enforced. **The generational stake is that a federation's data outlives the stores that hold it, and data whose ownership is a store's permission decays into whatever the next store's ACL says -- while data classified as a governed property the owner holds keeps its ownership provable across every custodian.** When a federation's data passes to a new generation, or migrates to a new store, its private/shared classification either travels with it as a governed fact or is re-derived from whatever the new store decides. A store's ACL does not survive the store. A governed classification does: a successor reads each datum's declared visibility and enforces it, with no store to trust. That is why the boundary must be the owner's governed classification -- so a federation's data ownership compounds across generations instead of resetting with each store. The rest of this volume builds the classification (Ch 2), private governance (Ch 3), shared governance (Ch 4), hybrid models (Ch 5), compliance (Ch 6), a comparison to legacy storage (Ch 7), and the generational synthesis (Ch 8).

title: Vol 05 Private Shared Storage Governance
text: You will classify a datum as private, shared, or hybrid -- a governed object under the owner's own mandate carrying a declared visibility and a sealed-P5 Merkle integrity root -- so the private/shared partition is a built classification, not a store's ACL.

title: Vol 05 Private Shared Storage Governance
text: **A private/shared boundary that the owner controls must first be a governed classification carried by the datum itself -- and `classify_datum` is the act that records it.** In a central store, a datum's visibility is an ACL entry the store holds. This volume moves the classification onto the datum: `classify_datum(reg, owner, chunks, *, visibility, mandate, author, source_ref, at)` records the datum as a governed object on the sealed registry, under the owner's own mandate, carrying its declared visibility and a Merkle root over its content. The datum's classification stops being a store's permission and becomes a governed property the owner holds. **`classify_datum` records the datum as the owner's OWN governed object, composing the sealed object registry's append under the owner's mandate -- so a datum's classification exists only because the owner, acting under its own authority, declared it.** The function calls `reg.append(f"datum:{owner}:...", payload, mandate=mandate, kind="ratify")` -- the same sealed registry the object model is built on. The classification is ratified under the owner's mandate; no central classification authority assigns it, and no store administers it. This is the first line against a second classification authority: a datum's visibility is the owner's own declaration on the sealed record, not a store's ACL. **The datum carries a declared visibility -- 'private', 'shared', or 'hybrid' -- and a Merkle integrity root over its canonical chunks, computed via the sealed P5 `MerkleTree`, so its classification and its integrity travel with it.** The payload records `{"visibility": visibility, "owner": owner, "root": _merkle_root(chunks)}`. The visibility is the governed classification: private data the owner keeps, shared data the owner federates, hybrid data partly each. The root is a commitment over the content, so a reader can verify the datum is intact from its own bytes. A datum thus carries both what it is classified as and proof of what it contains -- neither trusted to a store. **An empty owner, empty content, or a visibility outside the three classes is refused -- there is no unowned datum, no empty datum, and no visibility a store might invent -- so every governed datum names its owner, commits to real content, and declares a valid classification.** `classify_datum` raises `GovernanceError` if `owner` is empty (a datum needs an owner to classify it), if `chunks` is empty (a datum needs content), or if `visibility` is not one of `('private', 'shared', 'hybrid')`. The three classes are the whole governed vocabulary; a fourth ("public", "internal", whatever a store might add) is refused. This keeps the classification a closed, governed set -- not an ACL's open-ended tags. **This is the built topology the distribution-matrix idea describes -- which data is private, which is shared or federated, is a governed classification declared per datum, not a diagram or a convention -- so the partition is a fact the node enforces, not a picture of intent.** The claim that a federation's data is partitioned into private and shared shards is, in most systems, an architecture diagram. `classify_datum` makes it a built governed classification: each datum's visibility is recorded on the sealed registry, and every access re-checks it (Ch 4). The matrix of what is private vs shared is not drawn -- it is the set of governed classifications, per datum, that the node enforces deny-by-default. That is the resonant-shard partition, built. **In the acceptance test, an owner classifies a datum hybrid and the governed object carries its visibility and a real Merkle root, and each of the empty-input and invalid-visibility cases is refused -- so the classification is executable, not asserted.** `test_classify_datum_records_governed_object_with_partition` classifies a datum and asserts the object id, the version hash, and a non-empty root with the declared visibility. `test_classify_datum_refuses_empty_or_bad_visibility` proves an empty owner, empty content, and an invalid visibility ('public') each raise. The classification-as-governed-partition is proven in code, in the suite pushed to the starter. **For the Ridgeline family office, `classify_datum` is the moment a record is filed -- the family classifies its ledger 'private' and a partner report 'shared', each as its own governed object with a provable integrity root -- so the boundary between what stays private and what is shared is a classification the family holds, not an ACL a store administers.** When Ridgeline files a record, the legacy path stores it and sets a store ACL. This volume gives it a governed classification: the ledger is a private governed object, the report a shared one, each carrying a Merkle root. The family's own declaration is the boundary; a store cannot broaden it because there is no store ACL to broaden. The next chapters govern the private data (Ch 3), the shared data (Ch 4), and the hybrid case (Ch 5).

title: Vol 05 Private Shared Storage Governance
chapter_title: Private Storage Governance -- Data the Owner Keeps
text: You will protect strictly private data with sovereign controls by composing the sealed Object Model and the sealed P5 Merkle -- a private datum is the owner's own governed object, never shareable across mandates, its integrity provable from its bytes.

title: Vol 05 Private Shared Storage Governance
chapter_title: Private Storage Governance -- Data the Owner Keeps
text: **Strictly private data -- a ledger, a cost basis, a personal record -- must be governed by the owner and reachable by no one else, and in a sovereign system that means the private datum is the owner's own governed object, not a row in a store scoped by an ACL.** Privacy in a central store is an ACL that says "only this owner may read." The store enforces it, and the store can fail to. This chapter is explicit that private data governance composes sealed floors -- the Object Model for the record, the P5 Merkle for the integrity -- so a private datum is the owner's own governed object whose privacy is a governed classification, not a store's promise. **A private datum is the owner's own governed object, composed from the sealed Sovereign Object Model (S5 Vol 5), with its integrity provable from its bytes via the sealed P5 Merkle -- so private data is held, not stored.** When `classify_datum` (Ch 2) records a datum 'private', it is a governed object on the sealed registry under the owner's mandate, carrying a Merkle root. There is no separate private store; the record is the sealed Object Model, the integrity is the sealed Merkle, composed. Private data is held by the owner as a governed object, provable from its own bytes, not deposited in a store that scopes and vouches for it. The composition is the point: privacy needs no store engine, only the sealed floors governing the owner's own object. **Own-mandate access is whole -- the owner reads its own private datum without any rule -- and a private datum is NEVER shareable across mandates, refused regardless of any scope rule, so privacy is structural, not a permission that can be broadened.** `govern_shared_access` (Ch 4) makes this explicit: when the principal is the owner, access is whole. When the principal is anyone else and the datum is 'private', the access is refused -- even if a scope rule names it. A private datum cannot be shared by declaring a rule; it must be re-classified first. This is stronger than an ACL, which can be broadened to add a reader. Privacy here is a property of the classification, not an entry someone can edit. **Encryption-at-rest of a private value composes the sealed P5 Paillier (ready, compute-on-encrypted) or the node's own key runtime -- homed, not built here -- so the plaintext and the keys stay off any central store.** A private datum's bytes may need to be encrypted at rest. This volume does not build encryption; it composes the sealed P5 Paillier (which supports computation on encrypted values) where that fits, or homes on-disk encryption at the node's own key runtime (OUT, the node holds its keys). The classification and the integrity are built here; the encryption is composed or homed. Naming the home keeps the claim exact: private data governance is the governed classification and the unshareable boundary, and the encryption lives at a sealed or node-owned home, never a store that holds both the ciphertext and the keys. **No central store holds private data anywhere in this governance -- the datum is the owner's own governed object, the classification is the owner's declaration, and the integrity is the sealed Merkle -- so the kill-target holds: private data is held by the owner, provable and unshareable, never vouched for by a store.** The kill-target for this volume is explicit: no central store, no second classification authority, no standing trust across data. Private governance honors each. The datum is the sealed registry's -- not a store's. The privacy is a governed classification -- not an ACL. The integrity is recomputed from the bytes -- not a store's attestation. A grep of the module for a store or a standing-grant cache returns nothing. Private data is held by its owner and proven from its bytes; nothing central holds or vouches for it. **Because private governance composes sealed floors and adds only the unshareable-private rule, this chapter's contribution is precise -- it makes a private datum the owner's own governed object that no rule can share, and names the encryption home -- and it builds no private store of its own.** The honest account is a composition plus one rule. The record is the sealed Object Model (S5 Vol 5). The integrity is the sealed P5 Merkle. The encryption is sealed P5 Paillier or the node's key runtime. What this volume adds is the governed classification (Ch 2) and the structural rule that a private datum is never shareable across mandates (enforced in Ch 4). There is no private storage engine here -- only the sealed floors governing the owner's own private object, with privacy made a property that cannot be broadened. **For the Ridgeline family office, private storage governance is what keeps the family ledger the family's alone -- a governed object the family holds, integrity-proven, that no scope rule and no store administrator can share -- so a stolen credential or a broadened permission grants a reader nothing.** When Ridgeline keeps its ledger private, the legacy path trusts the store's ACL to keep others out. This volume gives it a governed private object: the ledger is the family's own, classified private, and the classification refuses any cross-mandate share, rule or no rule. There is no store ACL to misconfigure and no store to compromise. The family's private data is held by the family, provable and structurally unshareable. Chapter 4 governs the data the family does choose to share.

title: Vol 05 Private Shared Storage Governance
chapter_title: Shared and Federated Storage Governance -- govern_shared_access
text: You will govern shared storage deny-by-default -- a shared or hybrid datum is accessible to a named peer only by a scope rule the owner declared for exactly it, revocable by withdrawing the rule -- so a share is a declared grant, never a store ACL, and private data is never shareable.

title: Vol 05 Private Shared Storage Governance
chapter_title: Shared and Federated Storage Governance -- govern_shared_access
text: **Sharing a datum across a federation must be a grant the owner declares for exactly that datum and exactly that peer -- revocable, per-datum, deny-by-default -- not a store ACL that outlives the intent, and `govern_shared_access` is that grant.** A federation shares data to collaborate: a capacity figure, a compliance report, a shared record. In a store, sharing is an ACL entry that persists until someone removes it. This volume makes a share a governed grant: `govern_shared_access(reg, datum, rules, *, principal_mandate, want)` returns access only when the datum's classification permits and the owner declared a scope rule for exactly this datum and peer. Its default is refusal. A share is the owner's declared, revocable grant, not a store's standing permission. **`govern_shared_access` is deny-by-default -- own-mandate access is whole, and any other access needs a declared scope rule -- so a shared datum is reachable only by a grant the owner made, never by default.** The function is deny-first. If the principal is the owner, access is whole.
