Otherwise it requires a `SharingRule` the owner declared naming exactly this datum and this peer, and it returns the grant only if that rule authorizes the access. A shared datum with no declared rule for a given peer is refused. This is the difference from a store: a store shares if the ACL includes the reader; `govern_shared_access` shares nothing until the owner declares a rule for exactly this datum and peer, this classification permitting. **A 'private' datum is NEVER shareable across mandates -- refused regardless of any scope rule -- so the classification is enforced before any grant is even considered, and privacy cannot be broadened by declaring a rule.** Before checking any rule, `govern_shared_access` enforces the classification: if the datum is 'private' and the principal is not the owner, the access is refused outright, even if a `SharingRule` names it. Only 'shared' and 'hybrid' data can be granted to a peer. This ordering matters: privacy is not a rule that can be added or removed; it is a classification checked first. A store ACL can always be broadened to add a reader to private data; this governance cannot -- a private datum must be re-classified before it can be shared at all. **A share composes the sealed Federation Node Governance `authorize_crossing` (S5 Vol 28) -- the same per-datum, declared-rule scope check the storage model uses -- so there is no standing trust across data: a rule for one datum never grants another.** `authorize_crossing(reg, rules, principal_mandate=..., obj_id=datum["object_id"], want=...)` decides the grant for a shared or hybrid datum. The scope is per-datum: a rule granting one datum does not grant another, and an unknown datum denies. There is no standing trust that lets a peer read a stream of a node's data on the strength of one grant -- each share is authorized only by a rule declared for exactly that datum. The scope is the sealed federation-governance check, composed, not a store-wide role or group ACL. **Withdrawing the rule revokes the share -- because a share exists only as a declared rule and nothing caches it, revocation is simply removing the declaration -- so there is no store holding a lingering permission after the intent is gone.** In a store, revoking a share means editing an ACL and trusting no cached grant survives. Here, a share is a declared `SharingRule`; `govern_shared_access` consults the rules on every request and grants nothing a current rule does not authorize. Remove the rule, and the next request is refused. There is no standing-grant cache to invalidate, no store-side permission to lag behind the intent. Revocation is exact and immediate because the share was never anything but the owner's current declaration. **In the acceptance test, an owner reads its own datum whole, a peer reads a shared or hybrid datum only with a declared rule, a peer with no rule is refused, and a private datum is refused even with a rule -- so deny-by-default sharing and the unshareable-private boundary are executable.** `test_own_mandate_access_is_whole` proves the owner's access. `test_shared_datum_needs_declared_scope` and `test_hybrid_datum_shareable_by_declared_scope` prove a shared/hybrid datum is granted only by a declared rule and refused without one. `test_private_datum_is_never_shareable` proves a private datum refuses a cross-mandate share even with a rule. `test_access_refuses_no_real_datum` proves accessing nothing raises. The governance is proven in code. **For the Ridgeline family office, `govern_shared_access` is how the family shares a report with a partner -- a scope rule declared for exactly that report and that partner, revocable the moment the engagement ends -- while the family ledger, classified private, refuses any share no matter what rule is written.** When Ridgeline shares a report, the legacy path adds the partner to a store ACL that persists until someone remembers to remove it. This volume gives it a governed grant: a rule for exactly this report and this partner, consulted on every read, revoked by withdrawing the rule. The private ledger refuses sharing structurally. The family shares exactly what it declares, to exactly whom, for exactly as long as the rule stands -- and its private data stays private by classification, not by a store's good behavior. Chapter 5 governs the hybrid case, where a datum is partly private and partly shared.

title: Vol 05 Private Shared Storage Governance
chapter_title: Hybrid and Scoped Storage Models -- Partly Private, Partly Shared
text: You will manage data that is partially private and partially shared by composing the sealed objects.scope discipline over authorize_crossing -- a hybrid datum is classified once and governed per-request, so scoped replication and consistency stay a declared-rule matter, not a store's copy.

title: Vol 05 Private Shared Storage Governance
chapter_title: Hybrid and Scoped Storage Models -- Partly Private, Partly Shared
text: **Most real data is not cleanly private or cleanly shared -- a record whose summary is shared but whose detail is private, a dataset shared with one partner and withheld from another -- and a sovereign system needs a governed middle for it, which is the hybrid classification.** A family shares a report's totals but not its line items. A network shares capacity with a buyer but not its cost basis. This data is hybrid: partly private, partly shared, and the boundary runs through the datum. This chapter is explicit that hybrid governance composes the sealed scope discipline -- the same `authorize_crossing` and `objects.scope` the shared case uses -- so a hybrid datum is governed per-request by declared rules, building no new engine. **A hybrid datum is classified once as 'hybrid' and then governed per-request exactly like shared data -- accessible to a peer only by a declared scope rule -- so the middle ground is not a special store but a classification plus the same deny-by-default grant.** `classify_datum` (Ch 2) records a datum 'hybrid'; `govern_shared_access` (Ch 4) then grants a peer access to it only by a declared `SharingRule`, deny-by-default. There is no third mechanism for hybrid data: it is the shared-access grant applied to a datum classified hybrid. The distinction between shared and hybrid is one of intent and policy -- hybrid signals that only part of the datum, or only some peers, are in scope -- but the governance is the same declared-rule check. The middle ground is a classification, not a new store. **Scoping a hybrid datum composes the sealed `objects.scope` discipline over `authorize_crossing` (S5 Vol 28) -- a `SharingRule` names exactly this datum, this peer, and a scope at least as strong -- so which part of a hybrid datum a peer may read is a declared rule, not a store's partial-copy.** The sealed scope check evaluates a `SharingRule` naming the object, the peer, and the access strength. For a hybrid datum, the owner declares rules that scope exactly what each peer may reach. The scoping is the sealed federation-governance discipline, composed; this volume adds no partial-replication engine that copies the shared portion to a store. The peer reads what the declared rule authorizes, verified per-request, and nothing wider -- the hybrid boundary is a set of declared rules, not a store's view. **Consistency across scoped copies is a declared-rule matter, not a store's replication -- because a hybrid datum is one governed object read per-request by rule, there are no divergent copies to keep consistent, only the one object and the rules that scope it.** A store that shares part of a datum makes copies -- the shared view here, the private original there -- and must keep them consistent. A hybrid datum has no copies: it is one governed object on the sealed registry, and each peer's access is a per-request grant scoped by a rule. There is nothing to replicate and nothing to reconcile. Consistency is trivial because the datum is singular and the scoping is a declared rule, not a materialized partial view. The reconciliation problems of scoped replication do not arise, because there is no replication. **No store holds the hybrid copy anywhere in this governance -- the datum is one governed object, the scoping is the owner's declared rules, and each access is verified per-request -- so the kill-target holds: hybrid data is governed by declaration, not by a store's partial view.** The kill-target holds for the hybrid case as it does for private and shared. There is no store holding a shared partial copy, no second classification authority deciding the boundary, no standing trust letting a peer read the hybrid datum by default. The datum is the sealed registry's; the scoping is the owner's `SharingRule`s; each access is `authorize_crossing`, per-request. A grep for a replication engine or a partial-copy store returns nothing. Hybrid data is one governed object scoped by declaration. **Because hybrid governance composes the sealed scope discipline and adds only the classification, this chapter's contribution is precise -- it makes hybrid data one governed object scoped per-request by declared rules -- and it builds no replication engine or partial-view store.** The honest account is again a composition. The classification is `classify_datum`'s 'hybrid'. The scoping is the sealed `objects.scope` over `authorize_crossing` (S5 Vol 28). What this volume adds is the recognition that the middle ground needs no special machinery: it is the shared-access grant on a hybrid-classified datum, scoped by declared rules. There is no hybrid store here -- only the sealed floors governing one object by the owner's declarations, with the partial boundary expressed as rules rather than copies. **For the Ridgeline family office, hybrid governance is how the family shares a report's totals with a partner while keeping its line items private -- one governed object, scoped by rules that grant the partner the summary and nothing more -- so there is no shared copy for the partner to over-read and no divergence to reconcile.** When Ridgeline shares part of a record, the legacy path exports a partial view into a shared store and hopes it stays in sync. This volume gives it a hybrid governed object: the report is one datum classified hybrid, and the partner reads exactly what the family's declared rule authorizes -- the totals -- verified per-request. There is no partial copy to leak the line items and no second view to reconcile. The family governs the middle ground by declaration. Chapter 6 composes the compliance and audit that make all three classifications provable to a regulator.

title: Vol 05 Private Shared Storage Governance
chapter_title: Storage Governance Compliance -- Composed, Not Rebuilt
text: You will maintain compliance across private, shared, and hybrid storage by composing the sealed Compliance & Audit floor for the human gate and audit trail, and Analytics for monitoring -- this volume builds no compliance engine; it makes each classification and grant a governed, auditable fact.

title: Vol 05 Private Shared Storage Governance
chapter_title: Storage Governance Compliance -- Composed, Not Rebuilt
text: **Compliance for private/shared storage is proving, to a regulator or a successor, that every classification was the owner's governed declaration and every share was a declared, authorized grant -- and because those are already governed facts, compliance is a matter of composing the sealed audit floors, not building a new one.** A regulator asks: was this data properly classified, and was each share authorized? In a store, the answer is reconstructed from ACL history and access logs. This volume makes the answer a governed record: each classification is a `classify_datum` object, each grant a `govern_shared_access` decision. This chapter is explicit that compliance composes the sealed Compliance & Audit and Analytics floors over those governed facts, building no compliance engine of its own. **The human gate for a material share -- one that shares regulated or consequential data -- composes the sealed Compliance and Audit floor (S5 Vol 16), so a consequential grant passes a named human's deny-by-default assent with a receipt, not an automatic ACL edit.** Some shares are routine; others are material -- sharing regulated data, personal records, consequential figures. For those, the grant passes through the sealed human-approval gate: a named human ratifies the share, deny-by-default, with an audit receipt. This volume does not build that gate; it composes the sealed Compliance and Audit floor. A material share is thus a witnessed, receipted decision, exactly as the sealed floor enforces -- not a silent ACL change a store applies. **Monitoring the classifications and grants -- who classified what, who was granted access to which datum -- composes the sealed Analytics and Decision Intelligence floor (S5 Vol 19), so oversight reads governed facts, not a store's access log.** Oversight of storage governance means watching the classifications and the grants: a datum re-classified from private to shared, a burst of grants to one peer, a private datum someone tried to share. These are governed events, and Analytics consumes them. The monitoring surface -- classification changes, grant rates, refused shares -- is Analytics reading the governed record, homed at S5 Vol 19. This volume builds no monitor; it makes the governance observable and names the home. **The datum at rest composes the Sovereign Data Storage Model (S7 Vol 3), and identity, delivery, and the surfaces are homed too -- so this volume governs the classification and the sharing, and the storage, identity, and delivery live at their sealed homes.** A classified datum is stored at rest by the Sovereign Data Storage Model (S7 Vol 3), which this governance composes rather than duplicates. A node's identity is Trust Boundaries & Handoff (S6 Vol 5); delivery of a shared datum is Receipted Inter-Node Messaging (S6 Vol 1); the operator surface is six-sov.com/seeit. This volume's own contribution is the private/shared/hybrid classification and the deny-by-default grant; everything adjacent is named and homed at a real sealed volume, no soft home. **Because compliance composes sealed floors, the kill-target holds here trivially -- there is no second classification authority in an audit, no central store in a human gate, and no standing trust in a monitor -- the compliance reads governed facts the classifications and grants already are.** The risk in a compliance chapter is inventing a central governance authority that becomes the thing regulators trust. This volume refuses it. The human gate is the sealed Compliance floor; the monitoring is the sealed Analytics floor; the classifications and grants are governed objects and decisions. There is no compliance engine to capture, no store to compromise, no standing trust to exploit -- only sealed floors composing governed facts. Compliance is proven from the record the governance already keeps. **This chapter's contribution is precise -- it names the sealed Compliance, Analytics, and Storage homes and composes them over the classifications and grants -- and it builds no compliance, monitoring, or storage engine of its own.** The honest account is a set of compositions. The human gate is Compliance & Audit (S5 Vol 16). The monitoring is Analytics (S5 Vol 19). The at-rest storage is the Sovereign Data Storage Model (S7 Vol 3). What this volume adds is that the classification (Ch 2) and the grant (Ch 4) are already governed facts, so compliance is composing the sealed audit floors over them, not building a new one. Naming those homes -- specific sealed volumes, not "the platform handles compliance" -- keeps the claim exact and refuses a soft-home into an unbuilt engine. **For the Ridgeline family office, storage governance compliance is what lets the family prove to an auditor that its ledger was properly classified private, its report shared only with the named partner by a declared rule ratified by a named human, and every access recorded -- all from the governed record, not a reconstructed access log.** When Ridgeline faces an audit of its data handling, the legacy path reconstructs from store ACL history who could see what. This volume gives it a governed proof: each classification is an object, each material share a witnessed decision, each access a per-request grant -- read directly from the sealed Compliance and Analytics floors. The family proves its data was governed, not that its store's ACLs happened to be set correctly. Chapters 7 and 8 compare this to legacy storage and synthesize it as a generational data strategy.

title: Vol 05 Private Shared Storage Governance
chapter_title: Private vs Shared vs Legacy Storage
text: You will compare sovereign private/shared governance against traditional storage -- the store with its ACL -- seeing where the sovereign model's owner-held classification and declared, revocable grants hold guarantees an ACL cannot.

title: Vol 05 Private Shared Storage Governance
chapter_title: Private vs Shared vs Legacy Storage
text: **Legacy storage -- the database, the object store, the file share -- scopes data by an access-control list the store owns and administers: the store decides who may read, the store enforces it, and the store is trusted to honor the owner's intent.** These technologies are mature and widely proven, and for decades they have been how organizations keep and share data. But their model of the private/shared boundary is the store's ACL. Who may see a datum is an entry in the store's permission system, set by whoever administers it. The owner asks the store to keep something private or share it with a partner, and trusts the store to comply. The boundary belongs to the store, not the owner. **The sovereign model makes the private/shared boundary the owner's governed classification carried by the datum -- so who may see a datum is a property of the datum, checked at every access, not a store's ACL entry.** Where a store holds the boundary in an ACL, the sovereign model holds it in the datum's declared classification. `classify_datum` records each datum private, shared, or hybrid under the owner's mandate; `govern_shared_access` enforces it deny-by-default at every read. The boundary travels with the datum and belongs to its owner. A misconfigured store, a broadened ACL, a compromised admin -- none of these can share what the classification refuses, because the classification is the owner's governed declaration, not the store's editable permission. **A share is a declared, revocable grant -- a rule the owner declared for exactly this datum and peer, consulted per-request, revoked by withdrawal -- not a persistent ACL entry that outlives the intent and must be remembered to remove.** In a store, a share is an ACL entry that persists until someone removes it; forgotten entries are how data leaks. In the sovereign model, a share is a `SharingRule` the owner declared, checked on every access; remove it and the next read is refused. There is no persistent permission to forget, no standing grant to lag behind the intent. The share exists exactly as long as the declaration stands, and revocation is immediate and exact -- a guarantee a store's ACL, with its caches and its administrative lag, cannot make. **The honest scope is that the sovereign model governs the classification and the sharing -- it does not replace the storage that holds bytes or the encryption that protects them -- so it composes, rather than competes with, the mechanics of storage.** This volume does not store bytes at rest (that is the Sovereign Data Storage Model, S7 Vol 3) or encrypt them (that is sealed P5 Paillier or the node's key runtime). What it governs is the private/shared/hybrid classification and the deny-by-default grant. This is the boundary the volume holds against overclaim: the sovereign model is the governance layer over storage, not a new database or object store. The reader gets exactly a governance guarantee, and the storage and encryption stay at their honest homes. **Migration guidance is to classify existing data as governed objects and replace store ACLs with declared rules -- so a node adopts the sovereign model incrementally, gaining owner-held classification without discarding its storage.** A node need not replace its database or object store to adopt this governance. It classifies its data as governed objects (`classify_datum`), and it replaces the store's ACL-based sharing with declared `SharingRule`s enforced by `govern_shared_access`. The bytes may still rest in the existing store; the classification and the sharing move to the governed layer. Over time, the store becomes a byte-holder while the boundary becomes the owner's governed classification. The migration is additive: the governance is layered over the storage the node already has. **The realism is that owner-held classification has a cost -- a declaration to make, a rule to write and maintain, a per-request check to run -- and the sovereign model pays it deliberately where owning the boundary matters, not for every transient file.** Governing every datum's classification is not free: each datum is classified, each share is a declared rule, and each access is checked. For high-volume, low-sensitivity data, a store's ACL may remain the pragmatic choice. For the data where ownership of the boundary matters -- private ledgers, regulated records, selectively shared reports -- the cost buys a guarantee no ACL can: a boundary the owner holds, enforced per-access, revocable exactly. The sovereign model is honest about the tradeoff and governs the data that warrants it. **For the Ridgeline family office, the choice between a store ACL and an owner-held classification is the choice between trusting the store to keep the boundary and holding the boundary itself -- and for the data that must stay the family's, the family chooses to hold it.** Ridgeline keeps its ordinary files in ordinary storage. But for the data that matters -- the private ledger, the selectively shared report, the regulated record -- it classifies each as a governed object and shares by declared, revocable rule. When an auditor asks who could see what, or a partner's access must end, the family answers from its own governed classifications, not the store's ACL history. The boundary is the family's, held and enforced, not the store's to administer. Chapter 8 synthesizes owner-held classification as a generational data strategy.

title: Vol 05 Private Shared Storage Governance
chapter_title: Private vs Shared as a Generational Data Strategy
text: You will see private/shared governance synthesized as a balanced, generational data strategy -- each datum a governed object classified and shared by the owner's declaration -- so a federation's data ownership and its collaborations survive every store and every custodian.

title: Vol 05 Private Shared Storage Governance
chapter_title: Private vs Shared as a Generational Data Strategy
text: **This volume built one thing -- the private/shared boundary as a governed classification the owner holds -- and everything in it follows from that single idea: each datum is the owner's own governed object carrying a declared visibility, private data is never shareable, and a share is a declared, revocable grant.** The chapters are one capability seen from its faces: classify a datum private/shared/hybrid (Ch 2), govern private data as unshareable (Ch 3), grant shared access deny-by-default (Ch 4), govern the hybrid middle by declared rules (Ch 5), and prove it all through the sealed compliance floors (Ch 6). The synthesis is that a federation no longer entrusts the boundary between its private and shared data to a store -- it governs it as a classification the owner holds. **The volume rolls no cryptography and builds no store -- `classify_datum` and `govern_shared_access` compose the sealed Object Model, the sealed federation scope check, and the sealed P5 Merkle -- so the governance inherits audited foundations rather than adding unproven machinery.** The honest account of the volume's construction is a list of compositions. The record is the sealed Object Model (S5 Vol 5). The scope is the sealed `authorize_crossing` (S5 Vol 28). The integrity is the sealed P5 Merkle. What the volume adds is the private/shared/hybrid classification and the deny-by-default grant with its unshareable-private rule -- and nothing else. There is no storage engine, no ACL system, no cryptography of its own. The capability is real because the floors beneath it are sealed and proven. **The governance integrates with the rest of the federation -- storage holds the classified datum at rest, shields protect it, compliance witnesses material shares, and identity anchors the peers -- so classification is one governed act within a sovereign system, not an island.** A classified datum meets several sealed capabilities: the Sovereign Data Storage Model (S7 Vol 3) holds it at rest; Shields as Protective Layers (S7 Vol 2) protect it; Compliance & Audit (S5 Vol 16) witnesses a material share; Trust Boundaries & Handoff (S6 Vol 5) anchors the peers' identities; Analytics (S5 Vol 19) monitors. This governance composes each at its sealed home. The federation is coherent because each capability is a governed floor, and the classification governs which data crosses between them. **The generational handoff is that a successor node can enforce a datum's classification from the governed record alone -- the declared visibility and the declared rules -- without trusting any store's ACL or any administrator's memory of what was meant to be private.** This is the deepest reason owner-held classification matters for Lasting Generational Prosperity. When a federation passes to a new generation, or migrates to a new store, its private/shared boundary either travels with the data as a governed fact or is re-derived from whatever the new store's ACL says. A governed classification travels: a successor reads each datum's declared visibility and its declared rules and enforces them, with no store to trust and no administrator to ask. The boundary survives the store and the people, because it is a governed property of the data. **The final synthesis is that data ownership provable across generations is what lets a federation's private data stay private and its collaborations stay governed as it passes through custodians -- so a sovereign federation makes the private/shared boundary a classification precisely so its data ownership can outlast the stores that held it.** A federation's prosperity depends on keeping its private data private and its shared data governed across decades and custodians. If the boundary lived in a store's ACL, it would reset every time the store changed or the administrator left. Made a governed classification the owner holds, the boundary compounds: each datum's visibility and each share's rule are governed facts a successor enforces. That is how a federation's data ownership endures across generations instead of dissolving into whatever the next store permits -- the boundary between private and shared is the owner's governed classification, and it outlives the store. **For the Ridgeline family office, private/shared governance is the strategy that lets the family's private ledger stay the family's and its partner collaborations stay governed as the office passes to the next generation -- so the successors inherit a data estate whose boundaries they hold, not a store's ACLs they must trust.** When Ridgeline hands its office to the next generation, it hands over a data estate: private records, shared reports, hybrid disclosures. Because each is a governed classification with declared rules, the successors inherit boundaries they enforce from the record, not permissions they must reconstruct from a store. The family's private data stays private, its collaborations stay governed, and its ownership of the boundary survives every custodian and every store. That is the generational data strategy this volume built: the private/shared boundary made a governed classification the owner holds, so a federation's data stays its own across time.

title: Vol 06 Resilience Recovery Shields
chapter_title: The Resilience Problem -- Recovery Without a Custodian
text: You will see why a sovereign node must be able to survive failure and recover its authority without handing a copy of its root to a custodian who could be compromised, coerced, or simply lost.

title: Vol 06 Resilience Recovery Shields
chapter_title: The Resilience Problem -- Recovery Without a Custodian
text: **Every sovereign node faces the same hard problem the moment it takes its keys into its own hands: a phone is lost, a laptop dies, an operator steps away -- and the node must be able to recover its authority, but the usual way to make recovery possible is to give a copy of the root to someone else, which hands that someone the node.** A node that cannot recover from a lost surface is fragile: one failure and its authority is gone. But the standard fix -- escrow the key with a custodian, back it up to a recovery service, register a support path that can reset it -- creates a worse problem. Whoever holds the recovery path holds the node. This volume, the capstone of Zero-Trust Sovereignty, is about recovering without that custodian. **Legacy recovery hands the root to a custodian -- a cloud backup that holds the key, an escrow service that can release it, a support desk that can reset it -- so the very mechanism that makes recovery possible makes the node capturable.** The convenience of "forgot your key? we'll restore it" is a second party who holds the power to restore -- and therefore the power to take. A backup service that holds the plaintext key can be breached. An escrow that can release the key can be subpoenaed or coerced. A support desk that can reset access can be social-engineered. Each is a recovery path, and each is a second authority over a node that was supposed to be sovereign. The node's resilience is bought by surrendering its sovereignty. **Whoever holds the recovery path holds the node -- so a recovery design is a trust design, and a custodian who can restore your authority is a party who can assume it.** This is the insight the whole series has been building toward. Zero-trust means never trusting a party you have not verified -- and a recovery custodian is exactly such a party, trusted with the ultimate power over the node. A recovery path that routes through a custodian is a standing grant of authority to that custodian, dormant until invoked but always live. The question a resilient sovereign node must answer is not "how do we back up the key" but "how do we make recovery possible without granting anyone standing authority to perform it." **The sovereign opportunity is to make recovery a governed, human-gated ceremony the owner controls -- a declared policy of named guardians who must jointly assent, over a root that never leaves the owner's own iron -- so recovery is possible without any custodian holding the key.** This volume builds exactly that. The recovery policy is a governed constitution the owner declares: named guardians and an M-of-N threshold. A snapshot of a resource is the owner's own integrity-proven governed object, not a copy in a custodian's store. And recovery is a ceremony: the declared guardians give a human-gated assent, and only when the threshold is met is authority restored -- as a governed succession, never an escrow releasing a key. The root stays on the owner's iron; losing a phone is not losing the node. **Recovery as a composition of sealed floors, not a new engine, is the discipline that keeps it honest -- the plan is a sealed constitution, the assent a sealed human gate, the succession a sealed continuity handoff -- so resilience adds no new machinery to trust.** The temptation in a recovery system is to build a recovery service: a new engine that holds the plans, runs the ceremonies, and executes the restores. That engine would be the custodian all over again. This volume refuses it. The recovery plan composes the sealed Constitutions floor; the ceremony composes the sealed HumanApprovalGate; the succession composes the sealed Generational Continuity handoff. There is no recovery engine, no escrow, no central trust service -- only sealed floors composed at the moment of recovery, and a deny-by-default binding on top. **The generational stake is that authority a federation cannot recover without a custodian is authority that dies with a lost key or is captured by whoever holds the escrow -- while authority recovered by a governed, human-gated ceremony survives failure and succession on the federation's own terms.** Lasting Generational Prosperity depends on a federation's authority outlasting the failures and the successions that time guarantees. A node whose recovery routes through a custodian either loses its authority when the custodian fails or surrenders it when the custodian acts. A node whose recovery is a governed ceremony of named guardians keeps its authority recoverable across every lost surface and every generational handoff, with no custodian to trust or to fear. The rest of this volume builds the recovery constitution (Ch 2), the governed snapshot (Ch 3), the recovery ceremony (Ch 4), the cross-node and compliance compositions (Ch 5-6), a comparison to legacy DR (Ch 7), the generational synthesis (Ch 8), and -- the coherence seal of the series -- the honest boundary of what resilience does not claim (Ch 9).

title: Vol 06 Resilience Recovery Shields
text: You will declare the recovery constitution for a resource -- the named guardians who may authorize recovery and the M-of-N threshold -- as a governed policy that holds no keys and no escrow, only who may recover and how many must assent.

title: Vol 06 Resilience Recovery Shields
text: **Recovery that does not surrender the node must begin with a governed policy of who may authorize it -- named in advance, requiring several to agree -- and `declare_recovery_plan` is the declaration of that policy.** Before a node can recover without a custodian, it must say, in a governed and provable way, who is allowed to authorize a recovery and how many of them must agree. `declare_recovery_plan(reg, resource_id, guardians, *, threshold, ...)` records exactly that: a recovery constitution for the resource, naming its guardians and its M-of-N threshold. Recovery stops being a custodian's discretionary power and becomes the owner's declared, governed policy. **`declare_recovery_plan` opens the recovery constitution by composing the sealed `open_constitution` (Constitutions S5 Vol 30) over the sealed Object Model -- so the recovery policy is a governed constitution, versioned and owned by exactly one mandate, not a document in a drawer.** The function calls `open_constitution(reg, f"recovery:{resource_id}", articles, mandate=..., ...)` -- the same sealed Constitutions floor a federation uses to govern its rules. The recovery plan is thus a governed constitutional object: authored under the owner's mandate, integrity-hashed, versioned. It is not a config file a service reads; it is a governed constitution the owner holds, and changing it is itself a governed act. **The plan names the guardians -- the principals who may authorize recovery -- and the M-of-N threshold -- how many of them must assent -- so recovery requires the agreement of several named parties, never one custodian's action.** The articles record `{"guardians": [...], "threshold": M}`. The guardians are named in advance: the people or nodes the owner trusts to attest that a recovery is legitimate. The threshold is how many must agree -- two of three, three of five. This is the structural defense against a single custodian: no one guardian can recover the node, and no party outside the named set can. Recovery requires a declared quorum of named principals, set by the owner, in advance, and provable. **The plan holds NO keys and NO escrow -- its articles record `holds_keys: false` and `escrow: false` -- so the recovery constitution is a policy of authorization, never a container of the secret it protects.** This is the line that keeps the shield from becoming the custodian. The plan does not store the key, a copy of the key, or a way to reconstruct the key. It stores only the governed policy: who may authorize a recovery and how many. The root itself stays on the owner's own iron (Ch 4). A plan that held the key would be an escrow -- exactly the second authority the volume refuses. By holding only the policy, the plan makes recovery governable without making it capturable. **An empty resource, an empty guardian set, or a threshold below 1 or above the number of guardians is refused -- so every recovery constitution names the resource it governs, names real guardians, and sets a threshold that can actually be met.** `declare_recovery_plan` raises `ResilienceError` if the resource is empty (a plan governs a specific resource), if there are no named guardians (no anonymous recovery), or if the threshold is below 1 or exceeds the guardian count (an unmeetable or trivial threshold). These refusals keep the constitution honest: a recovery policy that named no one, or required more assents than there are guardians, would be either a back door or a dead end. The plan must name a real quorum that can, in a real emergency, actually recover the node. **In the acceptance test, an owner declares a recovery plan and the governed constitution carries its guardians and threshold with no keys and no escrow, and each of the empty and out-of-range cases is refused -- so the recovery policy is executable, not asserted.** `test_declare_recovery_plan_is_a_governed_constitution` declares a plan and asserts the constitution object, its guardians and threshold, and `holds_keys: false` / `escrow: false`. `test_declare_recovery_plan_refuses_empty_or_bad_threshold` proves an empty resource, an empty guardian set, and a threshold above or below the valid range each raise. The recovery policy is proven in code, composing the sealed Constitutions floor. **For the Ridgeline family office, `declare_recovery_plan` is the moment the family sets, in advance and in a governed constitution, that recovering the office's root requires two of its three named trustees to agree -- so no service, no support desk, and no single trustee can ever recover it alone.** When Ridgeline takes its keys into its own hands, the legacy path would register a recovery email or an escrow service -- a custodian. This volume gives it a recovery constitution: two of three named trustees must assent, recorded as a governed object the family owns. No custodian holds the key, and no one party can recover the office. The family has made recovery possible and kept it sovereign. The next chapter builds the governed snapshot that recovery restores from.

title: Vol 06 Resilience Recovery Shields
text: You will take a governed, integrity-proven snapshot of a resource -- the owner's own governed object carrying a Merkle root over its state -- so a resource can be restored from a verifiable snapshot the owner holds, not a copy in a central backup store.

title: Vol 06 Resilience Recovery Shields
text: **Recovering a resource requires a snapshot of its state that the owner can prove is intact -- and in a sovereign system that snapshot is the owner's own governed object with a provable integrity root, not a copy sitting in a backup service that could be altered or lost.** A recovery constitution (Ch 2) says who may recover; a snapshot is what they recover to. The danger is the same as with the key: if the snapshot lives in a central backup store, that store owns the resilience -- it can lose the snapshot, alter it, or hold it hostage. `snapshot_resource` makes the snapshot the owner's own governed object, integrity-proven, held on the owner's terms. **`snapshot_resource` records the snapshot as the owner's OWN governed object, composing the sealed object registry's append under the owner's mandate -- so a snapshot exists as a governed fact the owner holds, not a file in a backup service.** The function calls `reg.append(f"snapshot:{resource_id}:...", payload, mandate=..., kind="ratify")` -- the same sealed registry the object model is built on. The snapshot is ratified under the owner's mandate; no backup service mints it and no custodian holds it. It is a governed object like any other in the federation: versioned, attributed, integrity-hashed. Resilience data is thus part of the owner's own governed record, not an export to a store the owner does not control. **The snapshot carries a Merkle root over the resource's canonical state, computed via the sealed P5 `MerkleTree` -- so its integrity is provable from its own bytes, and a snapshot that was altered cannot be restored as if it were sound.** The payload records `{"resource": resource_id, "root": _merkle_root(chunks)}`. The root is a commitment over the resource's state: anyone holding the snapshot's bytes can recompute the root and compare. If they match, the snapshot is exactly what was captured; if a byte was altered, the roots diverge. A recovery restores from a snapshot whose integrity is proven, not trusted. This is the difference from a backup service, which asks the owner to trust that the restored bytes are the stored bytes -- here the owner verifies it from the snapshot's own commitment. **No central backup store holds or vouches for the snapshot -- the record is the sealed object registry, the integrity is the sealed Merkle, and the snapshot is the owner's own governed object -- so the kill-target holds: resilience data is held by the owner, provable, never a store's copy.** The kill-target for this volume includes no central store that holds the resilience data. `snapshot_resource` honors it: the snapshot is a governed object on the sealed registry, its integrity recomputed from its bytes. A grep of the module for a backup store or a central replica returns nothing. Where the snapshot is physically kept -- on the owner's iron, or (Ch 5) carried to a peer node by receipted messaging under a governed scope -- it remains the owner's own governed object, verifiable, never a backup service's asset. **An empty resource or empty state is refused -- there is no snapshot of nothing and no phantom snapshot -- so every governed snapshot names the resource it captures and commits to real state.** `snapshot_resource` raises `ResilienceError` if the resource is empty (a snapshot captures a specific resource) or if the state chunks are empty (a snapshot must commit to real content). A snapshot with no content would be a root over nothing -- an integrity commitment that proves nothing. The refusals keep the governed record free of empty snapshots that could give a false sense of resilience. **In the acceptance test, an owner takes a snapshot and the governed object carries its resource and a real Merkle root, and each of the empty cases is refused -- so the snapshot is executable, not asserted.** `test_snapshot_resource_carries_merkle_root` snapshots a resource and asserts the object id, the version hash, and a non-empty root. `test_snapshot_resource_refuses_empty` proves an empty resource and empty state each raise. The governed, integrity-proven snapshot is proven in code, composing the sealed registry and the sealed P5 Merkle. **For the Ridgeline family office, `snapshot_resource` is how the office keeps a verifiable snapshot of its root state -- a governed object the family holds, its integrity provable from the bytes -- so a recovery restores exactly what was captured, and an altered or substituted snapshot yields nothing.** When Ridgeline prepares for the possibility of a lost surface, the legacy path backs the state up to a service the family must trust to keep it intact. This volume gives it a governed snapshot: the state is the family's own governed object with a Merkle root, restorable and verifiable. A snapshot tampered with in storage is caught by the root; a substituted snapshot does not verify. The family's resilience data is its own, provable, held on its terms. The next chapter builds the ceremony that recovers authority.

title: Vol 06 Resilience Recovery Shields
chapter_title: Recovery and Failover -- recover_authority, the Human-Gated Ceremony
text: You will restore authority over a resource by a human-gated M-of-N ceremony -- the declared threshold of named guardians must assent, ratified as a governed succession -- with a dry-run that verifies the ceremony without ever touching the live root.

title: Vol 06 Resilience Recovery Shields
chapter_title: Recovery and Failover -- recover_authority, the Human-Gated Ceremony
text: **Restoring a node's authority after a failure must be a ceremony the node's own governed policy authorizes -- the named guardians assenting, in the open, several at once -- not an escrow releasing a key or a service resetting an account, and `recover_authority` is that ceremony.** A recovery plan (Ch 2) declared who may recover; a snapshot (Ch 3) is what they recover to; `recover_authority(reg, plan, approvals, ...)` is the act of recovery itself. It restores authority only when the plan's threshold of named guardians have assented, and it does so as a governed succession -- the sealed continuity handoff of authority -- never as a custodian releasing a secret. This is the B-10 key-recovery home the series has carried since S6, built at last as a composition. **`recover_authority` is deny-by-default and fail-closed -- it requires a real governed recovery plan, assents from named guardians, and a met M-of-N threshold -- so recovery is impossible unless the owner's own declared quorum authorizes it.** The function is deny-first. It confirms the `plan` is a real governed recovery constitution carrying its guardians and threshold. It counts the assents that name a guardian in the plan and carry a reference. It requires the count of distinct valid guardians to reach the threshold. Any failure raises `ResilienceError`; the default is no recovery. There is no path by which fewer than the declared quorum, or anyone outside the named guardians, can recover the node. Recovery is exactly as governed as the owner declared it, and no more permissive. **Each assent must name a guardian in the plan AND carry an approval reference -- the sealed human-gate convention, composing `HumanApprovalGate` (S5 Vol 16) -- so a recovery is authorized by real, attributable human assent, never a silent or forged approval.** `recover_authority` composes the sealed `HumanApprovalGate`: recovery is a high-materiality, human-gated action class. Each assent must name a guardian who is in the plan and carry an `approval_ref` naming the act -- the same approver-plus-reference convention a governed change carries. An assent from someone not named as a guardian does not count; an assent with no reference does not count. The threshold is met only by distinct named guardians each giving an attributable, human-gated assent. There is no way to reach the threshold with anonymous or unreferenced approvals -- the ceremony is a real quorum of named humans. **A dry-run verifies the ceremony WOULD succeed without ratifying anything -- it never touches the live root -- so a node can test its recovery readiness, and rehearse the ceremony, without performing a recovery.** `recover_authority(..., dry_run=True)` runs every check -- the real plan, the named guardians, the met threshold -- and returns that the recovery would succeed, but ratifies nothing: it appends no succession and touches the live root not at all. This is the KR dry-run discipline: a node must be able to prove its recovery plan works, that its guardians are reachable and its threshold meetable, without a real recovery ever occurring. A rehearsal that altered the live root would be a recovery; a dry-run that only verifies is a rehearsal. The distinction is enforced in the code. **Recovery is ratified as a governed succession, composing the object registry and the sealed Generational Continuity handoff discipline (S5 Vol 29) -- so authority is handed on as a governed, receipted act, never an escrow releasing a key or a second recovery authority acting.** When the threshold is met and it is not a dry-run, `recover_authority` ratifies the recovery as a governed succession object on the sealed registry -- the same discipline by which Generational Continuity hands authority to a successor: proof plus a human gate. There is no escrow that releases the secret, no recovery service that executes the restore, no second authority that acts. The recovery is the named guardians' own assent, ratified as a succession the owner's governed record carries. The root stayed on the owner's iron the whole time; what was restored is authority, by governed succession, not a key from a custodian. **In the acceptance test, an M-of-N quorum of named guardians recovers and the succession is ratified, a below-threshold attempt is refused, an unnamed guardian and an unreferenced assent do not count, a dry-run ratifies nothing, and a recovery with no real plan is refused -- so the ceremony is executable and fail-closed.** `test_recover_authority_m_of_n_met_ratifies` recovers with a met quorum and asserts the ratified succession. `test_recover_authority_below_threshold_refused`, `_unnamed_guardian_does_not_count`, and `_assent_without_reference_does_not_count` prove the deny-by-default quorum. `test_recover_authority_dry_run_never_touches_live_root` proves a dry-run ratifies nothing. `test_recover_authority_no_real_plan_refused` proves a recovery needs a real plan. The ceremony is proven in code, composing the sealed human gate and the continuity discipline. **For the Ridgeline family office, `recover_authority` is the ceremony that restores the office's authority after a lost surface -- two of the three named trustees assent, each with a referenced human approval, and authority is handed on by governed succession -- while no service, no escrow, and no single trustee could ever perform it.** When Ridgeline loses an operator's phone, the legacy path calls a support desk or invokes an escrow -- a custodian restores access. This volume gives it a ceremony: two of three named trustees assent in the open, each attributably, and the office's authority is restored as a governed succession the family owns. A single trustee cannot; a stranger cannot; a service cannot. The office recovered without a custodian, and the root never left its iron. Chapters 5 and 6 compose the cross-node resilience and the compliance audit around this ceremony.

title: Vol 06 Resilience Recovery Shields
chapter_title: Cross-Node Resilience and Failover -- Composed, Not Replicated
text: You will make a node's resilience survive the loss of the node itself by composing sealed inter-node floors -- a snapshot carried to a peer by receipted messaging under a governed scope, roots reconciled by federation governance -- with no central replica store.

title: Vol 06 Resilience Recovery Shields
chapter_title: Cross-Node Resilience and Failover -- Composed, Not Replicated
text: **A node must be able to survive its own total loss -- a destroyed machine, an unreachable site -- and that means its snapshot must live somewhere beyond it, but a central replica store that holds every node's data would be the custodian again, so cross-node resilience is a composition of sealed inter-node floors, not a replica service.** Ch 3's snapshot is the owner's governed object; if the node is destroyed, the snapshot must exist on another node. The wrong way is a central backup that replicates everyone's snapshots -- a single store that becomes the thing everyone trusts. This chapter is explicit that cross-node resilience composes the sealed messaging and federation floors, homing failover there and building no replica engine. **A snapshot crosses to a peer node by the sealed Receipted Inter-Node Messaging (S6 Vol 1) -- a governed, integrity-proven message each peer validates independently -- so a snapshot held by a peer is a receipted governed object, not a copy in a shared store.** When a node arranges for a peer to hold its snapshot, the transfer is a receipted inter-node message: the snapshot crosses as a governed object with its provenance and its Merkle root, and the receiving peer validates it from its own bytes. This is the sealed messaging floor, composed. The peer holds the snapshot as a governed object it received and verified, not as a row a central replica store pushed to it. There is no shared store; there is a governed transfer between two nodes. **Which peer may hold a node's snapshot is a governed scope -- composing the sealed `authorize_crossing` (S5 Vol 28) -- so a node chooses, by declared rule, exactly which peers may hold its resilience data, and no peer holds it by default.** Holding a peer's snapshot is a cross-node access, and it is governed like any other: by a `SharingRule` the owner declared naming exactly this snapshot and this peer. A node picks its resilience partners deliberately and grants each a scoped, revocable hold. No peer holds a node's snapshot without a declared rule, and the hold can be revoked by withdrawing the rule. Cross-node resilience is thus a set of governed, chosen relationships -- not an automatic replication to a store the node did not choose. **Divergent roots after a failover reconcile by the sealed `reconcile_roots` (S5 Vol 28) -- so when a recovered node and a peer that held its snapshot disagree, the divergence is resolved against verifiable roots, not a replica store's version.** After a failover, a recovered node and the peer that held its snapshot may have divergent roots -- the recovered node acted, the snapshot is older. The divergence is detectable and resolved by the sealed `reconcile_roots`, which compares the two roots and identifies the difference. This volume composes that sealed mechanism; it builds no reconciliation engine. The recovered state resolves against what the verifiable roots prove, with a human witness for a material difference (Ch 6), not against whatever a central replica store happened to hold. **No central replica store exists anywhere in this composition -- the snapshot crosses by receipted messaging, the hold is a governed scope, and the reconciliation is federation governance -- so the kill-target holds: cross-node resilience is chosen, governed, and composed, never a central replica everyone trusts.** The kill-target forbids a central trust service, and a central replica store would be exactly that. This chapter composes only sealed inter-node floors: messaging for the transfer, `authorize_crossing` for the scope, `reconcile_roots` for the divergence. A grep for a replica engine or a backup cluster returns nothing. Cross-node resilience is a node's chosen, governed relationships with named peers -- each a composition of sealed floors -- and no central store holds the federation's resilience. **Because cross-node resilience composes sealed floors, this chapter's contribution is precise -- it homes failover at the sealed messaging, scope, and reconciliation floors -- and it builds no replica store or failover engine of its own.** The honest account is a set of compositions. The transfer is Receipted Inter-Node Messaging (S6 Vol 1). The scope is `authorize_crossing` (S5 Vol 28). The reconciliation is `reconcile_roots` (S5 Vol 28). The material-difference witness is Compliance & Audit (S5 Vol 16, Ch 6). What this volume adds is the governed snapshot (Ch 3) and the recovery ceremony (Ch 4); the cross-node carriage and failover are sealed floors it composes. Naming those homes -- specific sealed volumes, not "the platform replicates it" -- keeps the claim exact and refuses a soft-home into an unbuilt replica engine. **For the Ridgeline family office, cross-node resilience is how the office survives the loss of its own site -- a chosen partner node holds a receipted, scoped copy of its snapshot, and after a failover their roots reconcile against what the records prove -- with no central backup cluster holding the family's data.** When Ridgeline guards against losing its own machines, the legacy path replicates to a cloud backup the family must trust. This volume gives it a chosen relationship: a named partner node holds a receipted, scoped, revocable copy of the family's snapshot, and after a recovery their views reconcile by governed comparison of roots. The family chose its resilience partner, governs the hold, and reconciles by proof. No central cluster holds the office's data. Chapter 6 composes the compliance and audit that witness a material recovery.

title: Vol 06 Resilience Recovery Shields
chapter_title: Compliance and Audit of Recovery -- Composed, Not Rebuilt
text: You will make every recovery provable to a regulator and a successor by composing the sealed Compliance & Audit human gate and Analytics monitoring -- a material recovery is witnessed by a named human and recorded, and the recovery record is a governed fact, not a reconstructed log.

title: Vol 06 Resilience Recovery Shields
chapter_title: Compliance and Audit of Recovery -- Composed, Not Rebuilt
text: **A recovery is one of the most consequential acts a node can perform -- it restores the authority everything else depends on -- so it must be witnessed by a named human and provable to a regulator or a successor, and because the recovery ceremony is already a governed act, that compliance is a composition of the sealed audit floors, not a new engine.** A recovery that happened silently, or that could not be proven legitimate afterward, would undermine the whole point of governing it. This chapter is explicit that the compliance around recovery composes the sealed Compliance & Audit and Analytics floors over the governed recovery facts -- the plan, the assents, the succession -- building no compliance engine of its own. **A material recovery -- one that restores authority over a consequential resource -- composes the sealed Compliance & Audit human gate (S5 Vol 16), so the recovery passes a named human's deny-by-default assent with a receipt, over and above the guardian quorum.** The guardian quorum (Ch 4) authorizes that a recovery may proceed; for a material recovery, the sealed human-approval gate adds the compliance witness -- a named compliance human ratifies the recovery act itself, deny-by-default, with an audit receipt. This volume does not build that gate; it composes the sealed Compliance & Audit floor. A material recovery is thus doubly governed: the owner's declared guardian quorum, and the compliance human gate -- both sealed, composed, and receipted. **Monitoring recoveries and dry-runs -- who recovered what, which guardians assented, how often a plan is rehearsed -- composes the sealed Analytics & Decision Intelligence floor (S5 Vol 19), so oversight of resilience reads governed facts, not a reconstructed log.** Oversight of recovery means watching the governed record: a recovery that occurred, the guardians who assented, the dry-runs that rehearsed a plan, a threshold that was nearly met. These are governed events, and Analytics consumes them. The resilience-monitoring surface -- recovery counts, guardian participation, rehearsal frequency -- is Analytics reading the governed recovery record, homed at S5 Vol 19. This volume builds no monitor; it makes recovery observable and names the home. **The recovery succession is a governed object -- it records the resource, the assenting guardians, and the threshold -- so the audit trail of a recovery exists by construction, not by reconstruction from scattered logs.** When `recover_authority` ratifies a recovery (Ch 4), it appends a governed succession object recording the resource, the guardians who assented, and the threshold met. That object is the audit trail: a regulator or a successor reads it and sees exactly who recovered what, under which quorum, when. There is no reconstructing the story from access logs and support tickets; the governed succession is the record. Compliance reads the fact the recovery already produced. **Because compliance composes sealed floors, the kill-target holds here trivially -- there is no second recovery authority in an audit, no escrow in a human gate, and no central trust service in a monitor -- the compliance reads the governed facts the recovery already is.** The risk in a compliance chapter is inventing a central recovery-oversight authority that becomes the thing everyone trusts to bless recoveries. This volume refuses it. The human gate is the sealed Compliance floor; the monitoring is the sealed Analytics floor; the recovery record is a governed succession object. There is no compliance engine to capture, no escrow, no central trust service -- only sealed floors composing governed facts. A recovery is proven from the record it already keeps. **This chapter's contribution is precise -- it names the sealed Compliance and Analytics homes and composes them over the recovery facts -- and it builds no compliance, monitoring, or oversight engine of its own.** The honest account is a set of compositions. The human witness is Compliance & Audit (S5 Vol 16). The monitoring is Analytics (S5 Vol 19). The recovery record is a governed succession object. What this volume adds is the recovery ceremony (Ch 4) whose acts are governed facts, so compliance is composing the sealed audit floors over them, not building a new one. Naming those homes -- specific sealed volumes, not "the platform audits recovery" -- keeps the claim exact and refuses a soft-home into an unbuilt oversight engine. **For the Ridgeline family office, compliance of recovery is what lets the office prove to an auditor that a recovery was authorized by two named trustees, witnessed by a named compliance officer, and recorded as a governed succession -- all from the record, not a reconstructed support-ticket trail.** When Ridgeline faces scrutiny of a recovery, the legacy path reconstructs from support logs who did what. This volume gives it a governed proof: the guardian quorum, the compliance witness, and the succession object are all governed facts on the sealed floors. The office proves its recovery was legitimate from the record the ceremony produced. Chapters 7 through 9 compare this to legacy disaster recovery, synthesize it, and hold the honest boundary of what resilience does not claim.

title: Vol 06 Resilience Recovery Shields
chapter_title: Resilience the Sovereign Way vs Legacy DR, Backup, and Escrow
text: You will compare sovereign resilience against legacy disaster recovery, backup services, and key escrow -- seeing where a governed, human-gated, custodian-free recovery holds guarantees that a custodian-based recovery cannot.

title: Vol 06 Resilience Recovery Shields
chapter_title: Resilience the Sovereign Way vs Legacy DR, Backup, and Escrow
text: **Legacy resilience -- disaster-recovery services, cloud backups that hold the keys, key-escrow providers -- buys the ability to recover by handing a custodian the power to recover, so the resilience and the vulnerability are the same mechanism.** These services are mature and effective at what they do: they keep a copy, they can restore it, they can reset access. But every one of them works by holding what it takes to recover -- the key, the backup, the reset authority. That holding is the vulnerability. A backup service that holds the key can be breached; an escrow that can release it can be compelled; a DR provider that can restore access can be socially engineered. The recovery capability is a standing power in a third party's hands, and that party is a second authority over the node. **Sovereign resilience recovers by a governed quorum of named guardians, with the root staying on the owner's own iron -- so recovery is possible without any party holding standing power over the node.** Where legacy DR gives a custodian the power to restore, sovereign resilience distributes the authorization across named guardians who must jointly assent, and keeps the root itself on the owner's iron the whole time. No single party can recover the node; no party outside the named guardians can; and no custodian holds the key. The recovery is a ceremony the owner's governed policy authorizes, not a power a service holds. The resilience is real, and it costs no sovereignty. **The recovery plan is a governed constitution the owner holds, not a service's configuration -- so who may recover is a provable governed fact, versioned and owned, not a setting in a provider's console.** In a legacy service, the recovery policy is a config: a recovery email, an escrow agreement, an admin list -- set in the provider's system, changeable by whoever administers it. In the sovereign model, the recovery policy is a governed constitution (Ch 2): authored under the owner's mandate, versioned, integrity-hashed. Changing who may recover is itself a governed act. The recovery policy belongs to the owner and is provable, not a provider's mutable setting. **The honest scope is that the sovereign model governs recovery -- it does not replace the storage that holds the snapshot or the transport that carries it -- so it composes, rather than competes with, the mechanics of resilience.** This volume does not store the snapshot at rest (that is the Sovereign Data Storage Model, S7 Vol 3) or carry it between nodes (that is Receipted Inter-Node Messaging, S6 Vol 1). What it governs is the recovery policy, the integrity-proven snapshot, and the human-gated ceremony. This is the boundary against overclaim: sovereign resilience is the governance layer over recovery, not a new storage or transport system. The reader gets exactly a governed-recovery guarantee, and the storage and transport stay at their honest homes. **Migration guidance is to replace the escrow with a guardian quorum and keep the root on the owner's iron -- so a node adopts sovereign resilience by changing who holds the recovery power, not by discarding its storage or transport.** A node need not replace its infrastructure to adopt this model. It replaces the custodian -- the escrow, the recovery service -- with a declared guardian quorum (Ch 2), and it keeps the root on its own iron, snapshotting to its own governed objects (Ch 3) carried to chosen partners (Ch 5). The storage and the network may be unchanged; the recovery authority moves from a custodian to the owner's declared quorum. The migration is a change of trust, not of infrastructure. **The realism is that a guardian quorum has a cost -- guardians must be chosen, reachable, and willing to assent, and a recovery takes several people rather than one call -- and the sovereign model pays it deliberately because the alternative is a custodian who can take what it can restore.** Recovering by quorum is not as frictionless as calling a support desk: the guardians must exist, be reachable in an emergency, and give attributable assent. That friction is the price of having no custodian. For a node whose sovereignty matters -- whose authority a custodian must never be able to assume -- the price is worth paying, and the volume is honest that it is a price. The convenience of a custodian is exactly the vulnerability of a custodian; the quorum trades a little friction for the removal of a second authority. **For the Ridgeline family office, the choice between an escrow service and a guardian quorum is the choice between a custodian who can restore the office and one who could therefore take it, versus three named trustees of whom two must agree -- and for the authority the office runs on, the family chooses the quorum.** Ridgeline could register an escrow and recover with a phone call. But that escrow could be breached or compelled, and whoever holds it holds the office. Instead the family names three trustees, requires two to assent, and keeps its root on its own iron. Recovery takes a little more -- two trustees, in the open, attributably -- and in exchange no custodian can ever assume the office's authority. The family bought resilience without buying a master. Chapters 8 and 9 synthesize this and hold the honest boundary of what resilience does not claim.

title: Vol 06 Resilience Recovery Shields
chapter_title: Resilience as Generational Continuity of Authority
text: You will see resilience synthesized as the generational continuity of a federation's authority -- recoverable by a governed quorum across every failure and succession -- so a federation's authority survives the loss of any surface and the passing of any custodian, on its own terms.

title: Vol 06 Resilience Recovery Shields
chapter_title: Resilience as Generational Continuity of Authority
text: **This volume built one thing -- the recovery of a node's authority by a governed, human-gated quorum of named guardians -- and everything in it follows from that single idea: the recovery policy is a governed constitution, the snapshot is the owner's own integrity-proven object, and the ceremony is the named guardians' own assent, ratified as a succession.** The chapters are one capability seen from its faces: declare the recovery constitution (Ch 2), snapshot the resource (Ch 3), recover by the human-gated ceremony (Ch 4), extend it across nodes (Ch 5), and prove it through the sealed compliance floors (Ch 6). The synthesis is that a federation no longer buys resilience by surrendering its root to a custodian -- it recovers by a governed quorum it holds. **The volume rolls no cryptography and builds no recovery engine -- `declare_recovery_plan`, `snapshot_resource`, and `recover_authority` compose the sealed Constitutions, Object Model, P5 Merkle, HumanApprovalGate, and Continuity floors -- so resilience inherits audited foundations rather than adding unproven machinery.** The honest account of the volume's construction is a list of compositions. The recovery policy is the sealed `open_constitution` (S5 Vol 30). The snapshot's integrity is the sealed P5 Merkle. The ceremony's assent is the sealed `HumanApprovalGate` (S5 Vol 16). The succession is the sealed Generational Continuity handoff (S5 Vol 29). What the volume adds is the deny-by-default binding that turns these into a custodian-free recovery -- and nothing else. There is no recovery engine, no escrow, no cryptography of its own. The capability is real because the floors beneath it are sealed and proven. **Resilience is the completion of zero-trust -- the whole series argued for never trusting an unverified party, and a recovery custodian is the last such party a node usually keeps, so removing it completes the architecture.** Zero-Trust Sovereignty built, volume by volume, a node that verifies rather than trusts: its access (Vol 1), its shields (Vol 2), its storage (Vol 3), its flows (Vol 4), its private/shared boundary (Vol 5). But a node that still escrows its key to a custodian has kept one trusted party -- the most powerful one. This capstone removes it. Recovery by a governed quorum, with the root on the owner's iron, is zero-trust applied to the last place it was missing: the recovery path itself. The architecture is complete when even recovery trusts no custodian. **The generational handoff is that a successor can recover a node's authority by its governed recovery plan alone -- the named guardians assenting -- without any custodian holding the key or any service performing the restore.** This is the deepest reason resilience matters for Lasting Generational Prosperity. When a federation passes to a new generation, the authority it runs on must be recoverable by the successors -- but not by a custodian who outlived the founders. A governed recovery plan makes the handoff clean: the successors are (or name) the guardians, and they recover by the ceremony the founders declared, with no custodian to trust and no escrow to inherit. The authority survives the succession because its recovery is a governed policy the federation holds, not a custodian's standing power. **The final synthesis is that authority which can be recovered by a governed quorum outlasts every failure and every succession, while authority that depends on a custodian dies when the custodian fails or is taken when the custodian acts -- so a sovereign federation makes recovery a governed ceremony precisely so its authority can endure across generations on its own terms.** A federation's prosperity rests on its authority persisting -- through lost machines, lost surfaces, and the passing of the people who held them. Authority escrowed to a custodian is only as durable as the custodian and only as sovereign as the custodian allows. Authority recoverable by a governed quorum endures every failure and every succession without a custodian to trust or to fear. That is how a federation's authority compounds across generations instead of dying with a lost key or being captured by an escrow: recovery is a governed, human-gated ceremony the federation holds, and the root never leaves its iron. **For the Ridgeline family office, resilience is what lets the office's authority pass intact to the next generation -- recoverable by the trustees the family named, across every lost surface and every handoff -- so the successors inherit an office they can recover on their own terms, not one held hostage by an escrow the founders signed.** When Ridgeline hands its office to the next generation, it hands over a recovery constitution: named trustees, an M-of-N quorum, a root on the family's own iron. The successors can recover the office's authority after any failure by the ceremony the founders declared, with no custodian to trust and no escrow to inherit. The office's authority survives every lost phone and every generational handoff, on the family's own terms. That is the resilience this volume built -- and Chapter 9 holds the honest boundary of what it does not claim.

title: Vol 06 Resilience Recovery Shields
chapter_title: What Resilience Does NOT Claim -- The Held-G3 Boundary
text: You will read the honest non-goals of this volume and of Zero-Trust Sovereignty -- what resilience does not claim, what stays on iron, and what is held for later -- so the capstone seals the series with an accurate boundary, not an overclaim.

title: Vol 06 Resilience Recovery Shields
chapter_title: What Resilience Does NOT Claim -- The Held-G3 Boundary
text: **A capstone earns its place by holding the boundary as honestly as the series held its claims -- so this chapter states plainly what resilience does NOT claim, what stays on the owner's own iron, and what is held for later, because the coherence of Zero-Trust Sovereignty rests on claiming exactly what was built and no more.** Every volume of this series ended with a receipt marking what runs today and what is homed elsewhere. The series as a whole earns the same discipline: a final, honest boundary. This chapter is that boundary -- the Held-G3 seal -- and it is deliberately a chapter of non-goals, because an architecture that over-claims at its capstone undermines every honest claim it made along the way. **Resilience does not claim to prevent failure -- it claims to make recovery a governed, human-gated, custodian-free ceremony -- so a reader must not mistake this volume for a promise that nothing will break.** Machines fail; surfaces are lost; sites go down. This volume does not prevent any of that, and it does not claim to. What it provides is that when a failure happens, recovery is possible without a custodian: a governed quorum of named guardians, over a root on the owner's iron. The honest statement is narrow and exact -- resilience here is the governance of recovery, not the prevention of failure. A reader who took it as a guarantee against failure would be trusting something the volume never built. **The root stays on the owner's own iron -- this volume governs who may authorize a recovery and how, but it does not manage keys, run key ceremonies at the hardware level, or hold the secret -- so the actual custody of the root is the owner's, on the owner's hardware, outside this governance layer.** The whole point of custodian-free recovery is that the root never leaves the owner's iron. This volume governs the policy and the ceremony of recovery; it does not store the key, generate it, rotate it, or perform hardware-level key operations. Those are the owner's, on the owner's hardware. The volume is a governance layer over recovery, not a key-management system. Confusing the two would put the root back where the volume worked to keep it out of -- a managed store. **Recovery is a composition of sealed floors -- there is no recovery engine, no escrow, and no central trust service anywhere in this volume -- so a reader must not look for, or build, a service that holds the plans and runs the restores.** The volume's three acts compose the sealed Constitutions, Object Model, Merkle, HumanApprovalGate, and Continuity floors. There is no new engine that centralizes recovery, no escrow that holds keys, no trust service that blesses restores. The kill-targets held throughout, and they hold at the capstone: recovery is composition, not an engine. A reader who built a central recovery service on top of this would recreate exactly the custodian the volume removed. **What is held for later is named honestly -- automated failover orchestration across a live fleet, hardware-level key ceremonies, and the operator surfaces that make a guardian ceremony convenient are homed at the surface (six-sov.com/seeit) and at the node's own key runtime, not claimed here -- so the boundary between what is built and what is designed-toward is exact.** This volume builds the governed recovery policy, the snapshot, and the ceremony. It does not build automated fleet-wide failover orchestration, the hardware key ceremonies that generate and hold the root, or the operator UX that makes convening guardians easy in an emergency -- those are the node's own key runtime and the sovereign surface, named and homed, not claimed as present. Naming what is held keeps the capstone honest: the recovery governance is real and complete; the operational conveniences around it are homed, not overclaimed. **The series coherence seal is that Zero-Trust Sovereignty claims exactly what it built -- access, shields, storage, flows, private/shared governance, and now custodian-free recovery -- each a composition of sealed floors, each with its boundary named, and nothing beyond.** Across six volumes, the series built a node that verifies rather than trusts, all the way down to its recovery. Each capability is a composition of audited, sealed foundations; each named what it did not own; none rolled its own cryptography or built a central authority. This capstone completes the arc and seals it with the same honesty: the architecture is what it built, and its boundary is where it said. A reader can take Zero-Trust Sovereignty as an exact account of a self-verifying node, because at every step, including this last one, it claimed precisely what was proven and held the rest honestly. **For the Ridgeline family office, the Held-G3 boundary is the honest promise the whole series makes -- the office can verify its access, protect its records, govern its data, prove its flows, hold its private/shared boundary, and recover its authority without a custodian, and it is told exactly where each capability ends -- so the family trusts the architecture because the architecture never overclaimed.** When Ridgeline adopts Zero-Trust Sovereignty, it gets a node it can verify at every layer, including recovery.
