The choice to build for the novice and the heir -- and to make the check simple enough for the resourceless -- is the choice to make the node a lasting asset rather than a one-operator instrument. **Migration is to declare levels and a handoff over the same records -- not to rebuild the data -- so a node becomes generationally legible without changing what it stores.** A node adopting the generational surface does not restructure its records; it declares a `LevelSet` over them and exposes a handoff view. The novice level, the operator level, and the handoff are all windows onto the existing object; the weakest-party check comes free from rendering through the Lens. The migration adds legibility and verifiability on top of the records the node already holds, leaving the data unchanged and making it inheritable. **For the Ridgeline family office, the choice between an expert-only interface and Generational UX is the choice between a node only its current operator can read and one an heir can inherit, read, and verify -- and for a node meant to last generations, they choose the surface built for whoever comes next.** Ridgeline keeps its records but refuses the expert-only surface over them. Its generational UX renders the same records at every level, hands an heir the complete whole, and lets the weakest reader check that what they see is current. The office builds a node its successors can actually inherit. Chapter 8 synthesises the surface as one a successor can inherit and verify.

title: S8 05 Generational Ux
chapter_title: A Surface a Successor Can Inherit and Verify
text: You will see Generational UX synthesised -- the same governed object rendered at every level, a complete handoff, deny-by-default and read-only guards, and a weakest-party green light -- so a node is legible to a novice, complete for an heir, and verifiable by the resourceless; a surface built so a node outlives its operator.

title: S8 05 Generational Ux
chapter_title: A Surface a Successor Can Inherit and Verify
text: **This volume built one thing -- the same governed object rendered at every level, complete for a successor and verifiable by the weakest reader -- and everything in it followed from that: the level rendering, the omit-not-distort discipline, the guards, the whole-object check.** The chapters are one discipline seen from its faces: the same object at every level (Ch 2), omit-not-distort and the complete handoff (Ch 3), deny-by-default and read-only (Ch 4), and weakest-party verifiability (Ch 5). The synthesis is that a node's records become legible to whoever inherits them, at the depth they can handle, and checkable by a green light anyone can read. **`progressive_view` composes the Sovereign Lens and adds only levels and a whole-object check -- no new renderer, no data restructuring, no estate logic, and no cryptography.** The honest account is a thin composition. The rendering is the Lens, at every level; the host is the Atrium; continuity is S5 Vol 29; onboarding is S6 Vol 6; estate logic is OUT to S12. To all of that the surface adds exactly two things: a declared set of levels over the same object, and the weakest-party check that falls out of fingerprinting the whole. It restructures no records, owns no estate logic, and rolls no cryptography. Its whole contribution is making a node legible across expertise and checkable by the least-equipped. **It gives the operator layer its generational face -- the earlier volumes governed how a person sees, acts, styles, hosts, federates, and verifies; this volume governs whether a successor can read and trust it.** Interface Sovereignty built the operator layer for the person operating a node now. This volume extends it to the person who will operate it next. The same records the Lens renders honestly are rendered at the successor's level; the same verification that made a view trustworthy is degraded to a green light the heir can check. The operator layer is no longer only for the present operator; it is for the whole line of people a sovereign node passes through. **The generational handoff is that an heir inherits a node they can read and verify -- not a mystery they must trust -- because the surface shows them the whole at their level and lets them check it with a green light.** Lasting Generational Prosperity asks that a node pass to a successor as a living asset. A surface built for its expert hands an heir records they cannot read and cannot check. The generational surface hands them the complete object at the level they can handle, and a fresh-or-drifted signal they can verify without expertise or a second device. The heir inherits not a promise about the node but the node itself -- legible and checkable in their own hands. **A surface a successor can inherit and verify -- so a node's legibility is as sovereign as its records, its actions, and its verification, all the way to the person who inherits it.** The series built the operator layer face by face, and this volume gives it the face that makes a node last: one a successor can read at their level, inherit in full, and check with a green light. A node running Generational UX is not a one-operator instrument; it is an inheritable, verifiable asset whose surface serves every reader it will ever have. That is a node a family can hand down, and it is the foundation of a prosperity meant to last. On this volume's seal, S8 stands at 7 of 8. **For the Ridgeline family office, Generational UX is how the family makes its node inheritable -- the same records at every level, a complete handoff, and a green light an heir on a borrowed screen can check -- so the node passes to the next generation as an asset they can operate and trust, not a mystery they must decode.** When Ridgeline hands its node to an heir, the heir reads the office's real records at their level, inherits the complete object, and verifies it is current with a signal they can check anywhere. The family's node survives its operator, legible and verifiable in the hands of whoever comes next.

title: S8 06 Federation Ux
chapter_title: Seeing Across Sovereign Nodes -- A View That Owns None of Them
text: You will see why an operator layer that spans a federation of sovereign nodes must render the whole picture read-only -- a view assembled from what each node supplies, owning no authority over any of them -- rather than a central console that reaches into every node and becomes the one that owns them all.

title: S8 06 Federation Ux
chapter_title: Seeing Across Sovereign Nodes -- A View That Owns None of Them
text: **The earlier volumes governed the operator's surface onto one node; this volume governs the surface onto many -- a federation of sovereign nodes seen together, without any of them being owned.** An operator rarely works with a single node in isolation. A family office coordinates with the nodes of its advisors, its entities, its next generation; a business spans the nodes of its divisions and partners. The operator layer must show that whole picture. The discipline of this volume is that showing the federation must never become owning it: the view is assembled from what each node chooses to supply, and it holds no authority over any node it renders. **Legacy federation is a central console -- one surface that reaches into every node, pulls their state, issues commands, and becomes, in practice, the owner of the federation.** The usual way to build a multi-node view is a hub. A central console holds credentials to every node, fetches their state on a schedule, and offers operators the power to act on any node from one place. It is convenient and it is fatal to sovereignty: the console accumulates the authority of every node it touches, until the federation is not a set of sovereign peers but a set of subordinates to the hub. The node that runs the console owns the rest. **A console that owns the federation is the single point that un-sovereigns every node -- the exact collapse the operator layer was built to refuse, now across the whole federation.** Volume 4 refused the god-object host that owns one node; a central federation console is that god-object multiplied. When one surface can reach into and command every node, each node's sovereignty is nominal -- it holds until the hub decides otherwise. The boundaries the earlier volumes built (honest read, human-gated write, read-only watch) are not just weakened; they are relocated to a hub that sits above every node. Federation done this way is centralization wearing a federated name. **The sovereign opportunity is a view assembled from what each node supplies -- a read-only composite that renders cross-node state and owns no cross-node authority.** This volume builds that. `federated_view` takes the snapshots that nodes supply -- each node offering its own governed state -- and renders each through the Sovereign Lens into a single frozen composite. It renders the whole federation and holds power over none of it: it cannot reach into a node, cannot command one, cannot change one. The view is a window onto a federation of peers, not a throne above them. What an operator does with what they see is an action, and an action on a node goes through that node's own gate. **The honest scope is that this volume renders the federation; it does not transport between nodes, coordinate them, or hold their authority -- those are sealed floors it composes, named plainly.** The federation view is deliberately thin. It does not move messages between nodes -- that is the Sovereign Port. It does not coordinate the nodes' shared work -- that is Resonance Coordination (S6 Vol 4). It does not hold the write path -- that is the Atrium's gate. What it adds is the operator's cross-node sight: a read-only, honest, mandate-scoped composite of supplied state. Every other capability is a floor beneath it, and the volume names each one rather than absorbing it. **The generational stake is a federation a node joins without being owned -- a successor's node can be seen alongside others, and can see others, while remaining fully its own.** Lasting Generational Prosperity asks that a node be operable by a successor and able to work with others without surrendering itself. A federation built on a central console cannot offer that: to join is to be owned by the hub. A federation built on `federated_view` can: a node supplies what it chooses, sees what it is admitted to, and holds its own authority throughout. A family can federate across generations and entities without any node becoming the master of the rest. The chapters build it: the federated view (Ch 2), each node sovereign (Ch 3), mandate scope over fields and nodes (Ch 4), and honest drift (Ch 5), with what it composes (Ch 6), the contrast with a central console (Ch 7), and the synthesis (Ch 8).

title: S8 06 Federation Ux
text: You will see how a cross-node view is built by composition -- federated_view renders each node's supplied snapshot through the Sovereign Lens into a frozen composite that owns no cross-node authority and exposes no way to act on a node -- so the federation surface renders the whole picture and holds power over none of it.

title: S8 06 Federation Ux
text: **A cross-node view that owns nothing begins as a composition -- each node's state rendered through the same honest Lens, assembled into a frozen composite with no power to act.** Before an operator can see a federation safely, the surface that shows it must be the right kind of thing: not a hub with authority over nodes, but a read-only assembly of what nodes supply. This chapter builds it. `federated_view` renders a mapping of node snapshots into a `FederatedView`, and the shape of that object -- frozen, methodless of any write -- is what makes cross-node sight safe. **`federated_view(node_states, ...)` renders each node's supplied snapshot through the Sovereign Lens -- one call, many nodes, each rendered the same honest way.** The signature is a mapping: `node_states` is `{node_id: that node's supplied governed snapshot}`. For each node, `federated_view` calls the Lens's `render_view` on the supplied snapshot and keys the resulting View by node id. `test_renders_each_node_through_the_lens_readonly` proves it: two nodes' states render into two Lens Views, each carrying that node's content. The operator sees every node through the identical read-only, honest projection the Lens gives a single node -- now assembled across the federation. **The result is a frozen `FederatedView` -- a read-only window onto the federation, not a mutable console an operator edits.** `FederatedView` holds the per-node Views and offers exactly two ways to read them: `node_ids` (which nodes are present) and `node(id)` (one node's View). It is a frozen dataclass -- `test_federated_view_is_frozen` proves its fields cannot be reassigned. There is no growing internal state, no accumulated cross-node authority, nothing the surface owns that could be turned against a node. The composite is a snapshot of sight, not a seat of power. **It exposes NO write or act method -- no write, save, apply, mutate, run, command, send, or act -- so the federation surface can render a node but never command one.** The kill-target of the volume is enforced at the surface's API. `test_no_write_or_act_method_on_the_federation_surface` reads `FederatedView`'s public methods and asserts none of the forbidden authority verbs -- including `command`, `send`, and `act` alongside the usual mutation verbs -- appears. The absence is the guarantee: there is no method by which the federation surface reaches into a node. To act on a node is to go to that node's own Atrium and its human-gated write path; the cross-node view offers no shortcut around a node's sovereignty. **Its rendering IS the Lens's `render_view`, composed by identity -- the federation surface builds no renderer of its own, so cross-node sight is exactly as honest and read-only as single-node sight.** The composition is literal. `test_composes_the_lens_by_identity` proves that the module's `render_view` is the Lens's `render_view` -- the same imported function, not a re-implementation. Every node in the federation is rendered through the sealed Lens: read-only, content-agnostic, drift-fingerprinted. There is no federation-specific rendering path that could diverge from the honest single-node one. The federation inherits the Lens's discipline whole, once per node. **In the acceptance tests, the federation surface renders each node through the Lens, is frozen, exposes no write or act method, and composes the Lens by identity -- so the render-cross-node-own-no-authority posture is executable and proven, not asserted.** `test_renders_each_node_through_the_lens_readonly` proves the composite render. `test_federated_view_is_frozen` and `test_no_write_or_act_method_on_the_federation_surface` prove it owns and commands nothing. `test_composes_the_lens_by_identity` proves the borrowed honesty. The federation surface is proven in code. **For the Ridgeline family office, the federated view means the family sees its advisor, entity, and successor nodes together in one read-only window -- and that window holds no power to reach into any of them.** When Ridgeline views its federation, it gets a `FederatedView` composing each node's supplied state through the Lens: the whole picture, honest and read-only, with no method by which the family's console could command a partner's node or a successor's. Chapter 3 makes the sovereignty concrete -- the surface renders only what a node supplies, and can never fetch or mutate it.

title: S8 06 Federation Ux
chapter_title: Each Node Sovereign -- Render the Supplied, Never Fetch or Command
text: You will see how the federation surface keeps every node sovereign -- it renders only the snapshots a node supplies, imports no client that could fetch or command a node, and never mutates a node's state -- so a node in the federation is seen exactly as much as it chooses to show, and is never reached into.

title: S8 06 Federation Ux
chapter_title: Each Node Sovereign -- Render the Supplied, Never Fetch or Command
text: **A federation stays sovereign only if the surface that shows it cannot reach into a node -- so the deepest discipline of this volume is that `federated_view` renders the supplied and fetches nothing.** It is not enough that the federation surface merely chooses not to command nodes; it must be structurally unable to. This chapter shows how: the surface renders state that nodes hand it, and it imports nothing that could pull state or issue a command. Sovereignty is preserved not by policy but by construction. **The surface renders snapshots the caller supplies -- each node offers its own governed state, and the federation view renders what it is given.** `federated_view` takes a mapping of node id to snapshot. Those snapshots are supplied to it -- by each node, on that node's terms, through the node's own channels. The federation view does not go and get them. It is a rendering function over provided data, exactly as the single-node Lens renders an object handed to it. A node that supplies nothing appears not at all; a node that supplies a partial snapshot is seen partially. What the operator sees of a node is precisely what that node offered. **It imports no messaging, transport, or port client -- so it structurally cannot fetch a node's state or reach across the wire.** The guarantee is enforced at the module's imports. `test_renders_only_supplied_snapshots_imports_no_transport_or_messaging` reads the module's imports and asserts it composes only the Lens -- and imports none of messaging, collaboration, transport, port, socket, or any network client. The federation surface has no code path to the wire. It cannot open a connection, cannot poll a node, cannot pull state a node did not hand it. The delivery of snapshots is the job of the sealed inter-node floors (Chapter 6); the federation view only renders what those floors, under each node's sovereignty, deliver to it. **It cannot command a node -- there is no path from the federation view into a node's authority, because the view holds none and imports none.** Rendering and commanding are different powers, and the federation surface has only the first. It produces read-only Views; it holds no write path (Chapter 2); and it imports no client through which a command could travel. An operator studying the federation cannot, from that surface, tell a node to do anything. To act on a node, they compose that node's Atrium, and the action is the node's own core executing on a human's gated assent. The federation view is sight without command. **Rendering never mutates a node -- the Lens deep-copies every snapshot, so a node's state is untouched by being seen.** Sovereignty includes integrity: seeing a node must not change it. Because `federated_view` renders through the Lens, and the Lens returns a deep copy, the rendered content shares no mutable state with the node's snapshot. `test_rendering_does_not_mutate_a_node_state` proves it: mutating a rendered node's View leaves the source snapshot unchanged. A node can be rendered into a thousand federation views and remain exactly itself. Observation is inert. **Each node is seen exactly as much as it supplies and no more -- so a node joins a federation without exposing more than it chooses, and without being reachable through the view.** Put together, the sovereignty guarantee is complete. A node controls what it supplies; the federation view renders only that; it cannot fetch more, cannot command the node, and cannot change it. The node is a full peer in the federation, visible on its own terms, reachable only through its own gate. This is what it means for a federation to be sovereign at the surface: the view shows the peers without subordinating any of them. **In the acceptance tests, the surface imports no cross-node client and does not mutate a node's state -- so the render-the-supplied, never-fetch discipline is executable and proven, not asserted.** `test_renders_only_supplied_snapshots_imports_no_transport_or_messaging` proves the surface cannot fetch or command. `test_rendering_does_not_mutate_a_node_state` proves seeing is inert. Node sovereignty is proven in code. **For the Ridgeline family office, node sovereignty means a partner's node or a successor's node appears in the family's federation view only as much as that node supplies -- and the family's surface can neither pull more from it nor command it.** When Ridgeline federates with an advisor's node, the advisor supplies what they choose; Ridgeline's view renders exactly that, fetches nothing more, and holds no power over the advisor's node. Each party sees the other as a sovereign peer. Chapter 4 scopes that sight further -- by mandate, over both fields and nodes.

title: S8 06 Federation Ux
chapter_title: Mandate-Scoped Federation -- Which Fields, and Which Nodes
text: You will see how the federation view is scoped by a mandate over two axes -- which fields each node exposes, and which nodes are visible at all -- both deny-by-default, so an operator sees exactly the cross-node picture their mandate admits and nothing beyond it.

title: S8 06 Federation Ux
chapter_title: Mandate-Scoped Federation -- Which Fields, and Which Nodes
text: **A federation view must be scoped, because not every operator may see every node or every field -- so `federated_view` carries a mandate over two axes: which fields each node exposes, and which nodes appear at all.** Seeing across a federation multiplies the access question: it is no longer only "which fields of this node," but also "which nodes." This chapter scopes both, deny-by-default, so the cross-node picture an operator sees is exactly the one their mandate admits. **The federation view carries the Lens's mandate scope -- each node is rendered under the same field-level scoping the Lens gives a single node.** Because `federated_view` renders every node through `render_view`, it passes the mandate and scope through to each. A mandate with a scope map admits only the named fields of each node's snapshot; everything else is withheld. `test_mandate_scopes_which_fields_each_node_exposes` proves it: an auditor mandate scoped to `posture` and `balance` sees those fields of every node and never the `secret` field. Field-level access, governed once by the Lens, applies uniformly across the federation. **An un-mapped mandate is admitted nothing -- deny-by-default, per node, inherited from the Lens.** The scoping is deny-by-default. A mandate not present in the scope map is admitted no fields at all -- it sees each node as empty, not as fully exposed. `test_unmapped_mandate_is_admitted_nothing_deny_by_default` proves a `stranger` mandate, absent from the map, renders each node's content as empty. The federation never leaks a node's fields to a mandate it does not recognize; the default is to show nothing, and access is granted only by explicit mapping. **A second axis scopes which nodes are visible at all -- `admits(node_id)` decides node-level membership, deny-by-default the caller's to express.** Federation adds the node axis, and `federated_view` scopes it with an `admits` predicate: only nodes for which `admits(node_id)` is true are rendered into the composite. `test_admits_scopes_which_nodes_are_visible` proves that with `admits` admitting only `node-a`, the federation view contains `node-a` alone and asking for `node-b` raises -- it was never admitted. A mandate can thus be confined to a subset of the federation: an operator responsible for one region's nodes sees those nodes and not the others. **The two axes compose -- a mandate admits some nodes, and within each admitted node, some fields -- so scope is expressed exactly, at both the federation and the node level.** Together, `admits` and the field scope give precise cross-node access. A mandate might admit three of a federation's ten nodes, and within those three, only the fields an auditor may see. The composite the operator receives is that intersection: the right nodes, each showing the right fields, everything else withheld deny-by-default. There is no coarse all-or-nothing federation view; access is scoped on both axes at once. **An operator sees exactly the cross-node picture their mandate admits and nothing beyond it -- the federation is as access-governed as a single node, across every node.** The scoping closes the federation's access question. Whatever an operator's mandate, the federation view they receive shows the nodes they may see and the fields they may read, and refuses the rest by default. A broad mandate sees broadly; a narrow one narrowly; an unrecognized one sees nothing. The cross-node picture is never more than the mandate admits, which is what lets a federation include operators of many different scopes without any of them over-seeing. **In the acceptance tests, the federation view scopes fields per node and nodes per mandate, both deny-by-default -- so the two-axis mandate scope is executable and proven, not asserted.** `test_mandate_scopes_which_fields_each_node_exposes` and `test_unmapped_mandate_is_admitted_nothing_deny_by_default` prove field scope. `test_admits_scopes_which_nodes_are_visible` proves node scope. The two-axis federation scope is proven in code. **For the Ridgeline family office, two-axis scope means a regional operator sees only their region's nodes, and only the fields their role admits of each -- the federation includes them without over-exposing it.** When Ridgeline grants an operator a mandate, that mandate admits a subset of the federation's nodes and a subset of each node's fields; everything else is withheld by default. The family can bring many operators into one federation view, each scoped precisely, none seeing beyond their mandate. Chapter 5 makes the view honest over time -- a node that moves reads as drift.

title: S8 06 Federation Ux
chapter_title: Honest Federation -- A Node That Moves Reads as Drift
text: You will see how the federation view stays honest over time -- verify_federated reports each node's freshness against its current state, and a node whose state moved since render, or that stopped reporting, reads as drift rather than silently stale -- so a federation picture never quietly lies about a node.

title: S8 06 Federation Ux
chapter_title: Honest Federation -- A Node That Moves Reads as Drift
text: **A federation view is a snapshot of many nodes at one moment, and nodes move -- so the last discipline of the surface is that a view which has gone stale must say so, per node, rather than quietly misrepresent the federation.** The danger of a cross-node view is that it ages unevenly: one node's state advances while the view still shows the old value, and the operator, trusting the picture, acts on a node that has moved. This chapter makes the federation view honest over time -- staleness is detected and named, never hidden. **`verify_federated(fed, current_states)` reports each node's freshness against that node's current supplied state -- honesty checked node by node.** The Lens fingerprints the full source at render time; `verify_federated` uses that to check each node. Given the federation view and the nodes' current snapshots, it re-fingerprints each and returns a per-node status: fresh if the node's state is unchanged since render, drift if it moved. `test_verify_federated_flags_a_node_that_moved` proves it: when one node's balance changes after render, that node reads drift while the unchanged node reads fresh. The federation's honesty is not global; it is resolved to the node, so the operator learns exactly which part of the picture has aged. **A node whose state moved since render reads as drift -- the change is named, not silently absorbed into a stale view.** Drift is the honest verdict. A federation view showing a node's old posture, after that node's posture changed, does not silently keep showing the old value as if current; `verify_federated` flags that node as drifted. The operator is told, precisely, that this node's rendered View no longer matches the node, and can re-render before acting. The view never pretends a moved node is current -- the same read-only-honesty the Lens gives one node, resolved across the federation. **A node that stopped reporting reads as drift too -- its rendered View can no longer be confirmed, so it is surfaced, never assumed still-true.** Federation adds a failure mode a single node does not have: a node can drop out. `verify_federated` handles it honestly -- a node present in the view but absent from the current states reads as drift, because its rendered View can no longer be confirmed against a live source. `test_verify_federated_flags_a_departed_node_as_drift` proves a departed node reads drift. The federation view does not quietly keep displaying a vanished node's last state as if it were still true; it surfaces that the node can no longer be confirmed, which is the honest thing to show. **A federation picture never quietly lies about a node -- every node's freshness is checkable, and staleness is surfaced per node rather than smoothed over.** The guarantee closes the federation's honesty question. Whatever the operator sees, they can verify each node against its live state, and any node that has moved or departed is named as such. There is no aggregate "the view is roughly current" that hides a single stale node. The picture is honest at the granularity that matters -- the node an operator is about to act on -- so a cross-node view can be trusted to say plainly which of its parts are fresh. **This composes the Lens's drift discipline across the federation -- the honesty that made a single View trustworthy now makes a many-node view trustworthy, node by node.** The federation view builds no new honesty mechanism; it applies the Lens's fingerprint-and-verify across every node. What made a single node's View safe to act on -- that it cannot lie by going stale without saying so -- is exactly what makes the federation safe: each node's View carries the same guarantee, and `verify_federated` reads them together. The federation inherits honesty the same way it inherits rendering: from the Lens, once per node. **In the acceptance tests, a moved node and a departed node both read as drift while an unchanged node reads fresh -- so the honest-federation discipline is executable and proven, not asserted.** `test_verify_federated_flags_a_node_that_moved` proves a moved node drifts and an unchanged one stays fresh. `test_verify_federated_flags_a_departed_node_as_drift` proves a vanished node drifts. Federation honesty is proven in code. **For the Ridgeline family office, honest federation means the family can check its cross-node picture and see exactly which nodes have moved or dropped out since it last rendered -- and act only on the parts it has confirmed current.** When Ridgeline reviews its federation, `verify_federated` tells it which advisor, entity, and successor nodes are still fresh and which have drifted; the family re-renders the drifted ones before acting, and knows a departed node by name rather than trusting its stale last state. The cross-node picture is honest per node. Chapter 6 names exactly the sealed floors this federation surface composes.

title: S8 06 Federation Ux
chapter_title: What Federation UX Composes -- The Lens, the Host, and the Inter-Node Floors
text: You will see exactly what the federation surface composes -- the Sovereign Lens for rendering, the Atrium for the gated host it presents through, and the sealed inter-node floors that deliver cross-node state -- so every capability the surface appears to have is a sealed floor beneath it, and transport is named OUT.

title: S8 06 Federation Ux
chapter_title: What Federation UX Composes -- The Lens, the Host, and the Inter-Node Floors
text: **The federation surface looks capable -- it shows many nodes, honestly, scoped -- but it is a composition of sealed floors, and naming them exactly is how the reader sees it owns nothing across the federation.** This chapter is the honest inventory. The federation view's rendering, its host, and the cross-node state it displays are each a governed floor it composes; listing them, with their series-qualified homes, proves the surface adds cross-node sight and nothing more. **The rendering is the Sovereign Lens (Series 8, Volume 1), and the host it presents through is the Atrium (Series 8, Volume 4) -- the federation view's sight and surface are the operator layer it already has.** The federation view renders every node through the Lens; that is its sight, unchanged from the single-node case. And the federation view is shown through the Atrium -- the composed host whose write path is the human breath-gate. So the cross-node surface inherits both the honest read of Volume 1 and the gated write of Volume 4: an operator acts on a node in the federation only through that node's Atrium, human-gated, never through the federation view itself. **The cross-node substrate the view renders is delivered by the sealed inter-node floors of Series 6 -- the federation view renders their output; it does not build the federation's plumbing.** The federation view renders snapshots that nodes supply, but something must carry those snapshots between sovereign nodes. That is Series 6, Inter-Node Sovereignty, and the federation view composes its sealed floors rather than reinventing them. The plumbing is not this volume's; this volume is the operator's cross-node sight over what that plumbing delivers. **Coordination composes Resonance Coordination (Series 6, Volume 4); shared work composes Sovereign Collaboration (Series 6, Volume 2); the receipted message layer composes Receipted Inter-Node Messaging (Series 6, Volume 1).** Named precisely: when nodes coordinate their aligned work across the federation, that is Resonance Coordination (S6 Vol 4) -- the sealed floor the federation view composes for cross-node coordination, and the only place the word belongs. When nodes collaborate on shared artifacts, that is Sovereign Collaboration (S6 Vol 2). When they exchange receipted messages, that is Receipted Inter-Node Messaging (S6 Vol 1). The federation view displays the state these floors produce; it composes them and holds none of their authority. **Transport is OUT -- the wire between nodes, the actual delivery across the network, is the Sovereign Port (Series 6, Volume 7), not this volume.** The one thing the federation view must be clearest about not being is transport. It does not move bytes between nodes; it does not open connections; it imports no network client (Chapter 3). The wire is the Sovereign Port (S6 Vol 7), sealed and separate. The federation view sits above transport, rendering what arrives; it never becomes the thing that carries. Marking transport OUT is what keeps the surface a view and not a hub. **Every power the federation surface appears to have is a sealed floor beneath it, and it owns none of them -- which is the whole claim of the volume, made concrete by the inventory.** Read the list and the federation view disappears as an owner: sight is the Lens (S8 Vol 1); the gated host is the Atrium (S8 Vol 4); coordination, collaboration, and messaging are Series 6 floors (V4, V2, V1); transport is the Port (S6 Vol 7), OUT. What the federation view adds is the assembly -- one read-only, scoped, honest composite of supplied state. It owns no node, holds no cross-node authority, and carries no plumbing. The inventory closes with nothing left over that the surface owns. **For the Ridgeline family office, the inventory means the family can audit its federation surface floor by floor -- the Lens, the Atrium, the Series 6 inter-node floors -- and know transport is the Port, not the view.** When Ridgeline reviews how it sees its federation, it reviews sealed floors: the Lens renders, the Atrium gates any action, Series 6 carries the cross-node state, and the Port moves it. There is no owned federation hub in the middle. Chapter 7 contrasts this composed federation surface with the central console it replaces.

title: S8 06 Federation Ux
chapter_title: The Federated View vs the Central Federation Console
text: You will see the contrast that defines the volume -- a view assembled from what nodes supply, owning no cross-node authority, against a central console that holds every node's credentials, pulls their state, and commands them -- so the reader sees why rendering-not-owning is a sovereignty choice, not a convenience.

title: S8 06 Federation Ux
chapter_title: The Federated View vs the Central Federation Console
text: **The contrast that defines this volume is between a view assembled from what sovereign nodes supply, owning no authority over any, and a central console that holds every node's credentials, pulls their state, and commands them -- and the difference is sovereignty, not convenience.** Every multi-node surface must show the federation. The question is whether it does so by rendering what nodes offer or by reaching into them. This chapter sets the federated view against the central console so the reader can see that rendering-not-owning is the point, and that the alternative subordinates every node. **The legacy federation surface is a central console -- it holds credentials to every node, and in holding them, it holds every node's authority.** The default multi-node tool is a hub with keys. To show and operate many nodes from one place, the console is given access to each: credentials, endpoints, the power to read and write. The moment it holds them, it owns the federation -- every node is reachable and commandable from the center, and each node's sovereignty lasts only as long as the console permits. The convenience of one-place control is identical to the centralization of all authority. **A console pulls state and issues commands -- it reaches into each node on a schedule and acts on any node from the center, so each node is subordinate to the hub.** The console's mechanics are the opposite of the federated view's. It fetches: it polls each node, pulling state the node did not choose to push. It commands: it offers operators the power to act on any node directly. Both make the node subordinate -- its state is taken, its actions can be taken for it, from a surface above it. The federation is a hierarchy with the console on top, whatever the org chart says. **The federated view renders state that nodes supply and holds no command -- so each node stays a peer, seen but not subordinated.** The federated view inverts both mechanics. It does not fetch; it renders what nodes supply (Chapter 3). It does not command; it holds no write path and imports no client (Chapters 2-3). A node in a federated view is seen exactly as much as it offers and is reachable only through its own gate. There is no center that owns the federation, because the view owns nothing -- it is a read-only composite, and the authority over each node stays with that node. **Rendering-not-owning is a sovereignty choice, not a convenience -- the federated view is built so it can subordinate no node, and that constraint is the whole value.** The reason to render rather than own is not simplicity; it is that sovereignty can only survive if the shared surface holds no power over the nodes. A central console presents governance with a hub that owns everything and asks it to behave; the federated view presents a surface that structurally cannot subordinate a node. The choice to render supplied state, import no client, and hold no command is the choice to keep every node sovereign while still seeing them together. The constraint is the product. **Migration is to render what nodes supply and act only through each node's own gate -- a federation moves off a central console by inverting fetch-and-command into supply-and-render.** A federation adopting the federated view does not lose its cross-node picture; it changes how it gets one. Nodes supply their state (through the Series 6 floors) rather than having it pulled; operators view the composite read-only; and any action on a node routes to that node's Atrium and its human gate rather than issuing from the center. The migration removes the hub's authority and leaves a view -- the same cross-node sight, now with every node sovereign. **For the Ridgeline family office, the choice between a central console and a federated view is the choice between a hub that owns the family's whole federation and a surface that sees it while owning none of it -- and for a federation meant to include partners and successors as peers, they choose the view that subordinates no node.** Ridgeline keeps its cross-node picture but refuses the hub beneath it. Its federated view renders what each node supplies, commands nothing, and routes every action through the acted-on node's own gate. Partners and successors join as peers, not subordinates. Chapter 8 synthesises the federation as one a node joins without being owned.

title: S8 06 Federation Ux
chapter_title: A Federation a Node Joins Without Being Owned
text: You will see Federation UX synthesised -- a read-only view assembled from what sovereign nodes supply, owning no cross-node authority, scoped by mandate over fields and nodes, and honest about drift -- so a node can be seen alongside others, and see others, while remaining fully its own; a federation a successor inherits as a peer, not a subordinate.

title: S8 06 Federation Ux
chapter_title: A Federation a Node Joins Without Being Owned
text: **This volume built one thing -- a read-only view across sovereign nodes, assembled from what each supplies and owning authority over none -- and everything in it followed from that: the composite render, the render-not-fetch, the two-axis scope, the honest drift.** The chapters are one discipline seen from its faces: the federated view (Ch 2), each node sovereign (Ch 3), mandate scope over fields and nodes (Ch 4), and honest federation (Ch 5). The synthesis is that an operator can see a whole federation of nodes at once without any node being owned by the surface that shows them. **`federated_view` composes the Sovereign Lens and adds only the cross-node assembly -- no hub, no credentials, no command, no transport, and no cryptography.** The honest account is a thin composition. The rendering is the Lens, once per node; the host is the Atrium; the cross-node state is delivered by the Series 6 floors; transport is the Port, OUT. To all of that the federation view adds exactly one thing: the assembly -- a frozen, scoped, honest composite of supplied state, with no write path and no client. It builds no hub and owns no node. Its whole contribution is letting an operator see the federation as one picture while it holds power over none of it. **It extends the operator layer to the federation -- Volumes 1 through 4 governed the surface onto one node; this volume governs the surface onto many, on the same terms.** Interface Sovereignty built the operator layer for a single node: honest sight, gated action, governed look, a composed host. This volume carries that layer across a federation without changing its terms. The many-node view is still read-only, still mandate-scoped, still honest about drift, still actionless except through each node's own gate. Federation does not relax the operator layer's discipline; it applies it across the whole federation, node by node, so a federation is governed exactly as a node is. **The generational handoff is that a node joins and leaves a federation as a peer -- a successor's node can be seen by others and see others, and can walk away, without ever having been owned.** Lasting Generational Prosperity asks that a node stay sovereign and inheritable even as it works with others. A central console makes federation a trap: to join is to be owned, and to leave is to be cut off from a hub that held your keys. The federated view makes federation free: a node supplies what it chooses, is seen only that much, holds its own authority throughout, and can stop supplying and leave as the peer it always was. A family can federate across entities and generations, and any node can join or exit with its sovereignty intact. **A federation a node joins without being owned -- seen without being seized -- so an operator's cross-node picture is as sovereign as the nodes it shows.** The series set out to build the operator layer, and this volume gives it a federation surface that matches its single-node discipline. An operator running the federated view sees every node they are admitted to, honestly and read-only, and can act on none of them except through that node's own human gate. There is no hub that owns the federation, because the view owns nothing. That is a federation a family can build across peers and hand on -- one where being seen never means being seized. On this volume's seal, S8 stands at 5 of 8. **For the Ridgeline family office, Federation UX is how the family sees its whole world of nodes -- advisors, entities, successors -- as one honest, scoped, read-only picture, while every one of those nodes stays fully its own.** When Ridgeline runs its federated view, it sees the federation it belongs to without owning any part of it: each node supplies its state, is seen only as much as the mandate admits, is checked for drift, and is reachable only through its own gate. The family federates as a peer among peers, across generations, seizing nothing and owning no node but its own. The federation is seen, and it stays sovereign.

title: S8 07 Zero Trust Ux
chapter_title: A Surface That Shows What It Can Prove -- Verified, Not Vouched
text: You will see why an operator layer over a zero-trust node must show only what has been VERIFIED -- what a sealed proof has cleared -- and mark everything else as unverified, rather than a status board that shows a green light because something vouched for it, hiding the difference between a proof and a promise.

title: S8 07 Zero Trust Ux
chapter_title: A Surface That Shows What It Can Prove -- Verified, Not Vouched
text: **The Sovereign Lens rendered a node's objects honestly, and the earlier operator-layer volumes governed how a person sees, acts, looks, hosts, and federates; this volume governs the last thing an operator must see truthfully -- the difference between what has been verified and what has merely been vouched for.** A zero-trust node makes claims about itself: this flow cleared its checks, this shield held, this action was attested. The operator layer must show those claims, and it must show them honestly -- distinguishing a claim a sealed proof has cleared from a claim that is merely asserted. This volume builds that surface, and its whole discipline is that it shows what it can prove and marks the rest unverified. **Legacy status surfaces show vouched-as-verified -- a green checkmark that means "someone said so," with no proof behind it, indistinguishable from a green checkmark that means "a proof cleared."** The usual status board is credulous. A component reports healthy, and the board shows green; a flow claims it passed, and the board shows a check. There is no distinction on the surface between a result backed by a verification and a result that is simply asserted. The green light for a proven claim and the green light for a vouched claim look identical, so the operator cannot tell which trust is earned and which is borrowed. The surface launders assertion into apparent proof. **A surface that cannot tell a proof from a promise is worse than no surface at all -- it manufactures false confidence, showing trust the system never actually established.** The danger is not merely a missing feature; it is an active harm. An operator trusts the board, and the board shows verified when the truth is only vouched. Decisions ride on that false green. In a zero-trust setting -- where the whole premise is that nothing is trusted without verification -- a surface that displays vouched claims as verified defeats the architecture at the last inch, at the pane of glass the human actually reads. The node may verify rigorously and still be operated on a lie, because the surface flattened proof and promise into the same color. **The sovereign opportunity is a surface that shows what a sealed proof cleared, and marks everything else unverified -- verified means a proof, and nothing else is allowed to look like one.** This volume builds that. `verify_surface` reads the verdicts the sealed zero-trust floors produce -- Shields (S7 Vol 2) and Verified Flows (S7 Vol 4) -- and renders them so that a claim reads **verified** only when a cleared proof from a named floor backs it. A failed proof reads **failed**. An absent, malformed, or merely-vouched claim reads **unverified**. The surface never shows a promise as a proof; the green of "verified" is reserved for what a sealed floor actually cleared. **The surface proves nothing itself -- it is not a second verification authority; it renders the verdicts the sealed floors produce, and adds only the honest display.** The honest scope is narrow and important. `verify_surface` does not run a check, re-verify a proof, or hold any verification authority of its own. It reads the verdict a sealed floor already reached and displays it. This matters because a surface that re-verified would become a second authority whose judgment could diverge from the floors' -- another thing to trust. The surface trusts the sealed floors' verdicts and its only job is to show them truthfully: verified where they cleared, failed where they failed, unverified everywhere else. **The generational stake is a surface a successor can trust because it shows only what it can prove -- a green light that always means a proof cleared, never that someone vouched.** Lasting Generational Prosperity asks that a successor operate the node and trust what they see. A surface that shows vouched-as-verified hands them a board they must second-guess -- every green light a maybe. A surface that shows only verified-means-proven hands them a board they can read at face value -- every green light a proof, every unverified an honest gap. That is a surface a family can operate across generations without inheriting hidden false confidence. The chapters build it: the verification surface (Ch 2), no second authority (Ch 3), fail-closed adversarial clarity (Ch 4), and evidence rendered read-only (Ch 5), with what it composes (Ch 6), the contrast with a trust-me console (Ch 7), and the synthesis (Ch 8).

title: S8 07 Zero Trust Ux
text: You will see how a verification surface is built -- verify_surface classifies each claim as verified only when a cleared proof from a named sealed floor backs it, and renders the verdicts read-only through the Sovereign Lens -- so what shows as verified is exactly what a sealed proof cleared, and a bare assertion is never dressed as a proof.

title: S8 07 Zero Trust Ux
text: **A verification surface begins with an honest classifier -- a rule that calls a claim verified only when a real proof backs it, and calls everything else what it is.** Before a surface can show verification truthfully, it must decide, per claim, what kind of trust each carries. This chapter builds that decision. `verify_surface` classifies every claim into verified, failed, or unverified, and the classifier's discipline -- verified requires a cleared proof from a named sealed floor -- is what keeps a promise from ever being shown as a proof. **`verify_surface(proofs, ...)` classifies each claim -- it reads the proof outcome the sealed floors produced, and marks the claim verified only when that outcome is a cleared proof from a named floor.** The input is a mapping of claim to its proof outcome. For each, the surface asks a narrow question: did a sealed floor clear a proof for this? A `cleared` proof carrying the name of the floor that cleared it (Shields, Verified Flows) classifies as **verified**. `test_cleared_proof_reads_verified` proves it: a flow whose outcome is a cleared proof from Verified Flows shows verified, attributed to that floor. The surface's green is earned by a proof, and the classifier is where that is enforced. **A bare assertion -- a claim with no proof, merely vouched for -- is classified unverified: a promise is not a proof, and the surface refuses to let it look like one.** The central discipline is what happens to the unproven. A claim that carries an assertion but no cleared proof is **vouched**, not verified, and the classifier marks it **unverified**. `test_vouched_claim_reads_unverified` proves a claim asserted with no proof reads unverified. There is no charitable default that treats a confident assertion as good enough; without a cleared proof from a named floor, the claim is unverified, full stop. The surface will show it -- honestly, as unverified -- but it will never color it as though a proof stood behind it. **The verdicts render read-only through the Sovereign Lens -- the surface's display inherits the Lens's honest, read-only, mandate-scoped rendering.** Once classified, the verdicts are rendered by `render_view` (Vol 1) into a read-only View. `test_composes_the_lens_by_identity` proves the surface's `render_view` is the Lens's own, composed by identity. So the verification surface is as honest and read-only as any Lens view: it does not mutate the outcomes, does not invent fields, and renders within the caller's mandate. The zero-trust verdicts are shown through the same honest pane the rest of the operator layer uses. **A verified claim carries the sealed floor that cleared it -- the proof is attributed, not anonymous, so an operator can see not just that a claim is verified but by which floor.** Verification without attribution is its own weak trust. `verify_surface` records, for each verified claim, the named floor whose cleared proof backs it (`verified_by`) -- Shields, or Verified Flows. A failed or unverified claim carries no such attribution, because none cleared it. The operator reads not only the color but the source: this flow is verified by Verified Flows (S7 Vol 4); that claim is unverified because nothing cleared it. Attribution keeps the verification honest all the way down to which floor did the proving. **What shows as verified is exactly what a sealed proof cleared -- nothing more -- so the surface's strongest signal is also its most trustworthy.** The result of the classifier is a surface where "verified" is a precise, earned word. It appears only where a named sealed floor cleared a proof; it never appears for a vouched claim, a failed proof, or an absent one. The operator can trust the green of verified completely, because the surface reserved it completely. That precision -- verified means proven, and the surface enforces it per claim -- is the foundation the rest of the volume builds on. **In the acceptance tests, a cleared proof reads verified with its floor, a vouched claim reads unverified, and the verdicts render through the Lens -- so the verified-not-vouched discipline is executable and proven, not asserted.** `test_cleared_proof_reads_verified` proves earned green with attribution. `test_vouched_claim_reads_unverified` proves a promise is not a proof. `test_composes_the_lens_by_identity` proves the honest read-only render. The verification surface is proven in code. **For the Ridgeline family office, the verification surface means the office sees, per claim, whether a sealed proof cleared it or someone merely vouched -- and only the proven ones show verified.** When Ridgeline reviews its zero-trust node, `verify_surface` shows each flow and shield as verified only where Shields or Verified Flows cleared a proof, and marks the rest unverified. The office never mistakes a vouched claim for a proven one. Chapter 3 shows that the surface reaches this honesty without becoming a verifier itself.

title: S8 07 Zero Trust Ux
chapter_title: No Second Verification Authority -- Render the Verdict, Run No Check
text: You will see how the surface stays honest without becoming a verifier -- verify_surface renders the verdicts the sealed floors produce and runs no check of its own, importing no shield, flow, attest, or crypto engine -- so it adds an honest display and not a second authority whose judgment could diverge from the floors'.

title: S8 07 Zero Trust Ux
chapter_title: No Second Verification Authority -- Render the Verdict, Run No Check
text: **A verification surface must be honest without being a verifier -- so the deepest discipline of this volume is that `verify_surface` renders the sealed floors' verdicts and runs no check of its own.** It would be tempting for a verification surface to verify: to re-run a proof, to hold its own notion of what counts as cleared. This chapter refuses that. The surface displays what the sealed floors decided, and it holds no verification authority itself -- because a surface that verified would be one more authority to trust, defeating the point. **The surface renders the verdicts the sealed floors produced -- it reads the outcome Shields or Verified Flows reached, and it does not re-verify that outcome.** `verify_surface` takes proof outcomes as input; those outcomes are the verdicts the sealed zero-trust floors already produced. The surface classifies and displays them; it does not re-derive them. When Verified Flows (S7 Vol 4) has cleared a flow via `attest_flow_clears`, the surface shows that flow verified because Verified Flows cleared it -- not because the surface re-checked it. The proving happened in the sealed floor; the surface is downstream of the proof, showing it. **It imports no shield, flow, attest, evidence, or crypto engine -- so it structurally cannot run a check, and its "verified" can only ever mean "a sealed floor cleared a proof."** The guarantee is enforced at the module's imports. `test_surface_runs_no_check_imports_only_lens_no_engine` reads the module's imports and asserts it composes only the Lens -- and imports none of shields, verified_flows, attest, evidence, zero_trust, crypto, or hashlib. The surface has no code path to a verifier. It cannot run a shield, clear a flow, or compute a hash. Its verdict of verified is therefore never its own judgment; it is always a report of a sealed floor's cleared proof. **A second verification authority would be another thing to trust -- a surface that re-verified could reach a verdict the floors did not, and an operator would not know which to believe.** The reason to run no check is architectural. In zero trust, every verifier is a trust anchor that must itself be trusted. A surface that held its own verification would add an anchor -- and worse, one whose verdict could diverge from the sealed floors': the floor says failed, the surface says verified, and now there are two truths. By holding no authority and only rendering the floors' verdicts, `verify_surface` adds no new trust anchor. There is exactly one place verification happens -- the sealed floors -- and the surface faithfully shows it. **Its rendering is the Lens's and its verdicts are the floors' -- the surface adds only the honest display, and rolls no cryptography.** The honest account is subtraction. The surface's render is `render_view` (Vol 1), composed. Its verdicts are the sealed floors' outcomes, classified. It rolls no cryptography, runs no check, and holds no authority. What it adds is the one thing missing between a rigorous zero-trust node and a person: an honest pane that shows the floors' verdicts truthfully -- verified where they cleared, failed where they failed, unverified elsewhere. Everything that could be trusted was already sealed; the surface only makes it legible. **The surface trusts the sealed floors' proofs and shows them -- nothing more -- so the trust boundary is exactly where it should be, at the sealed floors, and not at the pane of glass.** Put together, the discipline places trust correctly. An operator trusting the verification surface is, in effect, trusting the sealed floors that produced the verdicts -- which is exactly the right thing to trust in a zero-trust node. They are not additionally trusting the surface to verify, because it does not. The pane of glass is honest precisely because it is not an authority; it is a window onto the authorities that are sealed. **In the acceptance tests, the surface imports only the Lens and no verifier or crypto engine -- so the no-second-authority discipline is executable and proven, not asserted.** `test_surface_runs_no_check_imports_only_lens_no_engine` proves the surface holds no verification code and composes only the Lens. The no-second-authority discipline is proven in code. **For the Ridgeline family office, no second authority means the office trusts its sealed shields and verified flows -- not a status board that might reach its own, different verdict -- and the board only shows what those floors proved.** When Ridgeline reads its verification surface, it is reading the verdicts of its sealed zero-trust floors, faithfully displayed. The board adds no judgment of its own to second-guess. Chapter 4 sharpens the honesty at the hard edge -- a failed or absent proof.

title: S8 07 Zero Trust Ux
text: You will see how the surface behaves under adversarial conditions -- a failed proof reads failed and is never hidden, and an absent, malformed, or unnamed-floor claim reads unverified rather than passing -- so the surface's default is deny, and a missing or broken proof can never masquerade as a cleared one.

title: S8 07 Zero Trust Ux
text: **A verification surface earns its trust at the hard edge -- what it does with a failure, an absence, or a malformed proof -- so the last discipline is adversarial clarity: fail-closed, and never hidden.** The easy case is a clean cleared proof. The case that matters is the adversarial one: a proof that failed, a proof that is missing, a proof that is malformed or dressed to look cleared. A credulous surface softens or hides these; a zero-trust surface must show them plainly and default to deny. This chapter builds that behavior. **A failed proof reads failed -- it is surfaced, never hidden and never softened into a vague "unknown" that reads as fine.** When a sealed floor's proof outcome is a failure, `verify_surface` classifies the claim **failed** and shows it. `test_failed_proof_reads_failed_never_hidden` proves a failed proof reads failed, and carries no `verified_by` -- because a failed proof verified nothing. The surface does not drop failed claims, does not gray them into an ambiguous state, and does not let a failure quietly disappear from the board. A failed proof is one of the most important things an operator can see, and the surface shows it as failed, precisely. **An absent or malformed proof reads unverified -- never defaulted to passing, because the surface trusts nothing it cannot prove.** The absence of a proof is not the presence of one. A claim with no outcome, or an outcome that is malformed -- not a mapping, missing its fields, garbled -- is classified **unverified**, never verified. `test_absent_claim_is_unverified` and `test_malformed_outcome_is_unverified` prove it. This is the fail-closed default: when the surface cannot find a cleared proof from a named floor, it does not guess, does not extend the benefit of the doubt, and does not default to green. It marks the claim unverified and shows the honest gap. Nothing passes by default. **A cleared proof with no naming floor does not pass -- an outcome that says "cleared" but names no sealed floor is treated as unverified, fail-closed on ambiguity.** The subtlest attack is a proof that looks cleared but is not attributable. An outcome marked `cleared` but carrying no `verified_by` -- no named sealed floor that did the proving -- is not trusted: `test_cleared_but_unnamed_floor_is_not_verified` proves it reads unverified. The surface requires both a cleared result and the name of the floor that cleared it before it will show verified. An unattributable "cleared" is exactly the kind of dressed-up assertion the volume refuses; on that ambiguity, the surface fails closed. **`is_verified` is a fail-closed gate -- it returns True only for a cleared proof from a named floor, and False for an absent, failed, malformed, or vouched claim.** Where code needs to act on verification -- to gate a decision on whether something is proven -- `is_verified` gives a fail-closed boolean. `test_is_verified_is_fail_closed` proves it: True for the cleared-and-named case, False for failed, False for vouched, False for an unattributable "cleared." A caller that gates on `is_verified` gets the zero-trust default for free: unless a sealed floor actually cleared a proof, the gate is closed. There is no path by which an unproven claim opens it. **The surface's default is deny -- a missing, failed, or broken proof can never masquerade as a cleared one, so an adversary cannot turn absence or malformation into a green light.** Together, these behaviors make the surface adversarially honest. An attacker who suppresses a proof gets unverified, not verified. One who corrupts a proof gets unverified, not verified. One who forges a "cleared" with no floor gets unverified. A genuine failure is shown as failed, not hidden. There is no adversarial input that produces a false green, because the only thing that produces green is a real cleared proof from a named sealed floor. The default is deny, and green is earned. **In the acceptance tests, a failed proof reads failed, an absent/malformed/unnamed claim reads unverified, and is_verified is fail-closed -- so the adversarial-clarity discipline is executable and proven, not asserted.** `test_failed_proof_reads_failed_never_hidden` proves failures are shown. `test_absent_claim_is_unverified` and `test_malformed_outcome_is_unverified` prove the fail-closed default. `test_is_verified_is_fail_closed` proves the gate denies by default. Adversarial clarity is proven in code. **For the Ridgeline family office, adversarial clarity means a shield that failed shows failed, a proof that is missing shows unverified, and nothing green appears unless a sealed floor actually cleared it -- so no gap or failure can hide behind a false checkmark.** When Ridgeline's node is under pressure -- a check failing, a proof missing, an outcome garbled -- its verification surface shows exactly that: failed where it failed, unverified where it cannot prove. The family is never lulled by a green light that an adversary manufactured from an absence. Chapter 5 renders the supporting evidence, read-only and never as a floor.

title: S8 07 Zero Trust Ux
chapter_title: Evidence Rendered Read-Only -- Displayed, Never a Sealed Floor
text: You will see how the surface shows supporting evidence honestly -- evidence_view renders the in-tree evidence module's state read-only through the Lens, imports no evidence engine, and asserts no verified-floor status for what it shows -- so evidence is displayed as evidence, never dressed as a sealed proof.

title: S8 07 Zero Trust Ux
chapter_title: Evidence Rendered Read-Only -- Displayed, Never a Sealed Floor
text: **A verification surface often has supporting material to show -- an actions projection, an export packet -- and the honest thing is to display it as evidence, never to dress it as a sealed proof.** Alongside the verdicts, an operator wants to see the underlying material: what actions a flow took, what an export packet contains. This chapter renders that evidence -- and its whole discipline is that evidence is shown as evidence, read-only, and is never composed as a sealed floor or shown with a verified status it did not earn. **The in-tree `evidence` module is displayed, not composed as a sealed floor -- it has no press seal, so it is rendered, never claimed as a verified floor.** The `evidence` module lives in the tree, not in the sealed-floor ledger; it carries no press seal. Composing it as though it were a sealed floor would be exactly the overclaim the standing disposition forbids (the same pattern as an unsealed economic module). So V07 does not compose `evidence` as a floor. It renders it -- read-only -- and the volume names it plainly as an in-tree module, displayed, not a proof. **`evidence_view(evidence_state)` renders the module's state read-only through the Sovereign Lens -- a supplied snapshot, deep-copied, never mutated.** The mechanism is a read-only render. `evidence_view` takes a supplied snapshot of the evidence state -- the actions projection, the export packet -- and renders it through `render_view` (Vol 1). `test_evidence_rendered_read_only_not_a_floor` proves it: the packet renders faithfully, and mutating the rendered view leaves the source evidence untouched. The evidence is shown exactly as it is, read-only; the surface neither changes it nor reaches into the module that produced it. **It imports no evidence engine and runs nothing -- the surface displays a supplied snapshot and does not drive, compute, or re-derive the evidence.** As with the verdicts, the surface holds no engine. `evidence_view` renders a snapshot the caller supplies; the module's import discipline (Chapter 3) forbids importing the evidence engine at all. So the surface cannot run the evidence module, cannot generate an export packet, cannot re-project actions. It displays what it is given. The evidence, like the verdicts, is produced elsewhere; the surface is a read-only window onto it. **It asserts no verified-floor status for the evidence it shows -- evidence is not a proof, and the surface does not let it borrow the color of one.** The critical honesty is that evidence and proof are different. An export packet is material; it is not, by its presence, a cleared proof. `evidence_view` renders the evidence without attaching any verified/`verified_by` status -- `test_evidence_view_asserts_no_verified_status` proves the rendered evidence carries no verification verdict of its own. An operator sees the evidence as evidence and the verdicts as verdicts; the surface never lets a pile of supporting material read as though a sealed floor had cleared a proof over it. The two are shown side by side, never blurred. **Evidence is shown as evidence and proofs are shown as proofs -- the surface keeps the two categories distinct, so supporting material can never masquerade as verification.** This is the same discipline the whole volume enforces, applied to the supporting layer. Just as a vouched claim is never shown as verified, evidence is never shown as a proof. The operator gets both -- the verdicts that say what a sealed floor cleared, and the evidence that shows the underlying material -- with an honest wall between them. Evidence informs; proofs verify; and the surface never lets the first pretend to be the second. **In the acceptance tests, the evidence renders read-only and carries no verified status -- so the evidence-read-only-never-a-floor discipline is executable and proven, not asserted.** `test_evidence_rendered_read_only_not_a_floor` proves the read-only render leaves the source untouched. `test_evidence_view_asserts_no_verified_status` proves evidence carries no proof status of its own. The discipline is proven in code. **For the Ridgeline family office, evidence rendered read-only means the office can inspect the actions and export packets behind a flow -- as evidence -- without that material ever showing up as a verified proof it did not earn.** When Ridgeline drills into a flow, it sees the supporting evidence read-only, clearly marked as evidence, distinct from the verdict that says whether a sealed floor cleared a proof. The family reads the material and the proof separately, and never mistakes one for the other. Chapter 6 names exactly the sealed floors this surface composes -- and marks evidence as the in-tree module it is.

title: S8 07 Zero Trust Ux
chapter_title: What Zero-Trust UX Composes -- The Lens, the Host, and the Sealed Proof Floors
text: You will see exactly what the verification surface composes -- the Sovereign Lens for rendering, the Atrium for the gated host it presents through, and the sealed zero-trust floors whose verdicts it displays -- with the evidence module named as the in-tree read-only display it is, not a sealed floor.

title: S8 07 Zero Trust Ux
chapter_title: What Zero-Trust UX Composes -- The Lens, the Host, and the Sealed Proof Floors
text: **The verification surface looks authoritative -- it shows what is verified -- but it composes sealed floors and verifies nothing itself, and naming them exactly is how the reader sees where the trust actually lives.** This chapter is the honest inventory. The surface's rendering, its host, and the verdicts it shows are each a governed floor it composes; the evidence it displays is an in-tree module, not a floor. Listing them precisely, with their series-qualified homes, proves the surface adds an honest display and no verification authority. **The rendering is the Sovereign Lens (Series 8, Volume 1), and the host it presents through is the Atrium (Series 8, Volume 4) -- the surface's sight and pane are the operator layer it already has.** The verification surface renders its verdicts through the Lens: honest, read-only, mandate-scoped. And it is shown through the Atrium -- the composed host whose write path is the human breath-gate -- so any action an operator takes in response to a verdict goes through the node's own gate, never through the verification surface. The surface inherits the operator layer's sight and its gated action, unchanged. **The verdicts the surface displays are produced by the sealed zero-trust floors of Series 7 -- the surface is downstream of the proving, showing what those floors decided.** The whole point of the surface is to show verification, and the verification is Series 7, Zero-Trust Sovereignty. The surface composes those sealed floors' verdicts rather than reinventing verification. The proving is not this volume's; this volume is the operator's honest window onto what the sealed zero-trust floors proved. **Zero-Trust Node Architecture (Series 7, Volume 1), Shields (Series 7, Volume 2), and Verified Flows (Series 7, Volume 4) do the proving; the surface shows their cleared, failed, and absent outcomes.** Named precisely: the zero-trust posture is Zero-Trust Node Architecture (S7 Vol 1); the protective checks are Shields (S7 Vol 2); the flow attestations are Verified Flows (S7 Vol 4), whose `attest_flow_clears` produces the cleared-or-not verdict for a flow. The surface reads these floors' outcomes and shows them -- verified where they cleared, failed where they failed, unverified where none did. It composes their verdicts and holds none of their verification authority. **The `evidence` module is the in-tree read-only display, not a sealed floor -- it has no press seal, so the surface renders it as evidence and never composes it as a proof.** The one thing the surface is clearest about not treating as a floor is `evidence`. The `evidence` module lives in the tree and carries no press seal_ledger entry; composing it as a sealed floor would be the standing overclaim the disposition forbids. So the surface renders it read-only (Chapter 5) and names it as an in-tree module -- supporting material, displayed, not a cleared proof. Marking evidence as in-tree-read-only is what keeps the inventory honest. **Every proof the surface shows is a sealed floor's, and the surface verifies nothing itself -- which is the whole claim of the volume, made concrete by the inventory.** Read the list and the surface disappears as an authority: sight is the Lens (S8 Vol 1); the pane is the Atrium (S8 Vol 4); the proving is Series 7's sealed floors (V1, V2, V4); the evidence is an in-tree read-only display, not a floor. What the surface adds is the honest classification and rendering -- verified, failed, unverified -- of verdicts it did not produce. It owns no verification, holds no proof of its own, and shows evidence as evidence. The inventory closes with nothing left over that the surface verifies. **For the Ridgeline family office, the inventory means the office can trace every green light to a sealed Series 7 floor -- Zero-Trust, Shields, or Verified Flows -- and know the evidence beneath it is an in-tree display, not a proof.** When Ridgeline reviews its verification surface, it reviews the sealed floors that proved each claim, presented through the Lens and the Atrium; the evidence is clearly the in-tree material it is. There is no verification hiding in the surface itself. Chapter 7 contrasts this proving surface with the trust-me console it replaces.

title: S8 07 Zero Trust Ux
chapter_title: The Verification Surface vs the Trust-Me Console
text: You will see the contrast that defines the volume -- a surface that shows only what a sealed proof cleared against a trust-me console that shows a green light because a component vouched -- so the reader sees why showing-only-the-proven is a zero-trust choice, not a UI preference.

title: S8 07 Zero Trust Ux
chapter_title: The Verification Surface vs the Trust-Me Console
text: **The contrast that defines this volume is between a surface that shows only what a sealed proof cleared and a trust-me console that shows a green light because a component vouched for itself -- and the difference is zero trust, not visual taste.** Every status surface shows health. The question is whether green means a proof cleared or merely that something asserted it did. This chapter sets the verification surface against the trust-me console so the reader can see that showing-only-the-proven is the point, and that the alternative defeats zero trust at the pane of glass. **The legacy console is trust-me -- a green light means a component reported healthy, an assertion nobody verified, indistinguishable on the surface from a proven result.** The default status board takes claims at face value. A service says it is up; the board shows green. A flow says it passed; the board shows a check. None of this is verified; it is vouched, and the board renders vouched exactly like proven. The operator reading the board cannot tell which greens are earned. In a zero-trust node, that is a fatal flattening: the architecture verifies rigorously, and the console throws the verification away by showing assertion and proof in the same color. **It hides failures and defaults absences to green -- under adversarial pressure, the trust-me console is exactly wrong, showing calm where there is a gap.** The trust-me console fails worst when it matters most. A check that failed is often dropped or grayed rather than shown as failed. A proof that is missing defaults to green, because absence of a red is read as health. An adversary who suppresses a proof, then, gets a green light for free. The console's credulity -- take claims at face value, treat absence as fine -- is precisely the behavior a zero-trust surface must invert, because it lets a gap or a failure hide behind a checkmark. **The verification surface shows verified only on a sealed proof, and absence and failure read plainly -- it inverts every one of the console's credulous defaults.** `verify_surface` is the trust-me console's opposite. Verified appears only where a named sealed floor cleared a proof (Chapter 2). A failure reads failed, never hidden (Chapter 4). An absence reads unverified, never defaulted to green (Chapter 4). And it verifies nothing itself, so its greens are the sealed floors' proofs, not its own assertions (Chapter 3).
