For Ridgeline, this means a harvest cannot be provisioned without naming its field, and its origin cannot be swapped after the fact — the source on the receipt is the source it came from. Chapter 5 turns the receipt into a green light the weakest receiver can read.

title: S9 03 Food Water
chapter_title: Verify by Receipt -- A Green Light on Every Harvest
text: **A verifiable harvest is one you can check from its receipt alone -- verify_sustenance re-derives the good's receipt and confirms the good and its origin, with no registry and no second device.** A receipt that can only be checked against a chain is no better than the chain. This chapter builds the check that needs neither. `verify_sustenance` takes the receipt and the good's facts — item, quantity, kind, origin — and returns a verdict: verified if the receipt re-derives and the good and origin match, tampered if not, using only what the receiver holds. **`verify_sustenance(receipt, item, quantity, *, kind_of, origin)` returns verified when the receipt re-derives and the good and origin match, tampered when either fails -- one signal, computed from the receipt itself.** The signature is the whole idea. `test_verify_sustenance_by_receipt_no_registry` proves that a receiver holding only the receipt and the good's facts gets `provisioned: True` — no registry passed, none needed. The verdict is a plain boolean with a reason, not a chain to query. A person reads one signal: is this the harvest that was sovereignly provisioned, from the source it claims? Green, yes. Amber, something is wrong. **The check re-derives the receipt via the Material Primitive -- so it composes the primitive's integrity and rolls no cryptography of its own.** The verification reuses the floor. `verify_sustenance` rebuilds the canonical sustenance good and passes it to the primitive's `verify_provision`, which re-derives the receipt's hash and compares. This is the Material Primitive's hashing, composed — `verify_sustenance` rolls no cryptography itself. The check answers "does this receipt re-derive?" using the exact machinery that produced it. **A change to the origin, item, or quantity flips the verdict to tampered -- a swapped source, a substituted item, an altered amount all fail, so a good cannot be quietly relabeled.** The guarantee is that tampering shows, and here it especially protects the origin. `test_verify_sustenance_detects_a_tampered_origin` proves a swapped origin fails. Because the good binds the item, quantity, kind, and origin, a receiver cannot be told a different source than the receipt records, or shown a receipt altered to claim a different food. A good cannot be quietly relabeled to disguise where it came from. **The check is weakest-party verifiable -- no registry, no second device, no expertise -- so the person least equipped to audit a good can still confirm it is sovereignly provisioned from a known source.** This is the standing lens of the sovereign layer, on sustenance. Sovereignty you cannot check is sovereignty you do not hold — and a person receiving food or water should not need a distributor login or a specialist to confirm where it came from. `verify_sustenance` degrades the check to a single signal from the receipt in hand. A recipient with no access to the provisioning node, no second machine, and no technical skill still answers the only question that matters — is this the good it claims to be, from the source it claims? The weakest receiver is handed the same certainty as the grower. **Verify-by-receipt is what makes a locally-held good universally checkable -- the sustenance stays with its node, but its proof and its origin travel to whoever holds the receipt.** This closes the circle. Because the receipt carries everything, including the origin, and `verify_sustenance` needs nothing else, a good provisioned at one node (Chapter 3) is confirmable by anyone who receives its receipt. The origin was required and bound in (Chapter 4); the receiver sees the real source. Local holding and universal verifiability coexist precisely because the check is against the receipt, not a chain. **A good verifiable by its own receipt is sustenance you can trace and verify -- provisioned locally, origin-bound, and confirmable by the weakest receiver, which is what the whole primitive was for.** The result is the promise of the volume, made checkable. A harvest is provisioned as a receipted governed object, held by its node, with a required origin, and verifiable by whoever receives it — all without a central chain anyone must trust. A receiver does not take the origin on faith; they read its light. Chapter 6 names exactly what this primitive composes and what it homes out. **In the acceptance tests, a good verifies by receipt with no registry, and a swapped origin flips to tampered -- so the verify-by-receipt, weakest-party discipline is executable and proven, not asserted.** `test_verify_sustenance_by_receipt_no_registry` and `test_verify_sustenance_detects_a_tampered_origin` prove the cases. For Ridgeline, this means anyone the homestead hands food or water to — a family member, a neighbor, a buyer — can confirm from the receipt alone that it is the good the homestead provisioned, from the field or spring it claims, with no call to Ridgeline and no expertise. Chapter 6 draws the map of composed floors.

title: S9 03 Food Water

title: S9 03 Food Water
chapter_title: What Regenerative Food & Water Composes -- The Material Primitive and the Origin
text: **A domain volume is defined by what it composes -- Regenerative Food & Water stands on the Material Primitive and adds exactly one thing: a required, traceable origin.** The third volume of the series is a composition. This chapter draws the map. `provision_sustenance` builds on the Material Primitive for the governed object, the local holding, the provenance rule, the human gate, and the by-receipt verification — and it adds one new thing, the required origin. Naming the composition is how the volume stays honest about where each guarantee lives. **It composes the Material Primitive (S9 Vol 1) -- every food or water good is a receipted, locally-held, human-gated, receipt-verifiable good, so sustenance inherits all of the opener's guarantees.** The primitive is the foundation. `provision_sustenance` provisions through `provision_local`, and `verify_sustenance` verifies through `verify_provision`. The receipted governed object, the no-central-provisioner locality, the human gate, the verify-by-receipt — all of it comes from the Material Primitive. The sustenance volume does not rebuild the harness; it points it at food and water. **Through the primitive it composes the Object Model, the provenance rule, the mandate, and the human gate -- so sustenance is hash-chained, its source citation honest, scoped to one mandate, and gated by a human.** The deeper floors travel with the primitive. Because it composes the Material Primitive, `provision_sustenance` inherits the Object Model's hashing (S5 Vol 5), the provenance rule (P5), the mandate scope (S5 Vol 28), and the HumanApprovalGate (S5 Vol 16). `test_human_primacy_gated_sustenance_refused_without_approval` proves a gated provision is refused without a human. Sustenance is governed by the same floors as records and goods. **It owns exactly one thing -- the required origin -- a food or water good must name a traceable source, bound into its identity.** What the volume adds is the mandatory provenance. `provision_sustenance` contributes the requirement that a good name where it came from, and the binding of that origin into the good's identity. That — and only that — is the sustenance volume's own. Everything else is composed. The claim is small and exact: the required origin, on top of the primitive. **It homes the good's economic value OUT to Sovereign Economy (S10) and its material estate to Generational Transfer (S12) -- the primitive provisions the sustenance, it does not price it or inherit it.** The honest boundary. A food or water good has an economic value — what it is worth, how it trades — and that homes OUT to Sovereign Economy (Series 10). A good is also part of an estate that passes on, and that homes to Generational Transfer (Series 12). `provision_sustenance` provisions and traces the good; it does not price it, trade it, or inherit it. **Drawing the boundary precisely is what makes the volume trustworthy -- it claims exactly the required origin, composes its guarantees from named sealed floors, and points every other concern at its real home.** The value of the map is that nothing floats. The governed object, locality, provenance rule, gate, and verification are the Material Primitive's (and through it the Object Model's, P5's, the mandate's, and the compliance gate's). Economic value is S10's, estate is S12's. What is left for this volume is the required origin. A domain volume that names its boundary this precisely is one a reader can trust exactly. **In the composition, Regenerative Food & Water owns the required origin and cites the rest by their series-qualified homes -- so the volume is a precise assembly, not a monolith.** The receipt of this chapter is the map itself: Material Primitive (S9 V1), Object Model (S5 V5), provenance (P5), mandate (S5 V28), human gate (S5 V16); economic value OUT to S10, estate OUT to S12. For Ridgeline, the homestead's sustenance is provisioned by a primitive that borrows its governance from the volumes it already trusts, and points the value and inheritance of that food to where they belong. Chapter 7 sets the whole thing against the opaque supply chain.

title: S9 03 Food Water
chapter_title: Sovereign Sustenance vs the Opaque Supply Chain

title: S9 03 Food Water
chapter_title: Sovereign Sustenance vs the Opaque Supply Chain
text: **The choice is between sustenance you are told about and sustenance you can trace -- a chain's label versus a locally-held receipted good with a bound origin -- and the difference is whether a node controls the truth about its own food and water.** Every node accounts for its sustenance somehow; the question is whether the truth lives in a system it controls. This chapter sets the two side by side. The opaque supply chain keeps the truth in a distributor's system and a printed label. Sovereign sustenance keeps it in the node's own registry, in a receipt whose origin is bound in. The contrast is the argument of the whole volume. **The supply chain keeps the truth in a system and a label the node cannot audit -- the node trusts a printed origin it does not control, and confirmation means trusting the distributor.** An opaque chain is a claim, not a holding. The origin is a label, the record lives in the distributor's system, and the node holding the food cannot audit either. To confirm where its food came from, the node reads a label and trusts it. The truth about the node's own sustenance lives outside the node. **Sovereign sustenance keeps the truth in the node's own registry and the good's own receipt -- the node holds the origin and confirms it without asking anyone.** The sovereign answer moves the truth home. `provision_sustenance` records the good in the node's own registry with the origin bound into its identity, and the receipt carries its own proof. The node holds the origin and can confirm it — or hand a receiver the means to — without querying any chain. The truth lives where the food was grown. **The supply-chain record can change without the node -- a label can be mislabeled or a source substituted, and the node has no independent record -- while the primitive's receipt re-derives or fails.** With a chain, the record is the distributor's to alter. A label can be wrong, a source swapped, and the node has no independent copy to check against. With the primitive, the origin is bound into a hash-chained receipt: it either re-derives or it does not, and any substitution shows as tampered. A record someone else can quietly change versus one that cannot be changed invisibly. **The supply chain requires trust to confirm an origin -- while the primitive's receipt is verifiable by the weakest receiver with no access at all.** A chain serves those with access. To confirm an origin, you trust the label or query the distributor. The primitive lowers that to nothing: `verify_sustenance` checks the receipt in hand, so a receiver with no access and no expertise still confirms the good and its source. Verifiability by anyone who holds the receipt replaces verifiability by the chain. **Choosing sovereign sustenance is a sovereign choice -- it is what lets a node control the truth about its own food and water, held and traceable rather than labeled and trusted.** This is the sovereignty frame. Sustenance known only through a chain's label is sustenance the node does not fully own — the chain controls its origin and its confirmation. Sustenance provisioned as a locally-held, origin-bound, receipt-verifiable object is owned in full: held on the node's storage, under its mandate, with its source bound in, confirmable without permission. The sovereign asset is not the label; it is the food you hold and the origin you can verify. **The contrast is not convenience versus features -- it is labeled-and-trusted versus held-and-traceable, which for a node's own sustenance is the whole game.** It would be easy to read this as a nicer traceability app. It is not. The opaque chain and sovereign sustenance differ on the one axis that matters: whether the node controls the truth about its own food and water. A node whose origins can be mislabeled or substituted by a chain it cannot audit does not sovereignly hold its sustenance, however polished the label. Sovereign sustenance makes food and water sovereign by making them held and traceable. Chapter 8 draws the primitive together. **In the composition of the whole volume, sovereign sustenance is what the opaque chain cannot be -- provisioned with a required origin, held locally, and verifiable by anyone -- which is why it is the third brick of the material layer.** The receipt of this chapter is the contrast itself, pointing back to the runnable proof: `provision_sustenance` requires and binds the origin, and `verify_sustenance` confirms it by receipt — properties a chain's label structurally lacks. For Ridgeline, adopting sovereign sustenance means the food and water it provisions are traceable by every receiver and successor, not trusted from a label. Chapter 8 closes the volume.

title: S9 03 Food Water
chapter_title: Sustenance You Can Trace and Verify
text: **Regenerative Food & Water makes present one thing -- a food or water good provisioned as a receipted, mandate-scoped governed object a node holds, traces, and can verify by receipt -- and that one thing is the material layer's third brick.** The opener made a good sovereign; this volume makes sustenance sovereign. `provision_sustenance` provisions a food or water good as a governed object in the node's own registry, with a required origin; `verify_sustenance` confirms both the good and its source from its receipt alone. A harvest becomes as held and traceable as a record — which is what Material Sovereignty reaches toward: not just goods you can hold, but sustenance you can trace and prove. **The good is provisioned as a receipted governed object -- hash-chained, mandate-scoped, provenance-true -- so a harvest carries the same verifiable receipt as any good, with its origin bound in.** The first pillar is the governed object. `provision_sustenance` composes the Material Primitive to provision a food or water good as a hash-chained version bound to one mandate, keyed to its kind, item, and origin. Its receipt travels with the food and re-derives or fails. Sustenance inherits the exact integrity goods and records hold. **It is held locally with no central provisioner -- each node provisions into its own registry, so no node depends on a chain it does not control, and yet a receipt verifies anywhere.** The second pillar is local holding. `provision_sustenance` writes into the node's own registry; two nodes provision independently; and a receipt from one verifies at another by receipt alone. There is no central chain whose outage, capture, or mislabeling breaks the whole. Sustenance is held where it is grown, and its proof travels. **The origin is required and immutable -- a good must name a traceable source, and a swapped origin fails verification -- so a good's provenance is never absent, faked, or substituted.** The third pillar is the origin. `provision_sustenance` refuses a good with no source and binds the origin into the good's identity and its tamper-evident receipt, so a provenance cannot be blank or later swapped. The origin on the receipt is the source the good came from — required at entry and immutable after. **The check is weakest-party verifiable -- verify_sustenance re-derives the receipt and confirms the good and its origin, so a resourceless receiver reads a green light with no registry, no second device, no expertise.** The fourth pillar makes sustenance universally trustworthy. `verify_sustenance` degrades the confirmation to a single signal computed from the receipt in hand: green, this is the good it claims to be, from the source it claims; amber, it is not. A change to the origin, item, or quantity flips the light. The person least equipped to audit a harvest is handed the same certainty as the grower. Sovereignty you cannot check is sovereignty you do not hold. **It composes the sealed floors and names its boundary -- the Material Primitive and its governance, with economic value and estate homed to their own series -- so every guarantee has a stated, checkable home.** The fifth pillar is honesty about the boundary. The primitive borrows its governed object, locality, provenance rule, gate, and verification from the Material Primitive (S9 Vol 1), and through it the Object Model (S5 Vol 5), the provenance rule (P5), the mandate (S5 Vol 28), and the human gate (S5 Vol 16); economic value homes OUT to Sovereign Economy (S10) and the material estate to Generational Transfer (S12). The volume owns exactly one thing — the required origin — and points everything else at its real home. Nothing floats. **With this volume the material layer gains its sustenance brick -- origin, on top of provision -- a node sovereign not only in its goods and power but in the food and water it grows.** This is the third volume of Material Sovereignty. A node's records, rules, surface, goods, and energy were made sovereign; now its sustenance is too. Shelter, logistics, and the covenant that binds them will each stand on the same primitive, held and verified. Food and water join matter under one sovereignty. **The generational payoff is sustenance a receiver can trace AND verify -- not a label they must trust -- because provisioning itself is now sovereign and checkable by the weakest party.** Lasting Generational Prosperity asks that what a node provides passes on intact and confirmable. A node's food and water are among the most vital things it hands on, and until now their origin lived in a chain's label. This volume makes them pass on as governed objects with portable, origin-bound receipts: a receiver inherits sustenance they can trace and confirm from its receipt alone. Provisioning stops being a reference to a chain and becomes the holder's verifiable possession. **In the acceptance tests, a good provisions as a receipted object, holds in the node's own registry, requires and binds its origin, and verifies by receipt -- so the sustenance-primitive discipline is executable and proven, and the sustenance brick lands on runnable proof, not assertion.** The ten tests of `test_provision_sustenance.py` prove every claim of this volume, and the whole kernel suite stays green around them. For the Ridgeline homestead, the primitive means every harvest and every tank it provisions is a governed object it holds on its own storage, with a bound origin, and hands on with a receipt any receiver can trace and verify. This is the sustenance brick's word: a node whose food and water are as sovereign as its goods — sustenance you can trace and verify, not a label you trust. That is the foundation of a prosperity meant to last.

title: S9 04 Shelter Manufacturing
text: You will see why a sovereign node's structures must be provisioned as receipted, verifiable governed objects -- held locally, honestly conditioned, checkable by whoever inherits them -- rather than titled in a registry a node cannot audit, so shelter can be held and inherited, not merely titled.

title: S9 04 Shelter Manufacturing
text: **The opener made a physical good a receipted governed object a node holds and verifies; this volume points that primitive at the built world -- the shelter and manufactured structures a node raises, holds, and hands on.** The Material Primitive made any good sovereign: receipted, mandate-scoped, held locally, verifiable by receipt. A dwelling is a good like any other, and this volume provisions it exactly so — with the additions the domain demands: a location, a capacity, and an honest condition. A cabin becomes a governed object with a receipt and a known state, not a titled line in someone else's registry. **A dwelling is usually a line in a title registry and a condition somebody asserts -- recorded in a system the node cannot audit.** This is how shelter is normally accounted. The structure exists, its ownership is a title in a registry, and its condition is a claim on an inspection report. The node holding the cabin does not hold the record of its ownership or its state; to know they are theirs, it reads a registry. The most rooted good a node has — the roof over its head — carries an ownership and a condition it cannot independently confirm. **Shelter verifiable only by a registry is shelter you do not fully hold -- ownership and condition depend on a system you do not control, and the record can change without you.** This is the shelter failure. If the only proof that a dwelling is yours is a row in a registry, then the registry — not the holder — controls the truth about it. The title can be clouded, revised, or disputed, and the condition can be misrepresented, and the node has no independent record to check. Sovereignty over shelter you cannot verify without the registry's permission is not sovereignty; it is tenancy on someone else's ledger. **The sovereign opportunity is to provision the structure as a receipted, mandate-scoped governed object the node holds itself -- the Material Primitive applied to the built world.** This volume builds that. `provision_shelter` provisions a structure — a dwelling, at a location, with a capacity and a condition — as a governed object in the node's own registry, through the Material Primitive (S9 Vol 1). The cabin becomes a receipted object the node holds, with its ownership bound to one mandate and its condition stated honestly. The opener built the harness; this points it at the built world. **There is no central housing authority and the condition is honest -- each node provisions its own structures locally, and a capacity cannot be negative while a condition must be a known value.** Two disciplines guard the primitive. No central housing authority: `provision_shelter` writes into the node's own registry, so no node depends on a registry it does not control. And honest condition: a structure's capacity must be a real, non-negative number, and its condition must be one of a known set — habitable, needs-repair, uninhabitable — so a structure cannot be provisioned in an impossible or vague state. The shelter is provisioned locally, conditioned honestly. **The weakest-party stake is an heir who can verify a structure is theirs and in the stated condition by a green light -- from the shelter's receipt alone, no registry, no expertise.** Lasting Generational Prosperity asks that what a node holds can be confirmed by whoever inherits it. `verify_shelter` gives exactly that: it re-derives the structure's receipt and checks that it is under the right mandate, at the stated location, in the stated condition, returning a plain verified-or-tampered verdict. A person inheriting a dwelling confirms it is theirs and in the condition it claims — with no call to a registry and no expertise. The chapters build the discipline: the receipted structure (Ch 2), no central authority (Ch 3), honest condition (Ch 4), and verify-by-receipt (Ch 5), with what it composes (Ch 6), the contrast with the title registry (Ch 7), and the synthesis (Ch 8).

title: S9 04 Shelter Manufacturing
chapter_title: provision_shelter -- A Structure as a Receipted Governed Object
text: You will see how a built structure becomes a governed object -- provision_shelter provisions it as a receipted, mandate-scoped version keyed to its dwelling and location, with its condition bound in -- so a structure you hold carries the same verifiable receipt as any good.

title: S9 04 Shelter Manufacturing
chapter_title: provision_shelter -- A Structure as a Receipted Governed Object
text: **A verifiable structure begins with one governed object and one honest receipt -- the dwelling is provisioned as a Material Primitive good, hash-chained and mandate-scoped, keyed to its dwelling and location.** Before shelter can be verified it must be provisioned as a governed object. This chapter builds that. `provision_shelter` takes a structure — a dwelling, a location, a capacity, a condition — and provisions it through the Material Primitive (S9 Vol 1) as a receipted version. The cabin becomes an object the node governs, and the version it produces is its receipt. **`provision_shelter(dwelling, *, location, capacity, condition, mandate, ...)` provisions the structure as a receipted good -- one call, one governed object, and the version it returns is the structure's receipt.** The signature is the whole idea. Given a dwelling, a location, a capacity, a condition, a mandate, a provenance-checked source, and the node's registry, `provision_shelter` provisions the structure and returns it. `test_provisions_shelter_as_receipted_object` proves it: the receipt carries `kind: provision`, the mandate, the capacity, and the condition, keyed to `MaterialGood:shelter:<dwelling>@<location>`. The cabin is now a governed object with a receipt — not a line in a title registry. **The structure's identity is its dwelling and its location -- a cabin on a parcel is `MaterialGood:shelter:<dwelling>@<location>`, one governed object, not a re-titleable row.** Identity is content, not a registry index. `provision_shelter` keys the structure's identity on the dwelling and the location, so a structure at a place is one object. A dwelling is not "parcel 4,812 in the county registry"; it is a named object whose identity binds the structure to its place. This is what lets a receipt be checked and not confused: the identity ties the structure to exactly one dwelling at one location. **The good carries the capacity, the unit, and the condition -- so the receipt states exactly what the structure is, how much it holds, and in what state, with nothing implicit.** The shelter good is explicit. It records the capacity, the unit (persons), and the condition, so the receipt is self-describing: a receiver reads not a bare title but a governed structure with a stated capacity and condition. There is no implicit state to trust. What the structure is, and what condition it is in, is exactly what the receipt says. **The version is hash-chained, mandate-scoped, and provenance-checked -- provision_shelter composes the Material Primitive, so the structure inherits the primitive's integrity, scope, and honest citation.** The primitive does the governance. Because `provision_shelter` provisions through `provision_local`, the structure is hash-chained (tamper-evident), bound to exactly one mandate (S5 Vol 28) — this is what makes it *theirs* — and carries a source that must resolve (P5). The shelter volume adds the condition; the integrity, scope, and provenance are the sealed primitive's, composed. A structure record is as governed as any record the node keeps. **The receipt is the deed that travels with the structure -- a portable, verifiable record a holder or heir can present, not a lookup into a registry they cannot reach.** The point of a receipt is that it moves. When Ridgeline provisions a cabin, the version `provision_shelter` returns is a self-contained record — dwelling, location, capacity, condition, mandate, hash — that can be presented by whoever holds or inherits it. The heir does not need the registry to prove the cabin is theirs; they hold the receipt. Ownership travels with the structure. **One structure, one receipted governed object -- the harness that made a good verifiable, now holding the built world, which is the foundation the rest of the volume builds on.** The result is shelter governed like a record: receipted, hash-chained, mandate-scoped, honestly conditioned. That is what makes the deeper guarantees possible — because the structure is a governed object with a portable receipt and a bound condition, it can be provisioned locally with no central authority (Chapter 3), conditioned honestly (Chapter 4), and verified by its receipt (Chapter 5). The structure is one; its receipt travels; its ownership is a mandate. **In the acceptance tests, a structure provisions as a receipted object with its capacity, condition, and mandate -- so the receipted-structure discipline is executable and proven, not asserted.** `test_provisions_shelter_as_receipted_object` proves the receipt's shape and content. For the Ridgeline homestead, this means a cabin is provisioned as `MaterialGood:shelter:north-cabin@ridge-parcel-3`, a hash-chained object under the homestead's mandate, with a receipt the structure carries. Chapter 3 shows why that registry is the homestead's own — and why there is no central housing authority in the loop.

title: S9 04 Shelter Manufacturing
chapter_title: No Central Housing Authority -- Each Node Provisions Its Own
text: You will see the first discipline that makes provisioned shelter sovereign -- provision_shelter writes into the node's OWN local registry, never a central authority -- so no node depends on a registry it does not control, and its structures are held, not merely titled.

title: S9 04 Shelter Manufacturing
chapter_title: No Central Housing Authority -- Each Node Provisions Its Own
text: **Sovereignly provisioned shelter is held by the node itself -- provision_shelter writes into the node's own registry, so there is no central housing authority any node depends on.** The danger with shelter is the registry: a single authority every node must go through to record or confirm its structures. This chapter refuses it. `provision_shelter` takes the node's own registry and writes there — inheriting the Material Primitive's no-central-provisioner discipline, now applied to the built world. Each node provisions into the registry it holds. **The registry is the node's own -- provision_shelter takes it as a parameter and writes there, so a structure is recorded where the node holds it, not in a central registry across a network.** The locality is explicit. `provision_shelter` knows about no central title store; it writes to the registry the caller passes, the node's own. A cabin is recorded where it stands. There is no moment where the node must reach an authority to make an ownership real. **Two nodes provision independently into their own registries -- each structure lives only in the node that holds it, with no shared registry either depends on.** The primitive scales by not sharing. `test_no_central_housing_authority_two_local_registries` proves it: Ridgeline provisions a cabin into its registry and Cedar provisions a barn into its own; each structure lives in exactly one node's registry, and neither node's provision touches the other's store. Two sovereign nodes holding structures are two independent holders, not two entries in one registry. **A receipt from one node still verifies at another -- because verify_shelter checks the receipt itself, a structure provisioned at one node is confirmable at any node, with no shared registry.** Locality of holding does not mean isolation of proof. Although each structure lives only in its own node's registry, its receipt is portable: `test_no_central_housing_authority_two_local_registries` proves one node's structure verifies from its receipt alone at another. `verify_shelter` needs no registry at all. So shelter is held locally and proofs travel freely — with no central authority that all ownership depends on. **No central housing authority is what keeps ownership sovereign -- there is no single system whose outage, capture, or revision breaks every node's ability to hold or confirm its structures.** A central registry is a single point of failure and control. If every ownership had to be recorded in one system, that system's outage would freeze conveyance everywhere, its compromise would cloud every node's title, and its operator would hold power over all of them. By writing to each node's own registry, `provision_shelter` removes that point. There is nothing to capture that would break the whole. **Local provisioning mirrors the sovereignty of local records, goods, power, and sustenance -- a node holds its structures as it holds its records, on its own storage, under its own mandate, answerable to no central authority.** The primitive is consistent with the whole stack. A sovereign node keeps its records, goods, energy, and sustenance on its own storage under its own mandate; now it keeps its structures the same way. There is no more a central housing authority than there is a central records authority. Ridgeline's cabin is Ridgeline's — provisioned and governed locally, held under its own mandate. **A structure held locally with a portable receipt is both sovereign and conveyable -- the node depends on no authority, and any receiver can still verify, which the rest of the volume builds on.** The result is provisioning that is neither centralized nor siloed. A structure is held by exactly one node, dependent on no external authority, and yet its receipt lets any receiver confirm it is theirs. Because provisioning is local and the receipt is portable, the condition can be honest (Chapter 4) and the weakest heir can verify it (Chapter 5). Held locally; provable anywhere. **In the acceptance tests, two nodes provision into their own registries and each verifies the other's structure by receipt -- so the no-central-authority discipline is executable and proven, not asserted.** `test_no_central_housing_authority_two_local_registries` proves the independent local registries and the cross-node verification by receipt. For Ridgeline and its neighbor Cedar, this means each homestead provisions its own structures on its own storage, and either can confirm the other's structure from the receipt that travels with it — no shared registry. Chapter 4 makes the condition honest.

title: S9 04 Shelter Manufacturing
chapter_title: Honest Condition -- A Structure's State, Known and Immutable
text: You will see the discipline that makes a structure's state trustworthy -- a capacity must be a real, non-negative number and a condition must be a known value, and a change to the condition flips verification to tampered -- so a structure cannot be provisioned in an impossible state or misrepresented after the fact.

title: S9 04 Shelter Manufacturing
chapter_title: Honest Condition -- A Structure's State, Known and Immutable
text: **Honest condition means a structure's state is well-formed -- provision_shelter refuses a negative capacity or an unknown condition, so a structure cannot be recorded in an impossible or vague state.** A record of shelter is only as trustworthy as its stated condition. This chapter builds the guard that fits a structure. `provision_shelter` refuses a negative capacity and a condition outside the known set — habitable, needs-repair, uninhabitable — so a structure enters the receipt in a real, well-formed state, or not at all. **A negative capacity or unknown condition is refused -- provision_shelter fails closed on an impossible state, so a structure cannot be recorded as holding fewer than zero or in an undefined condition.** The guard is fail-closed. `test_negative_capacity_refused` and `test_condition_must_be_known` prove it: a negative capacity and an unrecognized condition each raise before anything is recorded. A structure holds a non-negative number of people and is in one of a defined set of states, and the primitive enforces both — so no impossible or vague condition ever enters a receipt. The structure is recorded in a real state, or not at all. **The condition is drawn from a known set -- habitable, needs-repair, uninhabitable -- so a structure's state is a defined value, not a marketing adjective.** Honesty is also about clarity. A condition is one of three defined values, not free text that can flatter. `test_condition_must_be_known` proves an unknown condition — a flattering "palatial" — is refused. A structure's state is a governed category, so a receiver reads a defined condition, not a seller's prose. What state the structure is in is unambiguous. **A condition upgraded or altered after the fact flips verification to tampered -- because the condition is bound into the hash-chained receipt, a changed state does not re-derive.** The strongest guarantee is tamper-evidence. `test_verify_shelter_detects_a_tampered_condition` proves it: a structure provisioned as needs-repair but presented as habitable fails to verify. Because the condition is part of the hash-chained receipt, any change to it — an upgrade to inflate value, a downgrade to reduce it — is detectable, and `verify_shelter` flips to tampered. A structure's state cannot be quietly changed to claim a condition it is not in; the receipt either re-derives with the real condition or fails. **Honest condition matters because shelter is a shelter -- a misrepresented state is not a harmless error but a false claim about whether a person can safely live there, which is why the guard is strict.** It matters that this lands on shelter. Condition is not decoration; it is a claim about safety, about whether a roof will hold, about whether a person can live under it. A misrepresented condition is a false claim about that. Refusing impossible states and catching altered ones is not fussiness — it is what keeps a structure record from becoming a way to sell a failing building as sound. The strictness is proportionate to the stake. **The condition guard composes the primitive's integrity -- provision_shelter adds the well-formed-state checks, and the hash-chained tamper-evidence is the Material Primitive's, so honesty is layered, not re-implemented.** The primitive rolls no new integrity. `provision_shelter` adds exactly the domain guards — capacity non-negative, condition known — and inherits the tamper-evidence from the Material Primitive's hash-chained receipt. So an honest condition is guarded twice: at entry (well-formed) and forever after (tamper-evident), the second borrowed from the sealed floor. The shelter volume contributes the physical honesty of a structure's state; the cryptographic honesty is the primitive's, composed. **A condition that cannot be impossible or altered is a structure a node can stand behind -- which the heir, and the safety it rests on, can rely on.** The result is a stated condition trustworthy at both ends: it could not have been impossible when recorded, and it cannot have been changed since. An heir checking a structure's receipt reads the condition it is actually in. That is what makes shelter safe to hand on: the state is well-formed at entry and immutable after. Chapter 5 shows how any heir — even the weakest — verifies all of this from the receipt alone. **In the acceptance tests, a negative capacity and an unknown condition are refused, and a swapped condition fails verification -- so the honest-condition discipline is executable and proven, not asserted.** `test_negative_capacity_refused`, `test_condition_must_be_known`, and `test_verify_shelter_detects_a_tampered_condition` prove the cases. For Ridgeline, this means a cabin cannot be recorded in an impossible state, and its condition cannot be upgraded after the fact — the state on the receipt is the state the cabin is in. Chapter 5 turns the receipt into a green light the weakest heir can read.

title: S9 04 Shelter Manufacturing
chapter_title: Verify by Receipt -- A Green Light That the Structure Is Theirs
text: You will see how a provisioned structure becomes verifiable to the weakest heir -- verify_shelter re-derives the receipt and confirms the structure is theirs and in the stated condition, returning a green light with no registry -- so a resourceless person confirms a dwelling is sovereignly provisioned and inheritable, no second device, no expertise.

title: S9 04 Shelter Manufacturing
chapter_title: Verify by Receipt -- A Green Light That the Structure Is Theirs
text: **A verifiable structure is one you can check from its receipt alone -- verify_shelter re-derives the structure's receipt and confirms it is theirs and in the stated condition, with no registry and no second device.** A receipt that can only be checked against a registry is no better than the registry. This chapter builds the check that needs neither. `verify_shelter` takes the receipt and the structure's facts — dwelling, location, capacity, condition — and returns a verdict: verified if the receipt re-derives and the facts match, tampered if not, using only what the heir holds. **`verify_shelter(receipt, dwelling, *, location, capacity, condition)` returns verified when the receipt re-derives and the structure matches, tampered when either fails -- one signal, computed from the receipt itself.** The signature is the whole idea. `test_verify_shelter_by_receipt_no_registry` proves that a receiver holding only the receipt and the structure's facts gets `provisioned: True` — no registry passed, none needed. The verdict is a plain boolean with a reason, not a title to interpret. A person reads one signal: is this the structure that was sovereignly provisioned, theirs and in the condition it claims? Green, yes. Amber, something is wrong. **The check confirms it is theirs -- the receipt is mandate-scoped, so verifying it proves the structure belongs to exactly one mandate, and it re-derives via the Material Primitive, rolling no cryptography of its own.** The verification reuses the floor and proves ownership. `verify_shelter` rebuilds the canonical shelter good and passes it to the primitive's `verify_provision`, which re-derives the receipt's hash and confirms the mandate. Because the receipt binds the structure to one mandate, a valid verification is a proof that the structure is *theirs* — under exactly that mandate, no other. This is the Material Primitive's hashing and scope, composed — `verify_shelter` rolls no cryptography itself. **A change to the condition, capacity, or location flips the verdict to tampered -- an upgraded condition, an inflated capacity, a moved location all fail, so a structure cannot be quietly misrepresented.** The guarantee is that tampering shows, and here it protects the heir. `test_verify_shelter_detects_a_tampered_condition` proves a swapped condition fails. Because the good binds the dwelling, location, capacity, and condition, a receiver cannot be told a better condition than the receipt records, or shown a receipt altered to claim a different structure. A structure cannot be quietly misrepresented to inflate its worth. **The check is weakest-party verifiable -- no registry, no second device, no expertise -- so the person least equipped to audit a structure can still confirm it is theirs and in the stated condition.** This is the standing lens of the sovereign layer, on shelter. Sovereignty you cannot check is sovereignty you do not hold — and a person inheriting a home should not need a registry login or a specialist to confirm it is theirs. `verify_shelter` degrades the check to a single signal from the receipt in hand. A recipient with no access to the provisioning node, no second machine, and no technical skill still answers the only question that matters — is this structure theirs, in the condition it claims? The weakest heir is handed the same certainty as the builder. **Verify-by-receipt is what makes a locally-held structure universally checkable -- the shelter stays with its node, but its ownership and condition travel to whoever holds the receipt.** This closes the circle. Because the receipt carries everything, including the mandate and the condition, and `verify_shelter` needs nothing else, a structure provisioned at one node (Chapter 3) is confirmable by anyone who receives its receipt. The condition was honest by construction (Chapter 4); the heir sees the real state. Local holding and universal verifiability coexist precisely because the check is against the receipt, not a registry. **A structure verifiable by its own receipt is a structure you can hold and inherit -- provisioned locally, honestly conditioned, and confirmable by the weakest heir, which is what the whole primitive was for.** The result is the promise of the volume, made checkable. A cabin is provisioned as a receipted governed object, held by its node, honestly conditioned, and verifiable by whoever inherits it — all without a central registry anyone must trust. An heir does not take ownership on faith; they read its light. Chapter 6 names exactly what this primitive composes and what it homes out. **In the acceptance tests, a structure verifies by receipt with no registry, and a tampered condition flips to tampered -- so the verify-by-receipt, weakest-party discipline is executable and proven, not asserted.** `test_verify_shelter_by_receipt_no_registry` and `test_verify_shelter_detects_a_tampered_condition` prove the cases. For Ridgeline, this means whoever inherits the homestead's structures — a family member, a successor — can confirm from the receipt alone that a dwelling is theirs and in the condition it claims, with no call to a registry and no expertise. Chapter 6 draws the map of composed floors.

title: S9 04 Shelter Manufacturing
chapter_title: What Shelter & Manufacturing Composes -- The Material Primitive and the Condition
text: You will see exactly what this primitive builds on and what it deliberately leaves out -- it composes the Material Primitive (and through it the Object Model, mandate, and human gate) and adds the honest condition, homing economic value and estate to their own series -- so the boundary is drawn as precisely as its center.

title: S9 04 Shelter Manufacturing
chapter_title: What Shelter & Manufacturing Composes -- The Material Primitive and the Condition
text: **A domain volume is defined by what it composes -- Shelter & Manufacturing stands on the Material Primitive and adds exactly one thing: an honest, well-formed condition.** The fourth volume of the series is a composition. This chapter draws the map. `provision_shelter` builds on the Material Primitive for the governed object, the local holding, the ownership mandate, the human gate, and the by-receipt verification — and it adds one new thing, the honest condition. Naming the composition is how the volume stays honest about where each guarantee lives. **It composes the Material Primitive (S9 Vol 1) -- every structure is a receipted, locally-held, human-gated, receipt-verifiable good, so shelter inherits all of the opener's guarantees.** The primitive is the foundation. `provision_shelter` provisions through `provision_local`, and `verify_shelter` verifies through `verify_provision`. The receipted governed object, the no-central-provisioner locality, the human gate, the verify-by-receipt — all of it comes from the Material Primitive. The shelter volume does not rebuild the harness; it points it at the built world. **Through the primitive it composes the Object Model, the mandate, and the human gate -- so a structure is hash-chained, bound to one mandate (which is what makes it theirs), and gated by a human.** The deeper floors travel with the primitive. Because it composes the Material Primitive, `provision_shelter` inherits the Object Model's hashing (S5 Vol 5), the mandate scope (S5 Vol 28), and the HumanApprovalGate (S5 Vol 16). `test_human_primacy_gated_shelter_refused_without_approval` proves a gated provision is refused without a human. The mandate is doubly meaningful here: it is what binds the structure to its owner, so verifying the receipt proves the structure is theirs. **It owns exactly one thing -- the honest condition -- a well-formed capacity and a known condition, bound into the structure's receipt.** What the volume adds is the condition. `provision_shelter` contributes the requirement that a structure's state be well-formed — a non-negative capacity, a condition from a known set — and the binding of that state into the receipt. That — and only that — is the shelter volume's own. Everything else is composed. The claim is small and exact: the honest condition, on top of the primitive. **It homes the structure's economic value OUT to Sovereign Economy (S10) and its inheritance to Generational Transfer (S12) -- the primitive provisions the structure, it does not price it or convey it in an estate.** The honest boundary. A structure has an economic value — what it is worth, how it trades — and that homes OUT to Sovereign Economy (Series 10). A dwelling is also the archetypal thing passed down in an estate, and the logic of that inheritance homes to Generational Transfer (Series 12). `provision_shelter` provisions and conditions the structure and makes it verifiably theirs; it does not price it or run the estate that conveys it. **Drawing the boundary precisely is what makes the volume trustworthy -- it claims exactly the honest condition, composes its guarantees from named sealed floors, and points every other concern at its real home.** The value of the map is that nothing floats. The governed object, locality, ownership mandate, gate, and verification are the Material Primitive's (and through it the Object Model's, the mandate's, and the compliance gate's). Economic value is S10's, inheritance is S12's. What is left for this volume is the honest condition. A domain volume that names its boundary this precisely is one a reader can trust exactly. **In the composition, Shelter & Manufacturing owns the honest condition and cites the rest by their series-qualified homes -- so the volume is a precise assembly, not a monolith.** The receipt of this chapter is the map itself: Material Primitive (S9 V1), Object Model (S5 V5), mandate (S5 V28), human gate (S5 V16); economic value OUT to S10, inheritance OUT to S12. For Ridgeline, the homestead's structures are provisioned by a primitive that borrows its governance from the volumes it already trusts, and points the value and inheritance of that shelter to where they belong. Chapter 7 sets the whole thing against the title registry.

title: S9 04 Shelter Manufacturing
chapter_title: Sovereign Shelter vs the Title Registry
text: You will see the two approaches set side by side -- structures titled in a registry a node cannot audit versus provisioned as locally-held, honestly-conditioned, receipt-verifiable governed objects -- so the sovereign choice between them is explicit, not implied.

title: S9 04 Shelter Manufacturing
chapter_title: Sovereign Shelter vs the Title Registry
text: **The choice is between shelter you are titled to and shelter you hold -- a registry's title versus a locally-held receipted structure -- and the difference is whether a node controls the truth about its own dwellings.** Every node accounts for its structures somehow; the question is whether the truth lives in a system it controls. This chapter sets the two side by side. The title registry keeps the truth in a central system and an inspection report. Sovereign shelter keeps it in the node's own registry, in a receipt that binds ownership and condition. The contrast is the argument of the whole volume. **The title registry keeps the truth in a system the node cannot audit -- the node trusts a title and a report it does not control, and confirmation means trusting the registry.** A registry is a reference, not a holding. Ownership is a row, condition is a report, and the node holding the structure cannot audit either. To confirm it is theirs and sound, the node reads a registry and an inspection. The truth about the node's own shelter lives outside the node. **Sovereign shelter keeps the truth in the node's own registry and the structure's own receipt -- the node holds ownership and condition and confirms them without asking anyone.** The sovereign answer moves the truth home. `provision_shelter` records the structure in the node's own registry, bound to its mandate and stamped with its condition, and the receipt carries its own proof. The node holds ownership and condition and can confirm them — or hand an heir the means to — without querying any registry. The truth lives where the structure stands. **The registry record can change without the node -- a title can be clouded or a condition misreported, and the node has no independent record -- while the primitive's receipt re-derives or fails.** With a registry, the record is the authority's to alter. A title can be clouded, a condition misreported, and the node has no independent copy to check against. With the primitive, ownership and condition are bound into a hash-chained receipt: it either re-derives or it does not, and any change shows as tampered. A record someone else can quietly change versus one that cannot be changed invisibly. **The title registry requires trust to confirm ownership -- while the primitive's receipt is verifiable by the weakest heir with no access at all.** A registry serves those with access. To confirm ownership, you query the registry and trust it. The primitive lowers that to nothing: `verify_shelter` checks the receipt in hand, so an heir with no access and no expertise still confirms the structure is theirs and in the stated condition. Verifiability by anyone who holds the receipt replaces verifiability by the registry. **Choosing sovereign shelter is a sovereign choice -- it is what lets a node control the truth about its own dwellings, held and verifiable rather than titled and trusted.** This is the sovereignty frame. Shelter known only through a registry's title is shelter the node does not fully own — the registry controls its ownership and its confirmation. Shelter provisioned as a locally-held, receipt-verifiable object is owned in full: held on the node's storage, bound to its mandate, honestly conditioned, confirmable without permission. The sovereign asset is not the title; it is the structure you hold and the receipt you can verify. **The contrast is not convenience versus features -- it is titled-and-trusted versus held-and-verifiable, which for a node's own shelter is the whole game.** It would be easy to read this as a nicer property app. It is not. The title registry and sovereign shelter differ on the one axis that matters: whether the node controls the truth about its own dwellings. A node whose ownership can be clouded and whose condition can be misreported by a registry it cannot audit does not sovereignly hold its shelter, however polished the record. Sovereign shelter makes structures sovereign by making them held and verifiable. Chapter 8 draws the primitive together. **In the composition of the whole volume, sovereign shelter is what the title registry cannot be -- provisioned with an honest condition, held locally, and verifiable by anyone -- which is why it is the fourth brick of the material layer.** The receipt of this chapter is the contrast itself, pointing back to the runnable proof: `provision_shelter` conditions honestly and binds ownership to a mandate, and `verify_shelter` confirms both by receipt — properties a registry title structurally lacks. For Ridgeline, adopting sovereign shelter means the structures it holds are verifiable as theirs by every heir, not trusted from a title. Chapter 8 closes the volume.

title: S9 04 Shelter Manufacturing
chapter_title: A Structure You Can Hold and Inherit
text: You will see the whole volume drawn together -- a structure provisioned as a receipted governed object, held locally with no central authority, honestly conditioned, and verifiable by receipt -- and with it the material layer's fourth brick: the sovereign discipline of goods extended to the built world.

title: S9 04 Shelter Manufacturing
chapter_title: A Structure You Can Hold and Inherit
text: **Shelter & Manufacturing makes present one thing -- a built structure provisioned as a receipted, mandate-scoped governed object a node holds, conditions honestly, and can verify by receipt -- and that one thing is the material layer's fourth brick.** The opener made a good sovereign; this volume makes the built world sovereign. `provision_shelter` provisions a structure as a governed object in the node's own registry, bound to its mandate and honestly conditioned; `verify_shelter` confirms it is theirs and in the stated condition from its receipt alone. A cabin becomes as held and inheritable as a record — which is what Material Sovereignty reaches toward: not just goods you can hold, but shelter you can hold and inherit. **The structure is provisioned as a receipted governed object -- hash-chained, mandate-scoped, provenance-true -- so a dwelling carries the same verifiable receipt as any good, and the mandate is what makes it theirs.** The first pillar is the governed object. `provision_shelter` composes the Material Primitive to provision a structure as a hash-chained version bound to one mandate, keyed to its dwelling and location. Its receipt travels with the structure and re-derives or fails, and its mandate binds it to its owner. Shelter inherits the exact integrity goods and records hold, plus the ownership the mandate provides. **It is held locally with no central housing authority -- each node provisions into its own registry, so no node depends on a registry it does not control, and yet a receipt verifies anywhere.** The second pillar is local holding. `provision_shelter` writes into the node's own registry; two nodes provision independently; and a receipt from one verifies at another by receipt alone. There is no central authority whose outage, capture, or revision breaks the whole. Shelter is held where it stands, and its proof travels. **The condition is honest -- a capacity cannot be negative, a condition must be known, and an upgraded condition fails verification -- so a structure cannot be recorded in an impossible state or misrepresented.** The third pillar is the condition. `provision_shelter` refuses impossible states at capture and binds the condition into a tamper-evident receipt, so a structure's state cannot be vague or later inflated. The condition on the receipt is the state the structure is in — well-formed at entry and immutable after. **The check is weakest-party verifiable -- verify_shelter re-derives the receipt and confirms the structure is theirs and in its condition, so a resourceless heir reads a green light with no registry, no second device, no expertise.** The fourth pillar makes shelter universally trustworthy. `verify_shelter` degrades the confirmation to a single signal computed from the receipt in hand: green, this structure is theirs and in the condition it claims; amber, it is not. A change to the condition, capacity, or location flips the light. The person least equipped to audit a dwelling is handed the same certainty as the builder. Sovereignty you cannot check is sovereignty you do not hold. **It composes the sealed floors and names its boundary -- the Material Primitive and its governance, with economic value and inheritance homed to their own series -- so every guarantee has a stated, checkable home.** The fifth pillar is honesty about the boundary. The primitive borrows its governed object, locality, ownership mandate, gate, and verification from the Material Primitive (S9 Vol 1), and through it the Object Model (S5 Vol 5), the mandate (S5 Vol 28), and the human gate (S5 Vol 16); economic value homes OUT to Sovereign Economy (S10) and the dwelling's inheritance to Generational Transfer (S12). The volume owns exactly one thing — the honest condition — and points everything else at its real home. Nothing floats. **With this volume the material layer gains its shelter brick -- condition, on top of provision -- a node sovereign not only in its goods, power, and sustenance but in the structures it raises.** This is the fourth volume of Material Sovereignty. A node's records, rules, surface, goods, energy, and sustenance were made sovereign; now its shelter is too. Logistics and the covenant that binds them will each stand on the same primitive, held and verified. The built world joins matter under one sovereignty. **The generational payoff is a structure an heir can hold AND verify as theirs -- not a title they must trust -- because provisioning itself is now sovereign and checkable by the weakest party.** Lasting Generational Prosperity asks that what a node holds passes on intact and confirmable. A node's shelter is the archetype of what it hands on, and until now its ownership lived in a registry's title. This volume makes it pass on as a governed object with a portable receipt: an heir inherits a structure they can hold and confirm is theirs from its receipt alone. Ownership stops being a reference to a registry and becomes the holder's verifiable possession. **In the acceptance tests, a structure provisions as a receipted object, holds in the node's own registry, conditions honestly, and verifies by receipt -- so the shelter-primitive discipline is executable and proven, and the shelter brick lands on runnable proof, not assertion.** The ten tests of `test_provision_shelter.py` prove every claim of this volume, and the whole kernel suite stays green around them. For the Ridgeline homestead, the primitive means every structure it raises is a governed object it holds on its own storage, honestly conditioned, and hands on with a receipt any heir can verify is theirs. This is the shelter brick's word: a node whose structures are as sovereign as its goods — a structure you can hold and inherit, not a title you trust. That is the foundation of a prosperity meant to last.

title: S9 05 Logistics
text: You will see why a sovereign node's movements must be provisioned as receipted, verifiable governed objects -- held locally, honestly custodied, checkable by whoever receives them -- rather than tracked by a central dispatcher a node cannot audit, so a movement can be traced and verified, not merely tracked.

title: S9 05 Logistics
text: **The opener made a physical good a receipted governed object a node holds and verifies; this volume points that primitive at movement -- the shipments and supply transfers a node sends, receives, and hands on.** The Material Primitive made any good sovereign: receipted, mandate-scoped, held locally, verifiable by receipt. A movement is a good's journey, and this volume provisions it exactly so — with the additions the domain demands: an origin, a destination, and a carrier. A shipment becomes a governed object with a receipt and a known custody, not a tracked line in someone else's system. **A shipment is usually a line in a carrier's tracking system -- its origin, route, and custody recorded by a dispatcher the node cannot audit.** This is how movement is normally accounted. The good moves, and the record of its journey — where it started, who carried it, where it went — lives in a carrier's system. The node holding the shipment does not hold the record of its custody; to know where it came from, it reads a tracking number. The most consequential fact about a delivered good — its provenance and chain of custody — carries a record the holder cannot independently confirm. **A movement verifiable only by a carrier's system is a movement you do not fully hold -- origin and custody depend on a dispatcher you do not control, and the record can change without you.** This is the logistics failure. If the only proof of a shipment's origin is a row in a carrier's database, then the carrier — not the receiver — controls the truth about it. The origin can be relabeled, the custody misrecorded, and the node receiving the good has no independent record to check. Sovereignty over a movement you cannot verify without the dispatcher's permission is not sovereignty; it is a tracking number you are asked to trust. **The sovereign opportunity is to provision the movement as a receipted, mandate-scoped governed object the node holds itself -- the Material Primitive applied to logistics.** This volume builds that. `provision_shipment` provisions a movement — a good, an origin, a destination, a carrier — as a governed object in the node's own registry, through the Material Primitive (S9 Vol 1). The shipment becomes a receipted object the node holds, with its custody bound in. The opener built the harness; this points it at movement. **There is no central dispatcher and the custody is honest -- each node provisions its own movements locally, and an origin and destination are required and must differ while a carrier must be named.** Two disciplines guard the primitive. No central dispatcher: `provision_shipment` writes into the node's own registry, so no node depends on a carrier's system it does not control. And honest custody: a movement must have an origin and a destination that differ — a movement goes somewhere — and a named carrier, so a shipment records a real journey by a real party. The movement is provisioned locally, custodied honestly. **The weakest-party stake is a receiver who can verify a movement's origin and custody by a green light -- from the shipment's receipt alone, no dispatcher, no expertise.** Lasting Generational Prosperity asks that what a node sends can be confirmed by whoever receives it. `verify_shipment` gives exactly that: it re-derives the movement's receipt and checks its origin, destination, carrier, and quantity, returning a plain verified-or-tampered verdict. A person receiving a shipment confirms where it came from and how it was carried — with no call to a dispatcher and no expertise. The chapters build the discipline: the receipted movement (Ch 2), no central dispatcher (Ch 3), honest custody (Ch 4), and verify-by-receipt (Ch 5), with what it composes (Ch 6), the contrast with the dispatcher (Ch 7), and the synthesis (Ch 8).

title: S9 05 Logistics
chapter_title: provision_shipment -- A Movement as a Receipted Governed Object
text: You will see how a logistics movement becomes a governed object -- provision_shipment provisions it as a receipted, mandate-scoped version keyed to its good, origin, and destination -- so a shipment you send carries the same verifiable receipt as any good, with its custody bound in.

title: S9 05 Logistics
chapter_title: provision_shipment -- A Movement as a Receipted Governed Object
text: **A verifiable movement begins with one governed object and one honest receipt -- the shipment is provisioned as a Material Primitive good, hash-chained and mandate-scoped, keyed to its good, origin, and destination.** Before a movement can be verified it must be provisioned as a governed object with its custody bound in. This chapter builds that. `provision_shipment` takes a movement — a good, an origin, a destination, a carrier, a quantity — and provisions it through the Material Primitive (S9 Vol 1) as a receipted version whose identity includes the route. The shipment becomes an object the node governs, and the version it produces is its receipt. **`provision_shipment(good_ref, *, origin, destination, carrier, quantity, mandate, ...)` provisions the movement as a receipted good -- one call, one governed object, and the version it returns is the shipment's receipt.** The signature is the whole idea. Given a good reference, an origin, a destination, a carrier, a quantity, a mandate, a provenance-checked source, and the node's registry, `provision_shipment` provisions the movement and returns it. `test_provisions_shipment_as_receipted_object` proves it: the receipt carries `kind: provision`, the mandate, the origin, the destination, and the carrier, keyed to `MaterialGood:shipment:<good>:<origin>-><destination>`. The shipment is now a governed object with a receipt — not a tracking number. **The movement's identity is its good and its route -- a shipment is `MaterialGood:shipment:<good>:<origin>-><destination>`, one governed object, not a re-labelable tracking row.** Identity is content, not a tracking index. `provision_shipment` keys the movement's identity on the good and the route, so a movement of a good from one place to another is one object. A shipment is not "tracking number 4,812 in the carrier system"; it is a named object whose identity binds the good to its origin and destination. This is what lets a receipt be checked and not confused: the identity ties the movement to exactly one good on exactly one route. **The good carries the carrier and the quantity -- so the receipt states exactly what moved, how much, by whom, from where to where, with nothing implicit.** The shipment good is explicit. It records the carrier and the quantity alongside the route, so the receipt is self-describing: a receiver reads not a bare tracking number but a governed movement with a stated carrier, quantity, and route. There is no implicit custody to trust. What moved, and how it was carried, is exactly what the receipt says. **The version is hash-chained, mandate-scoped, and provenance-checked -- provision_shipment composes the Material Primitive, so the movement inherits the primitive's integrity, scope, and honest citation.** The primitive does the governance. Because `provision_shipment` provisions through `provision_local`, the movement is hash-chained (tamper-evident), bound to exactly one mandate (S5 Vol 28), and carries a source that must resolve (P5). The logistics volume adds the custody; the integrity, scope, and provenance are the sealed primitive's, composed. A movement record is as governed as any record the node keeps. **The receipt is the bill of lading that travels with the shipment -- a portable, verifiable record a receiver can present, not a lookup into a carrier they cannot reach.** The point of a receipt is that it moves with the good. When Ridgeline provisions a shipment, the version `provision_shipment` returns is a self-contained record — good, origin, destination, carrier, quantity, mandate, hash — that travels with the shipment to whoever receives it. The receiver does not need the carrier's system to check its custody; they hold the receipt. Provenance travels with the movement, bound in. **One movement, one receipted governed object -- the harness that made a good verifiable, now holding logistics, which is the foundation the rest of the volume builds on.** The result is a movement governed like a record: receipted, hash-chained, mandate-scoped, honestly custodied. That is what makes the deeper guarantees possible — because the movement is a governed object with a portable receipt and a bound route, it can be provisioned locally with no central dispatcher (Chapter 3), custodied honestly (Chapter 4), and verified by its receipt (Chapter 5). The movement is one; its receipt travels; its custody is bound in. **In the acceptance tests, a movement provisions as a receipted object with its origin, destination, and carrier -- so the receipted-movement discipline is executable and proven, not asserted.** `test_provisions_shipment_as_receipted_object` proves the receipt's shape and content. For the Ridgeline homestead, this means a wagon of grain to market is provisioned as `MaterialGood:shipment:heirloom-wheat:north-field->cedar-market`, a hash-chained object under the homestead's mandate, with a receipt the shipment carries. Chapter 3 shows why that registry is the homestead's own — and why there is no central dispatcher in the loop.

title: S9 05 Logistics
chapter_title: No Central Dispatcher -- Each Node Provisions Its Own
text: You will see the first discipline that makes provisioned movement sovereign -- provision_shipment writes into the node's OWN local registry, never a central dispatcher -- so no node depends on a carrier's system it does not control, and its movements are held, not merely tracked.

title: S9 05 Logistics
chapter_title: No Central Dispatcher -- Each Node Provisions Its Own
text: **Sovereignly provisioned movement is held by the node itself -- provision_shipment writes into the node's own registry, so there is no central dispatcher any node depends on.** The danger with logistics is the dispatcher: a single carrier or broker every node must go through to record or confirm its movements. This chapter refuses it. `provision_shipment` takes the node's own registry and writes there — inheriting the Material Primitive's no-central-provisioner discipline, now applied to movement. Each node provisions into the registry it holds. **The registry is the node's own -- provision_shipment takes it as a parameter and writes there, so a movement is recorded where the node holds it, not in a carrier's system across a network.** The locality is explicit. `provision_shipment` knows about no central dispatch store; it writes to the registry the caller passes, the node's own. A shipment is recorded by the party that sent it. There is no moment where the node must reach a dispatcher to make a movement real. **Two nodes provision independently into their own registries -- each movement lives only in the node that made it, with no shared registry either depends on.** The primitive scales by not sharing. `test_no_central_dispatcher_two_local_registries` proves it: Ridgeline provisions a grain shipment into its registry and Cedar provisions a water delivery into its own; each movement lives in exactly one node's registry, and neither node's provision touches the other's store. Two sovereign nodes moving goods are two independent holders, not two accounts on one carrier system. **A receipt from one node still verifies at another -- because verify_shipment checks the receipt itself, a movement provisioned at one node is confirmable at any node, with no shared dispatcher.** Locality of holding does not mean isolation of proof. Although each movement lives only in its own node's registry, its receipt is portable: `test_no_central_dispatcher_two_local_registries` proves one node's movement verifies from its receipt alone at another. `verify_shipment` needs no dispatcher at all. So movements are held locally and proofs travel with the goods — with no central dispatcher that all logistics depends on. **No central dispatcher is what keeps logistics sovereign -- there is no single system whose outage, capture, or relabeling breaks every node's ability to move or confirm its goods.** A central dispatcher is a single point of failure and control. If every movement had to be recorded in one system, that system's outage would halt confirmation everywhere, its compromise would corrupt every node's custody, and its operator would hold power over all of them. By writing to each node's own registry, `provision_shipment` removes that point. There is nothing to capture that would break the whole. **Local provisioning mirrors the sovereignty of local records, goods, power, sustenance, and shelter -- a node holds its movements as it holds its records, on its own storage, under its own mandate, answerable to no central authority.** The primitive is consistent with the whole stack. A sovereign node keeps its records, goods, energy, sustenance, and shelter on its own storage under its own mandate; now it keeps its movements the same way. There is no more a central dispatch authority than there is a central records authority. Ridgeline's shipments are Ridgeline's — provisioned and governed locally. **A movement held locally with a portable receipt is both sovereign and confirmable -- the node depends on no dispatcher, and any receiver can still verify, which the rest of the volume builds on.** The result is provisioning that is neither centralized nor siloed. A movement is held by exactly one node, dependent on no external dispatcher, and yet its receipt lets any receiver confirm its custody. Because provisioning is local and the receipt travels with the good, the custody can be honest (Chapter 4) and the weakest receiver can verify it (Chapter 5). Held locally; provable anywhere. **In the acceptance tests, two nodes provision into their own registries and each verifies the other's movement by receipt -- so the no-central-dispatcher discipline is executable and proven, not asserted.** `test_no_central_dispatcher_two_local_registries` proves the independent local registries and the cross-node verification by receipt. For Ridgeline and its neighbor Cedar, this means each homestead provisions its own movements on its own storage, and either can confirm the other's shipment from the receipt that travels with the good — no shared dispatcher. Chapter 4 makes the custody honest.

title: S9 05 Logistics
chapter_title: Honest Custody -- Origin and Destination, Required and Distinct
text: You will see the discipline that makes a movement's custody trustworthy -- an origin and a destination are required and must differ, a carrier must be named, and a change to the origin flips verification to tampered -- so a movement cannot be provisioned pointing nowhere or relabeled after the fact.

title: S9 05 Logistics
chapter_title: Honest Custody -- Origin and Destination, Required and Distinct
text: **Honest custody means a movement actually goes somewhere by someone -- provision_shipment refuses a shipment with no origin or destination, with an origin equal to its destination, or with no carrier.** A record of a movement is only as trustworthy as its custody. This chapter builds the guard that fits a shipment. `provision_shipment` refuses a movement that lacks an origin, lacks a destination, has an origin equal to its destination, or names no carrier — so a movement records a real journey by a real party, or not at all. **An absent or self-referential route is refused -- provision_shipment fails closed on a movement with no origin, no destination, or an origin equal to its destination, so a movement cannot point nowhere.** The guard is fail-closed. `test_origin_and_destination_required` and `test_origin_destination_must_differ` prove it: a missing origin or destination, or a route from a place to itself, each raise before anything is recorded. A movement goes from somewhere to somewhere else by physical fact, and the primitive enforces that fact — so no null or circular journey ever enters a receipt. The movement records a real route, or not at all. **A carrier must be named and the quantity must be real -- so a movement is carried by a stated party in a non-negative amount, not by nobody.** Honesty is also about who carried it. `test_carrier_required` proves a movement with no carrier is refused, and `test_negative_quantity_refused` proves a negative quantity is refused. A movement is carried by a named party and moves a real amount — not an anonymous custody or an impossible quantity.
