text: Bringing Your PESTLE Analysis Together Similar to your SWOT analysis, and potentially considered an extension of it, this external environment scan is meant to identify areas where your business is particularly sensitive. As you independently, you should note where you see potential or real risks and opportunities. Decide how you are going to respond to each of these. From there, look inward to your strengths and weaknesses and append your assessment of what those look like. If these are weaknesses, you should consider how to counteract the issue to either close the weakness gap or minimize any potential threats. See Figure 1.5 – PESTLE Analysis Framework for a visual radial diagram of the six macro-environmental factors. Porter’s Five Forces This is a competitive analysis framework developed by Michael E. Porter and published in his 1980 book Competitive Strategy: Techniques for Analyzing Industries and Competitors. It breaks down five competitive forces that shape every industry. With this model you will identify the strengths, weaknesses, environment incumbents face and navigate. These factors ultimately drive an industry’s profitability profile, where higher competition naturally leads to reduced profits. The model is normally used at the industry level but can also be applied at higher levels of the economy as well as down to market segments. The five forces are: (1) competition in the industry, (2) threat of new entrants into the industry, (3) threat of substitute products, (4) power of suppliers, and (5) power of customers. The number and power of each of these areas influences the profitability of your business. Competition in the Industry: A firm’s power in the industry depends on the number of incumbents, their relative size, and therefore any one firm’s ability to affect the market price. As a general rule, a higher number of competitors and competitive products in the industry will result in less power for any one company or product to set its own price and profit. A situation where there are few competitors and few products will result in a greater opportunity for the firm to set its own market price. In economic terms, this is diagrammed with a flat supply curve for high competition and a steep downward-sloping curve for low competition, and an upward-sloping demand curve in both situations. Threat of New Entrants Into the Industry: Limiting new entrants in an industry will result in higher profits for incumbents. Barriers to entry might include intellectual property protections, high capital investments, special tax provisions to existing firms, learning curves, brand identity, customer loyalty, and high customer switching costs. Any gating requirements that pose a substantial cost or risk to a new entrant or that require a waiting period before entry will benefit the incumbents, providing higher prices and margins. Threat of Substitute Products or Services: In addition to the threat of new entrants, the threat of substitute products will limit your ability to control your own pricing and profitability. Customer switching costs are an important consideration, but the closer the substitute product comes to your own, the easier it might be for customers to switch to the lower-cost substitute. This places a cap on the amount you can charge your customers and therefore limits your ability to maintain a premium price structure. Intellectual property protections can create an effective barrier for a period, but market and technological disruptors can quickly undercut your pricing power. Power of Suppliers: This aspect of the model reflects the ability of suppliers to control the price of process inputs. The uniqueness of the good or service they provide will also impact their ability to control pricing. When few suppliers are present and/or the product they supply is highly unique, you can expect that they will implement a premium price structure. If you are able to negotiate a similar product with multiple suppliers, and your switching cost is low, their premium price structure will be eroded and you will attain higher profitability. Power of Customers: In a similar vein, the number and size of customers and the uniqueness of your product or service will determine your ability to control the price. If your customer base consists of few large customers, your ability to negotiate a premium price is limited. And if you have a differentiated product and many customers to sell to, then you will have the power to control pricing and profitability. See Figure 1.6 – Porter’s Five Forces Model for the classic fiveforces diagram with key factors annotated for each force.

The Entrepreneurial Strategy Compass This model was developed by Joshua Gans, Erin L. Scott, and Scott Stern and published in the May-June 2018 issue of the Harvard Business Review. The model frames a set of plausible market entry strategies an entrepreneur might consider and implement. Often entrepreneurs make hasty decisions about what strategy to implement without considering alternatives or trade-offs that might result in greater success. Collaborate or Compete Decision Depending on your product or service idea, you have a decision on how you might compete in your industry. You could elect to work closely with established firms in the industry by providing a value-added activity for them. Or you could decide to go it alone and attempt to create your own value stream. Each of these alternatives comes with a trade-off between how much of the value chain you will attempt to control. Collaborate: If you choose to collaborate, you might find yourself in a long-term situation where you are dependent on larger players in the industry. However, this strategy might enable you to move into and grow quickly in your given industry. Compete: If you choose to compete with the industry incumbents, you have the opportunity to grow to their size or larger and take a market-leading position in the industry. However, in order to reach that level you might face barriers to entry or a competitive disadvantage due to capital constraints and the competitive response of firms with more resources at their disposal. Build a Moat or Storm a Hill Decision Do you want to move quickly into the industry and risk imitation, or do you want to ensure that your ideas are protected? Build a Moat: This path will enable you to protect your product or technology from competition and imitation, but it will take time and will require that you have the finished product prior to entering the market or that you develop and manage the vertical integration of your value chain. The reward for taking this approach is an extended period free of direct competition, or at least limited competition. Storm a Hill: Taking this approach will put your product or technology at risk to competition in the market but might allow you to get a head start on the competition, as you can continue to evolve and iterate the product with customer feedback. Speed to market is a key differentiator here, as you might expect to quickly begin your growth trajectory and use your ingenuity to develop complementary products and services as you evolve. The Four Strategy Compass Quadrants Intellectual Property: A collaborative and patient approach to the market where you will obtain legal protection for your product or technology for an extended period. This approach allows you to maintain control of your product and use it to create value within your industry as you direct it. Value Chain: A collaborative but fast approach to the market where you will work with incumbents, review the current value chain, and extract opportunities to provide a valueadded product or service. Architectural: A competitive and slow approach to create control of a new value chain. This is often done with a platform business that applies a vertical integration approach attempting to make the current industry model obsolete and thereby defend against competitive threats. Due to the larger scale and capital requirements, this approach requires a longer time horizon to implement. Disruption: A competitive and quick approach that attempts to take incumbents by surprise. This requires very fast execution, and gains made might be short-lived if the surprise and execution elements are unable to be sustained. Select Your Quadrant So which of these approaches best fits your mission and goals? You might go back to your SWOT analysis as a reference to evaluate your own competitive landscape and identify what your strengths and weaknesses are. Using those as a reference, you can consider each of these four approaches by reviewing your product, resources available, operational capabilities, and time horizons, then decide what is the most advantageous path for you. See Figure 1.7 – Entrepreneurial Strategy Compass for the 2x2 compass matrix of these four quadrants. title: 01 Strategic Finance
text: strategy comes from a book by the same name written by W. Chan Kim and Renee Mauborgne and published in 2005. The basic concept is that industries and markets are composed of two types of oceans: red oceans and blue oceans. Red oceans include all of the industries in existence today, whereas blue oceans are not yet in existence. Existing industries are composed of cutthroat rivals who attack each other and bleed each other of relative profit. Unexplored or untapped industries lack the competitive rivalries found in established industries. Consider this framework if you are starting up your business or are pivoting as an established business to neutralize your competition and grow. Value Innovation: This is the core principle of the Blue Ocean Strategy with an equal emphasis on both value and innovation. Effective strategies redefine the industry problem and cross market boundaries to unlock exceptional value for buyers. The starting point to identifying and developing a blue ocean is the strategy canvas. The Strategy Canvas: This is a diagnostic and action framework to analyze the current state of a known red ocean and then reconstruct buyer value. The canvas starts with a line chart where the horizontal axis lists each area that an industry competes on and the vertical axis measures the relative value that buyers receive across each factor. Each business is represented by a separate horizontal line as each competitive factor is evaluated. The curve of the line for each business is a visual representation of their market strategy. See Figure 1.8 – Blue Ocean Strategy Canvas for an example showing how Red Ocean competitors cluster together while the Blue Ocean strategy diverges dramatically. Reorient the Strategy Canvas: This is where the power of the strategy canvas is realized. Rather than attempting to outcompete the other businesses, blue ocean strategies attempt to reconstruct the industry value proposition by asking four questions: 1. Which of the factors that the industry takes for granted should be eliminated? Factors that industry customers no longer value should be eliminated. 2. What factors should be reduced well below the industry’s standard? Factors that are currently over-delivered can be reduced. 3. Which factors should be raised well above the industry’s standard? Factors that customers find appealing should be raised. 4. What factors should be created that the industry has never offered? Factors that can bring never-before customers into the market should be created. See Figure 1.9 – Blue Ocean: Four Actions Framework (ERRC Grid) for the Eliminate-Reduce-Raise-Create decision matrix. Redefine Market Boundaries: The next step in creating a Blue Ocean is to look outside of and across current industry boundaries. Red oceans entail evaluating the current industry, viewing the industry the same way as competitors, and finding ways to outperform rivals. Blue Ocean suggests looking across the current market using the six paths framework: 1. Look alternative industries to identify attributes that can be applied to your industry. Use the strategic canvas to combine the industries, then identify which attributes you will keep and which you will eliminate to create your uncontested market. 2. Look across strategic groups within industries: Within your industry, group those businesses with similar strategic identities using the strategy canvas. Compare two of these strategic groups and decide what attributes to combine and what to eliminate to create your uncontested market. 3. Look across the chain of buyers: In an industry, the buyers and customers are often part of a chain that might consist of influencers, purchasers, and users. Industries normally converge to one of the chain members, targeting them and excluding the others. By identifying which customers are being targeted in an industry and focusing your marketing strategy on an uncontested buyer, you can find yourself competing in uncontested waters. 4. Look across complementary product and service offerings: Evaluate the context in which your customers use complementary products. Identify what happens before, during, and after and whether there are any pain points. Create eliminates the pain points to create your uncontested product. 5. Look across functional or emotional appeal to buyers: Products and industries will often appeal to customers either through functional or emotional means. Identify if your product appeals to one at the exclusion of the other, then determine which attributes you will combine and eliminate to create a new space for your product. 6. Look across time: All industries are impacted by external trends that affect their business over time. Technological advances are constantly rising and can redefine how your industry operates. Identify what these trends are, how they might impact your industry in the future, and position your business to take advantage of the trend before your competition does. See Figure 1.10 – Blue Ocean: Six Paths Framework for the sixspoke radial diagram of market boundary redefinition. Attract Non-Customers to Expand Your Blue Ocean: Another way to think about Blue Oceans is in regards to customers or, as this strategy calls them, “non-customers” – customers who are not currently being targeted or have never been consumers. These customers are segmented into three groups: 1. “Soon-to-be” noncustomers who are on the edge of your market waiting to jump ship. These customers have familiarity with the product and a need; however, they have Understanding why these customers want to stop being customers presents a blue ocean for the company that can provide a solution that meets their needs. 2. “Refusing”

text: Understanding why these customers want to stop being customers presents a blue ocean for the company that can provide a solution that meets their needs. 2. “Refusing” against your market. These customers do not use the current market offering for some reason. The reason could be that they are priced out of the market or that they have a fundamental issue with the product as it stands. Again, there is an opportunity to bring them into a blue ocean by identifying what this pain point is. 3. “Unexplored” noncustomers who are in markets distant from yours. These customers may be active in another adjacent market but for some reason have never been targeted by competitors in your market. By focusing on key commonalities and pain points across these noncustomers and existing customers, companies can alter the market dynamics and standard set of product offerings to identify how to pull them into their new blue ocean. The Blue Ocean Strategic Sequence: The next step in developing your strategy is to send your idea through a set of four simple and dependent questions designed to ensure your idea is viable: 1. Buyer Utility: The starting point is to ensure your idea unlocks exceptional value in such a way that target buyers are compelled to buy it. Is there exceptional buyer utility in your business idea? If the answer is no, you need to rethink your idea by reviewing your strategy canvas and reframe it in a way that the utility becomes exceptional. If the answer is yes, proceed to the second question. 2. Strategic Price: Choose a strategic price that will instantly capture almost all of your target buyers. Is your price easily accessible to the mass of buyers? If the answer is no, you need to rethink your pricing strategy so it will be accessible by the mass of buyers. If the answer is yes, proceed to the third question. 3. Target Cost: You need to be able to produce the product, with its predetermined utility, at the target cost while still earning a healthy profit margin now and in the future. Can you attain your cost target and be profitable at your strategic price? If the answer is no, you need to rethink either your production process, your pricing strategy, or both your utility and pricing strategies so that you reach your cost and profit targets. If the answer is yes, proceed to the fourth question. 4. Adoption Hurdles: Even with compelling product utility and an achievable profit model, there will be reluctant and resistant stakeholders including employees, business partners, investors, and the general public. What are the adoption hurdles in actualizing your business idea, and have you addressed each of these upfront? Once you have addressed these and assuming that they do not affect the product utility and profitability, you should have a commercially viable Blue Ocean idea. See Figure 1.11 – Blue Ocean Strategic Sequence for the decision flowchart that validates commercial viability. Four Hurdles to Strategy Execution: The final step in effecting organizational hurdles that may be present or creep in: 1. The Cognitive Hurdle: This involves waking employees up to the need for a strategic shift. Team members may be complacent in the current operating model – the red ocean – and not see the path to future profitable and uncontested growth. This can be because the current product and process have served the organization well historically, and they do not feel the need to change. There is no silver bullet, but face-to-face interactions with the worst operational problems and disgruntled customers may be a way to get the point across and drive action. 2. The Resource Hurdle: Implementing a seismic change in the strategic plan of your company can be daunting and costly. Large changes to your organization can be expensive and you most likely are constrained by some limitation in your resources. To make the case for the Blue Ocean idea, you will want to propose a reallocation of resources, via your capital budget, to activities that provide the greatest return on investment – and that should include your Blue Ocean idea at the top of the list. 3. The Motivational Hurdle: You need to motivate key players to move fast and with determination to achieve this change in the status quo. Use your natural leaders who have the ability to identify and unlock key resources or unblock obstacles. 4. The Political Hurdle: The final obstacle might be the most daunting: the political landscape within your own organization. Enlisting the help of those who have the most to gain and navigating around those who have the most to lose is critical. Often you will want to gain the support of a highly respected insider in order to implement the change. In summary, a Blue Ocean strategy can lead to radical shifts in your business and the strategic environment you operate in, as well as the product and value proposition you provide your customers. Although the effect of this strategy might result in a disruptive business or product, the strategy is non-competitive in nature as you identify gaps and innovative adaptations in your industry and market structure.

Set Up an Advisory Board or Find a Mentor As a startup CEO, surrounding yourself with experienced advisors can accelerate your decision-making and help you avoid costly mistakes. Whether you establish a formal advisory board or find an individual mentor, the perspective of seasoned leaders is invaluable during this formative stage. In my experience, the best advisory relationships are ones where the advisor has built and exited a business in a related industry or has deep functional expertise in your weakest area. If you are a product visionary, find a financial mentor. If you are a finance person launching a product company, find an operator. The advisory board does not need to be large – two to four individuals with complementary expertise is sufficient. Compensate them with equity (typically 0.25-1.0% vesting over two years) and respect their time with structured quarterly meetings that come with a clear agenda and specific questions. Financial Leadership of the Start-Up At this point of operations, your finance support is most likely on your shoulders. As detailed in your business plan, your financial needs might be simple or complex. For the simpler case, this might entail sitting at your kitchen table to set up a QuickBooks account, a bank account, and using predefined online software to manage the smaller levels of transactions the business is incurring. You will probably reach out to a local CPA firm to help you with annual state and federal taxes, payroll, and potentially your bookkeeping. However, affordable small business software is often available to help you do these activities yourself. Your level of sales is still in infancy, and your ability to access higher service levels is both high cost and likely unnecessary – the juice is not worth the squeeze when it comes to paying for a lot of professional financial support. For the more complex startup, you might have large upfront financial needs for machinery, equipment, IP protection, R&D, or the like. Depending on the viability of your product or service, you may be able to acquire funds from other types of investment. Your basic needs for accounting software, tax filings, and bookkeeping are the same as for the simple startup; however, acquiring the funds you need is a far higher hurdle and may call for CFO assistance to both acquire the necessary financing and to ensure you are prepared to meet the reporting requirements and potential debt covenants according to the financing arrangement you enter into. Financing types, terms, and availability vary greatly based on the risk/reward level of the business as well as other factors such as leadership and management structure, stage of growth, track records, and the like. The following nonexhaustive list of funding sources might be available to the start-up firm and may or may not necessitate that you enlist a CFO. Although some of these types may not be available to the start-up firm, I have included all of them here to provide a consolidated view. Business Funding Estimation Concepts Estimating the amount of capital that your business needs is a balancing developing cash flow projections that forecast your expected sales requirements for inventory, payables, and receivables. You may be in a negative cash flow position where your cash burn rate exceeds your incoming cash. You should determine the level of sales you need to reach in order to start generating a positive cash flow, and any negative differences prior to reaching this breakeven point will increase your financing requirements. In addition, you need to identify any capital assets you might need to develop, purchase, and install in order to deliver your targeted service level. To summarize, you should estimating your capital requirements: • Negative cash flow prior to breakeven for labor, raw materials, overheads, salaries, etc. • Working capital for inventory, payables, and receivables • Capital investment in technology, production equipment, real estate, and any other long-term assets • A risk factor for learning curve, missed early targets, and any other headwinds you might face. This contingency might be more difficult to sell to investors but is an important aspect.

text: • Capital investment in technology, production equipment, real estate, and any other long-term assets • A risk factor for learning curve, missed early targets, and any other headwinds you might face. This contingency might be more difficult to sell to investors but is an important aspect. Debt vs. Equity Your CFO can provide guidance around the optimal level and type of invested funds. If your business produces a stable and consistent level of cash flows, investors will be willing to support your financing needs with debt financing. These are essentially loans you commit to repay. The benefit of this type of financing is that your debt investor does not ask for an ownership stake in your business, and the agreed rate of return is usually fixed at a set percentage that is normally far below the cost of equity financing. Start-ups normally receive a limited amount of debt financing and provide their investors higher rates of return. Debt financiers’ obligations are met once the investment is repaid in full with accumulated interest. Equity financing is available to most profitable businesses. Investors agree to make long-term and indefinite investments in your business in exchange for long-term and indefinite rates of return. The trade-off is that you are selling a portion of your company in order to receive the capital financing you need. Equity investors in early-stage companies expect higher rates of return than in mature businesses, as the risk of their investment is higher than in a mature firm. Valuation Summary A business valuation is an estimate of the market value of your business. You will need to develop a strong grasp of your business’s value when seeking financing, selling your business, engaging in M&A activity, navigating divorce proceedings, or performing tax/legal analysis. Multiple valuation methods are used to estimate your business’s worth, and normally a composite of these methods is used to arrive at the most accurate estimate. Valuations can be developed by external and internal financial professionals, such as your CFO, who have access to your financial results and projections. Where variables used in these projections are known and properly accounted for in the valuation model, the more accurate the valuation estimate. Business risk is a key factor in your valuation. Investors discount the amount they are willing to pay for an investment according to their perceived risk. As your business grows, various methods of valuation become more or less relevant in the valuation process. The following types of valuations are used regularly in practice: Comparable Market/Multiples Value: This method compares your business to other businesses that have recently been sold. The comparison is made to your total sales levels and operating cash flows. Industry market multiples are applied to your sales and operating cash flows to determine a market value. Small business brokers often use a regularly published index that provides these multiples by industry and business type. This valuation method does not account for local market, industry, or customers, nor does it account for potential growth outside of that implied by the multiples. Public companies utilize Price/Earnings ratios in a similar fashion to evaluate whether a stock is over- or undervalued. Asset-Based Value: This looks at the market value of the assets you have employed less the amount of your liabilities. If your business sale would not impact your operations as a “going concern” – allowing the business to continue to operate – the valuation would be higher. If your business asset sale would result in discontinuation, then your valuation would reflect the liquidation value of the sale of assets. All things being equal, a going-concern business should command a higher valuation. ROI-Based Value: This valuation is determined by the amount an investor is willing to pay for a set percentage of your company. This “backed-into” valuation is helpful to quickly determine a negotiated sale price. For example, if you negotiate with an investor to sell 50% of your business for $500,000, then the implied ROI-based valuation is $1,000,000. This method applies on a forward-looking basis to what an investor is willing to pay for a percentage of ownership. Discounted Cash Flow Value: This model begins with a future cash investments, working capital, and any other financial impacts. These cash flows are discounted using a risk-adjusted discount rate and the time value of money to estimate the amount an investor should be willing to pay for the future cash flows. For example, if you expected to cash flow $200,000 per year perpetually and your business risk requires a 30% discount, then each of these future cash flows would be discounted

These cash flows are discounted using a risk-adjusted discount rate and the time value of money to estimate the amount an investor should be willing to pay for the future cash flows. For example, if you expected to cash flow $200,000 per year perpetually and your business risk requires a 30% discount, then each of these future cash flows would be discounted based on that risk-adjusted discount rate. In the first year, the value of the cash flow would be $200,000 / (1 + 30%) or $153,846, and the second-year cash flow would be discounted with a compounded discount rate: $200,000 / ((1 + 30%)^2) or $118,343. The sum of all of the future cash flows are taken together to provide the total valuation. This model depends on the accuracy of the financial projections and the factor applied for your business risk. Capitalization of Earnings Value: This simple valuation method takes recent historical performance and projects these cash flows forward using the recent ROI performance. This model assumes stable and consistent cash flows, so it is less relevant for start-up and growing businesses. Book Value: This model simply values the net assets of your business. This is done by taking total assets and subtracting liabilities and equity. This method is useful for businesses with significant asset values that outstrip the cash-flow-generating activities. Sources of Start-Up Business Funding Bootstrapping with Little Capital: Many owners start their businesses with very little investment, going so far as to sell anything they can find around their house to fund the business. This type of financing is considered “pre-seed financing,” meaning that the funding is coming from nonaccredited investors. Or they take personal savings to start their business. They often start their business on the side until they can bear the risk of jumping into their start-up full time. Often this strategy involves reinvesting their earnings back into the business by taking little out as compensation. Friends and Family: A similar strategy is to seek funding from friends or family, which is also a pre-seed source of funding. These investors might be willing to take more risk in you and feel a need to help you succeed. These investments may come in the form of debt or equity and might be made with little care about seeing the funds returned. All parties should beware disappointing results and broken relationships. Start-ups are extremely high risk, so unless the investor can part with the invested funds with little impact to the relationship or their personal balance sheet (investment is below 10% of total assets), this type of investment is not advised. Crowdfunding: Many investors are sourced by large online crowdfunding platforms such as Kickstarter, GoFundMe, and Indiegogo. Each investor can invest a relatively low amount per investor, thereby avoiding accredited investor legislation restrictions; however, these sites are regulated by the SEC. Restrictions apply on who can contribute equity into your business as well as how much they can invest. The crowdfunding sites earn commission from a portion of the invested funds, and this source of funding can be considered pre-seed or seed depending on whether investors receive an equity stake. Angel Investors (Seed Investors): These investors are highnet-worth individuals or groups of high-net-worth investors that fund startups at the early stages of growth with their own assets. Businesses receiving this type of funding normally have a baseline level of proven results. This form of investment is preferred to friends and family as the agreements are at arm’s length and therefore do not risk personal relationships. It is also a sub-category of Private Equity/Venture Capital. Angel investors are among the primary sources of funding for startups and are preferred to some of the other more predatory forms of funding such as hard money lenders. Angel investors prefer to take an equity stake in the start-up, so be prepared to give up a percentage of the company that could limit your decision-making ability. As such, some angel investors prefer to invest in businesses where they have some expertise to provide in addition to the funding. This arrangement can be very beneficial or the opposite, so it is important to align expectations up front and in writing so that there is no miscommunication. Since these investments come with high risk, an angel investor or angel group will rarely invest more than ten to fifteen percent of their total available capital in one start-up. SAFE Agreements (Simple Agreement for Future Equity): A SAFE is one of the most widely used funding instruments for seed-stage and early-stage companies. Originally developed by Y Combinator in 2013, the SAFE has largely replaced convertible notes as the preferred vehicle for pre-priced rounds because of its simplicity and founder-friendliness. Under a SAFE, the investor provides capital today in exchange for the right to receive equity in a future priced round — typically at a discount or subject to a valuation cap that rewards the early investor for taking on higher risk. Unlike a convertible note, a SAFE is not debt: it carries no interest rate, no maturity date, and no repayment obligation. This makes it cleaner for both parties and avoids the awkward scenario where a note matures before the company has raised a priced round.

Originally developed by Y Combinator in 2013, the SAFE has largely replaced convertible notes as the preferred vehicle for pre-priced rounds because of its simplicity and founder-friendliness. Under a SAFE, the investor provides capital today in exchange for the right to receive equity in a future priced round — typically at a discount or subject to a valuation cap that rewards the early investor for taking on higher risk. Unlike a convertible note, a SAFE is not debt: it carries no interest rate, no maturity date, and no repayment obligation. This makes it cleaner for both parties and avoids the awkward scenario where a note matures before the company has raised a priced round. There are several common SAFE structures to understand. A valuation cap SAFE sets a maximum company valuation at which the investor’s funds will convert — if the company raises its next round at a higher valuation, the SAFE investor gets a better price per share. A discount SAFE gives the investor a percentage discount (typically 15–25%) to the price per share in the next round. Some SAFEs include both a cap and a discount, with the investor receiving whichever produces the better outcome. The post-money SAFE, the current Y Combinator standard, defines the cap as a postmoney valuation, making dilution math clearer for both founders and investors. Your CFO should model the dilution impact of each SAFE structure before you sign — stacking multiple SAFEs without understanding cumulative dilution is one of the most common mistakes founders make at the seed stage, and it can leave you with far less ownership than you expected when the priced round arrives. SAFEs are particularly well-suited for situations where you need to close capital quickly from multiple investors without negotiating a full term sheet for each. They are standard for angel investments, accelerator programs (many accelerators invest via SAFE), and small institutional seed checks. However, because SAFEs defer the actual equity issuance to a future event, they require careful tracking — your cap table should reflect all outstanding SAFEs and their conversion terms so that you and your future investors have a clear picture of the fully diluted ownership structure. Grants: Application for grants is an early source of funding for many smaller enterprises. These are awarded by federal and state agencies as well as some private companies. Normally these sources are meant to incentivize growth in areas of the economy that are competitive weaknesses, underutilized infrastructure, or to progress some broader aim of that organization. Customers and Vendors: At times a large customer or vendor will have a business need that is not aligned with their core business, or that is too small profit-wise to be troubled to manage but is still required for them to carry on their core offerings. If they cannot find a suitable subcontractor with the needed capacity, they may elect to invest in your start-up. Often these arrangements involve buying the assets and placing them under your watchful care. This has a twofold benefit to the start-up in that it relieves the start-up from arranging and obtaining financing but also nearly guarantees a consistent revenue stream. You should, however, anticipate that the investor will rightfully try to negotiate a lower market price for your product or service since they are taking on more risk. You would not, for instance, include in your price a factor for asset recovery since they are providing the asset. The funding level is usually dependent on a Loan-to-Value (LTV) ratio of the underlying property. These investors are usually only interested in providing debt

You receive the funds secured by the property and are expected to return the funds over a short one-to-three-year period through a periodic payment, a final lump sum, or a combination. These investors are usually only interested in providing debt financing and have little long-term interest in your operation’s success beyond recovering their investment. Since the use of the funds is high risk, they normally charge interest rates higher than conventional commercial or residential property loans. Lease Financing: This is similar to debt financing whereby you agree to make a set periodic payment for the use of an asset. You have probably seen or heard of this type of financing with automobiles, but it is often available for machinery and equipment. The lender may be the original manufacturer, could be a lender that works closely with the manufacturer, or could be completely unaffiliated and only brought in after you have identified the need. The amount you pay usually includes full recovery of the asset cost as well as additional interest expense; however, the breakdown of the cost is usually not provided. Failure to meet the lease repayment obligation usually includes the loss of ability to use the noncompliance that could reach up to the full value of the underlying asset with interest. Ownership of the asset at the end of the lease period is negotiable and defined in the lease agreement and may require a nominal charge to assume the asset at the end of the term. Financial Statements Overview Another key component for a CFO to support your business with is aligning a financial plan with your strategic plan. Without going into too much detail, I would like to discuss the primary elements of the financial statements. I will keep it simple to help you understand the use of the statements rather than get caught up in terminology and definitions. Every strategic plan needs this standard financial framework as the basis of its corresponding financial plan. Later we will go through some basic planning techniques that you can use to flesh out your financial budget (see Concepts for Forecasting and Budgeting in Chapter 2). Profit and Loss Statement Net Sales is your Gross Sales less any discounts, returns, or allowances you provide to your customers. The Gross Sales portion is the price you sold a good or service to your customer multiplied by the number of goods you sold. Each of these elements are levers you can use to impact this element of the P&L. Cost of Sales includes your cost of raw materials, labor, plant overhead, and freight to fulfill the sale. Each of these has a rate and quantity component that you use to improve your business. Understanding the cost elements in this form is crucial in driving performance. Gross Profit is the difference between your Net Sales and Cost of Sales. This is also referred to as Contribution Margin, as you use this profit amount to “contribute” profit to cover your overheads. This area is generally variable in nature, meaning that if you do not make a sale you do not incur the cost; however, there are some fixed cost components. Overheads include labor for selling, R&D, and administration such as HR, finance, and engineering. Also included is any other cost not directly related to the cost of the product or service you are selling. This section is generally fixed, meaning that you will have the cost regardless of whether you make a sale. EBITDA Depreciation, and Amortization and is a close approximation to the operating performance of the company. In our example it is Gross Profit less Overheads. As we dig into the cash flow statement, this measure will hopefully make more sense. Often this figure is used in the valuation estimate of a firm or the sale price you might expect in the market. Interest, Taxes, Depreciation, and Amortization: This area represents the non-operational performance of your company. These non-operational areas consider the impacts of financing (interest) and investing (depreciation and amortization) to your business. Taxes are payments to the government, which is also non-operational. It is also important to note that depreciation and amortization are non-cash impacts, meaning that although you show an expense on your P&L for the period, the actual expenditure happened in the past. Investors care about actual cash flows from your primary selling and fulfillment activities, which is why this expense is excluded from the EBITDA calculation. Net Profit represents the amount returned to equity shareholders after all revenues and expenses are accounted for. See Figure 1.12 – Income Statement (Profit & Loss) Structure for a waterfall chart showing the flow from Net Sales to Net Profit.

Balance Sheet Retained Earnings represent the accumulated net asset balance held by shareholders after all liabilities are deducted from the value of the assets. What is not necessarily accounted for here is that the market value of the company might be well in excess of the dollars represented as net equity or could be worth far less than reported. This amount is a pure financial accounting measure. Liabilities represent the total amount owed to vendors and lenders. In the event of a business sale, these stakeholders would be first in line to be repaid from sale proceeds. Assets represent the value of cash, inventory, customer receivables, fixed assets, and the accounting value of any other previously purchased goods that have not been consumed via P&L expense. These represent current, future, or potential benefit to the business. See Figure 1.13 – Balance Sheet Structure for a T-account style diagram of Assets, Liabilities, and Equity. Cash Flow Statement Operating Cash Flow includes cash activities related to the operations of the business reflected as income. The net impact of cash generated from the sale of goods (revenue) and cash paid for labor or products (expense) is a key metric for the valuation of your business. This cash flow also includes the impact of your working capital (AR, AP, Inventory) as well as the interest cost of your long-term debt, as these are key elements of your operations. If you were to buy a business, you would be primarily concerned with how much cash you would receive from your initial cash investment in order to understand your ROI percentage and payback period. Investing Cash Flow includes cash activities related to capital investing assets such as long-term investments, real estate, machinery, and equipment, as well as the principal amount of loans made to other entities. Investing activities include the purchase or sale of these assets. Use of cash to purchase another business is also classified here. One clarifying note is that interest received from loans made here is actually classified as Operating Cash Flow. Financing Cash Flow includes cash activities related to the acquisition or repayment of financing you have received from owners and lenders (non-current liabilities and owners’ equity). Non-current liabilities include the principal amount of long-term debt, and owners’ equity items include stock sales, repurchases, and dividend payments. See Figure 1.14 – Cash Flow Statement: Three Components for a diagram showing how Operating, Investing, and Financing cash flows combine to produce the Net Change in Cash. Statement of Changes in Equity The Statement of Changes in Equity is the reconciliation between the opening balance and closing balance of shareholder’s equity during a reporting period. It is a standard financial statement but not considered essential and is not normally issued as frequently as the P&L, Balance Sheet, and Statement of Cash Flows. It summarizes the transactions related to changes in the shareholders’ equity accounts over the period as follows: Beginning Equity + Net Income - Dividends +/- Other Changes = Ending Equity The statement of changes in equity details any movement in retained earnings, other reserves, and changes in share capital such as the issue of new shares and payment of dividends. The report is useful to owners in that it breaks down the equity portion of the balance sheet. Other Start-Up Financial Leadership Aspects Regulatory and Tax Reporting and Payments: When it comes to legal filing requirements of your business, a CPA can help you stay compliant. It is not common that you have a special need that they cannot assist with. There are also tax benefits that you may be eligible for that they can ensure you receive. It is important that if you have employees, you prepare for and stay current on payroll tax filings and payments as well as annual W-2 and 1099 filings. Standard accounting software can help you manage the process, filing documentation, and making the payments directly to the government agency. Alternatively, you could enlist the support of a CPA firm to manage the filings and payments for you. CFOs Are Cost-Effective As your business grows, the need for enhanced financial management skills does as well. A full-time CFO will come with a hefty price tag (and you need to be wary of the candidate’s skill level), so unless your business needs are significant enough to justify the position or the business is bringing in an excess of cash, you may not be able to justify the expenditure. You should be able to get by with targeted CFO support focused on your most critical needs and strategic vision. An experienced CFO will be able to get up to speed quickly, as their business consists of jumping in and out of situations and figuring things out rapidly. They can enter a situation midprocess in order to quickly assess the case at hand and identify the best financial path forward, lending their perspective to the dynamics of the situation. This can involve information gathering, improving financial processes. A CFO likely has at their disposal a team or teams of experienced but lower-level financial professionals. Other financial functions such as accounts receivable and payable can either be managed internally or through third parties. A corporate controller can be acquired at a price well below a CFO; however, their capabilities are likely lacking the strategic guidance a CFO will bring. You likely also have a CPA firm you have contracted with to provide tax payment and reporting. Your CPA firm has probably been a helpful resource as you have considered various business decisions; however, if they are not affiliated with your business directly, their lack of skin in the game may prevent them from fully considering the complete picture. Decades in the Making A CFO will handle the complex financial aspects that your business faces each day. The CFO has considered many issues similar to those that you face as well as the complex strategic decisions you have likely been considering. Getting a leg up on these bigger decisions will help your business grow in a healthy way, shortening and alleviating growing pains. You should expect your CFO to provide sound financial leadership in the following areas: • Strategic planning • Growth initiatives including mergers and acquisitions • Business partnering and performance management • Stakeholder management including investor relations, board, vendors, customers, and banking • Profitability and cash flow planning and performance • Capital allocation decision-making • Statutory compliance including regulatory reporting and internal controls • Risk management and internal controls • Manage financial staff including controller, bookkeeper, and reliable results Although not an exhaustive list, these technical capabilities of a CFO will enable your firm to grow safely and quickly. You need a seasoned veteran whom you can trust, not just someone to fill a role. The CFO will be able to quickly see into your business and identify those areas that need focused attention. These reports utilize best practices providing direct and relatable information to inform your business decisions. As a trusted business partner, they will help you quickly understand the issues and the impact to the business’s strategic plan. Implement Your Vision Your role as the CEO has been to determine everything related to your vision for the direction of the company. By bringing in a CFO, this role likely will not change; however, you will now have a business partner who can provide sound consideration to your ideas, goals, and overall ambitions. They are skilled in developing these plans and the mechanisms required to successfully implement them. They will help you understand the impact to profitability, stakeholders, and compliance. Many of these limiting factors you might find through trial and error, ultimately wasting your most valuable asset of time and also suffering financial losses. Together with the CFO, you will discuss and detail the strategic plan prior to rolling out and together plan around potential pitfalls. In addition, the CFO can help develop the tools, systems, and processes required to carry out the strategy. They have worked with many organizations that differ in size, industry, financial stability, and culture. They will assist with breaking down the vision statement into achievable targets (Key Performance Indicators) whereby performance can be measured. They will help make decisions related to human capital, financial capital, investment decisions, sales, marketing and operations planning, and other impacts as they relate to the overall business plan. They will consider and provide analysis of the various risks to the plan and opportunities that can give you a leg up. They consider your vision statement and provide insight that will streamline the implementation of this vision and ensure that key considerations are in place to achieve the strategic plan. Some of the most basic but critical aspects of executing these strategic activities are the long-term and short-term financial plans. These plans integrate all of the tactical activities and resource allocations required to best achieve the expected outcomes outlined in your strategic plan. Successful leadership teams strictly adhere to the plans by closely monitoring performance. rebalancing and rethinking the plan based on actual performance, changes in the market, and external and internal factors. Maximize Your Valuation As the CEO and other executive leadership desire, the CFO’s primary focus is to increase shareholder value. The key outcome that all firms strive for is to increase the value returned to shareholders. This is not to say that operations are carried out at the expense of other stakeholders through negative environmental, legal, and social impacts. The strategic plan takes into account these potential impacts, enabling the company to navigate smoothly through potential business disruptions. Ultimately, shareholder value must be increased if the business is to thrive. Profitability and cash flow management are critical to the success of the business. Growth often involves obtaining sufficient capital to enable the company to acquire the necessary assets – working capital such as inventory and customer credit (A/R), long-term assets such as land, buildings, machinery, and equipment. Without adequate cash available, businesses are not able to fund the growth. At times and with the right revenue and profitability structure, or sale of previously acquired assets, a firm is able to acquire this cash funding without the need to reach out to external investors. Often the business is left with few other options to obtain the funding and will need to seek external financing partners through debt or equity offerings. A seasoned CFO knows how to acquire the requisite cash, where to economically source the cash, what type of funding will best preserve and expand existing shareholder value, and lastly how to effectively negotiate the terms and amounts of cash to best enable the strategic initiatives. Having the business in a strong financial position with strong internal controls and risk management enables the firm to attract the most advantageous sources of funds. The CFO is best positioned to direct the CEO and leadership team to put the business on a solid financial footing. In fact, having a seasoned senior leader may be the difference between obtaining adequate funding or not from banks and external lenders. As the key financial executive of your company, the CFO is your liaison with external stakeholders, investors, lenders, and professional additional level of reassurance to reported figures and analysis during the due diligence phase of investing and lending confidence to the external party, as they should have a reputation for success and proven business partnering. How a CFO and CPA Differ As a business owner, you may be questioning: what is the difference between a CFO and a CPA? Although the answer is not cut and dry, the main differences include experience, particularly as it pertains to taxation, audit, and business strategy. Many CFOs carry the CPA designation, but the capacity of a CFO is far more strategic in nature. CPAs are primarily trained to manage statutory reporting and taxation. All businesses in the US must file annual and/or quarterly tax statements at both the Federal and State level. The CPA is trained businesses of all sizes and to ensure that reports are in accordance with Generally Accepted Accounting Principles (GAAP for US, or IFRS, which are international reporting standards). They also help to assist with external audits from government or third parties. The work of the CPA for smaller businesses is mostly done as a third party where involvement in daily operations or strategic development is limited. As part of the accreditation process and continuing education requirements (CPE credits), a CPA will get exposure to other financial aspects of business. They may also have the excellent experience of working for a major accounting firm such as the Big Four. However, unless a CPA is actively involved in the daily operations of a business, they will likely lack the experience levels required of a competent CFO. Eventually, with enough operational experience within a business and professional growth, a CPA can reach a level of expertise required to lead an organization as a CFO. Conversely, there are other CFOs who lack the CPA designation completely. More often than not, they have earned a Master of Business experience track within a business that could involve financial planning and analysis, general accounting, cost accounting, internal controls, or other managerial accounting activities. These CFOs may not be taxation experts like their CPA counterparts; however, they will often have decades of experience growing businesses from within and providing the business partnering a CEO of a growing company absolutely needs. Similar Is Not the Same As shown, the key difference between a CFO and a CPA is breadth of experience and capability. A CFO enhances and shapes the strategic direction of the firm in ways that CPAs may not be qualified to do. A CFO’s wide range of industry knowledge, operations within a company, and ability to obtain external financing clearly separates the two, and the gap can be very wide. CPA vs. CMA: Your CPA is an expert in preparing and reporting your financial statements. A CPA (public accountant) deals more with laws, governance, and technical components of accounting. They use financial accounting to communicate with external parties who will use them to assess tax liabilities, prepare audit statements to lenders and other requirements such as due diligence during a sales transaction. Their expertise is to measure historical performance. The CMA deals more with higher-level concepts and business applications with a track to CFO, such as budgeting, forecasting, investing, profitability analysis, cost accounting, and generally applying the strategic vision to the financial data of performance and use managerial accounting data to drive internal decisions of your company that will lead to increased shareholder value. Business Partnering Is Shared Decision-Making Another important differentiator between a CFO and CPA is that of business partnering abilities. Key to the ability of a firm to grow and expand operations is the linkage between the executive functions of the organization. It is incredibly difficult and potentially unsafe for a company to rely on the same CPA they picked up when they were just getting started to lead the financial strategy of the firm. The executives need a sophisticated partner who can advise them to reach the vision. The previous financial focus on taxation and compliance is now expanded to require strong financial and strategic planning. The CFO is acutely aware of the cross-functional needs of your organization including the sales and operating plan, marketing strategy, operations capacity allocation and utilization, and the issues you face running your business day to day. Business partnering is working together as CEO/CFO toward common goals and sharing in the decision-making as if your roles were reversed. This is not the same relationship you may have been used to when you brought your CPA in to “keep your nose clean.” You need someone you can trust to help make the day-to-day decisions you are accustomed to making alone. Operational Leadership of the Start-Up Hire and Manage Employees Hiring Pipeline: Depending on your budgeted sales forecast and growth projections, your strategic plan should include a plan to staff your business by role, indicating what roles and responsibilities each will cover. You will need to consider the lead time to get candidates in for interviewing and the amount of time per interview you will need to devote for each role. Your plan should consider the lag between approving and posting the role to the day that you need this person in the building to begin their training and onboarding. The more skilled the role, the more time it will likely take for you to search and hire the right person. A general rule of thumb is to bring in a dedicated and experienced HR manager between twenty and thirty full-time employees in order to have a baseline level of utilization for new and existing employees. However, if your growth expectations are to grow quickly, you may elect to bring on this person earlier for them to develop and execute a demanding hiring schedule. Employee Classification: From a federal and state law perspective, it is important that you classify each role correctly in classifications include regular full-time, part-time, temporary, and seasonal. You will also need to classify employee status between exempt and non-exempt employees, which applies to their eligibility for overtime pay. This status is determined by the federal Fair Labor Standards Act (FLSA), where nonexempt employees are entitled to overtime and exempt employees are not. Payroll and Benefits: Fringe benefits including healthcare, flexible spending accounts, 401(k), and other benefits offered to employees can be a large overhead expense for your startup. As you grow, you will want to offer a full suite of benefits to attract a qualified and skilled workforce. Relatively low-cost outsourced benefits providers are available to help take some of the administrative burden. Company procedures that govern your business. Onboarding Process: You should have a standardized onboarding process developed for bringing new employees into your business. The process should outline your steps, preferably in checklist form, including communication steps you will take with the new hire from the day they accept until the day they arrive. Other considerations in your checklist include any workspace IT, uniform, company credit cards, ID scans, and signatures. Terminations and Offboarding: Similar to your onboarding process, you need a standard set of guidelines including final paycheck, reimbursements, commissions, and confirmation that company equipment is returned. You should have a separation agreement that outlines the conditions of the termination including a potential separation amount. Exit interviews with terminated employees can be a valuable resource to understand potential issues or dysfunctions within your team. From time to time, these interviews can help resolve issues that your key employees have and prevent their early departure. DISCLAIMER: As with all aspects of your employee relations processes, you should consult with legal counsel to ensure you have all of your bases covered. This book does not provide and should not be interpreted as providing legal counsel. Standardized Processes for Efficiency In addition to your employee onboarding and offboarding processes, you should also consider standardizing other critical operating processes. By “critical operating process,” I mean that it is probably not time to document end-to-end every process in your business. Some recommended processes include your revenue model and your business processes – the process by which you fulfill a customer order. Revenue standardizing your revenue model is to ensure profitability targets are met and that sales transactions are efficient for both your business and your customers. Standardizing your revenue model should include the sales pipeline, pricing strategy including rules, methods, and guidelines you provide to your sales staff, and how these are communicated to your customers. Sales staff need to understand what activities and size of business they are authorized to commit the company to and how to elevate any issues. A standardized process might include quotation templates, pricing models, fulfillment and billing timelines. You should take the time to document your workflow including stages of business templates, email follow-ups, contract signatures, and any other items as required. Depending on your business need and stage, you should consider implementing a Customer Relationship Management (CRM) tool to track and automate this workflow. Depending on the system you select, this could pose a fairly significant financial and time investment, so you should be patient in reviewing your options and consider your growth trajectory so that you do not end up transitioning to a different CRM down the road. Also, depending on the CRM, you should consider how it will integrate with your ERP and/or accounting software. Business standardizing your business process is to be efficient and to scale. Before hiring for a new role, you should consider exactly what business activities you need the role to manage. For nonskilled labor, the manager should create detailed work instructions in advance of the hire in order to efficiently onboard them into the operations. This standard work should easily and straightforwardly communicate how to efficiently perform their duties, create quality products/services, and communicate Documenting the process should lead to improvements in performance and lower your cost as clarity in the process will help standardization should also help you develop time studies for how quickly an activity should be performed. Employee turnover is a fact of business and should be planned for. For skilled labor, it should be the responsibility of each team member to create detailed work instructions of their responsibilities so that others can backfill their role in their absence, resignation, or termination. In preparation for scaling your operation, you should clearly delegate roles and responsibilities across your organization. To create clarity in business functions, it is important for your employees to understand what level of accountability they have according to their role for each process. At a high level, you should outline all roles and responsibilities for your business using a Responsibility Assignment Matrix (RACI Matrix). RACI stands for Responsible, Accountable, Consulted, and Informed. The columns in the matrix represent the roles of your organization and the rows represent your business processes. At the intersection of each role and process, you designate what level of accountability the role is responsible for. Where the accountability is R, the person or people involved should develop and follow a standardized process. Without going overboard with too much detail, the level of detail you decide to go into should help remove any confusion about who is responsible for what. See Figure 1.17 – RACI Matrix Template for a sample responsibility assignment matrix you can adapt for your business. Short of implementing an Enterprise Resource Planning tool (ERP), these business process standardizations should help you reduce your cost and complete more with fewer employees.

IT Security, Web Presence, and Content Delivery Without going into too much additional detail around IT strategy, as I do not have a lot of expertise here, I want to cover a few of the tactical activities your startup should at least be aware of and consider implementing. Ensuring that your customers have a safe platform to interface with is an absolute must for any business that transacts through the internet. Content Delivery Networks (CDNs) can provide not only a secure environment for your business but also help you maintain a broader and more reputable presence with the search engines. This security can help you rank higher in search results as well. Perhaps the most important aspect CDNs provide is timely alerts and response to cybersecurity threats. Whatever platform you engage through, you should review the security risks and opportunities and place the highest priority on the financial and demographic information you store regarding your customers, employees, vendors, and your business. Summary Where You Are: Pre-revenue to early revenue. Cash is tight. You are wearing every hat. The goal is breakeven and a path to the Growth stage. Key Financial Decisions at This Stage: • Develop a written business plan with financial projections • Determine your cash burn rate and months of runway • Identify your breakeven sales level • Choose your funding strategy (bootstrap, angel, grants, etc.) • Set up basic accounting (QuickBooks or equivalent) and engage a CPA • Understand the difference between a CPA and CFO – know when you need each • Determine your entity structure with legal counsel Key Strategic Frameworks to Deploy: • SWOT Analysis (internal strengths/weaknesses, external opportunities/threats) • PESTLE scan (macro-environmental factors) • Porter’s Five Forces (competitive intensity of your industry) • Entrepreneurial • Blue Ocean Strategy (if your concept creates uncontested market space) Key Operational Priorities: • Standardize your revenue model and pricing approach • Document critical business processes • Build RACI matrix for role clarity • Establish employee onboarding/offboarding processes • Secure your IT infrastructure and web presence When to Move to Stage 2: You have achieved consistent positive cash flow, your sales are growing, and you are making financial decisions that exceed your comfort level or your CPA’s capabilities. It is time for a CFO. Key Questions to Ask Yourself: 1. Can I articulate my breakeven point in dollars and timeline? 2. Do I have a written business plan that I have reviewed in the last 90 days? 3. Am I spending my time on the highest-value activities? 4. Is my funding strategy aligned with my growth ambitions and risk tolerance? 5. If I were hit by a bus tomorrow, could someone else run this business for 30 days? Chapter 2: Stage 2 – Growth Your phone has not stopped ringing. Orders are coming in faster than you can fill them. Last month was your best month ever – and you are terrified. Not because the business is failing, but because you can feel the wheels starting to wobble. Fortunately your sales have increased, and with a portion of your margins you can afford to hire a part-time or full-time financial Controller. The Controller takes on the burden to manage the bookkeepers and clerks hired previously and, using your accounting experience and simple financial systems, runs this cash forecast for you and pulls together the financials required to prove to the bank that you are “good for it.” You also have your Controller develop your annual operating budget based on historical trends, and growth is still good. It is at this point where you are beginning to make significant financial decisions that may exceed your experience and/or comfort level. You also realize that your start-up investments provide insufficient capacity to reach the sales levels you believe you can achieve. You ask your controller for help but realize they have not faced these types of investment or planning questions before, nor do they have the knowledge of how to effectively obtain the requisite funding or the ability to help interdependencies to decide how to take the business to the next level. It is at this point that you likely need a CFO, but you may not be in a position to hire one full time. See Figure 2.1 – Growth Stage Transition Diagram for a visual showing the organizational evolution from Start-Up to Growth, including the key trigger points. The right CFO is the perfect fit in this situation. Regrettably, many entrepreneurs make hasty decisions in the moment due to lack of financial leadership in circumstances where they need to make high-impact decisions. They either do not know how to get the support they need or consciously decide to “go it alone” as they did in the early stages of their business. The pressing need for additional capital to continue the growth and expansion of their operations might be overlooked. Capital experienced in these circumstances, are incentivized to maximize their own returns, and rarely have or feel a fiduciary need to protect you, the entrepreneur. A CFO can provide strategic, financial, and operational leadership to support your growing operation. Strategic Support of the Growth Stage CFO As the strategic leader of your company, it has been your responsibility to determine the goals, vision, and objectives of your company. Although you may not have formally developed this strategy in-depth beyond your initial business plan, your efforts and insight have carried your business successfully to a level of growth that will potentially enable you to scale your business even further. An experienced CFO can help you expand and refine this vision and make it actionable. They have been through the strategic planning process many times and have helped other executives develop plans that align all of the functional areas and needs specific to your business. The planning process normally involves working together as an executive team through various strategic frameworks applicable to your business. As we discussed in the strategic models for startups (see Start-Up Phase: Strategic Frameworks in Chapter 1), a basic but powerful framework to start with is a SWOT analysis. This model helps to identify external risks and opportunities (market and industry) and internal strengths and weaknesses (your business) pertinent to your business. Together you will identify those areas that will help or prevent you from being competitive in the marketplace and that will enable your business to better gain and retain profitable customers. Next I will take you through a basic framework for strategy development that you can follow to develop your own strategic plan. Strategic Planning Process Overview Your Strategic Planning Process is a systematic way of executing the long- and short-term vision of your organization that combines your vision, goals, competitive environment, strategy operations execution, and governance activities. No two organizations manage their process exactly the same way; however, these general elements are the focus of most strategic planning and execution activities. As a startup you developed a business plan that included a purposely rudimentary version of your strategic plan where you considered alternative ways to operate in your industry and competitive environment. Now, as your business grows and greater resources are at your disposal, the formalization of this process with the support of executive steering becomes a critical focus of your business. Developing a strategic plan in this way enables you to have a high-level vision that ties back into your day-to-day activities and helps your business thrive financially. Step 1: Strategy Formulation In this first step you will determine the elements of your Strategic Planning Process and create your mission, vision, and value statements with corresponding strategic goals, objectives, and measurement methods. Strategic Planning Process is the systematic way your organization will think and organize itself to achieve your vision and goals. Planning is strategic when it melds long-term vision with short-term resources, capabilities, and tactics to achieve your chosen direction. The strategic planning process takes alternatives your business can decide to execute or not in order to realize your long-term vision. You do this by scanning your internal, external, and customer environments, assessing gaps between your current state versus your vision, and prioritizing your needs and allocating resources to implement strategic change. Mission, Vision, and Values Statements: Within your business plan you developed a mission statement and should now also include vision and values statements. • Mission Statement: Your organization’s purpose and reason for existence. It defines your business identity, what it will do (objectives), and your approach to achieving developed your mission statement, it was a natural outcome of your internal and external environment review (see Your Mission Statement, Goals, and Objectives in Chapter 1). • Vision Statement: Describes the future state of your company in terms of a shared vision of your strategic direction. It inspires a compelling future at the highest level of your organization and is used to drive change management as a team-based shared vision. It should be motivating, forward-looking, and reflect your purpose and core competence. • Core Values Statement: Reflects your fundamental beliefs that guide correct behavior of your organization. These values act as guides in determining your strategic direction and are used as a filter or litmus test as you select your core strategies. Together, these three statements provide guideposts as you select your core strategies, develop and execute the strategic goals and objectives of your strategic plan. The regular reviews as part of the strategic planning process will normally not attempt to adjust these statements, but you can and should modify them as your business evolves so that they continue to be accurate assessments. Strategic Goals and Objectives were also included in your startup business plan. These are a reflection of your mission, vision, and values statements and define what success looks like from an outcome viewpoint. As part of your strategic review process, you will take your mission and vision and decide what strategies you will employ to achieve the vision of your organization. You do this through Operational Planning. Operational Planning is the process of converting your strategic goals and objectives to tactical goals and objectives. Goals are similar to and directly related to your mission and vision statements, are stated in actionable outcomes that you want to achieve, and can be broken down into milestones. Objectives transform your goals into measurable outcomes that include SMART elements (simple, measurable, actionable, realistic, and time-bound). Together your Goals and Objectives apply functionally to your strategic plan and are tracked in areas that might include sales and marketing, operations, people, culture, and product. Goals and Objectives are either strategic and longer-term (three-to-five-year time horizon) or tactical, which are supporting and shorter in duration. Tactical Objectives use the OKR framework. To achieve strategic objectives you should identify three to five Key Results. A crucial deliverable from these plans is a working financial model that will serve as the basis for your budget. Each plan by itself may have many detailed parts, so together with your CFO and other leadership you will determine a handful of critical metrics you will use to guide your operating activities. Targets, Performance Indicators (KPIs), and each ties back into one or more of your OKRs and financial budget. These metrics focus your attention on those activities that will give your business the greatest benefit and guide your efforts to achieve your OKRs to keep the executive team focused. These metrics are reported as often as is feasible and effective (hourly, daily, weekly, monthly, annually) and laser-like focus together as an executive team should result in step-function improvements to reach your objectives.
