Strategy Formulation Frameworks: In the startup strategies, we discussed a number of models that are helpful to identify opportunities and risks with your business model such as the SWOT model. You can continue to use these models to reevaluate your situation and adjust course if needed. As you enter your growth stage, you may want to consider additional alternative strategic frameworks that will help you effectively take your operation to the next level. Strategy Formulation Frameworks BCG Growth-Share Matrix: This framework is a product portfolio planning tool that maps each of your products or services into one of four categories. The matrix is a 2x2 with the Y-axis representing market growth rate and X-axis representing market share. It helps you decide what products to keep, sell, or invest more resources into. This tool is observational in nature and does not measure market competition or disruptive products that could quickly change the categorization of your product portfolio. • Dogs: Low market share, low growth. These should be sold or repositioned but most likely divested. Investing too much in these products can be risky as the opportunity for growth is small. • Cash Cows: High market share, low growth. These are normally segments of the business that cover your company’s fixed costs. Because market growth potential is low, these products should be lightly refreshed from time to time and market share protected. Predictable cash flow should be reinvested in Stars. • Stars: High market share, high growth. These products provide substantial cash to your company that is quickly increasing the value of your business. They are prime candidates for reinvestment and should continue to be invested in until the market growth rate declines and they eventually become Cash Cows. • Question Marks: Low market share, high growth. These products are not market leaders and consume a large amount of company resources. These should be reviewed frequently maintaining. See Figure 2.4 – BCG Growth-Share Matrix for the classic 2x2 portfolio matrix with the ideal product lifecycle flow. The growth matrix is observational in nature and does not measure all market variables you should consider, including changes in competition levels or disruptive products that could alter your product positions in the matrix. Ansoff’s Grid: Originally developed by H. Igor Ansoff in 1957 and also known as the Product/Market Expansion Grid, this is a tool to analyze and plan your growth. The 2x2 model focuses on four options for growth along with their related risk profiles. Strategic leaders have two decisions for organic growth direction: whether to focus on existing or new products, and whether to pursue new or existing markets. • Market Penetration: Existing products, existing markets. This focuses on increasing sales to become more competitive in the markets you currently operate in. Strategies in this area can include price competition, increasing promotion and distribution, or competitor acquisition. • Product Development: New products, existing markets. This is a product development strategy to improve offerings and cater to current customers. Acquiring competitors technologies, or forming similar partnerships to gain access to additional brands or distribution channels, is another way to grow in this segment. • Market Development: Existing products, new markets. This includes market expansion into new customer segments as well as new domestic or international markets. This strategy is important for firms that own proprietary technology they can leverage into new spaces, reach new profitable customers, and that does not materially alter the format of the existing product. • Diversification: New products, new markets. This is the riskiest of all strategies, similar to a startup, where new capabilities, competencies, and customer relationships will need to be formed. Firms engaging in this segment will often focus on related competencies and markets to extract potential synergies in order to minimize risk. Unrelated diversification is the highest-risk area and is not recommended unless your firm is unable to develop a core competence or access attractive markets otherwise. See Figure 2.5 – Ansoff Growth Matrix for the 2x2 matrix with risk gradient showing increasing risk from market penetration to diversification. Core Competency Analysis: These are the aspects of your business that give you a unique competitive advantage over your competition. Your core competence is strategically important for your business to fulfill its mission, goals, and effectively compete in your industry. If not, then it is not a core competence. • Difficult to Imitate: This allows you to outperform your competition, and since you are continuously reinforcing this advantage, it will be sustainable. • Breadth of Application: This allows you to potentially enter

Core competencies can be identified and developed. Use the following steps to review your competencies and develop a plan to execute on those: • Review and list your internal capabilities that are strategically positioned to deliver sustainable value • Compile a list of your competitors’ competencies • Create a horizontal line map for each competitor with a list of competencies along the horizontal axis and a high, medium, low ranking for each competency along the Yaxis for each competitor • Perform a Strategic Gap Analysis on each competence • Highlight which competencies you will target and which you will minimize or avoid (you cannot be everything to everyone) • Use the competency litmus test to ensure your targeted competencies are relevant, difficult to imitate, and have breadth of application • Use the strategic gap analysis to build a roadmap and action plan for competence development In the absence of a core competence, your strategy, mission, and goals will be far more difficult to achieve. Often those companies who lack a core competence or fail to maintain it are ill-fated. Collins Hedgehog Concept: This model was developed by Jim Collins in his 2001 masterpiece Good to Great. The concept is similar to that of Core Competence where you identify areas where you should focus your strategic planning. Through this analysis you will identify one or more things that you do extremely well. Rather than spread your efforts across a range of things, you will spend your time developing this concept and protecting it. Critical Path Method: You should consider the various organizational dependencies when evaluating the strategic organizational changes that will meet your vision and objectives. The critical path method (CPM) is a planning technique that focuses on the key activities and dependencies that will lead to the fastest completion time and allow for the most scheduling flexibility. A critical path is the amount of time to complete the longest sequence of dependent activities to complete the entire project. • Determine all tasks that must be completed for the project • Estimate industry standards, or making an educated guess • Identify any interrelated dependencies among these steps. For example, B is dependent on A completion, and C and D are both dependent on B completion. You would order your path beginning with A, then B, and then C and D can start in parallel. • Where dependencies are not required to start, you would order the start of the task to end whenever dependent activities are able to start. For example, step E is dependent on both D and B completion. In our example, step E would begin with enough lead time to complete just as D is planned to complete. • Create a network diagram to prioritize all steps according to these dependencies and independencies. Order all elements based on dependency. • Calculate the critical path by identifying the longest string of activities and dependent activities. See Figure 2.9 – Critical Path Method (CPM) Network Diagram for a sample network showing task dependencies and the critical path highlighted. Step 3: Strategy Execution Operational Excellence and Continuous Improvement: Operational excellence refers to strategically designing your organization to consistently beat the competition. Excellent organizations utilize continuous improvement principles to perpetually improve the strategic assets of their business. This strategic design might involve forming a center of excellence to focus on your target customers to understand and overdeliver on their value expectations. Your center of excellence analyzes your customers and market through problemsolving, teamwork, and leadership to create uninterrupted value streams. A natural extension of operational excellence is the concept of continuous improvement execution. Continuous improvement incrementally enhances the performance of your center of excellence to both eliminate waste and create value through the following elements: Strategic Vision: Your mission, vision, goals, and objectives drive your operational excellence ambitions. These guidelines provide a framework by which your operations will develop, adjust, and organize to deliver your value proposition. Leadership Alignment: Critical to the success of any strategic initiative, as line managers rely on your vision and that of your key leadership to emulate. Your support and engagement with operational excellence will permeate your organization to the level you place it as a priority. Your understanding and proficiency in operating excellence principles will enable you to inspire your operating leadership team to gain the same competence and implement this excellence. Commitment primary focus of excellent operations and the center of your shared undertakes is centered on creating and leveraging strategic assets that deliver this promise. This commitment leads to topline organic growth and can provide additional platforms to extract additional customer value. Operations Value Chain Activities: Your value chain includes all of the business activities and processes involved within and outside your organization to create your product or service. Michael Porter developed the concept in 1985 in his book The Competitive Advantage: Creating and Sustaining Superior Performance. continually improving the vital aspects that most impact your customers. The primary value chain activities include your suppliers, inbound logistics, business operations, outbound logistics, marketing and sales, and after-sales services. The secondary value chain activities include your organizational infrastructure, human resources, technological resources, and resource acquisition (procurement). All of these value chain activities drive your value proposition and shareholder value. Your strategic planning process should include what Business Model Innovations (a BCG strategic model) you will select to drive shareholder value. This includes focusing your value proposition, target segments, and revenue model, and with this also aligning your operating model, strategic assets, and cost structure. You will make strategic decisions of where to play along the value chain, how to align your cost structure, and what organizational design and capabilities will leverage your strategic assets to exceed customer expectations and deliver attractive returns. Value chain management first involves evaluating each activity along your value chain to understand both risks and opportunities as well as costs and value. At the highest level you will consider your business value stream, then you can conduct the same analysis at each of your product or revenue stream levels. As you consider each step, it is important to evaluate how each step adds value in the eyes of the customer and to consider the incremental cost at that step. Aligning the cost/benefit structure in this way will help you make important profitability trade-offs. Making these often difficult decisions will drive the long-term success of your business as your infrastructure and resources will be put to the most profitable use and avoid underutilization of your strategic assets. These decisions should also be accretive to your strategic asset positioning. From an operational excellence perspective, value chain management is more tactical than strategic. Your tactical activities will involve your day-to-day line managers to effect make/buy decisions, supplier selection and management (scorecards), product/service development and design for manufacturability, lean/Six Sigma, manufacturing footprint, customer targeting and management, and more. Your tactics should follow your strategic mission, goals, and OKRs with prioritization on those business innovations expected to drive the greatest stakeholder value. Any critical area along your value chain should have supporting KPIs to ensure your activities performance. There are a handful of common impediments to strategic execution: Poor Goal Setting: Broad and complex goals increase the level of difficulty to achieve your strategic priorities. Mile-wide and inch-deep goals will not drive your business forward. At the executive level, you should attempt to limit your strategic ambitions to three to five annual strategic objectives. This will enable you to concentrate and prioritize your available resources to deliver faster progress toward your targets. Using the OKR format and guidelines for your objectives will focus your attention on goal achievement. Success will breed additional success and a culture of performance. Lack of Aligned Resources: Habits are difficult to break. Human nature and organizational momentum may draw resources and energy away from strategic priorities. We humans like consistency and to continue doing things the way we have always done them. Disruptions due to strategic realignment might be interpreted as derailing immediate results. These directions may be interpreted as conflicting with day-to-day non-strategic work. Establishing clear alignment and accountability for OKRs will help line management and employees deprioritize non-strategic work. Provide room for your employees to determine what implementation of the OKRs means to them and to set their own OKRs. This will drive their Inability to Measure Progress: Strategies that lack objective definition or that cannot be quantitatively measured are bound to fail. “What gets measured gets improved” and “you manage what you measure” are two proverbs that apply to strategic execution. As your business’s strategic leader, it is your responsibility to determine the destination by clearly defining your strategic objectives. You provide this definition in a way that it is clear to your team where they are heading and they will recognize when they have arrived. Again, the OKR goal-setting framework will provide the basis for this definition. In addition to the OKR framework, you should validate your ability performance. Often systems limitations might prevent regular measurement or require additional expense to provide this measurement. You need to consider any capital budgeting and resource acquisition/allocation requirements when setting your strategic goals. Under-allocating resources in these areas will be an impediment to your success. Other Strategic Execution Frameworks Lean/Six Sigma/Kaizen: These are three toolsets used to develop Operational Excellence in your business. All three fall under the Lean Manufacturing umbrella but are distinct methodologies. Lean Manufacturing: This methodology originates from the Toyota Production System (TPS) in the 1940s with borrowed ideas from Henry Ford’s manufacturing processes and W. Edwards Deming’s statistical quality control methods. The manufacturing, line workers’ quality circles, and waste elimination controls (seven forms of waste). At its core, Lean Manufacturing focuses on the elimination of waste using the Five organization, reduce variability of production processes, and focus on customer value-added efforts. The Five Principles of Lean are the basis for any lean implementation: 1. Value: Defined by your customer and quantified by how much they are willing to pay for your product or service. You then use this definition to align all productive activities by eliminating waste and adding features to extract the maximum your customer is willing to pay. 2. Value Stream Mapping: Represents your entire chain of production events including every value-added step from supplier receipt to customer delivery. Once the stream is mapped out step by step, often via a flowchart diagram, you evaluate each step to identify key statistics such as cost and time to optimize the process. 3. Flow Creation: Consists of elimination of barriers that prevent the value stream from flowing consistently. Interruptions and inconsistent production processes result in higher cost of production. A flowing process ensures consistent production and service delivery resulting in higher sales and profitability. 4. Pull System: This type of flow initiates procurement and production only when demand calls for it, contrasted with a push system which builds inventory to forecast demand. In a push system, the demand forecast inaccuracy will result in over- or under-production. An effective pull system relies on flexibility, supply chain communication, and efficient operations to meet customer demand on time and in full. 5. Perfection: The pursuit of perfection via continuous improvement, also known as Kaizen, is the ultimate goal of Lean. This requires ongoing assessment of current processes Measurement systems must be in place to continuously monitor and measure the productivity, quality, and delivery aspects of your business. See Figure 2.11 – Lean Manufacturing: Five Principles for a circular continuous improvement cycle diagram. The Three Categories of Waste: Elimination of waste is a key feature of Lean. The three categories of waste are: • Mura: Unevenness in production processes resulting from fluctuations in demand • Muri: Overburdening of resources resulting in excessive task switching and demotivation • Muda: Non-value-add activities that do not support a value-add activity

text: The Three Categories of Waste: Elimination of waste is a key feature of Lean. The three categories of waste are: • Mura: Unevenness in production processes resulting from fluctuations in demand • Muri: Overburdening of resources resulting in excessive task switching and demotivation • Muda: Non-value-add activities that do not support a value-add activity The Seven Forms of Waste can be used both within and outside of a manufacturing environment to drive a lean operation: 1. Overproduction: The most egregious form of waste. This drives over-staffing, over-supplying, and over-shipping. It drives other forms of waste including excess inventory, warehousing cost, material waste, labor waste, and excess capital. Processes to minimize overproduction include Just-in-Time (JIT) delivery, Sales and Operating Planning (S&OP) with the support of Material Requirements Planning (MRP) and Labor Capacity Planning (LCP). 2. Inventory: Unprocessed inventory ties up storage space, manufacturing inventory is never consumed in production, it is pure waste unless some value can be recaptured through return, sale, or scrap. 3. Motion: Any operator or machine movement that does not result in value-add to the customer is waste. Examples include unnecessary walking across the production floor, bending, and minor tool calibration. This form of waste results in productivity losses, higher changeover times, ergonomic issues leading to absenteeism and employee turnover. production lines, and changeover processes can quickly reduce motion waste. 4. Defects: Products that deviate from design standards require excess handling, production, rework, materials and labor, documentation, and customer management. Defects must be corrected quickly to prevent repeated defects. When identified, they should be followed up with a root cause analysis that will prescribe countermeasures to prevent future similar deviations. 5. Over-Processing: Any aspect of the production process that is not value-added in the eye of the customer. This includes materials that customers do not notice or value. You should evaluate all aspects of your value proposition and eliminate any factors that do not influence the value. 6. Waiting: Any wasted labor or machine time in your production productive resources. Production processes should be balanced to maximize the utilization of labor and machinery. Line balancing is the process of evaluating all activities in your production workflow to coordinate the equal distribution of time to produce a unit. 7. Transport: Moving component materials and finished goods from one location to another. Any movements, handling, or high-cost transit modes that add cost above the base requirement is waste. See Figure 2.12 – Seven Forms of Waste (Muda) for a radial diagram of all seven waste categories. Although not mentioned specifically, employee safety is a fundamental tenet of lean as not only a humane principle but also as a driver of efficiency and employee retention. A business process that is free of waste is considered a lean process. In practice, it is next to impossible to eliminate all forms of waste due to geography, market dynamics, capital limitations, businesses who align their business with these principles early and consistently almost always thrive in their respective markets. Six Sigma: This toolset is considered an extension of Lean and utilizes statistical analysis and the DMAIC framework (built on W. Edwards Deming’s Plan-Do-Study-Act cycle) to drive improvements. The statistical tools help to analyze issues and identify root causes, which lead to effective countermeasures. The DMAIC framework is a process workflow that utilizes the statistical models to continuously monitor your business activities and drive improvements. DMAIC has the following elements: • Define: The first phase where you create a project charter that includes a high-level process map and voice of the customer. Common tools include A3, SIPOC, Value Stream Map, Swimlane Map, Voice of the Customer Translation Matrix (VOC), and Stakeholder Analysis. • Measure: Once your problem is clearly defined, you will scope the issue using available datasets or create new ones. You will identify your performance baseline prior to making any process changes. Common tools include Value Stream Map, Data Collection Plan, and Operational Definitions. • Analyze: Determine which key indicators are drivers resulting in favorable or unfavorable performance – to test your hypothesis. Understanding the root cause driving your performance is critical. Common tools include Histograms, and Pareto Charts. • Improve: Clearly describe the countermeasures you will put in place to resolve the root causes. Tools include Benchmarking, Value-Stream Maps, Swimlane Map, and Impact/Effort Matrix. • Control: Follow-up monitoring and measuring activities to ensure your improvements take hold. Tools include Control Plans/Control Charts and process documentation. See Figure 2.13 – DMAIC Process (Six Sigma) for the horizontal process flow with feedback loop. Kaizen: In Japanese this means “Good Change” and in practice refers to the concept of Continuous Improvement. The goal of Kaizen is to improve all aspects of business processes through standardization and then incremental improvements to these standardized processes. These continual changes focus on eliminating the three categories of waste (Muda, Mura, and Muri) and utilize all aspects of Lean and Six Sigma as needed. In practice, business problems are often addressed through short sprint projects called Kaizens to quickly implement process enhancements. A CI team might implement between twelve and twenty-five Kaizen projects in a calendar year depending on your business, depth of analytics, team bandwidth, project size, and need.

Step 4: Strategy Governance and Monitoring Governance Concepts: A key aspect of your strategic governance and monitoring process is a formal strategy review to ensure your plan is living and breathing. You should take a structured approach across all areas of your business to review performance, make updates, and align your strategy through the organization. You use these regular structured reviews to monitor your goals, objectives, and progress toward reaching these. However, the focus of these strategic reviews is to ensure you are working on the correct activities, whereas an operational review would focus on how you are performing to reach your stated goals. Strategic Reviews: These can be functional or business unitlevel reviews, or else goal-based reviews focused on each of your three to five long-term goals. Functional reviews focus on the objectives of the functional group, their performance toward those objectives, feedback regarding performance gaps as well as blockages, and then any solutions to close gaps. Similarly, goal-based reviews focus on the long-term goals and supporting short-term goals and objectives. Members of your leadership team who are accountable to achieve each goal report their performance against the goal, highlighting any impediments that require top leadership feedback and decision-making by providing proposed solutions. Tools to assist with these strategic reviews include balanced scorecards and X-matrices that provide visual accountability. Operational Reviews: These reviews are focused on the shortterm goals and objectives of your business and the segment of the business that is accountable. These reviews should occur as often as is naturally helpful to your business. The focus is performance to your goals and objectives using OKRs. Functions are responsible to speak to their KPIs, performance gaps, and detailed work plans to identify root causes and countermeasures to close those gaps. Strategic Governance Frameworks Hoshin Kanri and X-Matrix: This extremely valuable execution and governance tool will help you align your strategy and operational execution activities. This tool is critical in governance as it highlights and forces alignment on a single page your mission, vision, strategic and operational objectives, improvement initiatives, improvement target KPIs, and team accountabilities. Each of these elements is linked within the matrix to show how individual activities relate back to your organization’s long-term strategic objectives. In addition, each functional or accountable area within your organization should have their own cascading version of the X-matrix, and all of these levels will roll up into a high-level Xmatrix. These cascading X-matrices enable the lowest-level team members to visualize the impact of their individual contributions to your long-term strategies. Key Monitoring Activities: Your Strategy Performance Reviews are essential to ensure you are working on the right activities to deliver your vision and strategic goals. Other elements of strategic governance you will want to ensure get proper focus include: • Champions: Accountability for executing your strategic design is critical. Your strategic planning process should drive this accountability from your strategic leaders down through to the lowest levels of your organization. • Cadence: operational performance. These reviews help keep your strategic planning process living and breathing. • Vital Few: Prioritize your activities so you are focused on three to five objectives expected to drive eighty percent of the targeted impact. • Operational Level Metrics: Leading indicators of your financial performance. Identifying and capturing these operational metrics and aligning with your strategic KPIs will help you stay ahead of and reach your financial goals. • Stretch Goals/Targets: Using both baseline goals and stretch goals will help your governance process stay on track. • Celebrate: Momentum from achieving performance targets should be recognized and rewarded publicly through all levels of your organization. Hoshin Kanri Matrix / X-Matrix (Detailed): This governance and execution tool developed in the 1960s and 1970s will help you align your strategy and operational execution activities through all levels of your organization. The tool summarizes your strategy and operational execution plan on a single page. The elements include your mission, vision, strategic and operational objectives, improvement initiatives, improvement target KPIs, and top-to-bottom team member accountabilities. Linkages across these various elements are defined through open and closed circles in the matrix to show how tactical activities relate back to long-term strategic objectives. See Figure 2.14 – Hoshin Kanri X-Matrix for the detailed XMatrix template with correlation matrices. X-Matrix Structure: The matrix is structured like a compass with north, east, south, and west sections, as well as a resource/accountability section to the outside of the east section. • 3-5 Year Breakthrough Objectives (South): Your longterm matrices this section is similar, as it is set through your strategic planning process. • Annual

Catch-Ball Deployment: An important consideration when deploying the strategy is to ensure you have the buy-in and alignment from lower levels of your organization. Senior leaders pass the matrix down into their organization and allow the lower levels to define how they will structure their improvement projects. They reflect how they will achieve, what metrics and targets they will use, and pass those upward to get the senior buy-in. This back and forth continues until all parties are aligned with the goals, objectives, scope, and accountabilities throughout the organization. Balanced Scorecard: This model takes both financial and nonfinancial information to measure the performance of your organization across four focus areas: • Learning and Growth: Measures how well information is captured and how effectively it is transferred into competitive advantage. • Business Processes: Measures how efficiently products are manufactured, quality levels, and delivery times. • Customer Perspectives: Measures customer feedback regarding satisfaction with quality, price, and product availability. • Financial measured in dollars, ratios, and variances to target. See Figure 2.15 – Balanced Scorecard Framework for the fourquadrant framework centered on Vision and Strategy. These four areas encompass your strategic vision and consolidate your goals and objectives into an integrated scorecard. Note: In lean manufacturing, leaders often implement a derivation of this scorecard to measure the areas of Safety, Quality, Delivery, and Cost (SQDC). Strategy Map: Closely tied to the balanced scorecard, this is a visual representation of your overall objectives and how they relate to one another. The elements of the strategy map align with your balanced scorecard but in reverse order: Financial Data, Customer Perspectives, Business Processes, and Learning and Growth. The first two elements regard process outputs – what you are getting. The last two relate to process inputs – what you are doing. See Figure 2.16 – Strategy Map for a vertical four-layer diagram showing cause-and-effect relationships between objectives. There are many benefits of the strategy map. It provides a visual representation of your overall strategy, connecting the intangible drivers such as knowledge and relationships to shareholder value. Your strategy map gives employees a visual understanding of how their roles can contribute to the achievement of your strategic goals and corporate mission. Financial Leadership of the Growth Stage CFO A CFO will be able to accurately and quickly determine what financial support you need; however, this will depend on the availability and reliability of your existing reporting tools. In order to effectively assist you, they will need to start with a brief “audit” of your financial statements, your processes, and they should take some time to walk through your business with you. If the financial statements are too high-level or have shortcomings, that will likely be the best and first place for them to step in. Once they have an understanding of your business, they can help determine what your financial needs are. The support needed might include: 1. Cash cycle stabilization, management, and forecasting 2. Funding for growth including working and invested capital 3. Operating budgets and periodic financial forecasts 4. Information systems for enhanced operations control and fixed asset management 5. Structure and function of your accounting/finance team This is by far not an exhaustive list, as every business is different; however, these subject areas should be considered during the growth stage of your business. Cash Management and Forecasting There is an old accounting adage in business: “Cash is King.” Understanding the flow of cash in and out of your business is by far the most critical piece of your financial processes. Having steady and predictable flows of cash from customers, vendors, and investors will simplify the task of obtaining funding for growth as well as minimizing the business’s cost of capital. If this is not already in place, you should expect that your CFO will recommend a KPI be put in place around the length of time it takes to fund your operations and return the cash to your bank account, such as the Cash-to-Cash Cycle Time or Quick Ratio. The cash forecast is a critical financial report for almost any business, and your CFO can ensure that you have an effective and accurate forecast.

Having steady and predictable flows of cash from customers, vendors, and investors will simplify the task of obtaining funding for growth as well as minimizing the business’s cost of capital. If this is not already in place, you should expect that your CFO will recommend a KPI be put in place around the length of time it takes to fund your operations and return the cash to your bank account, such as the Cash-to-Cash Cycle Time or Quick Ratio. The cash forecast is a critical financial report for almost any business, and your CFO can ensure that you have an effective and accurate forecast. Growth Funding When it comes to funding your business’s growth, your CFO should be able to assess what the most advantageous funding would look like and what is likely available. The areas they will consider include the source of funds (via commercial or investment banks, public or private, debt or equity), what rates and terms will be most advantageous in the long term, and how to structure and negotiate these funds. They should address each alternative in a way that both preserves and maximizes your long-term ownership value. Additional growth opportunities in addition to the organic strategies you have applied thus far are available to those firms that have the proper amount of financial leadership and stability. Growing through acquisition is a bigger step that requires detailed strategic and financial analysis to ensure that the potential targets are a strong fit and will lead to significant increases to the valuation of your business. Operating Budgets and Profit Forecasting An important outcome of your strategic plan is a financial model that can be used as the basis for your annual financial plan (budget). The financial plan should consider each element of your strategic plan and the expected impact of each element on your financial statements (cash forecasts, balance sheet, and profit and loss statement). The basis for the plan is a sales forecast that will represent the targeted sales dollars and/or units you plan to achieve in the given period. From there, you will have an operational plan to determine the cost to support the targeted sales level. Together these two plans combined are called your Sales and Operating Plan and will drive your expected profitability and cash budget. It is recommended that businesses adjust these plans at least annually, while some adjust quarterly or monthly depending on the financing and operating needs. See Figure 2.20 – S&OP Process Flow for a diagram showing how demand and capacity forecasts converge to produce the financial budget. Information Systems for Control Having the systems and processes in place to track, measure, and forecast your business is critical to the success of your strategic plan. At this stage of business growth, you may have already invested in some reporting and analytics tools that, at a minimum, have helped you manage your current business model. Often these systems are plagued with workarounds, slowness, or inaccuracies. Integration of these tools and carrying multiple or excess software can be costly. Your CFO can review your existing information systems and identify and implement software tools and business processes to provide the necessary tracking and reporting. The prescribed systems improvements should give you enhanced visibility and control of your business processes, people, and capital assets. They should enable you to accurately measure your business’s performance; however, every mid- to large-sized business needs a team of accounting and business analysts to help their executives maintain and navigate the financial systems output. Accounting and Finance Functions Supporting your strategic plan with timely and accurate reporting should be among the CFO’s top responsibilities. They should lead all aspects of this performance measurement including statutory and regulatory reporting. They will need lower-level support to provide the analytics, as it would be very costly otherwise. The CFO can lead your existing finance staff, or you could also consider turning over your entire accounting, finance, analytics, and payroll function to a team of professionals through an outsourcing arrangement. Setting up the structure that is right for you, from cost-effectiveness to level of support, is a decision that you could reach together through your strategic planning activities. See Figure 2.17 – Growth Stage Organizational Structure for an expanded org chart showing the CFO, Controller, and FP&A functions. Sources of Growth Business Funding SBA Loan: An SBA loan is a government-backed loan (debt financing) intended to be used for start-up operating costs, purchase of machinery and equipment, or real estate. The loan is issued by a private lender but guaranteed by the federal government through legislation. Loans up to $5 million can be available depending on the use of the funds and collateral. The private lender issues the loan, but if you default, the federal government is on the hook. However, the SBA requires an unconditional personal guarantee from anyone who has more than a twenty percent ownership stake in the company, so you will have to provide your assets as collateral. This additional personal guarantee may make this loan unattractive if you can provide those same assets as collateral for a personal loan at a lower interest rate.

Placement Agents: A placement agent connects investors with companies seeking funding. They are usually hired by private equity, hedge, and real estate investors to quickly and efficiently acquire growth capital. They normally work with later-stage businesses with some level of historic performance but might sometimes work with high-potential startups where the risk level is low and the probability and potential scale of success is very high. A placement agent is a registered securities agent and may provide additional services such as marketing materials and negotiation support with investors. Placement agents receive a commission from the business for providing investors who make an investment. Venture Capital (VC): This falls into a sub-category of Private Equity but with a focus on early-stage startup firms as early as seed funding. This is provided to businesses that are highpotential with little to no performance track record. The expectation is that these businesses are positioned to grow significantly in short order. Similar to Angel Investing, the VC investor is usually only open to accredited investors and is usually part of a larger financial institution or investment bank that is managing pooled investment funding. These equity investments often involve the investor taking an active role in the day-to-day operations of your business to extract the highest expected return on their investment. Startups lack access to public capital and are unattractive to debt financiers, so this type of funding is very attractive to these businesses – even critical for continued success. As of the time of writing, the following three VC series funding had investment and business valuation profiles in the following ranges: • VC Series A (Idea Stage): $2-15 million equity investment for businesses with valuations between $5-15 million • VC Series B (Development Stage): $30-60 million equity investment for businesses with similar valuations around $50 million • VC Series C (Growth Stage, Pre-IPO): $60-150 million equity investment for businesses with valuations around $120 million See Figure 2.19 – VC Funding Series Progression for a visual showing the increasing scale of investment from Series A through C to IPO. Initial Public Offering (IPO): An IPO refers to the process your business will take to transition its ownership shares from privately held to a public sale. Although this is a source of invested funds, it is also considered an exit strategy for yourself and any other investors along the way to realize the big payout. You work with investment banks to market the initial sale of your shares including setting the sale price, gauging demand, and marketing the offering to buyers. You would also expect to earn a premium on this sale price. Companies must meet stringent registration and periodic reporting requirements set by the exchange as well as the SEC. text: Concepts for Forecasting and Budgeting Financial planning within your company can take many forms. In some organizations it may take six months or more to finalize their budget. In reality, budgeting, forecasting, and business planning follow very similar processes, and in some organizations they are indistinguishable. Some companies have a continuous or rolling twelve-month forecast that they reset each month. Other companies develop a three-to-fiveyear master business plan and break off the first year to begin their budget work. The process to develop the budget varies from company to company but has a few consistent elements. I have included below a number of frameworks and accountlevel detailed forecast methods that can help shape your budgeting process and improve your forecasting accuracy and process activities. The finished product of your budgeting activities should include at least a one-year projection of your financial statements (P&L, Balance Sheet, and Cash Flow) as well as detailed analysis and commentary around how you developed the budget assumptions. This should also include a quantified assessment of the opportunities or risks to these financial projections. Annual Profit Plan and Three Types of Budgets: On an annual basis your company should have a profit plan that includes a budget for the key elements of the cash flow statement: (1) Operations, (2) Investing, and (3) Financing. This annual profit plan is meant to be a longer-range planning tool that is integrated with your strategic plan to ensure that adequate cash is in place to meet all of your business needs. • Operational Budget relates to the profitability of your operations including revenue, fixed and variable costs, non-operating costs, taxes, interest, and other non-cash expenses. • Capital Budget is included as a subcomponent of the Financial Budget that details the projects that will be undertaken as investments in the long-term operations of the business. These infrastructural investments are normally recorded to the Balance Sheet as long-term assets and then subsequently recorded as non-cash expenses through the Operational Budgets. • Financial Budget is the last budget to be built during your annual planning process as it includes all aspects of your Operational and Capital budgets. This cash budget is performed at the Balance Sheet level and highlights the cash flow changes across Assets, Liabilities, and Owners’ Equity. Characteristics of an Effective Budget Process: Your financial budget is a quantified measurement of your strategic and operational plan. According to the Institute of Certified Management Accountants, the budget must have the following characteristics: • Is a motivating tool: A successful budget ensures alignment management rank and file. If goals are set too high, this can be frustrating and achievement will be limited. • Has the support of management: Budgets cannot be created in a vacuum or be just a task the finance team manages. There needs to be complete engagement with executive leadership. • Conveys a sense of ownership: Not only should the senior leadership own the budget, but everyone down to the hourly employees should also feel they have activities in their control to hit the budget commitments. • Should be flexible: Business needs change, and early estimates of what the economic environment will be in twelve to eighteen months are rarely accurate. The budgeting process needs to be fluid. • Should be a correct representation: Leadership should ensure that those creating the budgets accurately represent the estimated performance. Rainy day funds in the line manager’s budget are not helpful to senior leadership. • Should be coordinated: All areas of the business should be using the same set of assumptions such as sales growth, labor market inflation, and the like. Top-Down vs. Bottom-Up Budgeting: As you develop your strategic plan, you will want to consider what operational and performance goals to include or exclude in your budget. You can evaluate these goals using multiple scenarios and sensitivity analysis to see how certain variables might impact your future financial statements. Top-Down Budgeting often includes multiple scenarios in which the CFO would be responsible to assess the impact of certain variables in each scenario. The executives decide what they believe is feasible and what the profit needs to be, then leave it to the managers below them to develop a plan that meets those assumptions. This is often done using a base case, worst case, and best case scenario. The variables might be sales growth plus or minus a percent that is realistic, or materials cost inflation plus or minus a percent. The CFO would estimate the sensitivity of a one-percent change in each variable with the resulting profit impact. Bottom-Up Budgeting (Zero-Based Budgeting) is a grassroots approach where the lower-level managers develop their own budgets. They look at the lowest level, potentially even the transactional level, to develop their budget. From a cost standpoint, they go through each account in detail and decide what additional resources they will need and what cost reductions they will implement. Budgeting at this level will likely result in a budget that is higher than what the Top-Down process would provide. In my experience, I have used and requested a combination of both methods. Hoshin Kanri is a popular strategy for top-down/bottom-up alignment, also referred to as Policy Deployment. This is an alignment process to gain strategic and budget consensus throughout your organization using a “catch ball” process (see Hoshin Kanri and X-Matrix earlier in this chapter). Resource Allocation: From an operational standpoint, your budget is an agreement between you and your managers as to what resources they will be authorized to acquire or utilize during the budget period. For instance, a key driver in most budgets is the acquisition and utilization of labor. Regression Analysis: A common financial forecasting tool using statistical modeling. Regression analysis uses historical trending data of a given variable (a dependent variable) in relation to another potentially correlated variable (an independent variable) to predict future results. Although historical performance is never a completely accurate predictor of the future, the results from these estimates come with a given probability level. The Learning Curve: Your business is made up of at least one human, and unless we are hungry, we humans are lazy. We adapt to changes in our environment and develop aptitudes that help us navigate it efficiently. The Learning Curve (alternatively called the productivity or experience curve) refers to the way the efficiency of a business process increases over time as our experience with the process becomes more familiar. When developing a financial forecast, it is important to take this productivity lag into account and build it into your projections. Fixed vs. Variable Cost: Another important concept to understand when budgeting is the concept of fixed and variable costs in the application of activity-based budgeting and flexible budgeting. If the dollars in the account increase or decrease with a change in sales, it is considered a variable cost. If there is no change as a result of a change in sales, it is considered a fixed cost. See Table 2.1 – Fixed vs. Variable Cost Classification for a visual table with behavior indicators. Inadequately assessing the impact to cost from a given sales change can have catastrophic consequences to your profitability. Many companies were forced to make quick decisions around how many people to keep employed or how much office or warehouse space they would need. Inadequately assessing the impact to cost from a given sales change can have catastrophic consequences to your profitability. Flexible Budgeting uses the fixed and variable aspects of the revenue and cost structure to restate the budget due to the change in volume. All variance analysis uses this revised budget as a comparison. Activity-Based Budgeting uses an even more detailed variable cost analysis of your business. Every activity that results in a cost is analyzed to identify the specific cost driver and then using this driver, potential efficiencies are identified and a budget is developed using the summation of all activities. Risks and Opportunities: This section of your budget highlights those items that you considered as part of your budget process but that are late-breaking news, were not considered highly probable, or that were not included in the Policy Deployment agreements. A good way to highlight these is to start with the budgeted P&L profitability and then show the individual impact of each risk or opportunity area. See Table 2.2 – Risks and Opportunities Summary Template for a bridge chart format. Financial Account Forecasting Net Sales Forecasting: Gross Revenue Forecast is a projection of your expected future sales level and often uses your historical sales information as a starting point. • This forecast might be the most important strategic goal to get right. This should be a SMART goal with a high probability and accuracy expectation. • Many other key budget metrics and forecasts use the revenue forecast as the basis for driving the financial statement, especially cost of sales. • Extrapolating straight-line or using statistical frameworks such as linear and multivariate regression are tools used to forecast. • Revenue streams include the unique direct and indirect streams that bring in revenue, classified by type of good or service, including volume, mix, price, discounts, returns, allowances, and merchant fees. Cost of Sales Estimates Total Labor Cost Estimates: An extension of the tax filing issues is effectively planning for these costs so that you do not end up in a loss position on your P&L. As you develop your budget, financial statement pro formas, quotations for customers, underestimate the true cost of your labor. • Include in your estimated labor costs the full cost per hour or per year including fringe benefits • Know what the total “fully fringed” cost is per hour and per year • A quick rule of thumb: divide the annual cost by 2,080 hours (52 weeks multiplied by 40 hours per week) • Include base rate, payroll taxes, social security tax, federal and state unemployment, 401(k) or pension, health/life/ dental/vision insurance, anticipated bonuses, overtime premiums, vacation and sick paid time off, and any other compensation See Table 2.3 – Fully Fringed Labor Cost Breakdown for a detailed cost table paired with a pie chart of cost components. When considering the purchase of machinery, equipment, vehicles, software, web development, facility upgrades, or

title: 01 Strategic Finance
text: Capital Budgeting As you prepare to begin your operation, expand your capacity, or make a large investment in assets that will give you value over multiple years, you will want to ensure that the use of your acquired capital is put to the absolute best purpose. When considering the purchase of machinery, equipment, vehicles, software, web development, facility upgrades, or other high-cost investments, these should be a good fit for your business’s core competence, have an immediate need and will not sit around waiting for customer demand, be procured at a competitive price (by seeking bids from multiple vendors), and have an anticipated return and payback period commensurate with your investors’ expectations. Deciding which project and asset investments you will make or not make is part of what is referred to as a capital budget. The capital budget lists all of your planned investments and rank-orders them by highest and lowest priority according to your strategic and operational plan. This ranking process helps you identify those items that are most critical since once you spend the money, it is gone and likely can only be returned at a fraction of what you paid for it. If you are unsure about what is most critical or what will provide the greatest return, there are a couple of financial models that can help you quantify the trade-off: discounted cash flow and discounted payback methods using the net present value and internal rate of return financial methodologies. You will likely use the financing rate you have received from your debt structure and equity contributions as a combined rate referred to as your weighted average cost of capital to discount the expected returns from your capital investments. This is a lot of financial jargon, but in a nutshell you are calculating the amount of cash you will get back compared to the amount you put in. Imagine a cash machine where you put in $100 and get $120 back, but you receive it in $20 increments each month. The additional $20 you earned is a 20% ROI. The payback time is the amount of time to get your original investment back, or breakeven, which in this case would be five months. If you were to compare a separate investment that required the same $100 input and returned the same $120 but in $30 monthly payments, you would prioritize the second investment over the first since you would get payback in just over three months compared to five before. See Figure 2.18 – Capital Budgeting Decision Framework for a decision tree showing the evaluation criteria for capital investments. These capital assets are normally depreciated over a time period as defined through GAAP, and your CPA can help with the specifics, as these will have an impact on your annual taxes. The capital budget is often segmented by the purpose of the investment, whether for safety, quality, delivery, maintenance, systems, cost reductions, or capacity expansion. Part of the capital budgeting process may involve a plan around how to acquire the funding required for the investments. Some investments do not provide a financial return, such as safety or maintenance projects, but are a cost of doing business. Project Budgeting Development of project budgets differs from repetitive operations budgets. Projects are normally conducted as one-off development or implementation activities. Budgeting can be done as part of the capital budgeting process where trade-offs across many alternatives are made; alternatively, one or a handful of projects could encompass the entirety of all business activities. The elements of project budgeting include: • Project scope, schedule, and deliverables are the key elements of the project commitments. • Project funding authorization should be obtained prior to any labor resources beginning the activity and before any materials are procured or committed. • Procurement quotation, negotiations, and contracts should be reviewed through a separate approver than the individual requesting the product or service. Multiple vendors should be sourced whenever possible. • Activity-based costing is normally used to identify the resource requirements for each independent project activity. • Historical data can be used as a baseline or template for project costing. • Risk register and review cadence will help to quickly identify risks and roadblocks to the scope, schedule, and deliverables. title: 01 Strategic Finance
text: Operational Support of the Growth Stage CFO Not only can the CFO direct the efforts of your accounting and finance staff, they can also provide direction for the operational organizations fill the role of COO simultaneously. These analytics expand upon purely financial ratios and metrics into the realms of Safety, Quality, Delivery, Utilization, Employees, Vendors, and Customers. The KPI definitions and tracking in these areas should be determined during your strategic planning process. Your CFO with the support of your finance and accounting team should be well versed in reporting and monitoring activities, so it is a natural extension for the same team to manage the operational KPIs. Additionally, each of these metrics has a direct correlation to your budget performance and therefore should be applied to any reforecasting or annual budgeting process. This is not to say that the CFO and accounting team should be running the show. Their role is a supporting one where they act as a business partner to the operational manager. Just as the CFO is not the CEO, a financial analyst is not your quality manager but a business partner to support the successful performance of that area of your business. Growth initiatives should be the primary focus of your operating team and include developing internal capabilities and businesses, and streamlining the daily operating activities of your business. As your business and industry grows, eventually the number of opportunities becomes smaller and the size of these opportunities increases due to industry consolidation. These reduced growth opportunities lead to the next phase in the business growth lifecycle. A robust strategic planning process will help you successfully navigate this transition from top-line growth to bottom-line optimization. Summary Where You Are: Revenue is growing, customers are multiplying, and financial decisions are getting more complex. You need financial leadership beyond what your CPA or Controller can provide. Key Financial Decisions at This Stage: • Engage a CFO (fractional or full-time depending on scale) • Formalize the strategic planning process with CFO partnership • Develop integration • Establish cash management forecasting and KPIs (Cash-toCash Cycle) • Evaluate growth funding options (SBA, VC, PE, organic cash flow) • Implement investments • Build or outsource the accounting/finance function Key Strategic Frameworks to Deploy: • BCG assessment) • Core Competency Analysis and Hedgehog Concept • McKinsey 7S (organizational alignment) • Hoshin governance) • Balanced Scorecard and Strategy Map • Lean/Six Sigma/Kaizen (operational excellence) Key Operational Priorities: • Implement formal OKRs and KPIs across all functions • Establish improvement • Build S&OP process connecting sales forecasts to capacity • Implement information systems for control and reporting • Evaluate organic vs. inorganic growth opportunities When to Move to Stage 3: Your revenue growth is decelerating, competition is intensifying, and the focus is shifting from “how do we grow faster” to “how do we grow more profitably.” Your fixed cost structure needs serious attention. Key Questions to Ask Yourself: 1. Do I have a formal strategic plan that my entire leadership team can articulate? 2. Can my CFO tell me my Cash-to-Cash Cycle Time and WACC within 24 hours? 3. Am I measuring the right KPIs at the right frequency? 4. Is our growth funded sustainably, or are we outrunning our cash flow? 5. Have I evaluated whether to grow organically, through acquisition, or both? Chapter 3: Stage 3 – Maturity The champagne years are over. Your company has grown from a scrappy startup into a genuine market player, but the phone is not ringing as often as it used to. Last quarter’s revenue was flat. Your biggest competitor just cut prices by eight percent, and your sales team is panicking. Meanwhile, your cost structure – built for growth mode – is eating into margins that used to feel comfortable. This is the moment that separates good companies from great ones. Last quarter’s revenue was flat. Your biggest competitor just cut prices by eight percent, and your sales team is panicking. Meanwhile, your cost structure – built for growth mode – is eating into margins that used to feel comfortable. This is the moment that separates good companies from great ones. The decisions you make now about cost structure, operational efficiency, and strategic reinvention will determine whether your business becomes a durable franchise or a cautionary tale. Eventually your sales growth rate decreases and your firm reaches the shake-out period prior to maturity. This shake-out can be due to a number of industry or competitive forces such as reaching market saturation or the arrival of competitors or substitute products. These forces can create pressure in the industry and on your ability to even maintain your pricing levels and sales revenue year to year. See Figure 3.1 – Maturity Stage: Industry Forces Pressures for a visual showing the six convergent pressures on a mature business. • Industry growth is limited, leading to increased head-tohead competition (red ocean environment) • Customer bargaining power is increased, leading to market price pressure • Competitive entrants increase, foreign competitors arrive, and number of competitive products increases, leading to commoditization and market price/profitability pressure • Industry capacity slows as demand declines, leading to overcapacity and profitability declines to long-run lowmargin profile • Product innovation is limited and consumer sentiment decreases • Market consolidation occurs to reduce competition and stabilize industry prices • Competitors consolidate to cut overcapacity and reduce cost to drive out weak and inefficient firms Although your ability to grow your revenue internally may be limited, there may be opportunities to grow through acquisition. Other firms with similar, substitute, or adjacent products may be a good fit to be combined with your business. Alternatively, you may be an acquisition or merger target. Your strength in this phase and through these potential negotiations will depend on your financial stability and leadership, leading to your ability to source capital through external parties or preferably through your retained earnings. At this stage of growth, assuming that you have successfully navigated and expended most or many organic and growth opportunities, the slowing of your sales levels requires that you take another look at your internal operating strategies and cost structure. As you worked your way through the Growth phase, your focus was likely more around fulfilling customer orders by increasing your staffing and inventory levels and acquiring the capital and production capacity to feed this growing demand. During the shake-out and maturity phase, you do not have the same need for additional capital or staffing. The opportunities for growth are limited and less in your control; however, your internal cost structure is within your ability to influence. You enhance your focus on maximizing your profit levels. By paying more attention to your cost structure including your fixed and variable costs, you change your focus from top-line growth to bottom-line profitability and cash flow returns to your investors and shareholders. Strategic Leadership of the Maturity Stage CFO At the shake-out/maturity stage, you most likely have grown to the point where you can support a full-time CFO internally. In their role, they have partnered with you and your leadership team to provide the strategic, operational, and financial guidance to lead the business through your intense growth phase. Although there are still external growth opportunities, there are just fewer than before. Your business size likely now dwarfs what it was before, and you are in need of a more robust and regimented strategic plan. The CFO’s focus, and yours, is shifting toward a strategy of cash flow preservation and optimization. These profit-maximizing strategies can be daunting to implement, but a seasoned CFO can help guide you through to ensure that your business will stand the test of time. At this stage it is recommended that there be an additional financial function supporting the CFO that is focused on management accounting and internal financial reporting and analysis. This function is normally referred to as the FP&A group, which stands for Financial Planning and Analysis. The CFO would likely identify a strong candidate with industry experience to lead this team. Below I have highlighted a number of areas your CFO should maintain and review with you frequently during this stage: • Ongoing strategic audits and realignments • Organizational design optimization; engage and motivate employees • More intensive use of OKRs, KPIs, and internal/external benchmarking • Enhanced information technology tools including ERP and CRM • Robust Sales and Operating (S&OP) forecast process including demand forecasts and supply chain signaling and monitoring • Regular reviews of your pricing strategies and product portfolio • Assess and reduce Cost of Goods Sold (COGS) and overheads • Quality performance management • Working capital reductions Increased Use of OKRs, KPIs, and Benchmarking Early on as you brought in your CFO, you would have developed some high-level OKRs and resulting KPIs that were easily implemented with the small-scale technology assets at your disposal (see Targets, Measures, and KPIs in Chapter 2).

title: 01 Strategic Finance
text: Increased Use of OKRs, KPIs, and Benchmarking Early on as you brought in your CFO, you would have developed some high-level OKRs and resulting KPIs that were easily implemented with the small-scale technology assets at your disposal (see Targets, Measures, and KPIs in Chapter 2). As you grew, you likely would refine and adjust these strategic objectives, key results, and KPIs to meet new challenges. An important part of KPI monitoring is benchmarking. Depending on performance, budget targets, competitor data, or an industry standard. Benchmarking allows you to take your current or potential performance and drive improvements based on realistic expectations. See Figure 3.2 – KPI Dashboard Mockup for a sample executive dashboard showing six key metrics with trend indicators. Too often zealous executives set unrealistic goals and incentivize employees based on reaching such targets. This behavior can quickly become demoralizing, and any strategic initiatives presented by executive leadership are quickly dismissed. Conversely, some firms set targets too low and always pay out incentives regardless of whether actual performance improved. Executive leadership must find the right balance that engages their employees, rewards them for performance, and sets targets that can be reached through the employees’ control. Business Process Management (BPM) This is a way for your business to document the standard repetitive processes that make up the core of your operations. Once defined and the interrelated processes matched up, these processes can be analyzed and revised to streamline your operations. See Figure 3.3 – Business Process Management (BPM) Cycle for the five-step continuous improvement lifecycle. • Design: Complete a detailed process map to identify inputs, outputs, decisions, processes, and roles. • Model: Take the design analysis and place into a visual model using Universal Process Notation (UPN) and representing it visually through a diagram, flowchart, Gantt chart, or Petri net. • Execute/Test: Validate that your design and model are properly prototyped by testing each script. • Monitor: Use the standard processes to measure ongoing performance. • Optimize: Increase your efficiency by identifying the root cause for gains and losses in the monitor step, then develop countermeasures to drive improvement. A note of caution: failure in BPM implementation is often due to over-complicating the process. It is recommended to review your processes at the highest level and then break down into sub-elements that can be tracked and measured simply. Business Intelligence (BI) Business intelligence is the result of compiling and analyzing sales, operations, and financial data into actionable insights to inform strategic and operational decision-making. Effective BI tools enable faster decision-making for every area of your business and are the backbone for your KPI/OKR performance measurement processes. Companies that sufficiently invest in carefully designed BI infrastructure are able to quickly respond to economic changes, competitor threats, customer shifts, operational execution, and strategic realignments. Key Driver Analysis This is a statistical analysis that indicates the correlation between business drivers and potential outcomes. For instance, an X-point increase in the US inflation rate would have an X% impact on your cost per unit. Multivariate regression analysis is a statistical tool you can use to model business dependencies compared to key drivers. Leaders should avoid attempts to predict outcomes based on pure statistical analysis assuming causality, but rather use the models as informational data points that might require additional analytics. Strategic Gap Analysis This technique compares your business’s current state across a number of variables with a comparison against benchmarks, competitors, ideal outcomes, or strategic future states. The gap analysis attempts to identify what steps should be taken to close the gaps through root cause analysis, fishbones, 5 Whys, reverse engineering, and other gap closure tools. See Figure 3.4 – Strategic Gap Analysis Framework for the bridge diagram showing current state, desired state, and the analytical tools that bridge the gap. FP&A Function A mature firm should have an FP&A function in place to manage leadership of risks and opportunities. Planning and reporting of performance to the plan is the central element of this function. Most often these teams develop an annual budget, multiple business plan for future year outlooks and capital/capacity planning. Assess and Reduce Cost of Goods Sold and Overheads In order for a profit maximization strategy to work, effective cost controls must be in place. Various cost accounting practices are used to monitor cost and profitability. One of the primary goals is providing accurate product cost information that can be used in margin analysis to support the profitability strategy of the business. See comprehensive table of cost areas, drivers, strategies, and measurement KPIs. Key areas include: • Operations and Supply Chain FP&A: Focused on COGS control environment • Cost Accounting: Provides budgeting, forecasting, and standard costing of your product or service • Fixed Cost Absorption/Contribution: Understanding how products contribute to covering fixed costs • Materials businesses, manageable through commodity forecasting and statistical models • Labor Inflation: Monitor employee satisfaction, turnover, unemployment rates, and competitor wage rates • Distribution and Logistics Cost: Understanding your supply and value chains • Inventory and Cash Management: Monitoring inventory turnover via KPI dashboards • Cost inflationary forces, using tools such as lean/Six Sigma

text: businesses, manageable through commodity forecasting and statistical models • Labor Inflation: Monitor employee satisfaction, turnover, unemployment rates, and competitor wage rates • Distribution and Logistics Cost: Understanding your supply and value chains • Inventory and Cash Management: Monitoring inventory turnover via KPI dashboards • Cost inflationary forces, using tools such as lean/Six Sigma Enterprise Risk Management This methodology is used to identify, assess, prepare for, or respond directly to internal and external influences that could harm your organization and lead to losses. Your strategic planning and governance process should include a regular review of activities that might impact the risk profile of your organization. See Figure 3.5 – Enterprise Risk Management Framework for a 5x5 risk heat map matrix showing likelihood versus impact. Working Capital Optimization Working capital – the difference between your current assets and current liabilities – is the lifeblood of daily operations. At the maturity stage, optimizing working capital becomes a powerful lever for cash generation without requiring external financing. performance: Days Sales Outstanding (DSO): The average number of days it takes to collect payment from customers after a sale. Reducing DSO by even a few days can free significant cash. Strategies include tightening credit terms, offering early payment discounts (2/10 net 30), improving invoicing speed, and implementing automated collections follow-up. Days Payable Outstanding (DPO): The average number of days your business takes to pay its suppliers. Extending DPO – without damaging supplier relationships – keeps cash in your business longer. Negotiate extended payment terms with strategic suppliers, and use supply chain finance programs where available. Days Inventory Outstanding (DIO): The average number of days inventory sits before being sold. Excess inventory ties up cash and warehouse space. Implementing demand-driven replenishment, improving forecast accuracy through your S&OP process, and applying lean inventory principles can dramatically reduce DIO. The Cash Conversion Cycle (CCC) is the sum of DSO plus DIO minus DPO. This single metric tells you how many days it takes to convert a dollar invested in inventory and receivables back into cash. A lower CCC means faster cash generation. Your CFO should track CCC monthly and benchmark it against industry peers. In my experience managing supply chains at scale, the companies that treat working capital as a strategic KPI – not just a finance metric – consistently outperform their competitors in cash generation. The operational teams must own these metrics alongside the finance team. Technology-Enabled Finance As your business matures, the finance function itself must evolve from spreadsheet-driven reporting to technologyenabled strategic analysis. Several capabilities are becoming standard practice for mature-stage FP&A teams: Business Intelligence Platforms: Modern BI tools (Power BI, Tableau, Looker) can consolidate data from your ERP, CRM, and operational systems into real-time dashboards. The investment in a well-designed BI layer pays for itself within months through faster decision-making and reduced manual reporting labor. Automated platforms and close management tools can reduce your monthly close cycle from weeks to days. Faster close means earlier access to reliable data, which means faster strategic response. Predictive Analytics in FP&A: Statistical models and machine learning tools can enhance forecast accuracy by identifying patterns in historical data that human analysts might miss. These tools are particularly powerful for demand forecasting, cash flow prediction, and cost anomaly detection. Your FP&A team does not need to become data scientists – they need to become effective consumers of analytical tools. The CFO’s Technology Agenda: As your business evaluates technology investments, your CFO should champion the business case for finance technology that improves decision speed, reduces manual effort, and enhances data quality. The return technology is among the highest in the enterprise. Sources of Maturity Business Funding Private Equity: Similar to Angel Investors, Private Equity is an alternative form of equity financing whereby investors or investor groups make non-public investments in growth firms. Private equity firms usually expect a resale of their equity stakes within three to seven years at an attractive multiple of their original invested dollars. Leveraged Buy-Outs (LBO): LBOs are another type of Private Equity investment whereby investors purchase a stable cash flow business with a large amount of assets that can back a large amount of debt financing. The purchase price consists of a high percent of debt financing (approximately 90%) along with equity (approximately 10%). Asset Sales: This involves selling any assets that are not aligned with your core business or that are lagging in the industries they service. Divesting assets in ways that maximize your cash flow can position you to take advantage of higherreturn and high-growth expansion opportunities. Addition of COO and Other C-Level Roles At some point in your business evolution, you will want to consider the addition of a COO. The purpose of this role is to delegate the day-to-day internal activities of your business. This role works closely with the CEO, CFO, and other C-level executives and is often considered the number-two leader in a business. The COO manages functions such as: • A key leader in the strategic planning process • Leads the allocation of resource decisions to achieve strategic objectives • Operational planning, closely aligned with the CFO’s financial planning knowledge and skills, and incentive structures • Monitors performance measurements in conjunction with CFO See Figure 3.7 – Maturity Stage Organizational Structure for the fully developed executive org chart with Board of Directors, CEO, and C-level reporting.
