Table of Contents • Chapter 1: The New Org Chart • Chapter 2: The Trust Calibration Scale • Chapter 3: Human vs. Agent Role Definition • Chapter 4: The Delegation Playbook • Chapter 5: Accountability When Agents Err • Chapter 6: Change Management for AI Teams • Chapter 7: The Skills That Matter Now • Chapter 8: Briefing Agents Like Direct Reports • Chapter 9: Measuring Hybrid Team Performance • Chapter 10: When Agent Deployments Fail — Case Studies and Lessons Learned • Chapter 11: Building a Co-Intelligence Culture • Appendix A: The Leadership Prompt Library • Appendix B: The Human-Agent Team Charter Template • Sources & Further Reading • About the Author Chapter 1: The New Org Chart The org chart of the future has AI agents on it. “The technical challenges are solvable. The human challenges are harder. Most leaders are unprepared for the human side.” This is not a metaphor. It is a practical reality that every leader will face within the next two years. Most leaders are unprepared for the human side. The question is not whether AI agents will become members of your team. The question is whether you will lead the transition deliberately or let it happen to you. I have led teams directly and held operational responsibility for organizations of over a thousand people across multiple continents — at Ford, Agilent, Henkel, and Hunter Douglas. I have led through restruc‐ turings, mergers, international expansions, and technology transitions. None of those experiences fully prepared me for what it feels like to deploy AI agents alongside a human team. The technical challenges are solvable. The human challenges are harder. This playbook is about those human challenges. For the full technical foundation — agent architecture, API and MCP integration patterns, deterministic vs. non-deterministic frameworks, frontier model capabilities, and the governance model that runs through the entire series — see AI Agents for CFOs (Book 1). For the decision agent framework, context engineering, and scenario modeling covered in Book 2, see AI Agents for Executives. This playbook builds on those foundations and focuses entirely on the leadership dimension. And for the broader AI landscape, strategic finance frameworks, and sovereignty principles that inform this series, see the Mangum Executive Series: Strategic Finance For Growth, Harnessing Artificial Intelligence, Blue‐ print for Brilliance, and Cryptocurrency Decoded. Where Agents Sit in the Team Structure AI agents do not fit neatly into traditional organizational roles. They are not employees. They are not contractors. They are not software tools (though they run on software). They occupy a new category that organizations are still learning to define. In practice, agents fill four types of roles: The Assistant Role. The agent supports a specific human by handling routine tasks: scheduling, data gathering, report formatting, email drafting. The human directs. The agent executes. This is the simplest integration and the best starting point for most teams. The Analyst Role. The agent independently gathers data, identifies patterns, and produces analyses. The human reviews the analysis and makes decisions based on it. This is the model we built in Books 1 and 2 — the finance agent, the decision agent. The agent does the analytical heavy lifting. The human provides judgment. The Monitor Role. The agent watches systems, processes, or data streams continuously and alerts humans when intervention is needed. The variance detection agent from Book 1 is an example. The agent operates in the background, surfacing only when something requires at‐ tention. The Executor Role. The agent takes actions — sending communica‐ tions, updating records, triggering workflows — based on predefined rules or its own analysis. This is the highest-autonomy role and requires the most robust governance. Most teams will start with assistants and analysts, then gradually add monitors and executors as trust builds. Organizations deploying agents into defined roles see 3x higher adoption rates than those without clear role definitions. Figure 1.1 — Four Agent Roles in Your Team -- see images A principle worth stating explicitly: maintaining human in the loop should be a long-term commitment, not a transitional phase. Even as agent capabilities increase and autonomy expands across all functions — finance, operations, HR, supply chain — the human perspective remains irreplaceable. The trajectory toward full autonomy should be approached with deliberate caution. The organizations that thrive will be those that optimize the human-agent partnership, not those that remove humans from the equation. The Leadership Challenge The challenge is not configuring the agent. The challenge is leading the humans who now work alongside the agent.

title: 03 Leading Agents
text: The Leadership Challenge The challenge is not configuring the agent. The challenge is leading the humans who now work alongside the agent. Your team has questions they may not ask out loud: • “Is this agent going to replace me?” • “If the agent does my analysis, what is my job?” • “Who gets credit when the agent produces good work?” • “Who gets blamed when the agent makes a mistake?” • “Am I being evaluated against an AI that works 24/7 and never takes a sick day?” If you do not address these questions proactively, your team will answer them with assumptions — usually the worst-case version. That breeds re‐ sentment, resistance, and attrition that costs more than the agent saves. The leader’s job is to define the relationship between humans and agents explicitly, early, and with the kind of clarity that leaves no room for anxiety to fill. Your 5-Minute Quick Win Before you read another chapter, open Claude and paste this: ``` I am deploying an AI agent to assist my [team type, e.g., “FP&A”] team of [N] people. The agent will handle [task, e.g., “monthly variance analysis and reporting”]. What are the top 3 concerns my team likely has but won’t say out loud? For each concern, give me one sentence I should say in my announcement to address it proactively. ``` Replace the brackets with your real situation. Read the response. If it surfaces concerns you had not considered — or gives you language you would actually use — you have just experienced the value of thinking about the human side before the technology side. That is what this entire playbook is about. Industry Signal: MIT Sloan’s 2025 research on the AI-augmented organization validates four distinct agent role types in enterprise teams — assistant, analyst, monitor, and executor — with case studies showing that organizations deploying agents deliberately into defined roles see 3x higher adoption rates than those that introduce agents without clear role definitions. The org chart is changing. The leaders who define the new structure first will define the culture. Source: MIT Sloan Management Review, “The AI-Augmented Organization,” 2025. sloanreview.mit.edu Your Next Steps: 1. Look at your current team structure. Where would an agent add the most value? Which of the four roles (assistant, analyst, monitor, executor) fits best? 2. Before deploying any agent, have a direct conversation with the team members who will work alongside it. Address the unspoken questions listed above. 3. Write a one-paragraph “Agent Charter” that defines what the agent does, what it does not do, and how it relates to the human team. Share it with the team before the agent goes live. Chapter 2: The Trust Calibration Scale Skipping trust levels causes 4x more trust-destroying errors. Trust between a leader and an AI agent follows the same progression as trust between a leader and a new hire. “Teams that skip intermediate trust levels experience four times more trust-destroying errors than teams that progress deliber‐ ately.” You do not hand a new employee the keys to the company on day one. You should not hand them to an agent either. These five trust levels parallel the five autonomy levels from Book 2 (Chapter 2) — and the Agent Autonomy Trade-offs figure there maps how governance, context requirements, and risk scale at each level. The same principle applies here: as trust increases, human involvement decreases, but the governance framework must increase proportionally. Think of agent onboarding the way you would think of onboarding a new hire: IT access provisioning, training on your systems and processes, clear access privileges, confidentiality frameworks, and a probationary period where oversight is highest. The author’s Charter v1.0 and Consti‐ tution@A1 framework — centered on SOURCE, TRUTH, and INTEG‐ RITY — provide the governance structure for this onboarding. The optimal human-in-the-loop model: the agent promotes decisions requir‐ ing your attention with clear boundaries, while inconsequential items flow through without intervention. The Five Levels Level 1: Verify Everything. You check every output the agent produces before acting on it. Every number. Every recommendation. Every narrative. This is where every agent relationship starts. It is laborintensive, but it builds your understanding of what the agent does well and where it struggles. Duration: First 10 interactions or first 2 weeks, whichever is longer. Level 2: Spot Check. You review the agent’s conclusions and randomly check a sample of the underlying work — maybe 20-30% of outputs. You are building confidence that the agent’s reasoning is sound, not verifying every detail. Promotion criteria: Agent accuracy exceeds 85% at Level 1. Duration: Next 20 interactions or 2-4 weeks. Level 3: Review Output. You review the agent’s final output (reports, recommendations, analyses) without re-checking the data. You trust the data processing and focus on the strategic implications.

title: 03 Leading Agents
text: The Five Levels Level 1: Verify Everything. You check every output the agent produces before acting on it. Every number. Every recommendation. Every narrative. This is where every agent relationship starts. It is laborintensive, but it builds your understanding of what the agent does well and where it struggles. Duration: First 10 interactions or first 2 weeks, whichever is longer. Level 2: Spot Check. You review the agent’s conclusions and randomly check a sample of the underlying work — maybe 20-30% of outputs. You are building confidence that the agent’s reasoning is sound, not verifying every detail. Promotion criteria: Agent accuracy exceeds 85% at Level 1. Duration: Next 20 interactions or 2-4 weeks. Level 3: Review Output. You review the agent’s final output (reports, recommendations, analyses) without re-checking the data. You trust the data processing and focus on the strategic implications. Promotion criteria: No material errors during Level 2 spot checks. Duration: Ongoing for most strategic applications. Level 4: Act on Alerts. The agent operates continuously and you engage only when it surfaces something that requires your attention. Routine operations run without your review. Promotion criteria: Agent has operated at Level 3 for 30+ days with no significant errors. The domain is well-defined and bounded. Duration: Ongoing for monitoring and operational applications. Level 5: Full Autonomy. The agent makes decisions and acts without human review. Reserved for low-stakes, high-frequency decisions where the cost of a wrong decision is low and easily reversible. Promotion criteria: Level 4 operation for 60+ days. Clear rollback mechanisms. Low downside risk. Examples: Auto-categorizing expenses under $100. Scheduling meeting rooms. Sending routine acknowledgment emails. Why the Scale Matters Without a deliberate trust progression, organizations do one of two things: Under-trust. They verify everything forever. The agent becomes a burden rather than a benefit because it adds a step (review the output) without removing one — the human still does the analysis anyway, killing adoption. Over-trust. They hand the agent consequential decisions too early, based on a few impressive outputs. Then the agent makes a significant error in a domain where it lacks the context to succeed. Trust is destroyed, and the organization reverts to “AI is not ready.” The Trust Calibration Scale prevents both extremes. It creates a deliberate, evidence-based progression from full verification to appro‐ priate autonomy. Applying the Scale Across Your Team Different team members will be at different trust levels with the same agent. The analyst who has been working with the finance agent for six weeks may be at Level 3. The new hire who joined last week should be at Level 1. Trust is individual, not organizational. Set expectations accordingly. Consider maintaining a simple team matrix: each team member’s name, the agents they work with, and their current trust level for each. Review it monthly. Teams that progress deliberately experience 4x fewer trustdestroying errors than those that skip levels. Figure 2.1 — Trust Calibration Scale (5 Levels) -- see images Industry Signal: IBM’s Institute for Business Value research on human-AI team trust identifies a five-level trust progression that aligns closely with the scale above — from “supervised automa‐ tion” through “trusted autonomy.” Their key finding: teams that skip intermediate trust levels (jumping from verify-everything to full autonomy based on a few impressive outputs) experience 4x more trust-destroying errors than teams that progress deliberately. The calibration process is the trust-building process. Source: IBM IBV, “Trust Calibration in Human-AI Teams,” 2025. ibm.com Your Next Steps: 1. For each agent your team uses, determine the current trust level for each team member. Write it down. 2. Define the promotion criteria from your current level to the next. What evidence would you need to see? 3. Set a calendar reminder in 30 days to reassess trust levels. Chapter 3: Human vs. Agent Role Definition The most destructive thing you can do when deploying an AI agent is leave the role definition ambiguous. If the team does not know where the agent’s job ends and their job begins, they will either duplicate the agent’s work or abdicate their own — wasting time or creating risk. “The categories are not about capability. They are about account‐ ability. An agent might be capable – but accountability rests with a human.” The Role Definition Matrix For every task in your team’s workflow, assign it to one of four categor‐ ies: Monthly variance report, daily cash position update, competitive monitoring Data ingestion, routine calcu‐ lations, standard alert genera‐ tion Figure 3.1 — Human vs. Agent Role Definition -- see images The key insight: the categories are not about capability. They are about accountability. An agent might be capable of writing the board presentation. But the accountability for what it says rests with a human. That distinction — capability vs. accountability — should drive every role assignment decision. An agent might be capable of writing the board presentation. But the accountability for what it says rests with a human. That makes it “agent-assisted,” not “agent-led.” Worked Example: A 5-Person FP&A Team Here is the role matrix for a real finance team deploying their first agent: Present to leadership Approve budget ex‐ ceptions Cash flow monitoring CFO decides — agent provides analysis to support the decision Agent monitors 24/7, alerts team when thresholds crossed Agent produces first draft, team reviews and adds judg‐ ment Agent gathers data and pro‐ duces initial analysis, analyst adds interpretation

title: 03 Leading Agents
text: Present to leadership Approve budget ex‐ ceptions Cash flow monitoring CFO decides — agent provides analysis to support the decision Agent monitors 24/7, alerts team when thresholds crossed Agent produces first draft, team reviews and adds judg‐ ment Agent gathers data and pro‐ duces initial analysis, analyst adds interpretation The result: The junior analyst’s role shifts from data pulling to data validation and agent oversight. The senior analyst shifts from model building to model governance and assumption management. The FP&A manager shifts from writing commentary to reviewing and adding strategic context. The director and CFO see no change in their roles — but they get better inputs, faster. Nobody loses their job. Everyone’s job gets more interesting. Task-level accountability clarity correlates directly with team satisfaction and adoption speed. Practical approach: Take your team’s standard operating procedures and break each one down into its component tasks and subtasks. For each, assign a category: Human Only, Agent-Assisted, Agent-Led, or Agent-Autonomous. Many workflows will be shared — the human handles certain subtasks while the agent handles others within the same process. This SOP-level analysis is where the real deployment planning happens, and it requires the domain expertise of the people who do the work every day. What Humans Do Best Even with the most advanced agents, humans excel at: Relationship intelligence. Understanding the dynamics between people — politics, trust, history, motivation. An agent can analyze sentiment data. It cannot read a room. Ethical judgment. Making decisions that involve values, principles, and trade-offs where there is no “correct” answer — only choices with different consequences for different stakeholders. Creative synthesis. Combining insights from disparate domains to generate genuinely novel ideas. Agents are excellent at pattern recognition within domains. Humans are better at connecting across do‐ mains. Contextual adaptation. Adjusting communication, strategy, and ap‐ proach based on subtle environmental cues. The agent does not know that the CEO is having a bad day and this is not the meeting to propose a risky initiative. Accountability. Someone has to own the outcome. In every legal, ethical, and organizational framework, that someone is a human. Hands-on and subjective judgment. Anything requiring physical pres‐ ence, sensory evaluation (taste, smell, tactile quality), or deeply subjective assessment remains fundamentally human. The more subject‐ ive a topic becomes — the harder it is to quantify or narrate — the more humans excel. And while agents may be constrained by their context window, humans are not limited on context in the same way. Humans are limited on conscious memory, but they can draw on a lifetime of implicit knowledge that no context file can fully capture. This is why domain experts become more valuable, not less, in agent-augmented teams — their implicit knowledge is the context that makes agent output action‐ able. What Agents Do Best Agents excel at: Speed and scale. Processing volumes of data that no human team can match. Running one hundred scenarios while a human runs one. Consistency. Performing the same analysis the same way every time. No fatigue. No shortcuts. No forgetting a step. Pattern detection. Identifying patterns in large datasets that humans would miss — anomalies, trends, correlations. Availability. Working 24/7/365. No vacations. No sick days. No timezone constraints. Documentation. Automatically generating records of what was done, when, and why. Every agent action is inherently logged. The Value Intersection The highest value is at the intersection: tasks where human judgment and agent capability combine to produce results neither could achieve alone. A human analyst working alone might spend three days producing a market analysis. An agent alone might produce an analysis in thirty minutes that misses critical strategic context. Together — agent pro‐ duces the data analysis in thirty minutes, human adds strategic context and judgment in two hours — the result is both faster and better. The highest value is at the intersection — where human judgment and agent capability combine. This is co-intelligence. Not human OR agent. Human AND agent, each contributing what they do best. The organiza‐ tions that win will be the ones that find and optimize this intersection for every function. Industry Signal: Harvard Business Review’s 2025 research on defining roles in human-AI collaboration confirms that the role matrix approach — explicitly classifying every task by human vs. agent responsibility — is the single most effective tool for reducing role ambiguity and team anxiety during agent deployment. Their research across 200+ enterprise teams found that accountability clarity at the task level (not just the role level) correlates directly with team satisfaction and adoption speed. Source: Harvard Busi‐ ness Review, “Defining Roles in Human-AI Collaboration,” 2025. hbr.org Your Next Steps: 1. List the top 20 tasks your team performs. Assign each to one of the four categories (Human Only, Agent-Assisted, Agent-Led, AgentAutonomous). 2. For any task currently done by humans that you assigned to “Agent-Led” or “Agent-Autonomous,” define the transition plan: who trains the agent, who validates during transition, and who monitors after handoff? 3. Share the completed matrix with your team. Their input will im‐ prove it — they know their tasks better than you do. Chapter 4: The Delegation Playbook Delegating to an agent requires the same discipline as delegating to a person — but with different mechanics. This chapter provides the systematic framework. “Structured Agent Briefs produce sixty percent better output quality than unstructured prompts. Briefing agents like direct reports is not optional.”

title: 03 Leading Agents
text: “Structured Agent Briefs produce sixty percent better output quality than unstructured prompts. Briefing agents like direct reports is not optional.” Figure 4.1 — Delegation Decision Tree -- see images When a new task arrives, run it through this decision tree: Question 1: Is this task repeatable? If yes, it is a candidate for agent delegation. If it is a one-time, unique task, it may still benefit from agent assistance but probably not full delegation. Question 2: Is the task well-defined? Can you describe the inputs, the process, and the expected output clearly? If the task requires significant ambiguity resolution, keep it human. If the parameters are clear, an agent can handle it. Question 3: What is the cost of an error? If the cost of a wrong output is low and reversible (a draft email, a preliminary analysis), delegate confidently. If the cost is high and irreversible (a financial commitment, a public communication), keep the human in the approval loop. Question 4: Does the task require relationship context? If the task in‐ volves understanding interpersonal dynamics, organizational politics, or relationship history, keep it human. If it is data-driven and relationshipneutral, delegate. Question 5: Does the task require real-time adaptation? If the task occurs in a dynamic, interactive context (a negotiation, a live meeting, a customer interaction), keep it human. If it can be completed asynchronously, delegate. The Agent Brief When you delegate to an agent, provide the same clarity you would give a new direct report: Objective: What is the end result you need? Context: What background information does the agent need to do the job well? (See Chapter 5 of Book 2 on context engineering) Constraints: What are the boundaries? Budget limits, timeline, format requirements, data restrictions, tone. Quality criteria: How will you evaluate the output? What does “good” look like? Escalation triggers: Under what circumstances should the agent stop and ask for human input? The Agent Brief is the equivalent of a job description for a task — and it is fundamentally a context engineering exercise (see Book 2, Chapter 5 for the full framework, including the Blind Agent Test for validating context sufficiency and the Decision Handoff Protocol for structuring how agents present recommendations to human decision-makers). You can spend five minutes writing a good brief manually, or — better — have another AI write it for you. Tell a second agent: “Here are my objectives and constraints. Create an Agent Brief for this task.” Spend five minutes talking to it (voice-to-text works well for speed), let it draft the brief, then tweak anything it missed. The output quality of the ex‐ ecuting agent improves dramatically either way. A note on structured vs. unstructured prompts: The Agent Brief above is a suggested structure — fields with clear labels and descrip‐ tions, similar to a JSON schema. Structured prompts (where inputs follow a defined format) tend to produce more consistent agent output than unstructured narrative prompts. As you develop your briefing practice, consider standardizing your brief templates so agents receive consistent input formats across tasks. Delegating UP vs. DOWN An interesting pattern emerges when agents are deployed across levels: Delegating DOWN (leader to agent): “Produce the monthly variance report.” The agent does the analytical work that was previously done by a junior analyst. Delegating UP (agent to leader): “I detected an anomaly in the cash position that exceeds your defined threshold. Here is the analysis and three options. A decision is needed by end of business today.” The agent escalates to the leader with context, options, and urgency — a better escalation than most human direct reports provide. The best agent deployments include both directions — but the preferred model shifts over time. Early on, you delegate down: “Do this task.” As the agent builds context about your organization, your preferences, and your decision patterns, the relationship shifts to delegating up: the agent identifies variances, exceptions, and opportunities on its own, runs scenarios, develops risk-adjusted recommendations, and comes to you for approval. This is the mature state — the agent has enough contextual basis to frame the problem and the options. You provide judgment and authorization. That shift from “I tell it everything” to “it surfaces what matters” is the progression every leader should aim for. Industry Signal: Forbes Technology Council’s 2025 framework for delegating to AI agents mirrors the decision tree above — using task repeatability, definition clarity, error cost, and relationship requirements as the four primary filters. Their additional insight: the Agent Brief (structured task delegation) produces 60% better output quality than unstructured prompts, confirming that the discipline of briefing agents like direct reports is not optional — it is the primary driver of agent effectiveness. Source: Forbes Technology Council, “How to Delegate to AI Agents,” 2025. forbes.com Your Next Steps: 1. Take one task you are currently doing yourself and run it through the delegation decision tree. Is it delegable? 2. Write an Agent Brief for that task using the five-element frame‐ work. 3. Delegate it to your agent and evaluate the result against your quality criteria. Chapter 5: Accountability When Agents Err The agent will make mistakes — the framework you build before that moment determines everything. This is not a question of if, but when.

title: 03 Leading Agents
text: Chapter 5: Accountability When Agents Err The agent will make mistakes — the framework you build before that moment determines everything. This is not a question of if, but when. “Organizations that assign accountability before deployment experience seventy percent faster error resolution than those that assign it after the first failure.” Agent errors typically come from two sources: lack of context (the agent did not have the informa‐ tion it needed) or technical limitations (the task exceeded the agent’s current capability). Understanding which type of error occurred — and understanding how the agent works well enough to diagnose it — is more important than defending against errors. That understanding is one of the primary reasons this series exists: to give you, the leader, enough knowledge of agent archi‐ tecture, context engineering, and governance to diagnose problems rather than just blame the technology. The accountabil‐ ity framework you establish before the first error determines whether that error is a learning event or a crisis. The Accountability Principle The human who deployed the agent is accountable for its outputs. This is not negotiable. An AI agent is a tool deployed by a human decision-maker. If the agent produces a faulty analysis that leads to a bad decision, the human who deployed the agent and acted on its output bears accountability — not the agent, not the AI vendor, not the IT team. This principle has three practical implications: 1. You cannot deploy an agent and then blame it when things go wrong. “The AI told me to” is not a defense. You chose to act on the agent’s recommendation. 2. You must maintain sufficient understanding of the agent’s reasoning to evaluate its outputs. Delegating does not mean ab‐ dicating. If you cannot explain why the agent made a recommenda‐ tion, you are not ready to act on it. 3. You must have governance in place before deployment, not after the first failure. The governance framework (Book 2, Chapter 8) exists precisely for this moment. When the Agent Is Wrong: The Response Protocol Step 1: Contain the impact. If the error has downstream consequences (a report was distributed, a decision was communicated, an action was taken), address those consequences immediately. Correction first, investigation second. Step 2: Investigate the root cause. Was it a data quality issue (bad input)? A context gap (the agent did not have information it needed)? A reasoning failure (the model drew the wrong conclusion from correct data)? A governance failure (the human did not review when they should have)? Step 3: Fix the system, not just the symptom. Apply root cause coun‐ termeasure analysis — the same discipline used in lean manufacturing and Six Sigma. Understand the deterministic vs. non-deterministic aspects of your agent system: what in the process flow is systematic and repeatable? What was generated by the LLM and therefore variable? Where exactly did the process break? If it was a data issue, fix the data pipeline. If it was a context gap, update the context file. If it was a governance failure, adjust the trust level and approval gates. Good accountability leads to good results — and that principle applies far beyond AI agents. It is foundational to leadership in any domain. Step 4: Communicate transparently. If stakeholders were affected by the error, tell them what happened, why, and what changed. Hiding agent errors destroys trust faster than the errors themselves. Step 5: Update the failure log. Document the error, the root cause, the fix, and the lesson learned. This log becomes the agent’s institutional memory — preventing the same error from recurring. The Blame Vacuum In many organizations, agent deployment creates a “blame vacuum.” When an error occurs: • The executive says: “The agent did it.” • The IT team says: “We deployed the tool, but we did not design the use case.” • The data team says: “We provided the data, but we did not control how it was used.” • The vendor says: “Our model is general-purpose. The customer is responsible for their specific application.” Everyone points to someone else. No one owns the problem. The fix is the accountability principle stated above: the human who deployed the agent for this specific use case is accountable. Full stop. This must be documented in the Agent Charter and communicated to everyone involved. Industry Signal: MIT Sloan Management Review’s 2025 investig‐ ation into AI accountability — “Who Is Accountable When AI Makes a Mistake?” — documents the blame vacuum phenomenon across 150 enterprise deployments. Their finding: organizations that assign accountability before deployment experience 70% faster error resolution than those that attempt to assign account‐ ability after the first failure. The accountability principle is not a post-incident framework. It is a pre-deployment requirement. Source: MIT Sloan Management Review, “Who Is Accountable When AI Makes a Mistake?” 2025. sloanreview.mit.edu Your Next Steps: 1. Write the accountability statement for your agent deployment: “I am accountable for the outputs of [Agent Name] in the domain of [Use Case].” 2. Establish the Response Protocol before the first error occurs. Have the five steps documented and accessible. 3. Create a failure log file. Add it to the agent’s governance docu‐ mentation.

Chapter 6: Change Management for AI Teams Deploying an AI agent is a technology change. Managing the human response is a leadership change. The second is harder. Organizations ex‐ periencing more than 10% voluntary attrition within 90 days almost universally failed to address team fears proactively. “The difference between integration and resistance is almost entirely a function of leadership communication during the anxiety phase.” A structured implementation practice is essential — consider developing standard operating procedures (SOPs) for agent deployment and running pilot programs within your organization where a select group learns the protocols before broader rollout. Before any deployment, reassure your team that this change is for their benefit: less grunt work, more leadership, elevation from front-line execution to strategic guidance. The agents handle the repetitive data plumbing. Your people handle the thinking, the relationships, and the judgment. That is not a demotion. It is a promotion. The Three Phases of Team Response Phase 1: Curiosity (Days 1-14). When you first introduce an agent, most team members are curious. They want to see what it can do. They play with it. Some are excited. Some are skeptical. This is the honeymoon phase. Phase 2: Anxiety (Days 15-60). As the agent starts handling real work, anxiety emerges. “If the agent can do my analysis in ten minutes, why does the company need me to spend four hours on it?” The anxiety is about relevance, job security, and identity. It is real and it is legitimate. Phase 3: Integration (Days 60-90+). If leadership handles Phase 2 well, the team moves into integration: finding the collaboration patterns between human and agent that make both more effective. If leadership handles Phase 2 poorly, the team moves into resistance — working around the agent, undermining its outputs, or actively sabotaging its data. The difference between integration and resistance is almost entirely a function of leadership communication during Phase 2 — the leader’s words shape outcomes for months. What to Say (and When) Why does this section matter? Because words have meaning — espe‐ cially during a transition that affects people’s sense of security and identity. The language you use in the first week of an agent deployment shapes how your team perceives the change for months afterward. Get it right, and you build trust. Get it wrong, and you spend months recover‐ ing. Before deployment: • “We are deploying an AI agent to handle [specific tasks]. The purpose is to free up the team’s time for [higher-value work].” • “The agent is not replacing anyone. It is handling the repetitive data work so you can focus on analysis, strategy, and judgment.” • “Your expertise is what makes the agent useful. Without your context and review, the agent’s output is just data. Your job is evolving, not disappearing.” During Phase 2 (when anxiety peaks): • “I hear the concern. Let me be specific about what changes and what does not change.” • “Your role is shifting from [doing the analysis] to [directing the analysis and applying judgment to the results]. That is a more senior role, not a lesser one.” • “I need your help making this work. You understand the domain better than the agent does. title: 03 Leading Agents
text: Sample Day 1 Communication (Copy and Adapt) The following is an example of the kind of communication that prevents the anxiety, rumors, and resistance that derail agent deployments. Adapt it to your team, your culture, and your specific situation — but do not skip it. Case: Day 1 Communication for an FP&A Agent Deployment The finance director of a mid-market company sent this email to the FP&A team before deploying their first reporting agent: Subject: New addition to our FP&A workflow — starting Monday Team, Starting Monday, we are adding an AI agent to our monthly reporting workflow. I want to be transparent about what this means and what it does not mean. What the agent will do: - Pull actuals from the ERP daily (repla‐ cing the manual data extraction that currently takes four hours every Monday morning) - Generate a first draft of the monthly variance commentary - Monitor budget pace and alert us when a cost center exceeds thresholds What the agent will NOT do: - Replace anyone on this team Make decisions about our forecast assumptions - Communicate with anyone outside finance - Operate without human review (every output is reviewed before distribution) What this means for your role: - The analyst who has been doing the Monday data pull is moving to the scenario modeling project the team has been requesting. Domain expertise is what makes the agent’s output useful. - The senior analyst will review and edit the agent’s variance commentary instead of writing it from scratch. Time shifts from production to quality and strategic context. Everyone: I need your help calibrating this agent. For the first 30 days, please flag every output that is wrong, misleading, or missing context. Your feedback is how we make it better. Why we are doing this: Not because anyone is doing a bad job. Because I want this team spending 80% of its time on analysis and strategy — not 80% on data plumbing. The agent handles the plumbing. You handle the thinking. I am scheduling a 30-minute team meeting for Thursday to answer questions and hear concerns. Nothing is off-limits. This communication took ten minutes to write. It prevented weeks of anxiety, rumors, and resistance. The ROI on that ten minutes was in‐ calculable. But even with good communication, teams make predictable missteps during agent deployment. The following three are the most common — and the most preventable. The Three Change Management Mistakes Mistake 1: Surprise deployment. Introducing the agent without ad‐ vance communication. The team discovers they have a new “colleague” when they see outputs appearing that they did not produce. This triggers maximum anxiety. Mistake 2: Minimizing the change. “It’s just a tool, like a new spread‐ sheet.” It is not. It changes workflows, roles, and the definition of value in the team. Acknowledge the significance of the change. Mistake 3: Ignoring the identity question. (Note: these are the most common mistakes, but not the only ones. Review the industry signals and deployment case studies in your specific domain — each industry surface additional patterns.) For many professionals, their expertise IS their identity. The analyst who prides herself on building the best financial models is not just worried about her job. She is worried about her identity. Address this directly: “Your expertise in financial modeling is what allows you to direct and validate the agent. You are the quality control. The agent is the production line.” Industry Signal: Gartner’s 2025 research on leading through AI adoption identifies the unspoken fears — job displacement, skill obsolescence, and identity loss — as the primary drivers of AI resistance, not technical skepticism. Their data shows that organizations experiencing more than 10% voluntary attrition within 90 days of AI deployment almost universally failed to address these fears proactively. Communication strategy is not a nice-to-have. It is the deployment’s immune system. Source: Gart‐ ner, “Leading Through AI Adoption: Managing the Human Side,” 2025. gartner.com Your Next Steps: 1. Draft the “before deployment” communication for your next agent. Use the language above as a starting point, adapted to your team and culture. 2. Schedule a 30-day check-in with the team specifically to discuss how they feel about working with the agent. Ask open-ended questions. Listen. 3. Identify the team member most anxious about the agent deploy‐ ment. Have a private conversation. Address their specific concerns directly. Chapter 7: The Skills That Matter Now The skills that got your team here are not the same skills that will keep them relevant. AI agents change what matters — and leaders need to help their teams build new capabilities while honoring the expertise that brought them this far. “Domain experts become more valuable, not less, in agent-aug‐ mented teams – their implicit knowledge is the context that makes agent output actionable.” Skills That Increase in Value Prompt engineering and context curation. The ability to communicate clearly with an agent — providing the right context, asking the right questions, and structuring inputs for optimal output. This is not a technical skill. It is a communication skill applied to a new medium.

title: 03 Leading Agents
text: Skills That Increase in Value Prompt engineering and context curation. The ability to communicate clearly with an agent — providing the right context, asking the right questions, and structuring inputs for optimal output. This is not a technical skill. It is a communication skill applied to a new medium. Output validation. The ability to critically evaluate every agent re‐ commendation against domain reality. Does this analysis make sense? Are the numbers plausible? Is the recommendation sound? This requires domain expertise — the very expertise that some team members fear is becoming obsolete. Strategic synthesis. Taking multiple agent outputs and synthesizing them into a coherent strategic narrative. The agent produces analyses. The human produces meaning. Relationship management. Navigating the interpersonal dynamics that agents cannot perceive. Client relationships, stakeholder management, team motivation, negotiation — all become more valuable as analytical tasks shift to agents. Data capture and context feeding. How are you capturing communica‐ tions that happen outside the agent’s view? Meeting transcriptions, audio notes, email context, visual data — all of these feed the agent’s understanding. The tools for capturing this data (voice-to-text, meeting summarizers, email integrations) should be part of every team member’s toolkit. The agent is only as good as the context it receives, and most context lives outside the chat window. Ethical reasoning. Making judgment calls about what should be done, not just what can be done. As agents handle more of the “can,” humans must own more of the “should.” Skills That Decrease in Value Manual data gathering. If your value proposition is “I know where to find the data,” agents diminish that advantage. The data gathering is automated. Routine calculation. Building models from scratch, running standard analyses, performing calculations that follow established methodologies. Report formatting. Creating slides, formatting tables, designing charts for standard reporting. Information brokering. Being the person who has access to information that others do not. Agents democratize information access. Understanding WHY these skills decrease is critical for every team member evaluating their own trajectory. The pattern is consistent: agents automate the repetitive, pattern-based aspects of work. If your role is primarily about executing known patterns — pulling the same data, running the same calculations, formatting the same reports — that work is a candidate for agent automation. The question is not whether this will happen, but whether you will be the one who leads the transformation or the one who is surprised by it. Frame this as retraining and redeployment, not elimination. The skills that replace these are the ones listed above — and they are more senior, more valuable, and more interesting. Knowing which skills are at risk is only half the equation. The other half is leadership — actively guiding your team through the transition. The Upskilling Responsibility As a leader, you have a responsibility to help your team build the skills that increase in value. This is not optional — it is a leadership obliga‐ tion that comes with deploying agents. Practical approaches: • Pair human and agent on every task for the first 60 days. The human learns the agent’s strengths and weaknesses through direct collaboration. • Create “prompt workshops” where the team practices writing effective agent prompts and evaluating outputs. Make it a team exercise, not individual homework. • Redefine performance metrics. If you still measure people on hours worked or reports produced, you are incentivizing the old model. Shift to impact-based metrics: decision quality, speed to insight, strategic contributions. • Share failure stories. When the agent produces bad output and a team member catches it, celebrate the catch. “This is why we need your expertise. The agent could not have caught this.” • Invest in assumption-checking skills. Teach your team to interrog‐ ate agent output: What assumptions did the agent make? What data did it not have? How confident should we be in this recommenda‐ tion? These critical thinking skills become the core competency of the agent-augmented professional. • Make it personal. Help each team member identify their unique contributions — the things they bring that no agent can replicate. Those contributions should be valued, developed, and com‐ pensated. The leader’s imperative is not just to deploy agents. It is to ensure that every person on the team understands why they matter more, not less, in an agent-augmented world. Industry Signal: Harvard Business Review’s 2025 analysis of the new executive skill set confirms that relationship intelligence, ethical judgment, and creative synthesis — the uniquely human skills listed above — are not just surviving the AI transition. They are becoming the primary differentiators for career advancement. Executives who develop these capabilities alongside agent management skills are being promoted at 2x the rate of those who focus on technical AI skills alone. Source: Harvard Business Re‐ view, “The New Executive Skill Set for the AI Era,” 2025. hbr.org Your Next Steps: 1. List the top five skills your team currently relies on. Classify each as “increasing value” or “decreasing value” in an agentaugmented world. 2. For any “decreasing value” skills, identify the corresponding “increasing value” skill the team member should develop. 3. Have a team conversation about skills evolution. Frame it as growth, not obsolescence. Chapter 8: Briefing Agents Like Direct Reports Brief quality accounts for more output variance than model selec‐ tion. One of the most practical insights from deploying agents: treating them like direct reports — not like software — produces dramatically better results.

text: Chapter 8: Briefing Agents Like Direct Reports Brief quality accounts for more output variance than model selec‐ tion. One of the most practical insights from deploying agents: treating them like direct reports — not like software — produces dramatically better results. “Brief quality accounts for more output variance than model selection, framework choice, or prompt engineering technique.” The Agent Briefing Template When you give a task to a human direct report, you provide: 1. What you need (objective) 2. Why it matters (context) 3. How you want it done (approach, if you have a preference) 4. When you need it (deadline) 5. What good looks like (quality criteria) Give your agent the same briefing. Here is the template: ``` ROLE: You are [role description — e.g., “a senior financial analyst on my team”] OBJECTIVE: I need [specific deliverable — e.g., “a variance analysis for Q3”] CONTEXT: - We are a [company description] - This analysis is for [audience — e.g., “the board of directors”] - Recent developments: [anything the agent needs to know] - Prior decisions: [relevant history] APPROACH: [Optional — if you have a preference for methodology] CONSTRAINTS: - Timeline: [when you need it] - Format: [how you want the output — length, structure, tone] - Budget/scope: [any limits] Must include: [non-negotiable elements] - Must NOT include: [things to exclude] QUALITY CRITERIA: - What does “excellent” look like? - What would make this output not useful? ESCALATION: If you encounter [conditions], stop and ask me before proceeding. ``` This template works for any agent, any task, any domain. The more completely you fill it out, the better the output. Agents can also brief themselves. A well-configured agent can automat‐ ically generate briefs from incoming emails, documents, meeting transcripts, and data feeds — connecting each brief to your standing templates and organizational context. There is an entire architecture that can be built around the agent briefing concept, turning every piece of incoming information into a structured, actionable brief without manual effort. For standard, repeatable tasks, platforms like Anthropic offer prebuilt “skills” that encode common briefing patterns — worth exploring as you scale. Context windows and memory: A critical consideration for agent briefings is the context window — the amount of information the agent can hold in active memory during a conversation. When the context window fills, older information gets summarized or dropped, potentially degrading the agent’s understanding of your standing instructions. Persistent memory systems (like the hash-chaining approach at memory.six-sov.com) help bridge this gap by maintaining verified longterm memory that survives context window resets. As you deploy agent briefing systems, assess whether your agent’s memory architecture can sustain the context it needs across sessions — not just within a single conversation. Industry Signal: Anthropic’s engineering blog on building effect‐ ive agents emphasizes that the Agent Brief — structured context provided to the agent before task execution — is the single highest-leverage skill for agent-augmented teams. Their research shows that brief quality accounts for more output variance than model selection, framework choice, or prompt engineering tech‐ nique. The Agent Brief is not just a best practice. It is the new core executive skill. Source: Anthropic, “Building Effective Agents,” 2025. anthropic.com The “Direct Report” Mindset The shift from “using a tool” to “briefing a team member” is subtle but transformational. When you use a tool, you expect it to do exactly what you tell it. When you brief a team member, you expect them to bring their own intelli‐ gence to the task — to fill in gaps you did not specify, to flag issues you did not anticipate, to suggest approaches you did not consider. Modern AI agents can do all of these things — if you treat them as collaborators rather than command executors. The agent that receives a rich brief produces 60% better output quality than one given an unstructured prompt. The difference between “analyze Q3 revenue” and a full brief is the difference between useful output and noise. Your Next Steps: 1. Take the next task you delegate to your agent and write a full brief using the template above. 2. Compare the output quality to a task where you gave a minimal prompt. The difference will be obvious. 3. Save your best briefs as templates. Over time, you build a library of reusable briefing patterns for common tasks. Chapter 9: Measuring Hybrid Team Performance You cannot improve what you do not measure. But the metrics for a human-agent team are different from the metrics for a human-only team. “The real ROI is not in doing the same work faster. It is in doing different, higher-value work with the time freed up.” The Hybrid Team Dashboard Track these metrics for any team that includes AI agents: Efficiency Metrics: • Cycle time reduction. How much faster does the team complete key processes compared to the pre-agent baseline? Measure specific processes (forecast cycle, report production, close cycle).

title: 03 Leading Agents
text: The Hybrid Team Dashboard Track these metrics for any team that includes AI agents: Efficiency Metrics: • Cycle time reduction. How much faster does the team complete key processes compared to the pre-agent baseline? Measure specific processes (forecast cycle, report production, close cycle). • Volume throughput. How many analyses, reports, or decisions does the team produce per week? Has it increased? • Agent utilization. What percentage of the agent’s capacity is being used? If the agent is underutilized, the team may not trust it enough. If it is overloaded, you may need additional agents. Quality Metrics: • Output accuracy. What percentage of agent outputs are used as-is vs. requiring significant revision? Target: 80%+ used as-is by Level 3 trust. • Error rate. How often does the agent produce materially incorrect output? Track by category: data errors, reasoning errors, context misses. • Decision quality. Are decisions made with agent support producing better outcomes than decisions made without? This is hard to measure but essential to track. Human Metrics: • Time reallocation. How much time has shifted from routine work to strategic work? Measure in hours per week per team member. • Team satisfaction. How does the team feel about working with agents? Survey quarterly. Watch for early signs of resistance or anxiety. • Skill development. Are team members developing new skills (prompt engineering, output validation, strategic synthesis)? Track through self-assessment and manager observation. Agent Metrics: • Trust level progression. Are team members advancing through the Trust Calibration Scale? Or are they stuck at Level 1 (verify everything)? • Override rate. How often do humans override agent recommenda‐ tions? A high override rate may mean the agent needs better context. A zero override rate may mean humans are not exercising sufficient judgment. • Failure log entries. How many errors are being documented? A growing log in the early months is healthy (the team is learning). A growing log after 90 days suggests systemic issues. Worked Example: 90-Day Hybrid Team Dashboard Here is what a real dashboard looks like for a 5-person FP&A team after 90 days with a finance agent: as-is) Team trust level (avg) Team satisfac‐ tion (1-5) Override rate Failure log entries ✅ Re‐ covered ✅ Calib‐ rating ✅ Declin‐ ing Key observations: • Satisfaction dipped at Day 30 (Phase 2: Anxiety). It recovered because the leader addressed concerns directly at the Day 30 re‐ view. • Trust progressed from Level 1 to 2.8 over 90 days. This is a healthy pace — rushing to Level 4 would have skipped the calibra‐ tion that caught the 8 failure log entries in Month 1. • The ratio flip happened: at baseline, 40 hours gathering / 8 hours analyzing. At Day 90, 12 hours gathering / 28 hours analyzing. The team is now doing what it was hired to do. The real ROI is not in doing the same work faster. It is in doing different, higher-value work with the time freed up. This is the 80/20 flip in action — the same pattern described in Book 1’s financial context, applied here to team performance. Agents handle 80% of the data plumbing so your people spend 80% of their time on the analysis, judgment, and leadership that no agent can replicate. Industry Signal: IBM’s Institute for Business Value 2025 research on hybrid team KPIs validates the dashboard metrics above — and adds a critical finding: teams that measure only efficiency gains (cycle time, throughput) without measuring human realloca‐ tion (time shifted to strategic work) consistently undervalue their agent deployments. The real ROI is not in doing the same work faster. It is in doing different, higher-value work with the time freed up. Source: IBM IBV, “Measuring Human-AI Team Performance,” 2025. ibm.com Before and After: The Monday Team Meeting Dimen‐ sion Dura‐ tion Content Think of your AI agent implementation as a journey — similar to a lean manufacturing journey. Executive dashboards will increasingly include AI implementation KPIs: agent utilization rates, token consumption, autonomous vs. human-initiated actions, and the autonomy level of each agent. Measuring where you are on that journey — and how well the journey is progressing — may warrant its own dashboard. The SIX-SOV framework for hash-chained cryptographic receipts provides another KPI data source: verified, tamper-proof records of every agent action that can feed directly into compliance and performance dashboards. The Dashboard Review Cadence Review the hybrid team dashboard monthly for the first 90 days, then quarterly. Use the review to: 1. Celebrate improvements (publicly) 2. Identify bottlenecks (where is trust stuck?) 3. Adjust agent configuration (better prompts, more context, different thresholds) 4. Address team concerns (satisfaction declining? Address immedi‐ ately) 5. Plan the next phase of agent expansion Your Next Steps: 1. Create a simple hybrid team dashboard with the metrics above. A spreadsheet is fine to start. 2. Set baseline measurements for each metric BEFORE deploying the agent. You cannot demonstrate improvement without a baseline. 3. Schedule the first monthly review. Make it a team event, not just a management review. Chapter 10: When Agent Deployments Fail — Case Studies and Lessons Learned The following case studies are illustrative scenarios based on common deployment patterns observed across enterprise AI implementations. Dollar figures, organizational details, and timelines represent realistic composites drawn from industry experience. “The surprise deployment cost more than the entire first year of savings. The report was fine. The deployment process cost fortyfive thousand dollars and six weeks of team trust.” Industry Signal: McKinsey Digital’s 2025 analysis of enterprise AI deployment failures across 50+ organizations identifies three dominant failure modes in human-agent team deployments: sur‐ prise deployment without communication (Case Study 1 below), cognitive atrophy from over-reliance (Case Study 2), and adoption failure from poor distribution design (Case Study 3). Notably, all three are leadership failures, not technology failures. Source: McKinsey Case Study 1: The Surprise Deployment An FP&A team of five produced a weekly financial summary that went to all department heads. It took one analyst four hours every Monday morning. The format had not changed in three years. It was, by any measure, a perfect candidate for agent automation. The finance director built the agent. It produced a report that was technically superior to the human version — more data, better format‐ ting, automated charts, narrative commentary. The agent produced re‐ ports faster and with better formatting than any manual process. It was deployed on a Monday morning without warning. The backlash was immediate and personal. The surprise deployment cost more than the entire first year of savings. The analyst who had produced the report for three years — a talented, loyal team member who took pride in her work — felt publicly replaced. She did not say anything in the team meeting. She said it in her resignation letter two weeks later. Recruiting her replacement cost $45K in agency fees and three months of reduced productivity while the new hire got up to speed. The total cost of the “surprise deployment” exceeded the entire first year of savings from the automated report. Other team members saw the resignation as confirmation of their fears. Two more updated their resumes. Department heads who received the agent-produced report noticed it was “different” and questioned the numbers — the same numbers they never questioned when a human produced them. Trust in the finance team’s output dropped for six weeks. What should have happened: 1. The team should have been told in advance (the Day 1 Communication from Chapter 6) 2. The change should have been positioned as “freeing the analyst for higher-value work” — and she should have been given the scenario modeling project she had been requesting 3. The analyst should have validated and co-branded the first several agent-produced reports 4. The change should have been introduced gradually, not overnight The deeper lesson: The analyst should have been the quality gate, not the casualty. She should have been part of the validation process — poking holes in what the agent produced, bringing her three years of domain expertise to quality-check the agent’s output. That would have been an elevated responsibility on the same work she had always done. Instead, the organization lost a capable team member who could have been redeployed into higher-value strategic work. The report itself was fine. The deployment process cost $45K in recruiting, a $90K analyst, and six weeks of team trust. That is the price of skipping the human side. Case Study 2: The Team That Stopped Thinking A strategy team was given access to a strategic analysis agent. The agent was excellent — fast, comprehensive, well-structured. Within a month, a concerning pattern emerged: team members stopped doing their own preliminary analysis before consulting the agent. They went straight to the agent for every question. The result: the team’s outputs became uniform. Every analysis had the same structure, the same perspective, the same blind spots. The strategy quality score — measured by board feedback after each quarterly presentation — dropped from 4.2/5 to 3.1/5 in the month after the team stopped doing independent analysis. A board member said directly: “Your team’s work has gotten faster but less interesting. Every recommendation sounds the same.” The diversity of thought that comes from five different humans ap‐ proaching a problem from five different angles was replaced by one AI’s consistent (but singular) approach. The deeper issue: A truly strategic thinker should be focused on improving the context the agent receives, reading the assumptions embedded in the agent’s analysis, and pushing the quality of insight higher — not passively accepting whatever the agent produces. That assumption-checking, context-refining work is the analyst of the future. The fix: A “hypothesis first” rule was implemented: team members must form their own perspective before consulting the agent. The agent is for testing and refining thinking, not for skipping it. It took six weeks of the “hypothesis first” rule to recover to a 3.9/5 quality score. The team never fully returned to 4.2 — but speed had tripled, so the net value was still positive. The lesson: Agents should augment thinking, not replace it. When a team outsources its reasoning to an agent, it loses the cognitive diversity that produces breakthrough insights. The 80/20 flip (Book 1) means agents handle the data plumbing — not the thinking.

title: 03 Leading Agents
text: It is co-intelligence: a culture where humans and agents work together so naturally that the distinction between “human work” and “agent work” becomes irrelevant. What matters is the outcome. Think of it this way: today’s home framers carry a hammer and a saw, but they are the framers — not the tools. AI agents are the new tool set. They are extraordinarily efficient, but they need direction and will likely need direction for the foreseeable future. The capabilities will increase across every function — HR, operations, finance, supply chain — and we should stop separating “agents” and “humans” as opposing categor‐ ies. The humans are the resource we optimize. The agents are how we optimize them. One note that may sound surprising but matters more than most leaders expect: the way you communicate with an agent affects its output. Excess negativity, hostility, or carelessness in your inputs will reflect in the quality and tone of what the agent produces. Maintaining a high standard of ethical, clear, professional communication with your agents is not just good practice — it is a performance lever. For any significant culture shift, have a handful of human super users on hand — people who understand the agent system deeply enough to troubleshoot, guide their colleagues, and serve as the bridge between the technology and the team. These are your AI champions, and they will do more for adoption than any training program. The Four Hallmarks of a Co-Intelligence Culture Hallmark 1: Agents are named, not numbered. In high-performing teams, agents have names, roles, and reputations. “Ask Forecast Bot — it is really good at spotting seasonal patterns.” This humanization is not about pretending the agent is human. It is about integrating it into the team’s working vocabulary. Hallmark 2: Humans credit agents and agents credit humans. When presenting results, the team naturally attributes contributions: “The analysis was produced by our finance agent, with strategic context added by Sarah.” This transparency builds trust with stakeholders and establishes the collaborative model. Hallmark 3: Failure is investigated, not punished. When an agent makes an error, the team investigates the root cause (data issue? context gap? governance failure?) without blame. The failure log is a learning resource, not a disciplinary record. Hallmark 4: Skills evolve continuously. The team actively develops prompt engineering, output validation, and strategic synthesis skills. These are not afterthought training modules — they are core competen‐ cies that are practiced, measured, and rewarded. The 90-Day Culture Shift Building a co-intelligence culture does not happen overnight. But with deliberate leadership, the shift can begin within 90 days: Days 1-30: Introduction. Deploy the first agent with full communica‐ tion, training, and support. Set the tone: this is an addition to the team, not a replacement for the team. Measure: team members actively using the agent (target: 80%+ adoption), initial trust level assessments completed, and at least one “the agent caught something we missed” moment shared publicly. Days 31-60: Habituation. The team begins to use the agent naturally for routine tasks. The leader reinforces positive patterns (“great use of the agent for that analysis”) and corrects anti-patterns (“let’s not skip our own thinking step”). Measure: override rate stabilizing (indicates calibration is working), team satisfaction recovering from the Phase 2 dip, and at least two team members advancing from Level 1 to Level 2 trust. Days 61-90: Integration. The agent becomes part of the team’s work‐ flow. Team members begin suggesting new use cases. The culture shifts from “we have an agent” to “we work with an agent.” Measure: time reallocation visible (less data gathering, more analysis), agent-influenced decisions producing measurable outcomes, and the team requesting additional agent capabilities rather than resisting existing ones. Organiza‐ tions experiencing more than ten percent voluntary attrition within ninety days of AI deployment almost universally failed to address team fears proactively. The Agent Capability. AI agents fill four team roles: assistant (supports a human with routine tasks), analyst (independently produces analyses for human review), monitor (watches systems continuously and alerts on exceptions), and executor (takes actions within predefined governance boundaries). Organizations deploying agents deliberately into defined roles see three times higher adoption rates than those that introduce agents without clear role definitions. The Agent Brief – structured context provided before task execution – produces sixty percent better output quality than unstructured prompts. The Human Role. The leader’s job is to define the relationship between humans and agents explicitly, early, and with clarity that leaves no room for anxiety. This means writing the Day 1 Communication before deploy‐ ment, implementing the Trust Calibration Scale (five levels from verifyeverything to full autonomy), creating the Role Definition Matrix (Human Only, Agent-Assisted, Agent-Led, Agent-Autonomous for every task), and establishing the accountability principle: the human who deployed the agent is accountable for its outputs. The Cost of Slow Response Supply chain decision latency — the gap between when a disruption signal appears and when the organization responds — is one of the most expensive metrics in operations. A supplier who misses a delivery deadline by three days. If the signal appeared in the supplier’s own shipping data but nobody on your team saw it until the PO was already late, the organization scrambles. Expedited shipping costs 3-5x standard rates. An AI agent monitoring supplier shipping data would have flagged the delay signal 48 hours before the missed deadline — creating a response window instead of a scramble. The math is straightforward. title: 04 Supply Chain
text: “From signal detection to actionable response options in under ten minutes. The equivalent manual process: seven to ten days of response latency eliminated.” Before diving into architecture, a definition: supply chain in this playbook means end-to-end — from procurement of raw materials through resource acquisition, manufacturing operations (inbound and outbound logistics), warehousing, distribution, and final delivery to the customer. Supply chain is not just procurement and logistics. It includes your manufacturing operations, your quality systems, and every handoff between them. No two businesses are alike in their supply chain structure, and this variability across industries, geographies, and operating models means the agent frameworks we build must adapt to unique environments while leveraging proven best practices. A supply chain agent system has four layers, each mapping to a phase of supply chain operations. Understanding these layers — and critically, how humans interact with each one — is the difference between building something that adds value and building something that generates alerts nobody reads, flooding your team with noise. The agentic system must focus on high-value exceptions. The Four Layers Layer 1: Perception. The agent’s ability to monitor the supply chain environment in real time. This includes data from internal systems (ERP, WMS, TMS, procurement systems), external data feeds (shipping trackers, weather, commodity prices, news), supplier data (on-time delivery rates, quality metrics, financial health), and market signals (customer demand patterns, competitor actions, regulatory changes). The perception layer is the foundation — agents are only as good as the data they have access to. If your perception layer is inaccurate or incomplete, every downstream layer produces flawed results. Invest here first. The human role at this layer: defining which data sources matter, validating data quality, and identifying gaps the agent cannot see — tribal knowledge, relationship context, and market intuition that lives in your team’s experience, not in your systems. Layer 2: Forecasting. The agent’s ability to predict what will happen based on current data and historical patterns — demand forecasting, lead time prediction, risk probability estimation, and cost projection. The forecasting layer transforms raw perception data into actionable predictions with confidence intervals. The human role: reviewing assumptions, challenging forecasts that contradict market intelligence, and applying judgment about strategic priorities that the data alone cannot capture. Layer 3: Orchestration. The agent’s ability to coordinate responses across multiple supply chain functions. When the perception layer detects a supplier delay and the forecasting layer predicts a stockout, the orchestration layer coordinates the response: identify alternative suppliers, adjust production schedule, communicate to affected customers, update inventory positions. The human role: approving high-impact decisions, resolving conflicts between competing priorities (cost vs. speed vs. quality), and ensuring that automated responses align with strategic objectives. Layer 4: Action. The agent’s ability to execute responses — triggering purchase orders, rerouting shipments, adjusting reorder points, sending alerts, generating reports, or activating contingency plans. The scope of permissible actions is defined by the governance framework (see Book 1, Chapter 10, and Book 2, Chapter 8). The human role: setting the governance boundaries, reviewing actions that exceed thresholds, and retaining commitments, supplier relationships, or financial exposure above defined limits. When an action requires human review, the agent elevates it with full context — the data, the analysis, the options, and its recommendation — so the human can decide quickly rather than spending days assembling the same information manually. Figure 2.1 — Supply Chain Agent Architecture (4 Layers) The four layers mirror the decision agent architecture from Book 2 (Perception, Reasoning, Action, Memory) — adapted for the continuous, high-volume, multi-source nature of supply chain data. The key difference: supply chain agents operate in environments where the data volume is orders of magnitude higher and the latency requirements are tighter. A financial forecast can be updated daily. A logistics routing decision may need to be made in minutes. Note: the manufacturing operations dimension of supply chain is covered more extensively in AI Agents for Manufacturing (Book 8), which provides dedicated chapters on production scheduling, predictive maintenance, OEE optimization, and factory floor agents. This book focuses on the broader supply chain — procurement through logistics — with manufacturing touchpoints where they affect supply chain decisions. text: How the Layers Work Together Consider a practical scenario: a Tier 1 supplier in Southeast Asia reports a 15% production capacity reduction due to equipment failure. Perception: The agent ingests the supplier’s capacity alert via API (or detects the signal in the supplier’s shipping data — shipments are trending below historical volume). Cross-references with weather data (no weather event), commodity data (stable), and financial data (supplier’s credit rating unchanged — this is operational, not financial). Forecasting: The agent calculates the impact: this supplier provides 40% of a critical component. At 15% reduced capacity, the component supply shortfall over the next 60 days is approximately 6% of total demand. Current safety stock covers 18 days. If the capacity reduction persists beyond 30 days, stockout probability exceeds 70%. Orchestration: The agent identifies three response options: (1) Activate the qualified backup supplier in Vietnam (lead time: 21 days, cost premium: 8%). (2) Redistribute allocation across product lines — prioritize the highest-margin SKUs. (3) Accelerate an existing order with the primary supplier to build buffer before the capacity reduction takes full effect. Action: The agent generates a Supply Chain Alert with the three options, estimated costs, and timeline for each. It routes the alert to the VP of Operations and the procurement team. If the governance framework permits, it also initiates a quote request to the backup supplier — not a commitment, just a request — so the data is ready when the human decision-maker reviews the options. This entire cycle — from signal detection to actionable response options — executes in under 10 minutes. The equivalent manual process: a procurement analyst discovers the capacity reduction in a weekly supplier review call (3-5 days after the fact), escalates to the supply chain manager (1 day), who convenes a meeting with production planning and procurement (2 days), who collectively identify the same three options (1-2 days). Total: 7-10 days of response latency eliminated by the agent architecture. The difference is 10 minutes versus 7 days. In supply chain, that difference is measured in dollars. Frontier Models for Supply Chain The frontier models — the most capable large language models from leading AI labs — serve as the reasoning engine within the supply chain agent architecture. For a detailed comparison of frontier model capabilities, selection criteria, and the distinction between deterministic and non-deterministic frameworks, see AI Agents for CFOs (Book 1, Chapter 2). For supply chain applications specifically: • Claude (Anthropic) — strongest for complex multi-variable reasoning, long-context analysis of contracts and compliance documents, and nuanced narrative generation for executive reporting • GPT (OpenAI) — strong for structured data analysis, code generation for API integrations, and function calling in orchestration workflows • Grok (xAI) — real-time information access for current market conditions, shipping delays, and breaking supply chain news • Gemini (Google) — strong for multimodal analysis (interpreting shipping documents, invoices, quality inspection images) • Llama (Meta) — open-source, run locally for organizations with sensitive supplier data or sovereign deployment requirements • Mistral (Mistral AI) — European-based, strong for multilingual supply chain communications and GDPR-conscious organizations with EU operations The sovereign model tradeoff. Supply chain data — supplier pricing, logistics patterns, inventory positions, customer demand — is competitively sensitive. Sending this data to cloud-hosted frontier models creates an exposure risk that many organizations, particularly in defense, pharmaceuticals, and high-value manufacturing, cannot accept. The tradeoff: cloud-hosted frontier models offer the best reasoning capabilities but require data to leave your infrastructure. Local sovereign models (Llama, Mistral) keep data on-premise but may sacrifice some capability. For many supply chain teams, the practical answer is a hybrid approach: use frontier models for reasoning about non-sensitive data (market analysis, general recommendations), and sovereign models for processing sensitive data (supplier pricing, logistics costs, inventory positions). The SIX-SOV approach (six-sov.com) provides a framework for sovereign AI inference that keeps sensitive data within your control while maintaining frontier-model reasoning quality. The orchestration frameworks (LangGraph, CrewAI, n8n) and data integration patterns covered in Books 1-2 apply directly to supply chain agents. The primary difference is the data sources: instead of ERP financial data, you are connecting to WMS, TMS, procurement systems, supplier portals, and external data feeds.
