A.1 How to Read a Receipt Every substantive claim in this series is meant to arrive with a receipt — a small block that records the claim, marks its status, and names the way to check it. The whole discipline turns on one distinction, carried by two phrases: • Runs today. The capability exists in the platform’s code, is exercised by a test, and can be demonstrated on request. When a receipt marks something runs today, you are entitled to ask to see it run. • Designed-toward. The capability is specified and has a named home — a later volume, a spec file, or a planned surface — but it is not yet built. When a receipt marks something designed-toward, read it as a statement of direction, not a description of the present. A receipt that blurs the two is a receipt to distrust. The rule this series holds itself to is that the line is always drawn, in writing, on the same page as the claim. So when you meet one, find the line first: everything on the runs-today side you can verify now; everything on the designedtoward side you are being told is still ahead. A receipt has a small, stable shape. Read it in this order: 1. The claim — one sentence, stated plainly. 2. Runs today — what part of the claim is built and testable now. 3. Designed-toward — what part is planned, and where it closes (a named volume or spec, never “someday”). 4. Verify — the concrete thing you could ask to see: a record replayed, a test that passes, a value derived rather than asserted. If a receipt is missing the designed-toward line, it is claiming everything is built; confirm that before you rely on it. If it is missing the verify line, it is asking for faith; withhold it. To make the shape concrete, here is an illustrative receipt — not a claim about any one product, but an example of the form you will meet throughout the series: Claim. A new unit of value is created only after a person approves the specific mint. Runs today. The approval gate: a proposed mint is held until a human authorizes it, and the authorization is recorded on the append-only substrate. Designed-toward. The cross-operator settlement that would let two sovereign systems reconcile such a mint without a shared intermediary — planned, and homed in a later volume. Verify. Ask to see a proposed mint sit unapproved, then seal only on a person’s authorization; replay the record and confirm the authorization is present and unedited. Read that receipt the way you would read every other one: the approval gate is something you can watch happen now; the cross-operator settlement is a direction, not a present fact; and the verify line names the exact demonstration you are entitled to ask for. Nothing about the claim requires trust once you can run the check. A.2 The Four Constraints (K1–K4) in Plain Language The system rests on four constraints. They are not features to be switched on; they are limits the system places on itself, and they are meant to hold whether or not anyone is watching. • K1 — Human Primacy. A person, not an automated process, authorizes any act that creates or moves value. The machine may prepare a proposal, present it, and wait; a human decides. No autonomy is granted over the acts that matter most. For you as operator: the decision is yours, and it is designed to stay yours. • K2 — Default-Deny. Nothing is permitted unless a rule explicitly permits it. The starting position for any action is no; permission is granted narrowly, on purpose, and never assumed. For you: if you did not sanction it, it does not happen. • K3 — Audit-Immutable. The record of what happened is appendonly and hash-chained. Entries are added, never edited or erased; a later reader can replay the record and reach the same result the writer reached, or the record itself is visibly broken. For you: the past cannot be quietly rewritten, including by the person who wrote it. • K4 — Constitutional-Validated Extension. New capability may be added only in ways the governing rules already sanction. The system grows by validated extension, not by exception — a change the constitution does not allow does not ship. For you: the system can only grow by its own rules, so growth never silently loosens the other three. Read together, the four say a human is in charge (K1), the system withholds by default (K2), the past cannot be rewritten (K3), and the future can only be built by the rules (K4). Each one guards the others: primacy is worth little if the record can be edited, and an honest record is worth little if anything is permitted by default.

Each term is developed in the chapters; nothing here adds a claim. • Receipt. A block that records a claim together with its status — runs today or designed-toward — and the way to check it. • Runs-today / designed-toward. The two statuses a claim can carry: built-and-testable now, versus planned with a named home. The line between them is the point of the receipt. • Obligation. A unit of work or duty that is opened, approved by a human, and later closed with evidence — tracked so that what is owed and what is done stay clear over time. • Breath-gate (human approval gate). The point at which a proposed act pauses and waits for a person to approve it before it takes effect. The pause is the mechanism, not a delay to be optimized away. • Private mint. The creation of a new unit of value under human authorization, recorded on the operator’s own substrate rather than broadcast to a public network. • Substrate. The private, append-only ledger the value lives on — provable to the keyholder without being published to outsiders. • Replay. Deriving the present state by re-reading the sealed record from the beginning, rather than trusting a stored total. Two readers who replay the same record to the same point get the same answer, or the record is broken. • Yield organism. The image this series uses for value that compounds under governance: not a single ledger but a living arrangement of receipts, obligations, and gates that grows without shedding its rules. • Keyholder. The person or role that holds the authority to approve acts on the substrate. Primacy (K1) is exercised by the keyholder. A.4 How a Reader Verifies a Claim You do not have to take a claim on faith. Two checks, in order: 1. Check the book. Find the receipt for the claim. Confirm it is marked runs today, and read the verify line — the specific thing you could ask to see. For a runs-today claim, the verify line points at something a running system can show — a record replayed to a value, a test that passes, a figure derived rather than asserted. Ask for that demonstration. A claim that cannot be shown this way has not been verified, whatever the prose around it says. A short checklist you can carry: • Does the claim have a receipt at all? No receipt, no claim. • Is it marked runs today or designed-toward? Only the first is a present capability. • Does the verify line name something concrete you could watch happen? • When shown, does the demonstration match the sentence — no more, no less? No marketing language survives this procedure, which is the reason to have it. The book tells you where to look; the node shows you the thing; you decide. Read a worked example for three things. First, the problem before — what went wrong when the mechanism was absent, stated in terms a practitioner would recognize. Second, the mechanism applied — the specific gate, receipt, or replay that changed the outcome, named so you can trace it back to the chapter’s claim. What you do with it, you do; a human stays in charge by design. See It Work The closing volume’s claim is that a token can be inherited — legally hardened, forkable, exitable, and reducible to a single verifiable package. This walkthrough shows it in the cockpit (Atrium), each step bound to a real surface and marked for what runs today versus what is designedtoward. 1. Seal a jus cogens invariant. Declare “no participant can be permanently trapped” as a sealed constitutional rule; a policy that violates it cannot seal. (Surface: the governance view. Runs-today: the sealed rule + amendment discipline on the obligation ledger. Designed-toward: the jus cogens invariant checker at seal time.) 2. Propose an equity override (human-gated). An override surfaces as a proposal carrying its condition, the injustice it prevents, and the required consent; approve it and it seals, principal-stamped — the letter bent under discipline, not fiat. (Surface: the governance view. Runs-today: the human approval gate. Designed-toward: the equity-override review circuit.) 3. Simulate and gate a fork. Model a branch’s clean fork — value, history, reputation carried, subsidy drawn — then propose, review, consent, and execute it as a ceremony sealed on both sides. (Surface: the fork/exit console. Runs-today: portable sealed obligations + replay + the human gate. Designed-toward: the fork engine + continuity subsidy.) 4. Guarantee an exit. Propose a minority holder’s exit; it cannot be refused, carries value and history intact, is subsidized from the commons, and seals as a dignified departure. (Surface: the fork/exit console. Runs-today: the gated, sealed portable transfer. Designedtoward: the exit-guarantee + subsidy engine.) 5. Generate and verify the inheritance package. Produce the verifiable package; an heir or auditor replays the full chain from genesis and recomputes the cryptographic commitment — proof, not testimony, exposed to no outsider. (Surface: the inheritancepackage view + the integrity panel. Runs-today: deterministic replay + the Merkle commitment. Designed-toward: the oneartifact packaged export tooling.) That is the demonstration: an invariant sealed, an override disciplined, a fork and an exit walked through as ceremonies, and the whole history handed on as a package an heir can prove — with the enforceable law and the movement of money named as the operator’s own, not assumed. The mechanism is Chapters 2–8; this is what it looks like when it runs.
